en: *The Great Tang Dynasty Record of the Western Regions*, Volume One: Thirty-four Countries.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree;
compiled by the Śramaṇa Bianji of Dazongchi Monastery.
The thirty-four countries are: the country of Aṅga; the country of Kuci;
the country of Bāhlika; the country of Tukhāra; the country of Cīna; the country of Tāshi;
the country of Fānhan; the country of Sutrulisa; the country of Samarkand; the country of Maimargha; the country of Kapitha; and the country of Kustana.
The Kingdom of Hekhan, the Kingdom of Puhé, the Kingdom of Fadí, the Kingdom of Huólìxímíjiā,
the Kingdom of Jiéshāngnà, the Kingdom of Tánmì, the Kingdom of Chì’èyǎnnà, the Kingdom of Hūlùmó, the Kingdom of Yūsèmán,
the Kingdom of Jùhuóyǎnnà, the Kingdom of Huòshā, the Kingdom of Kēduōluó, the Kingdom of Jūmídíduó, and the Kingdom of Fúqié.

In the kingdoms of Langguo, Heluosimin, Jianguo, Hulinqi, Bohe, Ruimotuo, Hushi-jian, Dala-jian, Jiezhi, and Fanyana, as well as Kapisi, one may examine the imperial achievements in succession and survey the annals of the emperors from afar.

From the beginning when Pao-xi emerged from the eastern trigram Zhen, to the time when Xuan-yuan let fall his robes [in non-action]— [The text continues with a description of the transmission of the Dharma through various patriarchs and kings,

including the introduction of Buddhism by Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna during the Later Han, the flourishing of the faith under the Northern Wei, and the subsequent propagation of the teachings throughout the Tang dynasty.]
In the beginning, it was for the purpose of governing the common people and demarcating the boundaries of the various territories.

Reaching down to the time when Tang Yao received the mandate of Heaven, his glory extended to the four quarters; and when Yu Shun presented the maps of the lands, his virtue flowed across the nine regions.
From this point onward, there have been only empty records of events transmitted through books; listening afar to the former sages, one hears only the annals of recorded words.
How could this compare to encountering a time of the Way and being joined with an era of non-action?

Our Great Tang governs with sovereign majesty, seizing the opportune moment to grasp the chronicles of state. It has unified the six directions to establish its glorious reign and eclipsed the Three August Ones by its presiding light.

The profound transformation flows far and wide, and auspicious winds spread to distant lands; it shares in the encompassing and supporting of Heaven and Earth, and equals the moistening and nourishing power of wind and rain.

As for the Eastern Yi tribes coming to present tribute and the Western Rong tribes being brought into order, and for his founding of the dynasty and establishing a legacy that dispelled chaos and restored the correct way—this truly transcends former kings and encompasses all previous dynasties.

Sharing the same script and following the same tracks, this era of supreme governance and divine achievement could not have its great design extolled without records, nor could its flourishing legacy be glorified without clear proclamation.

I, Xuanzang, have followed my travels to record the customs and lands of these regions; though I have not yet exhaustively examined their directions or dialects, I believe I have already traversed more than five hundred and three thousand *li*.
All categories of living beings are uniformly graced by his gracious benevolence;
among those capable of speech, there are none who do not extol his merit.

From the celestial realm to all of India, even the remote and desolate regions with their divergent customs and distant, alien lands, all receive his calendar and are equally moistened by his enlightened teachings.
To extol the achievements of martial merit is merely to provide fodder for idle talk;
to praise the abundance of civil virtue results only in being stifled by those who claim preeminence.
Examining the records of the past, such a thing has never been heard of before.
Reflecting deeply upon maps and records, it is truly beyond compare.
Were there not this account, how could the harmonious transformation [of the people] be recorded?
Now, based on what I have heard and seen, I have here set it down in writing.
Thus, the Sahā world—formerly called the Saha world or the Sahe world—is in both cases a corruption; this trichiliocosm constitutes the sphere of transformation and guidance for a single Buddha.

Now, that which is illuminated by the sun and moon—the four continents—is situated at the center of the trichiliocosm; herein all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, manifest their transformative teachings, appearing both in birth and in extinction, guiding both the holy and the ordinary.
Mount Sumeru—translated into Chinese as Miaogao (Wondrous High)—was formerly called Xumi or Xumilou;

both are erroneous abbreviations. It is composed of four precious substances and stands within the great ocean upon the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanamaṇḍala*). It is the place where the sun and moon revolve and illuminate, and the abode where all the devas roam and dwell.
The seven mountains and seven seas stand encircling one another;
the seawater between the mountains possesses the eight meritorious qualities.
Beyond the seven golden mountains lies the salt ocean.
Within the great ocean, there are roughly four continents that are habitable.

To the east is Pūrvavideha (formerly called Fupotiti; also called Fuyudai, which is an error); to the south is Jambudvīpa (formerly called Yanzhuti Zhou; also called Yanfuzhou, which is an error); to the west is Aparagoyānī (formerly called Quoyeni; also called Digani, which is an error); and to the north is Uttarakuru (formerly called Yudanyue; also called Julou).
This is an error.

The Golden Wheel-turning King’s transformation extends over the four continents; the Silver Wheel-turning King’s governance excludes Uttarakuru; the Copper Wheel-turning King excludes both Uttarakuru and Aparagoyānī; and the Iron Wheel-turning King governs only Jambudvīpa.

Now, when a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) is about to ascend the great throne, a great wheel-treasure, manifested in accordance with his merit, appears floating through the air to respond to him. There are distinctions among these wheels—of gold, silver, copper, or iron—and correspondingly, there are differences in the extent of his realm, which may be four, three, two, or one continent. Because this is their primary auspicious omen, it serves as the basis for their title.
The central land of Jambudvīpa is Lake Anavatapta—translated into Chinese as "Free from Heat and Affliction" (Wu re nao).
The older transcription, "Lake Anouda," is erroneous.
To the south of Mount Gandhamādana and to the north of the Great Snowy Mountains, it extends for eight hundred *li* in circumference;
its shores are adorned with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
Golden sand spreads everywhere, and the clear ripples are as bright as a polished mirror.
By the power of their vows, Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage transform themselves into dragon kings and dwell therein in concealment.
They bring forth cool, clear water to provide for Jambudvīpa.

Therefore, from the silver ox-mouth on the eastern side of the lake flows the Gaṅgā River (formerly called Henghe; also called Henggā, which is an error), which circles the lake once and enters the southeastern ocean.
From the golden elephant-mouth on the southern side of the lake flows the Sindhu River (formerly called Xintouhe, which is an error), which circles the lake once and enters the southwestern ocean.
From the lapis lazuli horse-mouth on the western side of the lake flows the Vakṣu River (formerly called Bochaxihe, which is an error), which circles the lake once and enters the northwestern ocean.

From the lion’s mouth made of crystal on the northern side of the lake flows the Sītā River (formerly called the Siduo River, which is a corruption), which encircles the lake once before entering the North Sea; some say it flows underground and emerges at Mount Jishi, where it becomes the current of the Sītā River, serving as the source of the Yellow River in China.
At that time, as no Wheel-Turning King appeared to govern, the land of Jambudvīpa was divided among four rulers.

In the south was the Elephant Lord, where the climate was hot and humid, suitable for elephants; in the west was the Jewel Lord, bordering the sea and abundant in treasures; in the north was the Horse Lord, where the weather was cold and brisk, suitable for horses; and in the east was the Human Lord, where the climate was mild and pleasant, and the population was large.

Therefore, in the kingdom of the Elephant Lord, the people are impetuous and ardent in their studies, being particularly proficient in extraordinary arts; for dress, they wear turbans and bare the right shoulder; as for their hair, it is tied in a topknot with four strands hanging down; they dwell in clans within walled towns, and their houses consist of multi-storied pavilions.

In the land of Ratnapati, there is no propriety or righteousness; they value wealth and bribes. Their garments are short and worn with the lapel on the left; they cut their hair but grow long beards. They dwell in walled cities and towns and devote themselves to the pursuit of commercial profit.

The customs of the Horse-Lord (Huns) are by nature fierce and violent; their disposition is accustomed to slaughter. They dwell in felt tents and nomadic huts, living like birds as they follow their herds.

In the lands of the Human-Lord (Chinese), the customs are shrewd and benevolent, and benevolence and righteousness shine brightly. They wear caps and belts with garments fastened on the right, their carriages and robes follow a proper order, they find peace in their native soil and value stability over migration, and they strive to provide for all classes of beings.
Among the customs of the three principal regions, those of the East are considered superior; their dwellings have doors opening toward the east, and at dawn they perform obeisance facing east.
As for the land of the sovereign, the south-facing orientation is held in the highest honor.
The diverse customs of various regions constitute the general outline of this matter;
however, as for the rites between sovereign and subject, superior and subordinate, and the protocols of legal statutes and cultural standards, no place surpasses the land of the Son of Heaven.
The precepts for purifying the mind and shedding worldly burdens, and the teachings for transcending birth and death—these principles are preeminent in the land of the Elephant Lord (India).

All of these are recorded in the scriptures and edicts; they have been inquired about among the local customs, extensively related to both the present and the past, and carefully examined through personal observation and report.

Thus, the Buddha arose in the West while the Dharma flowed to the Eastern lands; yet in the process of translation, sounds became corrupted and dialects were mistaken. When sounds are corrupted, the meaning is lost; when dialects are mistaken, the principle is distorted.
Therefore it is said:
"It must be that names are rectified," for this values the absence of error and contradiction.

Now, humans possess differing natures of hardness and softness, and their speech and sounds differ; these are tied to the influence of climate and soil, and are also brought about by the result of customs and habits.

As for the peculiarities of its mountains, rivers, and products, as well as the differences in its customs and the dispositions of its people, these were recorded in detail by the national histories during the reigns of the lords of Men;
likewise, the customs of the lords of Ma and the regions of the lords of Bao are fully contained in the historical annals and may be briefly described here.

As for the land of the Elephant Lord (Hastināpura), it was not clearly detailed in ancient times; some records state that its terrain is largely hot and humid, while others describe its customs as favoring benevolence and compassion. Although these accounts remain somewhat preserved in local gazetteers, they cannot be cited in full detail. Is this not because the Way possesses the principle of appearing and withdrawing, and because the world is subject to the shifting currents of fortune?

Thus we know that those who observe the laws of the calendar to submit to transformation, who drink in the imperial bounty to come as guests, who traverse profound perils to pay their respects at the Jade Gate, and who present rare products of distant lands to prostrate before the Crimson Palace, are indeed few enough to be spoken of.
For this reason, while traveling afar to seek the Way and seeking instruction from my teachers, I have recorded the customs and geography of the lands.
From the Black Ridge onwards,
all are indeed of Hu (non-Chinese) custom.
Although the Rong people share a common lineage, they are divided into various clans; they demarcate boundaries and establish frontiers, for the most part being sedentary.
They construct city walls and moats, and devote themselves to agriculture and animal husbandry;
by nature they value wealth and goods, while their customs hold benevolence and righteousness in little regard.
Marriage lacks propriety and the distinction between the honorable and the humble is disregarded;
the words of women are followed, while men occupy subordinate positions.
Upon death, the remains are cremated, and mourning periods have no fixed duration.
They trim their faces and cut off their ears, sever their hair and tear their garments, slaughtering flocks of livestock to offer sacrifices to the spirits of the deceased.
In times of auspiciousness they wear plain white robes; in times of misfortune, they wear black clothing.
Regarding customs similar to those of our own region, I have briefly set forth their general principles;
as for differing administrations and unique regulations, I shall describe them separately according to their respective locations.
The customs of India are discussed in the subsequent record.
Departing from the old territory of Gaochang, beginning with those nearest, we reach the kingdom of Ākṣīṇa (formerly called Wūqí).
The kingdom of Ākṣīṇa is more than six hundred li from east to west and over four hundred li from south to north.
The capital city of the kingdom is seven to eight *li* in circuit.
Its four sides are backed by mountains, making it easy to defend due to its perilous paths.
Springs and streams wind around it, and water is diverted for irrigation in the fields.
The soil is suitable for growing panicled millet, broomcorn millet, winter wheat, fragrant dates, grapes, pears, crabapples, and various other fruits.
The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs of the people are honest and straightforward.
Their written characters are derived from those of India, and they have a small amount of silk and brocade.
For clothing, they wear felt and coarse wool; they cut their hair and do not wear head coverings.
Their currency consists of gold coins, silver coins, and small copper coins.
The king is a native of that country; he is brave but lacks strategic wisdom, and he is fond of boasting of his own military conquests. The state lacks governance and its laws are not orderly.

There are more than ten monasteries with over two thousand monks, who study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna teachings. As both their scriptural doctrines and disciplinary codes follow those of India, the students adhere closely to the original texts in their studies.
His observance of the precepts and moral discipline was pure and diligent;
however, his diet included the three kinds of "pure meat," indicating that he remained stuck at the level of the gradual teachings.

From here, traveling southwest for more than two hundred *li*, crossing a small mountain and two great rivers, one reaches a level plain to the west. After proceeding another seven hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Kuci (formerly called Qiuci).
The Kingdom of Kuci: The kingdom of Kuci is over one thousand li from east to west and over six hundred li from south to north.

The capital city has a circumference of seventeen or eighteen li. It is suitable for millet and wheat, and produces non-glutinous rice. It yields grapes and pomegranates, and abounds in pears, crabapples, peaches, and apricots.
The local products include gold, copper, iron, lead, and tin.
The climate is temperate, and the customs are simple and honest.
The written script is modeled after that of India, with some minor modifications.
Their musical performances on wind and stringed instruments are particularly excellent compared to those of other countries.
They wear clothing of brocade and coarse wool, with their hair cut short and covered by turbans or caps.
Their currency consists of gold coins, silver coins, and small copper coins.
The king is of the Qu-ji (Kucha) lineage; his wisdom and strategy are meager and obscure, and he is constrained by powerful ministers.
Regarding their customs, when a son is born, they press his head with a wooden board, desiring that it become flat and elongated.
There are over one hundred monasteries with more than five thousand monks, who study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna teachings.
Their scriptures, doctrines, and disciplinary codes follow the Indian models; those they practice and recite are the original texts themselves.
Still constrained by the gradual teachings, their food is mixed with the three kinds of pure meat.
They take pride in ritual purity and devote themselves to cultivation; people vie with one another in their meritorious efforts.
To the east of the kingdom’s border, north of the city, in front of a deva temple, there is a great dragon pond.
The various nāgas change their forms and mate with mares, subsequently giving birth to dragon-foals that are fierce and difficult to control.
Only the offspring of these dragon-foals become tame enough for harnessing; this is why this country produces many excellent horses.

I have heard from the records of former sages that in recent times there was a king named Jinhua (Golden Flower), whose governance and teachings were clear and discerning, so much so that he moved the dragon to serve as his mount.
When the king wished to pass away, he touched the dragon’s ear with his whip, whereupon it immediately withdrew into hiding, remaining so to this day.
There were no wells within the city, so they drew water from that pond.
The dragon transformed himself into a human and consorted with the women, fathering sons who were valiant and fierce, able to run as fast as galloping horses.
As this influence gradually spread, all the people became of dragon lineage; relying on their physical strength, they exercised their own power and did not respect the king’s commands.
The king then instigated the Turks to attack and slaughter the people of this city; both young and old were executed, leaving almost no survivors.
The city is now desolate and overgrown, and the smoke of human habitation has been cut off.

More than forty li north of the city of Huángchén, at the foot of a mountain range and separated by a river, there are two monasteries both named Zhàohùlǐ (Jyotiṣka), designated as "East" and "West" according to their respective locations.
The adornment of the Buddha images almost surpasses human craftsmanship.
The monastic community maintains a pure fast and is truly diligent in their practice.

Within the Hall of the Buddha Reliquary of the Eastern Radiance (Tōshō), there is a jade stone, over two feet wide in surface area, with a color ranging from yellowish-white; its shape resembles that of a sea clam.
Upon it are the footprints left by a Buddha, eighteen inches long and over six inches wide;
on certain days of fasting, they emit a brilliant light.
Outside the western gate of the great city, on both sides of the road, there stand statues of the Buddha, each over ninety feet in height.
Before these statues, a site was established for the Great Assembly held once every five years.
Every year during the ten days around the autumnal equinox, the monastics of the entire nation assemble there.

From the sovereign above down to the scholars and commoners below, they abandon worldly affairs, observe the fasts and precepts, receive the scriptures, and listen to the Dharma, forgetting their fatigue as they gaze upon the sun.

In various monasteries, they adorn Buddha images, embellishing them with rare jewels and decorating them with brocades and silks; these are carried upon litters and carriages in what is called the "Procession of Images," numbering in the thousands as they gather like clouds at the assembly sites.
On the fifteenth day and the final day of every month, the king and his ministers deliberate on state affairs and consult with eminent monks before issuing their proclamations.
Crossing the river to the northwest of the assembly hall, one arrives at the Aśokārāma (translated into Chinese as Qite).
Its courtyards and buildings are spacious and grand, and its Buddha images are exquisitely adorned.

The monks are solemn and reverent, applying themselves with diligent effort without slackening; they are all elderly men of long-standing virtue, men of profound learning and superior talent, and eminent scholars from distant lands who have come here out of admiration for its righteousness.
The king, ministers, scholars, commoners, and prominent families provided him with the four types of offerings, their reverence increasing as time passed.

According to the records of former worthies, it is said that in the past, the former king of this country, who deeply venerated the Triple Gem, was about to travel abroad to visit and pay homage to sacred sites; he therefore commanded his younger half-brother to take charge of the affairs remaining behind.
His younger brother, having received this command, secretly castrated himself to prevent the danger from sprouting.
He placed it in a golden casket and presented it to the king.
The king said:
"What does this mean? He replied,
"The day the carriage turns back, it may then be opened."
He immediately entrusted him to the officials to accompany and protect the army.
When the king returned, there was indeed one who incited trouble, saying:
"The king has ordered him to oversee the state, yet he is committing lewd acts within the inner palace."
Upon hearing this, the king was struck with rage and intended to impose a severe punishment.
His younger brother said, "I dare not evade my responsibility; I pray that you open the golden casket."
The king then opened it and looked inside; it was a castrated animal.
He asked, "What strange creature is this?"
"What do you wish to clarify?
He replied, "When Your Majesty previously traveled abroad, you charged me with the affairs of the palace. Fearing the calamity of slander, I castrated myself to prove my innocence."
"Now that there is indeed evidence of this result, I pray you will deign to examine it.
The King was deeply struck with wonder and his affection increased all the more; he entered and exited the inner palace without any restriction or hindrance.
Later, while traveling, the king’s younger brother encountered a man leading five hundred oxen who intended to offer them for the purpose of self-mutilation.
Seeing this, he reflected and his thoughts were stirred by a sense of kinship:
"My body is now impaired; could this not be the result of my past karma?"
He immediately used his wealth and treasures to redeem this herd of oxen.
Through the power of his benevolence and compassion, his male organs gradually developed.
Because his organs were now complete, he ultimately did not enter the palace.
The king, finding this strange, questioned him, whereupon he related the matter from beginning to end.
The king, considering it most extraordinary, subsequently established a monastery to commemorate these noble deeds and transmit their fragrance to future generations.
From here, traveling west for more than six hundred li, one crosses a small sandy desert and arrives at the kingdom of Bālukā (formerly called Gūhē or Jīhē).
The kingdom of Bālukā is more than six hundred li from east to west and more than three hundred li from south to north.
The capital city of the kingdom is five or six *li* in circuit.
Its soil, climate, the character of its people, and their customs are the same as those of the country of Kuci; only the spoken language differs slightly.
Fine felt and fine coarse woolen cloth are highly prized by neighboring countries.
There are several dozen monasteries with more than a thousand monks, who study and practice the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna teachings.
Traveling more than three hundred li northwest from the kingdom, crossing a stony desert, one reaches Mount Ling.
This is the northern plain of the Pamirs, where most waters flow to the east.
The valleys and mountains were covered in accumulated snow; they remained frozen throughout both spring and summer. Although the ice would occasionally melt away, it would soon freeze over again.
The journey was fraught with perilous obstacles, and the cold winds were bitterly fierce.
There are many perils from fierce dragons that assault and violate travelers.
Those who travel this road must not wear saffron-colored robes, nor carry gourds, nor call out with loud voices.
Should there be even the slightest transgression, one will witness calamity and disaster with one's own eyes.
Violent winds arise, scattering sand and raining stones; those who encounter them perish, finding it difficult to preserve their lives.
After traveling over four hundred li through the mountains, one arrives at the Great Clear Lake, also known as the Hot Sea or the Salt Sea.
It spans over one thousand *li* in circumference, being long from east to west and narrow from south to north.

Its four sides are backed by mountains, where various streams converge; its color is a dark blue-black, and its taste is both salty and bitter. The vast surges are immense and expansive, with startling waves crashing and swirling.

Dragons and fish dwell together, and numinous anomalies arise from time to time; therefore, travelers passing by offer prayers for blessings, and though aquatic creatures abound, none dare to fish there.
Traveling northwest from Qingchi for more than five hundred li, one arrives at Suyabshui City.
The city is six or seven li in circuit, where merchants and Hu people from various countries dwell together.
The soil is suitable for millet, wheat, and grapes; the forests are sparse.
The climate is windy and cold, and the people wear felt and coarse woolen garments.

To the west of Suyab are several dozen isolated cities, each with its own appointed governor; although they do not acknowledge one another’s authority, they all pay tribute and are subject to the Turks.
From the city of Suyab on the river to the kingdom of Kasanna, there is a place named Suli, which is also the name by which the people are called.
Their written characters and spoken language follow these very names.

The origins of these characters are concise, originally consisting of some twenty-odd words; as they evolved and gave rise to one another, their proliferation became vast. Having been roughly committed to writing, their texts are read vertically and passed down from teacher to student in succession, with the lineage of masters and disciples remaining unbroken.
They wear felt and coarse wool, and garments of leather and cotton; their lower robes are narrow and tight.

They either wear their hair parted with the crown exposed or shave it entirely; they bind their foreheads with silk and colored cloth. Their physical stature is imposing, yet their dispositions are timid. Their customs are corrupt and decadent, and they frequently practice deceit and fraud. For the most part, they are greedy and acquisitive; fathers and sons calculate profit together, regarding the possession of great wealth as noble, with no distinction made between the honorable and the lowly.
Although their wealth may reach tens of millions, their clothing and food are coarse and simple;
those who cultivate the land and pursue profit constitute about half the population.
Traveling more than four hundred li west from the city of Sule, one arrives at Thousand Springs (Qiànquán).
As for Thousand Springs (Qiànquán), its territory extends over more than two hundred *lǐ*. To the south it faces the Snow Mountains (*Himavat*), while its three borders consist of level plains.
The soil and water are rich and moist, and the forest trees grow luxuriantly; in the month of late spring, various flowers bloom like fine brocade.
There are a thousand springs and pools, hence it was named accordingly.
The Khans of the Turks frequently came here to escape the summer heat.
Within the park were herds of deer, many adorned with bells and rings; they were so tame and familiar with humans that they did not flee in alarm.
The Khan held this in high regard and issued a command to his subordinates: "Whoever dares to kill or harm it shall be executed without pardon.
For this reason, these deer have been able to live out their natural lifespans.
Traveling one hundred forty or fifty li west from Qianquan, one arrives at the city of Talasī.
The city is eight or nine li in circuit; merchants from various countries and Hu people dwell there together.
The local soil and climate are largely similar to those of Suyab.

Traveling south for over ten li, there is a small isolated city with more than three hundred households; its inhabitants were originally from China, who were formerly plundered by the Turks. Later, they gathered their compatriots together to jointly defend this city, where they now reside.
In matters of dress and deportment, he followed the customs of the Turks;
yet in speech and ceremonial etiquette, he still preserved the traditions of his own country.
From here, traveling southwest for more than two hundred li, one arrives at the city of Bai-shui.
The city is six or seven *li* in circuit.
Its local products and climate are even more excellent than those of Ta-lo-si (Tāraśī).
Traveling southwest for over two hundred *li*, one arrives at the city of Gong-yü (Kongyū).
The city is five or six *li* in circuit.
The plains and marshes are fertile, and the forests are lush and verdant.
Traveling forty or fifty *li* south from here, one arrives at the kingdom of Nuchien (笯赤建).
The country of Nuochijian (Nujkend) is over one thousand li in circuit.
Its soil is fertile and well-suited for cultivation; vegetation is lush and trees bear abundant fruit and flowers. Grapes are plentiful, which are also highly prized there.
There were hundreds of cities, each with its own ruler; their movements and comings and goings were not subject to one another’s commands.
Although the territories were demarcated and divided, they were collectively known as the Kingdom of Nuochijian.
From here, traveling west for more than two hundred *li*, one reaches the country of Jāṭī (in the language of Tang, Shiguó).
The country of Jāṭī is over one thousand *li* in circuit.
It borders the Ye River to the west;
it is narrow from east to west and long from south to north.
Its soil and climate are identical to those of the kingdom of Nuochijian.
There are several dozen cities and towns, each with its own ruler; as there is no sovereign overlord, they are subject to the Turks.
From here, traveling southeast for more than a thousand *li*, one reaches the country of Fuhu (also read fan).
The country of Fohan (Fahan) is over four thousand li in circuit, with mountains surrounding its four borders.
The soil is rich and fertile, crops grow in great abundance, flowers and fruits are plentiful, and it is well-suited for raising sheep and horses.
The climate is windy and cold, and the people are by nature fierce and courageous; their speech differs from that of other nations, and their physical appearance is coarse and unrefined.

For several decades, there has been no great sovereign, as chieftains and nobles compete for power, neither submitting to one another, relying on rivers and occupying strategic heights to demarcate territories and establish capitals.
From here, traveling west for more than a thousand *li*, one arrives at the country of Sthūleśvara.
The country of Sthūleśvara is approximately one thousand four or five hundred *li* in circuit.
To the east it borders the Ye River.
The Ye River originates from the northern plains of the Pamir Mountains and flows toward the northwest; it is vast and turbid, surging and rushing with great force.
As for its soil, crops, and customs, they are the same as those of the Zhashi country.
The local ruler was a subordinate of the Turks.
From here, traveling northwest, one enters a vast desert where water and grass are entirely absent.
The roads stretch out boundlessly and the frontiers are difficult to fathom; one must gaze toward distant mountains and seek out human remains to discern the direction and mark the path traveled.
After traveling more than five hundred *li*, he arrived at the kingdom of Samarkand (which in the language of Tang means "Kangguo").
The kingdom of Samarkand is one thousand six or seven hundred *li* in circuit; it is long from east to west and narrow from south to north.
The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty li in circuit; it is extremely secure and well-fortified, and is densely populated.
Precious goods from foreign lands are largely concentrated in this country.
The soil is fertile, and all varieties of crops are cultivated; the forests are lush and verdant, flowers and fruits grow in abundance, and excellent horses are produced in great numbers.
In the art of mechanical ingenuity, they excel above all other nations.
The seasonal climate is harmonious and pleasant, while their customs are fierce and vigorous.
Among all the various Hu kingdoms, this is the most prominent; its manners and deportment serve as a model for those both near and far.
The king was bold and valiant, and neighboring states obeyed his commands.
His army was powerful and strong, consisting largely of *Ṣaka* people.
These *Ṣaka* men were by nature fierce and courageous; they regarded death as returning home and had no enemy who could stand before them in battle.
From here, proceeding southeast, one reaches the country of Mi-mo-ha (in the language of Tang, "The Country of Rice").
The country of Mi-mo-ha is four or five hundred *li* in circuit.
It is situated in the midst of a river valley, being narrow from east to west and long from south to north.
The soil and customs are the same as those of the kingdom of Sāmbhī.
From here, traveling north, one reaches the kingdom of Kapitha (which in the language of Tang means Cao).
The kingdom of Kapitha is approximately one thousand four or five hundred *li* in circuit; it is long from east to west and narrow from south to north.
The soil and customs are the same as those of the kingdom of Sāmara.

From this country, traveling more than three hundred li to the west, one reaches the kingdom of Kūcā (pronounced with a departing tone on the final syllable; in the language of Tang, it means "He" [Hephthalite]).
The Kingdom of Kustana is fourteen or fifteen hundred *li* in circuit; it is narrow from east to west and long from south to north.
Its soil and customs are the same as those of the kingdom of Sāmara.
From this country, traveling west for more than two hundred li, one reaches the kingdom of Kāpiśī (in the language of Tang, Dong’an).
The kingdom of Kāpiśī is more than one thousand li in circuit.
The soil and climate, as well as the customs, are the same as those of the kingdom of Sāmbhī.
From here, traveling more than four hundred li to the west, one reaches the kingdom of Bolor (known in the language of Tang as Shou'an).
The Kingdom of Bost (Pohhe): The kingdom of Bost is approximately one thousand six or seven hundred *li* in circuit; it is long from east to west and narrow from south to north.
Its soil and climate, as well as its customs, are the same as those of the kingdom of Sāmarrakand.
From this country, traveling more than four hundred *li* to the west, one reaches the kingdom of Bāḍī (in the language of Táng, Xī'ān Guó).
The kingdom of Bāḍī is over four hundred *li* in circuit; its soil, produce, and customs are the same as those of the kingdom of Sāmarrakand.
From here, traveling more than five hundred li to the southwest, one reaches the country of Huoli-ximi-jia (Hulūśāpūrṇa).
The country of Huoli-ximi-jia borders both banks of the River Fuchu (Vakṣu), measuring twenty to thirty li from east to west and more than five hundred li from south to north.
The soil and climate, as well as the customs, are the same as those of the country of Bāḍhā, though their language differs slightly.
Traveling southwest from the country of Sāmakaṇa for more than three hundred li, one arrives at the country of Karashar (which in the language of Tang means "History").
The Kingdom of Kāśmīra: The kingdom of Kāśmīra is approximately one thousand four or five hundred *li* in circuit.
Its soil and customs are the same as those of the kingdom of Sāmbarī.
From here, traveling southwest for more than two hundred *li*, one enters the mountains.
The mountain paths were rugged and the stream trails perilous; being utterly devoid of human settlements, they also lacked water and grass.
Traveling southeast for more than three hundred li through the mountains, he entered the Iron Gate.

As for the Iron Gate, mountains flank it on both sides; these mountains are exceedingly steep and precipitous. Although there is a narrow path, it is further compounded by its treacherous nature; the stone cliffs on both sides are as dark in color as iron.
Having installed doors and panels, they further secured them with iron bolts; many iron bells were suspended from the door leaves, and because of its formidable fortifications, it was thus named.
Emerging from the Iron Gate, he arrived at the country of Tukhāra— formerly called Tuhuoluo, which is a corruption—
the land of which is over one thousand *li* from south to north and over three thousand *li* from east to west.

To the east it is hemmed by the Pamir Mountains; to the west it borders Persia; to the south lies the Great Snowy Mountains; and to the north it rests upon the Iron Gates. The great river Oxus flows through its center toward the west.

For several hundred years, the royal lineage has been extinct; local chieftains have vied for power, each asserting themselves as sovereigns, relying on rivers and occupying strategic heights, thereby dividing the land into twenty-seven kingdoms.
Although the territory is divided into distinct administrative districts, they are all collectively subject to the Turks.
Since the climate is temperate, epidemics are also frequent.
At the end of winter and the beginning of spring, heavy rains fall in succession.
Therefore, south of this region and north of Lanpā, the climate and soil of these countries are mostly characterized by heat and endemic diseases.

Consequently, the various monks enter the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) on the sixteenth day of the twelfth month and conclude the retreat on the fifteenth day of the third month; this is based on the prevalence of heavy rain and is also an instance of establishing the teachings according to the seasons.
As for their customs, their disposition is timid;
their appearance is coarse and unrefined; they have a rudimentary understanding of good faith and honor, and do not engage much in deception.
Their speech and social conventions differ somewhat from those of other nations.

The source of these characters consists of twenty-five syllables, which transform and generate one another to provide for all things; they are written horizontally, reading from left to right, and as the recorded texts gradually increase, they become increasingly extensive and refined.
They wear many cotton garments and few coarse woolen clothes.
Their currency consists of gold and silver coins, the designs of which differ from those of other countries.
Following the lower reaches of the Bindusū River, one arrives at the country of Tamiṣa.
The country of Ta-mi (Tami) is over six hundred li from east to west and over four hundred li from south to north.
The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit.
It is long from east to west and narrow from south to north.
There are more than ten monasteries with over a thousand monks.
As for the various *stūpas*—which are what were formerly called *futu*, or *tuyubo*, or *tabo*, or *siyubo*, or *soudoubu*—all of these are corruptions.
Furthermore, the Buddha statues there abound in spiritual wonders and possess divine discernment.
To the east lies the country of Che-wo-yan-na (Khotan).
The country of Che-wo-yan-na extends over more than four hundred li from east to west and more than five hundred li from south to north.
The capital city of the kingdom is over ten li in circuit.
There are five monasteries, and the monks are few in number.
To the east lies the kingdom of Huluo-mo.
The kingdom of Huluo (Hulūma) is over one hundred li from east to west and over three hundred li from south to north.
The capital city of the kingdom is more than ten li in circuit.
Its king is of the Xisu Turks.
There are two monasteries with over one hundred monks.
To the east lies the country of Yuman (pronounced *yú* and *shuò*, both reversed).
The country of Yuman lies more than four hundred li from east to west and over one hundred li from south to north.
The capital city of the country is sixteen or seventeen li in circuit.
Its king is of the Xisu Turks.
There are two monasteries with few monks.
To the southwest, bordering the Oxus River (Vakṣu), one reaches the kingdom of Kūhāvana.
The Kingdom of Kuvāṇa: The kingdom of Kuvāṇa is over two hundred li from east to west and over three hundred li from south to north.
The capital city of the kingdom is more than ten li in circuit.
There are three monasteries with more than one hundred monks.
To the east lies the kingdom of Khotan (Pōśa).
The kingdom of Khotan is over three hundred li from east to west and over five hundred li from south to north.
The capital city of the kingdom is sixteen or seventeen *li* in circuit.
To the east lies the kingdom of Khotan;
the kingdom of Khotan is over one thousand *li* from east to west and over one thousand *li* from south to north.
The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty li in circuit.
To the east it borders the Pamir Mountains (Congling), reaching the kingdom of Kūmīda.
As for the kingdom of Kūmīda, it is over two thousand li from east to west and over two hundred li from south to north.
Situated within the Great Onion Range (Pamir),
the capital city of the kingdom is over twenty li in circuit;
to the southwest it borders the Oxus River (Vakṣu), and to the south it adjoins the Śrīkṣetra kingdom.
Crossing southward over the Vakṣu River, he reached the kingdoms of Dharmasthiti, Badakshān, Yavugaṇa, Kulūta, Himatala, Parvata, Kṛṣṇa, Rāhu, Arni, and Maṅgala.
To the southeast of Jiva lies the country of Kustana and the country of Andarab; the accounts of these are recorded in the *Huiji* (Records of Retrospection).
To the southwest of Jiva lies the country of Bāklāng.
The country of Bāgalāṅga is over fifty *li* from east to west and over two hundred *li* from south to north.
The capital city of the country is more than ten *li* in circuit.
To the south, one reaches the kingdom of Hrilu-siminkien.
The kingdom of Hrilu-siminkien is over one thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit.
To the northwest, one reaches the kingdom of Hu-lin.
The kingdom of Hu-lin is over eight hundred *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is five or six *li* in circuit.
There are more than ten monasteries with over five hundred monks.
To the west lies the country of Bāhīka.
The country of Bāhīka is over eight hundred *li* from east to west and over four hundred *li* from south to north.
To the north it borders the Vakṣu River.
The capital city of the kingdom is more than twenty *li* in circuit; people all call it the "Lesser Rājagṛha.
Although the city is well-fortified, its inhabitants are very few.
The products of the land are particularly diverse; the various flowers of the water and land are too numerous to list in full.
There are more than one hundred monasteries with over three thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
To the southwest outside the city is the Navatāṅga (in the language of Tang, "New") Monastery, which was established by a former king of this country.
Among the masters who composed treatises north of the Great Snow Mountains, it is only in this monastery that the legacy of meritorious works has not declined.
The Buddha images were polished with famous jewels, and the halls and buildings were adorned with rare treasures;
consequently, the rulers of various kingdoms sought to plunder them for profit.
This monastery had long possessed an image of Vaiśravaṇa, whose spiritual discernment was reliable and which provided secret protection through its divine guardianship.
Recently, Siyehe Khan, the son of the Tujue Yehu Khan, mobilized his entire tribe and led his military forces to launch a sudden raid upon the monastery, seeking to seize its precious treasures.
Not far from there, while his army was encamped in the open fields, he dreamed that one night of Vaiśravaṇa Deva, who said to him:
"What power do you possess that you dare to destroy a monastery?"
Consequently, he was pierced through the chest and back with a long halberd.

The Khan was startled awake and immediately suffered excruciating pain in his heart; he then informed his followers of the ominous omen in his dream, dispatched messengers to invite the assembly of monks to perform rites of repentance and confession, but before he could return their command, he had already passed away.
In the southern Buddha hall within the monastery, there is a bathing pitcher for the Buddha, with a capacity of slightly more than one *dou*;
its variegated colors are dazzlingly brilliant, such that it is difficult to name the materials of stone or metal from which it is made.
There is also a tooth of the Buddha, over an inch in length and eight or nine *fen* in width; its color is yellowish-white, and its substance is lustrous and pure.
There was also a Buddha’s broom made of kāśa grass, over two chi in length and about seven cun in circumference, its handle adorned with various precious gems.

Whenever these three objects were brought forth on the six days of the *poṣadha*, both monastics and laypeople would assemble to arrange offerings; moved by their utmost sincerity, the images would sometimes emit radiance.
To the north of the monastery is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, coated with diamond-paste clay and adorned with various precious gems.
Within it are śarīra relics, which from time to time emit a divine radiance.
To the southwest of the monastery is a meditation hut that has stood for many years since its construction.

People from distant regions flock there like spokes converging at a hub, and those of high talent gather there in great numbers; it would be difficult to enumerate in detail those who have realized the four fruits of arhatship.

Therefore, when the various Arhats were about to enter nirvana, they manifested supernatural powers before those who knew them well; thus, there have been established some several hundred stūpas, their foundations and sites situated close together.
Although they have realized the fruits of sainthood, they ultimately manifest no supernatural transformations; there are likely thousands of them, yet no memorial markers have been erected for them.
Today, the monastic community numbers over a hundred, who are diligent day and night, such that it is difficult to discern whether they are ordinary or holy beings.
Traveling more than fifty li northwest from the great city, one reaches the city of Trapuṣa; more than forty li north of that city is the city of Bhallika.
Within each of these cities stands a stūpa, over thirty feet in height.
In the past, when the Tathāgata first realized the fruit of Buddhahood and rose from beneath the Bodhi tree, he was about to proceed to the Deer Park.

At that time, two elders encountered him and were moved by his majestic radiance; providing the provisions for his journey, they offered him parched grain and honey. The World-Honored One then preached to them the blessings of humans and devas, and they were the very first to hear of the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions.
Having heard the instructions of the Dharma, they requested what offerings they should present; the Tathāgata thereupon gave them his hair and nails.
The two elders, intending to return to their own country, requested the proper ritual for paying homage to these relics.

The Tathāgata placed his saṃghāṭī (formerly called *sengqili*, a corruption) folded square beneath [the base], followed by the uttarāsaṅga, then the saṃkakṣikā (formerly called *sengqizhi*, a corruption), and further covered it with an alms bowl; he then stood his khakkhara staff upright—arranged in this sequence, they formed a stūpa.

The two men, having received their orders, each returned to his own city; there they modeled themselves upon the sacred instructions and proceeded with the construction. This was the very first stūpa within the Dharma of Śākyamuni.
More than seventy *li* to the west of the city is a stūpa, over twenty feet high, which was built during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha.
From the southwest of the great city, one enters the valleys of the Snow Mountains and arrives at the country of Rāmmagrāma.
The country of Ra-mo-ṭa (Rāmatā) is fifty or sixty *li* from east to west and over one hundred *li* from south to north.
The capital city of the country is more than ten *li* in circuit.
To the southwest, one reaches the kingdom of Hu-shi-jian.
The kingdom of Hu-shi-jian is over five hundred li from east to west and over one thousand li from south to north.
The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty li in circuit.
It abounds in mountains and rivers and produces excellent horses.
To the northwest, one reaches the country of Tāla-kāṇa.
The country of Tāla-kāṇa is more than five hundred *li* from east to west and fifty or sixty *li* from south to north.
The capital city of the kingdom is over ten li in circuit;
to its west it borders on the kingdom of Persia.
Traveling south from the kingdom of Bāhīka for more than one hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Kapiśa.
The kingdom of Kie-chih (Kapiśī) is over five hundred li from east to west and over three hundred li from south to north.
The capital city has a circumference of four or five li; the soil is stony and barren, with hills and ridges stretching continuously.
Flowers and fruits are scarce, while beans and wheat abound.
The climate is bitterly cold, and the local customs are stern and fierce.
There are more than ten monasteries with over three hundred monks, all of whom study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna teachings.

To the southeast, one enters the Great Snow Mountains, where the valleys and gorges are high and deep, and the peaks and crags are perilous. Wind and snow follow one another; even in midsummer, the ground freezes, as accumulated snow fills the valleys and the mountain paths are difficult to traverse.
Mountain deities and malevolent spirits ran riot with demonic calamities, while bands of robbers roamed at will, making it their business to commit murder.
After traveling over six hundred li, he emerged from the borders of the kingdom of Tukhāra and arrived at the kingdom of Bamiyāna.
The Kingdom of Bāmiyān is more than two thousand li from east to west and over three hundred li from south to north; it is situated amidst the Snow Mountains.
The people dwell in valleys and settle in towns according to the terrain.

The capital city of the kingdom is situated on a cliff overlooking a valley, measuring six or seven *li* in length; it backs onto high crags to the north. There is winter wheat, but few flowers or fruits; the land is suitable for animal husbandry, and there are many sheep and horses.
The climate is bitterly cold and the customs are harsh and rugged; they mostly wear skins and coarse woolens, which is also appropriate for the conditions.
Their script, social customs, and the use of currency are the same as those of the country of Tukhāra.
Their language differs slightly, while their customs and appearance are largely the same.
Their sincerity and faith are particularly profound compared to neighboring countries.
From the Three Jewels above down to the hundred deities below, there are none to whom they do not offer their utmost sincerity and exhaust their hearts in veneration.
Merchants and traders who come and go witness auspicious signs manifested by celestial deities; they are shown portents and transformations so that they may seek merit and virtue.
There are several dozen monasteries with several thousand monks, who follow the teachings of the Lokottaravāda school of the Hinayana.
On a mountain slope to the northeast of the royal city stands a stone image of the Buddha, one hundred forty or fifty feet high, its golden hue radiant and its jeweled ornaments resplendent.
To the east is a monastery, built by a former king of this country.
To the east of the monastery is a standing image of Śākyamuni Buddha made of brass, over one hundred feet in height; it was cast in separate sections and joined together to form the whole.
Two or three *li* to the east of the city, within a monastery, is a reclining image of the Buddha entering nirvāṇa, over one thousand feet in length.

Whenever this king convenes an unrestricted great assembly (*paṃcavārṣika-mahāpariṣad*), he begins with his wife and children and extends down to the national treasures; having emptied the treasury, he further offers himself as a gift. The various officials and assistants then come to the monks to redeem him; such is the primary concern of his endeavors.

Traveling over two hundred li southeast from the monastery containing the reclining Buddha image, one crosses the Great Snow Mountains and reaches a small marshy valley to the east, where the springs and pools are as clear as mirrors and the forests are lush and verdant.
There is a monastery containing the tooth of the Buddha and the tooth of a Pratyekabuddha from the beginning of the kalpa, which is over five inches long and slightly less than four inches wide;
furthermore, there is the tooth of a Cakravartin King, three inches long and two inches wide;
and there is the iron alms-bowl held by the Great Arhat Śāṇakavāsa (formerly transcribed as Shannahexiu, which is erroneous), with a capacity of approximately eight or nine *sheng*.
All the personal effects left behind by the Three Sages and Holy Ones were sealed with gold leaf.
There was also the nine-panel *saṃghāṭī* robe of Śaṇakavāsa, which was crimson in color and woven from the fibers of the śaṇaka grass.
Śaṅkhābhāsa was a disciple of Ānanda. In a previous life, on the day of the conclusion of the rainy season retreat, he offered garments made of śaṅkha grass to the community of monks as a gift.
By virtue of this merit, throughout five hundred lifetimes—both during the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and at birth—he shall always wear these garments.
In his final existence, they shall emerge from the womb together with him; as his body gradually grows, the garments shall likewise expand.
When Ānanda brings him forth into the religious life, the garments shall transform into Dharma robes.
Upon receiving full ordination, it further transformed into a nine-striped *saṃghāṭī*.

As he was about to realize *nirvāṇa* and entered the *prāntakoṭika-samādhi*, he exercised the power of his wisdom-vow to leave behind this *kāṣāya*, so that it would endure until the end of Śākyamuni’s bequeathed Dharma.
Only after the Dharma has come to an end will it finally undergo transformation and decay.
That it has already suffered some slight deterioration is indeed a sign of this.
From here, traveling eastward into the Snow Mountains and crossing the Black Ridge, one arrives at the kingdom of Kāpiśī.
The Kingdom of Kāpiśī: The kingdom of Kāpiśī is over four thousand *li* in circuit; it has the Snow Mountains to its north and borders on the Black Range on three sides.
The capital city of the kingdom is over ten *li* in circuit.
The land is suitable for rice, wheat, and fruit trees, and produces fine horses and saffron.
Exotic goods from distant regions are gathered in great abundance in this country.
The climate is windy and cold; the people are violent and fierce by nature, their speech is vulgar and coarse, and their marriage customs are promiscuous.
Their script is largely the same as that of the country of Tukhāra,
though their customs, language, and social mores differ considerably.
For clothing, they wear wool and cotton, while their garments also include furs and coarse woollen cloth.
The currency consists of gold coins, silver coins, and small copper coins; their shape and design differ from those of other countries.
The king is of the Kṣatriya caste; he possesses strategic wisdom and a courageous and fierce nature, intimidating his neighbors and governing more than ten kingdoms.

He cherished and nurtured the common people and revered the Triple Gem; every year he commissioned a silver Buddha image eighteen feet tall and concurrently established an unrestricted great assembly (*amogha-mahāpariṣad*), providing for the poor and destitute and bestowing gifts upon widowers and widows.
There are more than one hundred monasteries with over six thousand monks, most of whom study and practice the Mahāyāna teachings.
The stūpas and monasteries are lofty and spacious, vast and magnificent, and pure and serene.

There are several dozen deva temples with more than a thousand followers of heterodox paths; some go naked, some smear themselves with ashes, and they string together skulls to form crowns and garlands.
Three or four *li* to the east of the great city, at the foot of a northern mountain, there is a large monastery with more than three hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna.

According to the records of former sages, it is said that in the past, King Kaniṣka of Gandhāra extended his majesty over neighboring countries and his transformation reached distant lands. Having mobilized his troops and expanded his territory to the east of the Pamir Mountains, the vassal states west of the river feared his power and sent hostages.

Once King Kaniṣka had received the hostage prince, he treated him with exceptional courtesy and honor, providing different residences according to the seasons: during the winter he resided in the various kingdoms of India, during the summer he returned to the kingdom of Kapīśa, and during the spring and autumn he stayed in the kingdom of Gandhāra.
Therefore, monasteries were established at each of the three locations where the hostage prince resided;
this present monastery is the one built at his summer residence.
Consequently, on the walls of the various chambers, portraits of the hostage prince have been painted, and his countenance and attire are quite similar to those of the Middle Kingdom (China).

Subsequently, although they were able to return to their own country, their hearts remained fixed on their former residence; thus, despite the barriers of mountains and rivers, they did not cease their offerings.

Consequently, the monastic community continues to this day to hold grand Dharma assemblies whenever the period of *varṣā* (the rainy season retreat) begins or concludes, praying for blessings and cultivating merit for all the hostages, a tradition that has continued without interruption until now.
Beneath the right foot of the Great Devarāja image to the south of the eastern gate of the monastery’s Buddha hall, there is a pit containing buried treasure, which was hidden by the hostage prince.
Therefore, its inscription reads:
"When the monastery falls into ruin, take this to repair it."
Recently, there was a neighboring king who was greedy and tyrannical; hearing that this monastery stored much precious treasure, he drove out the monks.

Just as he began the excavation, the parrot image upon the crown of the divine king stirred its feathers and cried out in alarm, causing the earth to tremble. The king and his soldiers were struck with terror and fell prostrate; after a long time they were able to rise, whereupon they apologized for their transgression and returned home.
On the northern ridge above the monastery are several stone chambers, the places where the hostage prince practiced meditative concentration.
Within them are stored many miscellaneous jewels; beside them are inscriptions guarded by yakṣas.

Should anyone wish to excavate and take the treasure within, this yakṣa deity manifests various transformations, appearing sometimes as a lion, sometimes as a python, a fierce beast, or a venomous insect; with such diverse forms and expressions of wrathful fury, no one dares to attempt its excavation.

Two or three *li* to the west of the stone chamber, atop a great mountain ridge, there is a statue of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. If anyone with sincere devotion wishes to see him, the Bodhisattva emerges from within the statue in a body of wondrous color to comfort the practitioner.

More than thirty li to the southeast of the great city, one reaches the Kalandaka Monastery. Beside it stands a stūpa over a hundred feet high, which occasionally emits a brilliant light on fast days.
From the crevices of the stone at the top of the overturned bowl-shaped structure, black fragrant oil flows out; in the stillness of the night, the sound of music is occasionally heard.
According to the records of former sages:
"In the past, this was built by the minister Aṭaḥkula of this kingdom."
When the work was completed, someone appeared in a dream at night and said to him:
"The stūpa you have erected contains no śarīra; tomorrow morning, there will be one offered as a gift, which you should request from the king."
At dawn, he entered the court and presented his request, saying:
"Without reckoning my own mediocrity and ignorance, I venture to have a wish.
The King said:
"What do you desire? He replied,
"Now that there is one who has presented himself first, I pray that you will bestow your grace upon me."
The king said, "So be it.
Elāra stood waiting at the palace gate, gazing toward wherever he might go.
Suddenly, a man appeared carrying a relic casket. A high minister asked him, "What do you wish to offer?
He replied:
"Buddha-relics.
The minister said, "I shall guard them for you; you ought first to inform the King."

Rāhula, fearing that the King might hold the śarīra in such high esteem as to regret his former kindness, hurried to the monastery and ascended the stūpa. Moved by his utmost sincerity, the stone *kapotaka* covering [the relic chamber] opened of its own accord; he placed the śarīra therein and then quickly departed, yet remained caught by his robe’s hem.
The king sent men to pursue him, but the stone had already closed over him;
consequently, black fragrant oil flows from the crevices between them.
More than forty *li* south of the city, one reaches the city of Śvetavatāra.
Whenever there is a great earthquake, the mountains and cliffs collapse; yet within the boundaries of this city, nothing is shaken.

About thirty li south of the city of Xibi Duofalaci, one reaches Mount Alunuo (pronounced with the second tone on "nu"). Its cliffs and ridges are steep and precipitous, and its rocky valleys are dark and profound.
Each year its peak rises several hundred feet, until it nearly rivals Mount Nakhila in the kingdom of Kāmarūpa; immediately thereafter, it collapses.
According to local tradition, it is said that in the beginning,
the deity Śunatā arrived from afar, intending to dwell upon this mountain.
The mountain god was struck with indignation and caused the valleys and gorges to tremble and shake.
The deity said:
"I do not wish to abandon you; therefore, I have caused this upheaval.
If you would deign to accept even a small portion as a guest's gift, your wealth and treasures shall be filled."
"I shall now go to Mount Śūnahila in the country of Koṭṭamati; every year, when I receive the sacrificial offerings of the king and his ministers, you should look toward me."
Thus, as soon as Mount Aruṇa had increased in height, it immediately collapsed.
Over two hundred li to the northwest of the royal city, one reaches the Great Snow Mountains.
At the summit of the mountain is a lake; whether for requesting rain or praying for clear weather, one’s wishes are fulfilled accordingly.
I have heard from the records of former sages that,
in the past, there was an Arhat in the kingdom of Gandhāra who constantly received offerings from the Dragon King of this lake.
Whenever it was time for the midday meal, he would use his supernatural powers to travel through the air, seated upon a corded couch.

The attendant śrāmaṇera hid himself secretly beneath the rope bed, clinging to it and remaining concealed; when the time arrived, the arhat went forth, and upon reaching the dragon palace, he saw the śrāmaṇera, whereupon the Dragon King invited him to stay for a meal.
The Dragon King served the Arhat with celestial ambrosia, while he provided the śrāmaṇera with human food.
When the Arhat had finished his meal, he expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the Dragon King.

The śrāmaṇera, as was his custom, washed his teacher’s bowl; seeing that there were grains remaining in it, he was struck by their fragrance and flavor. He immediately conceived an evil vow, resenting his teacher and feeling anger toward the dragon:
"May all the power of my merits manifest this very moment to end this dragon's life, so that I myself may become king."
When the śrāmaṇera made this vow, the dragon king already felt a headache.
Although the arhat preached the Dharma to admonish and instruct him, the dragon king apologized for his fault and reproached himself;
yet the śrāmaṇera harbored resentment and did not accept the apology.

Having returned to the monastery, he made a vow with utmost sincerity. By the power of this merit, at the end of that night his life came to an end, and he was reborn as a great dragon king. Possessing fierce and vigorous majesty, he entered the pond, slew the former dragon king, took up residence in the dragon palace, and assumed command over his subordinates, governing their lives.
Due to his past vows, he raised violent winds and rain, uprooting trees and intending to destroy the monastery.
At that time, King Kaniṣka, finding it strange, questioned him; the Arhat then explained everything in detail to the king.
The King then established a saṃghārāma for the dragon at the foot of the Snowy Mountains and constructed a stūpa over one hundred feet high.
However, harboring its former resentment, the dragon subsequently unleashed wind and rain.
The king’s heart was set on universal salvation, yet the dragon, driven by its venomous malice, wrought havoc, causing the monasteries and stūpas to be destroyed six times and rebuilt seven times.

King Kaniṣka, ashamed that his meritorious work remained unfulfilled, desired to fill the dragon’s pool and demolish its dwelling; he immediately raised a military host and arrived at the foot of the Snow Mountains.
At that time, the Dragon King was deeply struck with terror; he transformed himself into an old Brahmin, tapped the king’s elephant, and admonished him, saying:

"Great King, you cultivated the roots of goodness in past lives and planted many superior causes, whereby you attained the status of a human sovereign over whom none dare think themselves unsubmissive."
For what reason do you contend with a dragon today?
A dragon is but a beast, a lowly and ignoble creature; yet it possesses great majesty and cannot be overcome by mere physical force.
Riding upon clouds and driving the wind, treading on emptiness and walking upon water—these are not things that human power can control; how could they possibly be objects of Your Majesty’s wrath?

Now Your Majesty mobilizes the entire nation and raises an army to fight a single dragon; if victorious, Your Majesty will lack the majesty of one who subdues the distant; if defeated, Your Majesty will incur the shame of being no match for the foe.
"For the king's own sake, you ought to withdraw your troops.
King Kaniṣka did not follow this advice.

The dragon immediately returned to his pool, its roar shaking like thunder; violent winds uprooted trees, sand and stones fell like rain, and clouds and mist darkened the sky, terrifying the soldiers and horses.
The king then took refuge in the Triple Gem and entreated for their protection, saying:

"Having cultivated much merit in past lives, I have attained the status of a human king; my majesty has intimidated powerful enemies, and I have governed Jambudvīpa. That I am now humiliated by these dragon-beasts is truly due to my own meager merit."
"May the power of all merits manifest itself here and now!
Immediately, great smoke and flames rose from his two shoulders; the dragon retreated, the wind subsided, the mist rolled away, and the clouds dispersed.
The King ordered the soldiers to carry one *śata* of stone each to fill the dragon pond.
The Dragon King then transformed himself into a Brahmin and again entreated the King, saying:
"I am the Dragon King of that pond; fearing your majesty, I have come to take refuge. I only pray that Your Majesty will show compassion and forgive my former transgressions."
The King has nurtured and protected all living beings; why then do you alone inflict such evil harm upon me?

If Your Majesty kills me, both I and Your Majesty shall fall together into the evil realms. Your Majesty will incur the sin of taking life, while I will harbor a heart of resentment and enmity; the retribution of karma is clear, and the distinction between good and evil is manifest.
The King then established a solemn covenant with the dragon, stipulating that should it violate the agreement again in the future, it would certainly not be pardoned.

The dragon said, "Because of my evil karma, I have received this body as a dragon; the nature of dragons is fierce and violent, and I cannot restrain myself. Should a mind of anger arise, I may forget these constraints."
"Your Majesty may now establish monasteries once more, for we shall not dare to destroy them.

We shall each dispatch a person to keep watch upon the mountain ridges; should black clouds arise, they must strike the *gandī* drum with urgency. Upon hearing its sound, our evil intentions shall be stilled."
The king thereupon renovated the monastery and erected a stūpa; he has continued to observe the clouds and vapors without ceasing even to this day.
According to the records of former sages:
within the stūpa are the bodily relics of the Tathāgata, amounting to slightly more than one *sheng*; the accounts of its miraculous transformations are difficult to describe in detail.

At one time, smoke suddenly rose from within the stūpa, and after a short while, fierce flames burst forth. People of the time thought the stūpa had been consumed by fire; they gazed upon it for a long time until the fire was extinguished and the smoke had vanished. Thereupon, they saw the śarīra appearing like white pearl banners, circling around the central pillar and winding upward, rising to the edge of the clouds before spiraling back down.

Within the Old King’s Monastery on the southern bank of the Great River to the northwest of the royal city, there is the hair of Śākyamuni Bodhisattva from his youth, when he was still a child; it is over one inch in length.

To the southeast of that monastery is another monastery, also named Old King, which contains a fragment of the Tathāgata’s skull-bone; its surface is over an inch wide, its color is yellowish-white, and the pores of the hair are clearly visible.

Furthermore, there is hair from the Tathāgata; its color is deep blue-black, curling to the right in spirals. When extended, it is over a foot long, yet when coiled, it is only half an inch in diameter.
Regarding these three items, whenever the six fasting days (ṣaḍ-upavāsa) arrive, the king and his great ministers scatter flowers as an offering.
To the southwest of the Kālaṅka Monastery is the monastery of the former queen, which contains a gilded-bronze stūpa over one hundred feet high.

According to local tradition, this stūpa contains more than a *śu* of the Buddha’s relics. On the fifteenth day of every month, at night, it emits a circular light that illuminates the *āmalaka* pinnacle; the radiance continues until dawn, after which the light gradually withdraws and enters back into the stūpa.
To the southwest of the city is Mount Pilusāra, which in the language of Tang means "Elephant-Firm.
Because the mountain deity takes the form of an elephant, it is called Elephant-Firm.

Formerly, when the Tathāgata was in the world, the deity Elephant-Firm invited the World-Honored One and twelve hundred great arhats. On the summit of the mountain there was a large flat rock, whereupon the Tathāgata proceeded to receive the deity’s offerings.
Later, King Aśoka erected a stūpa upon this rock, over a hundred feet in height; people today call it the Elephant-Strong Stūpa.
It is also said that there are relics of the Tathāgata within, amounting to slightly more than one *sheng*.

To the north of the Kharaosta Stūpa, at the base of a mountain cliff, there is a dragon spring. This is where the Tathāgata, after receiving divine food, and the Arhats rinsed their mouths and chewed *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-sticks) therein; they subsequently planted them, which have now become a lush grove.
Later generations established a monastery here, named Vetravāṇa (translated into Chinese as *jiào yángzhī*, "chewing willow twigs").

From here, traveling east for more than six hundred li through continuous mountain valleys and steep, precipitous peaks and crags, one crosses the Black Ridge (*Kālācala*) and enters the territory of North India, arriving at the kingdom of Lampāka within the borders of North India.
The Great Tang Dynasty Record of the Western Regions, Scroll One.
The Great Tang Dynasty Record of the Western Regions, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Three Kingdoms, by Imperial Decree.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Bianji of Dazongchi Monastery.

Preface to the Kingdoms of Lanpo, Nagarahāra, and Gandhāra in the Three Kingdoms Period. To examine in detail the designation "Tianzhu" (India): opinions have long been conflicted and confused. Formerly it was called Shendu, or alternatively Xiandou; now, following the correct pronunciation, it should be called Indu.

The people of India designate their country according to its specific location; yet, when referring to distant regions with diverse customs by a general name to praise what is excellent therein, they call it "India."
India is called "Moon" (Candra) in the language of Tang.
The moon has many names, and this is one such appellation.

It is said that the various sentient beings revolve in saṃsāra without ceasing; in the long night of ignorance, there is none to herald the dawn. This is like when the sun has already set and the night lamp must follow; although there is the illumination of the stars, how can it compare to the brilliance of the bright moon?
If one follows this reasoning, one may thus liken it to the moon.
This is truly because the sages and worthies have followed one another’s tracks in that land, guiding the common people and governing all things like the moon’s illuminating presence.
For this reason, it is called India.

In India, society is divided into various castes and classes, among which the Brahmins are particularly pure and noble; following their elegant title, this has been passed down as a custom, and without distinguishing between specific boundaries, the land is collectively referred to as the Kingdom of the Brahmins.
As for its territorial boundaries, they may be described as follows:
the realm of the Five Indias spans over ninety thousand *li* in circumference;
it borders the great ocean on three sides and is backed by the Snow Mountains to the north.
It is broad in the north and narrow in the south, shaped like a half-moon; its territory is divided into more than seventy kingdoms.
The climate is particularly hot, and the land is mostly marshy with many springs.
To the north, the terrain consists of undulating hills and mounds, with salt-encrusted plateaus and low ridges;
to the east, the rivers and fields are lush and moist, with fertile plots and rich soil;
to the south, the vegetation flourishes and thrives.
The lands of the western regions are generally stony and barren;
this is the general outline, which may be stated briefly.
As for the designation of distance, it is called *yojana*, formerly translated as *youxun*.
It is also called *yojana*, and it is further called *youyan*; both are corruptions and abbreviations.
A *yojana* is the distance traveled by the army of an ancient sage-king in a single day.
According to ancient tradition, one *yojana* is forty *li*; however,
according to the local custom of the Indian country, it is thirty *li*,
while that recorded in the Noble Teachings is only sixteen *li*.
To calculate the subtlest of numbers, one *yojana* is divided into eight *krośas*.
A *krośa* is defined as the maximum distance to which the bellowing of a large bull can be heard; thus it is called a *krośa*.

One *krośa* is divided into five hundred *dhanus*; one *dhanus* is divided into four *hasta*; one *hasta* is divided into twenty-four *aṅguli*; one finger-joint (*aṅguliparvan*) is divided into seven barley grains; and this sequence continues through sevenfold divisions of louse, nit, mote of dust in a sunbeam, cow-hair, sheep-hair, rabbit-hair, gold-dust, and water-dust, until reaching the subtle particle (*paramāṇu*). Seven subtle particles constitute an extremely subtle particle (*paramāṇv-aṇu*).
The "extremely fine particle" (*paramāṇu*) is that which can no longer be further divided; if it were divided, it would return to emptiness, and is thus called the "ultimate atom.

As for the movements of the Yin and Yang and the cycles of the calendar, as well as the positions of the sun and moon—their designations may differ, yet the seasonal timing remains the same; according to the established lunar mansions, the names of the months are designated.
The shortest duration of time is called a *kṣaṇa*.

One hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* constitute one *tatkṣaṇa*; sixty *tatkṣaṇas* constitute one *lava*; thirty *lavas* constitute one *muhūrta*; five *muhūrtas* constitute one period (*yāma*). Six such periods compose one day and night, consisting of three daytime periods and three nighttime periods.
In the secular world, the day and night are divided into eight periods—four for the day and four for the night—and each of these periods is further divided into four sub-divisions.

The period from the waxing of the moon until it is full is called the "white portion" (śuklapakṣa), while the period from the waning of the moon until it is dark is called the "black portion" (kṛṣṇapakṣa).
