The black portion may consist of either fourteen or fifteen days, depending on whether the lunar month is short or long.
The dark [fortnight] preceding and the white [fortnight] following constitute one month.
Six months combined constitute one course.
When the sun moves within [the solstitial limits], it is the northern course;
The sun’s journey outside [the sphere] is its southern course.
These two courses together constitute one year.
Furthermore, one year is divided into six seasons:
From the sixteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the third month is the period of gradual heat;
from the sixteenth day of the third month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month is the period of intense heat;
from the sixteenth day of the fifth month to the fifteenth day of the seventh month is the rainy season.
From the sixteenth day of the seventh month to the fifteenth day of the ninth month is the period of flourishing;
from the sixteenth day of the ninth month to the fifteenth day of the eleventh month is the period of increasing cold;
and from the sixteenth day of the eleventh month to the fifteenth day of the first month is the period of intense cold.
According to the noble teaching of the Tathāgata, the year consists of three seasons:
from the sixteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month is the hot season;
from the sixteenth day of the fifth month to the fifteenth day of the ninth month is the rainy season.
From the sixteenth day of the ninth month to the fifteenth day of the first month is the cold season.
Alternatively, there are four seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter.
The three months of spring are known as Caitra, Vaiśākha, and Jyeṣṭha; these correspond to the period from the sixteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the fourth month.
The three months of summer refer to the months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and Bhādrapada; these correspond to the period from the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
The three months of autumn are known as Āśvayuja, Kārttika, and Mārgaśīrṣa; these correspond to the period from the sixteenth day of the seventh month to the fifteenth day of the tenth month.

The three months of winter are called the month of Pauṣa, the month of Māgha, and the month of Phālguna; these correspond to the period from the sixteenth day of the tenth month to the fifteenth day of the first month.
Therefore, the monastic community in India observes two periods of the rains retreat (*varṣā*) based on the Buddha’s holy teachings: either the first three months or the last three months.

The first three months correspond here to the period from the sixteenth day of the fifth month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month; the last three months correspond here to the period from the sixteenth day of the sixth month to the fifteenth day of the ninth month.

Among those who translated the sutras and vinaya in previous dynasties, some used the term "sitting summer" (zuò xià) and others used "sitting winter" (zuò lā). These were all due to the divergent customs of frontier regions and a failure to master the standard pronunciation of the Middle Kingdom; perhaps their local dialects had not yet been harmonized, resulting in errors in the transmission and translation.

Furthermore, when calculating the dates of the Tathāgata’s entry into the womb, birth, renunciation, attainment of Buddhahood, and parinirvāṇa, there are discrepancies in all of them; the details are recorded in the subsequent notes.
As for the towns and villages, their walls stand square and broad;
the streets and lanes wind in tortuous paths, while marketplaces occupy the thoroughfares and taverns line the roads.

Butchers, fishermen, pimps, actors, executioners, and scavengers—having marked their dwellings, they were expelled beyond the city limits; when traveling through the streets, they kept to the left side of the road.

As for the construction of dwellings and the building of walls and enclosures, because the terrain is low and damp, cities are mostly built with piled bricks; as for the various walls, they are sometimes made of woven bamboo or wood. The houses, palaces, and towers consist of plank-roofed structures with flat tops, plastered with lime and covered with brick tiles.
The various structures differ in their construction, yet their design conforms to that of the Middle Kingdom.

They are thatched with *māṇa* grass or common grass, using either bricks or wooden planks; the walls are adorned with lime plaster, the floors are smeared with cow dung for purification, and seasonal flowers are strewn about—these are the points of difference.
The various monasteries are exceedingly marvelous in their construction.

Corner towers rise on all four sides, and multi-storied pavilions reach three levels. The rafters, eaves, ridgepoles, and beams are carved with extraordinary shapes; the doors, windows, walls, and enclosures are painted with a multitude of colors.
The dwellings of the common people are extravagant within and frugal without;
the inner chambers and central halls vary in height and breadth, while the multi-storied terraces and layered pavilions are unrestricted in their architectural design.
The gates open toward the east, and the seats for the morning assembly face east.
As for the seating arrangements, all use corded couches (rajjupīṭha).
Whether they be members of the royal clan, great personages, scholars, commoners, or prominent elites, their ornaments and finery differ, yet the rules of decorum remain the same.
The sovereign’s throne was even more lofty and expansive, inlaid with pearls and gems, known as a lion-seat; it was spread with fine cotton cloth and approached by means of a jeweled footstool.
Among the various officials, each according to their own preference, carves diverse objects and polishes rare treasures.
As for clothing and ornaments, they are not tailored or fashioned; they value fresh white and hold variegated colors in low esteem.
Men wrap their waists and drape their armpits, crossing a cloth over the shoulder to leave the right side bare; women, however, wear robes that hang down low, covering both shoulders entirely.
They form a small topknot on the crown of the head, with the remaining hair falling downward.
Some even cut their mustaches as a peculiar and eccentric custom.
They wear flower garlands upon their heads and necklaces of jewels upon their bodies.
As for their clothing, they wear garments made of *kauśeya* silk and cotton cloth (*karpāsa*).
Kauśeya refers to wild silkworm silk;
kṣaumaka refers to a type of flaxen cloth;
kambala refers to woven fine wool.
The *he-là-li* garment is woven from the fur of wild beasts.
Because the animal fur is fine and soft, it can be spun and woven; thus it is prized and used for clothing.
In North India, the climate is harsh and cold; the people wear short and narrow garments that are somewhat similar to those of the Hu.

The dress of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) is diverse and varied in its styles: some wear peacock feathers and tails, some adorn themselves with necklaces of skulls, some go naked without clothing, and others cover their bodies with grass or wooden boards. Some pull out their hair or shave their mustaches; others have disheveled hair or wear topknots. Their lower garments and robes have no fixed style, and they do not consistently wear red or white.
The dharma-robes of a śramaṇa consist only of the three robes (*trīṇi cīvarāṇi*) and the *saṃkakṣikā* (also known as *nivāsana*).
Regarding the tailoring of the three robes, the various schools hold differing views: some have wide borders while others have narrow ones; some have small patches while others have large ones.
The *saṃkakṣikā*—in the language of Tang, *yan-yi* (掩腋)—was formerly called *saṃghāṭī*, which is an error.
It covers the left shoulder and conceals both armpits; it is open on the left and closed on the right, and its length is cut to extend past the waist.
*Nivāsana* (in the language of Tang, "skirt").

Formerly called *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*, which is an error; as it lacks bands or loops, when one is about to wear it, one gathers the cloth into pleats and secures them with a cord. Regarding the pleats, the various schools differ, and their colors vary between yellow and red.
The Kṣatriyas and Brāhmaṇas live in purity and simplicity, remaining clean, bright, and frugal.

Kings and high ministers, however, wear garments and ornaments of superior quality; they use flower garlands and jeweled crowns as head adornments, and rings, bracelets, and necklaces as body ornaments.
Among them, there are wealthy merchants and great traders who possess nothing but bracelets.
Most people go barefoot, with few wearing sandals.
They dye their teeth either red or black; they have even hair, pierced ears, high noses, and large eyes—such is their appearance.
Now, his maintenance of purity and self-restraint was not a pretension of his will.
Whenever there was food to be served, he would invariably wash his hands first; he would not partake of leftovers from the previous night, nor would he share his eating vessels with others.
As for utensils made of clay or wood, once they had been used, they were necessarily discarded.
Gold, silver, copper, and iron were each polished to a high luster.
Once the meal was finished, they chewed on willow twigs for purification.
Before the rinsing and washing were complete, no one would touch them.
Whenever they urinated or defecated, they invariably performed ritual ablutions.
Their bodies were anointed with various fragrances, namely sandalwood and turmeric.
When the king was about to bathe, drums were beaten and stringed instruments were played with song.
Regarding the rituals of sacrifice and ancestral worship, as well as bathing and ablution:
examining their script, it was devised by Brahmā; its original principles and established rules consist of forty-seven characters.
Manifesting through objects to form a synthesis, it shifts its application according to circumstances.

As it flows and evolves into branches and tributaries, its source gradually expands; though it undergoes slight modifications depending on the terrain and the people, in its general outline, it does not differ from its original source.

Central India, however, is particularly detailed and correct; its diction and cadence are harmonious and elegant, matching the celestial tones, and its spirit and resonance are clear and bright, serving as a model for all people.
In neighboring regions and foreign lands, errors have become established as tradition, and they compete in following degenerate customs, failing to preserve the pure and refined style.
As for recording words and chronicling events, each has its own designated office.

The general title for the historical records is *Nirvāṇa-bhadraka*, which in the language of Tang means "Pure Treasury" (*viśuddha-piṭaka*); therein both good and evil are fully set forth, and calamities and auspicious signs are exhaustively documented.
To open the minds of the ignorant and guide them forward, he first taught the Twelve Chapters.
After the age of seven, he gradually imparted the Great Treatises on the Five Sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*):
the first is *Śabdavidyā* (the science of grammar), which explains glosses and defines characters, providing commentaries and distinctions.
Second is the science of crafts (*śilpakarmasthāna-vidyā*), which includes technical arts, mechanical devices, and the calculation of yin-yang and calendrical astrology.
Third is the science of medicine (*cikitsā-vidyā*), which includes the use of incantations to ward off malevolent spirits, as well as medicinal herbs, minerals, acupuncture, and moxibustion.
The fourth is Hetuvidyā (Logic), which examines and determines what is correct or erroneous, and investigates and scrutinizes what is true or false.
The fifth is Adhyātmavidyā (Inner Science), which thoroughly explores and elucidates the subtle principles of cause and effect within the five vehicles.
As for the Brahmins, they study the four Vedas.
The old term was *Veda*, which is a corruption.
The first is called *Jyotiṣa* (Life), meaning the cultivation of life and the refinement of one's nature.
The second is called *Śrauta* (Sacrifice), meaning the offering of sacrifices and the performance of prayers.
The third is called "Equilibrium" (Ping), referring to ritual propriety, divination, military strategy, and battle formations.
The fourth is called "Art" (Shu), referring to extraordinary abilities, technical skills, incantations, and medical prescriptions.

The Master must extensively investigate the subtle and profound, thoroughly penetrate the mysterious and abstruse, demonstrate the great principles, and guide with subtle words; he shall uplift and encourage, skillfully lead, refine the decayed, and inspire the insincere.

If one possesses a penetrating and sagacious intellect yet harbors a desire for reclusion, then even those who are bound and confined shall find liberation, and their work will be completed only after their final passing.
At the age of thirty, his aspirations were established and his studies perfected; once he had attained a position of emolument and rank, he first repaid the virtue of his teacher.

There were those who possessed broad knowledge of antiquity and a refined love for the elegant; they lived in secluded retirement, maintaining their integrity, drifting in and out beyond the realm of things, and wandering carefree outside the affairs of the world. Unperturbed by honor or disgrace, their reputation spread far and wide, yet even kings and lords who held them in high esteem could not induce them to humble themselves and appear at court.

However, the state prizes sagacity and wisdom, and its customs esteem loftiness and brilliance; since praise and commendation are so abundant, the honors and mandates bestowed are likewise significant.

Consequently, people are able to strengthen their resolve and devote themselves to study, forgetting fatigue as they cultivate the arts, seeking the Way and relying on benevolence, traveling thousands of li without regard for distance.

Though their families were wealthy and noble, their aspirations were those of wanderers; for the sustenance of their bodies, they traveled about begging to survive, valuing the knowledge of the Way above all and feeling no shame in the lack of material wealth.

Indulging in pleasure-trips, neglecting one’s studies, eating gluttonously, and wearing extravagant clothes—possessing neither virtuous conduct nor practicing at the proper times—both shame and disgrace arrive together, and an ill reputation spreads far and wide.

The Tathāgata’s principles and teachings allow beings to attain understanding according to their respective capacities; though the Sage has been gone for a long time and the purity of the True Dharma has varied, those who follow their own inclinations of mind all obtain the awakening of hearing and wisdom.
The mountain peaks of the various schools stand tall, while the waves of debate surge; those specializing in heterodox studies follow divergent paths yet reach the same destination.
Among the eighteen schools, each excels in its own sharpness of argument;
as for the Great and Small Vehicles, their respective domains are clearly distinguished.

Whether in quiet contemplation, walking meditation, standing, or sitting, their concentration and wisdom were far-reaching and deep; as for the differences between the noisy and the tranquil, they established various regulations and safeguards according to the specific dwellings of each group.
Setting aside the Vinaya and Abhidharma, as for the Sūtras—these being the Buddha’s own discourses—if one lectures and proclaims one section, one is exempt from monastic administrative duties;
for two sections, one is additionally provided with housing and personal requisites;
for three sections, one is assigned an attendant to serve them.
The fourth division provided lay attendants for service;
the fifth division traveled in elephant-drawn carriages;
and the sixth division provided a surrounding escort.
As their moral character was thus lofty, their honors and mandates were likewise exceptional.
At that time, assemblies were held for discussion to examine their relative merits, clearly distinguishing between the good and the evil, and demoting the obscure while promoting the enlightened.

Whenever there were those who deliberated upon subtle words, exalted the wondrous principles, employed elegant and abundant diction, or displayed marvelous and agile eloquence, they would then mount the precious elephant, followed by a retinue as vast as a forest.

To the point that the gates of righteousness were left open in vain and the sharp edges of their rhetoric blunted; though their reasoning was meager and their words profuse, and their principles perverse while their speech was smooth, they were consequently smeared with red ochre and white lime on their faces, their bodies covered in dust and dirt, banished to the vast wilderness, and cast into ditches and ravines.
Having distinguished between the virtuous and the wicked, and likewise manifested the difference between the wise and the foolish,
people came to know the joy of the Way and families applied themselves diligently to the pursuit of learning.
Whether they left the household life or returned to secular life, they followed their own inclinations.

Having incurred guilt and violated the rules, one is subject to disciplinary punishment within the Sangha: in light cases, the assembly issues a formal reprimand; next, the assembly does not speak with the person; and in severe cases, the assembly does not cohabit with them.

Those who are not permitted to dwell together are expelled and cast out from the ranks; driven from their monastic residence, they find no place to set foot, enduring the hardships of a wandering exile, and some even return to lay life.
As for those of distinct lineages, there are four classes:
the first is the Brahmin, whose practice is purity.
They preserve the Way and abide in integrity, keeping their conduct immaculate.
The second is the Kṣatriya, the royal caste (formerly called *Chali*, which is an abbreviation).
For generations they have presided over the throne, taking benevolence and forbearance as their guiding principle.
The third is the Vaiśya (formerly called *Pisheshi*, which is a corruption); these are merchants and traders.
They trade goods for what they lack and pursue profit both far and near.
Fourth are the śūdras (formerly called shoutuo, which is a corruption), who are farmers.
They exert their strength in the fields and toil with their bodies at sowing and reaping.

Among these four castes, the pure and the turbid flow in separate streams; marriage and kinship are restricted, and the paths of the exalted and the lowly diverge. Within the internal and external branches of the lineage, matrimonial alliances are never intermingled.
Once a woman has been married, she never remarries.
As for the other miscellaneous surnames, their lineages are truly numerous; they each cluster according to their kind, making it difficult to record them in detail.
For generations, the sovereigns have been exclusively of the Kṣatriya caste.
Yet, as usurpations and regicides arise from time to time, those of different lineages claim the throne.
The warriors of the state are all selected for their prowess and heroism; fathers transmit their craft to their sons, who thus exhaust themselves in the arts of war.
When at rest, they occupied palaces and lodgings with surrounding guards; when on campaign, they led the vanguard as they mobilized their troops.
There were four types of military units:
infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants.

As for the elephant, it is clad in sturdy armor and its tusks are fitted with sharp spurs; a single general rides securely upon it, directing its movements, while two soldiers flank it on the left and right to manage and control it.
The chariot was then yoked with four horses; the military commander sat within it, surrounded by ranks of soldiers who guarded him, supporting the rims and clutching the hubs.
The cavalry dispersed to provide defense, pursuing the defeated enemy with all haste.

The infantry are light and agile, selected from among the bold and courageous. They carry large shields and wield long halberds, or hold swords and blades, charging forward at the head of the battle lines.

Among all their weapons, none are not sharp and keen; those known as spears, bucklers, bows, arrows, knives, swords, battle-axes, hatchets, *ge*, *shu*, long lances, and wheel-rope lassos are all skills they have practiced for generations.

As for their customs: although their nature is impetuous, their will is exceedingly upright and sincere. They do not seek gain through dishonest means regarding wealth, and they possess a surplus of yielding in matters of righteousness. Fearing the retribution of karmic destiny, they regard worldly pursuits as trivial; they do not practice deceit, taking oaths as their bond of trust. Their governance values simplicity, and their social customs remain harmonious.

When wicked and perverse scoundrels occasionally violate the laws of the state or plot to endanger the sovereign, and their deeds are clearly manifest, they shall be perpetually confined in prison without being subjected to corporal punishment; their lives are left to their own fate, and they are excluded from the ranks of human society.

Those who violate ritual propriety and righteousness, or act in rebellion against loyalty and filial piety, shall have their noses cut off, their ears severed, their hands amputated, or their feet mutilated; they may be driven out of the country or banished to remote frontiers.
For all other offenses and transgressions, one must pay a fine to redeem the guilt.

In adjudicating legal cases and interpreting testimony, corporal punishment shall not be added; rather, one shall proceed according to the confession elicited through questioning and impose a penalty proportionate to the facts.

When one denies or resists what they have committed, or when they feel shame over their errors and attempt to gloss over their faults, and it is necessary to investigate the actual facts through formal examination, there are four methods:
water, fire, the balance, and poison.
As for water, they place the accused and stones together in a net bag and sink them into a deep current to test their truth or falsehood;
if the person sinks and the stone floats, there has been an offense; if the person floats and the stone sinks, there is no concealment.
The fire burns the iron; the sinner squats upon it, then is made to tread upon it with his feet, pressed down by his palms, and further compelled to lick it with his tongue.
Though it is empty and insubstantial, it causes no harm; yet though it is solid and real, it inflicts actual injury.
A person of weak character cannot endure intense heat; holding an unopened flower, they scatter it toward the flames.
If it is hollow, the flower blooms; if it is solid, the flower withers.
When weighed, the person and the stone balance each other, allowing their relative weight to be verified.
If the case is false, the person will sink and the stone will rise; if it is true, the stone will be heavy and the person light.
For a poison ordeal, take a single black sheep, cut open its right thigh, and according to the amount of food consumed by the accused, place various poisons within that right thigh.
If the case is true, the poison will take effect and he will die; if it is false, the poison will subside and he will recover.
By citing these four examples, one may guard against a hundred paths of transgression.
The forms of paying respect consist of nine grades of ritual:

first, offering words of greeting; second, bowing the head to show reverence; third, raising the hands for a high salutation; fourth, joining the palms with arms held level; fifth, bending the knees; sixth, squatting low for a long duration; seventh, placing both hands and knees on the ground; eighth, bending all five limbs (the two feet, two knees, and two elbows); ninth, prostrating the entire body to the ground.
In all these nine grades of ritual, the ultimate expression is a single prostration.
To kneel and extol the virtues of another is called the height of reverence.
At a distance, one bows with the forehead touching the ground and the hands clasped; when near, one kisses the feet and strokes the heels.
Whenever they delivered their words or received instructions, they would lift their robes and kneel for a long time.

When honoring the worthy or receiving their prostrations, they invariably offered words of consolation; sometimes stroking the crown of their heads or patting their backs, they used kind words to instruct and guide them, thereby demonstrating their affection and intimacy.
When a renunciant śramaṇa has received a prostration, he should only offer virtuous wishes and must not stop them from kneeling and bowing.

According to the object of their devotion, there are many who perform circumambulations—either once or three times; if they have made a specific request based on their long-held intention, the number follows their wish.
Whenever one encounters illness, one should abstain from grain for seven days.
Within this period, many are completely cured;
only if recovery does not occur should one then take medicine.
The natures and categories of medicines differ in their names and species;
the skills of physicians vary in their methods of prognosis.
Upon the final passing and the arrival at the funeral, they wail and weep for one another, tearing their clothes, pulling out their hair, striking their foreheads, and beating their breasts.
The mourning garments are worn without interruption,
and the period of mourning has no fixed limit.
Regarding the rites for seeing off the deceased and performing the encoffining and burial, there are three types of ceremonies:
The first is cremation, piling firewood to burn the body.
The second is water burial, sinking the remains in flowing currents to drift away.
The third is wilderness burial, discarding the body in the forest to feed the beasts.
When a king passed away, a successor was first established to preside over the funeral rites and sacrifices, thereby determining the hierarchy of high and low.
During his lifetime, he established his own title and name; after death, there was no formal deliberation for a posthumous eulogy.
In households struck by mourning or calamity, no one would go to eat;
only after the encoffining and burial were completed did they return to their normal state, with no further prohibitions.
All who accompanied the dead were considered impure and thus bathed before re-entering the city from outside the outer walls.

As for those who have reached advanced age and senility, with the time of death drawing near, beset by chronic and grave illnesses and fearing the end of their lives, they grow weary of and seek detachment from worldly俗 matters, wishing to abandon the human realm; they look down upon birth and death as trivial and base, hoping to distance themselves from the paths of the world.

Thereupon, his kinsmen, elders, and friends held a farewell banquet with music; they traveled by boat, rowing across the Ganges River, where he submerged himself in midstream, believing that he would thereby be reborn in heaven.
One of these ten points remains incomplete according to my humble view.

For the monastic community, the regulations prohibit wailing and weeping; yet when parents pass away, reciting scriptures to repay their kindness serves as a means to honor the distant past and ensure a careful conclusion, truly providing merit for the afterlife.

Since governance and instruction were both lenient and state affairs were likewise simple, households were not registered in official records and the people were exempt from corvée labor. Within the royal fields, the land was divided into four parts: one portion was allocated for state expenditures, such as the sacrificial grain offerings for rituals; the second was for the King’s personal use; the third was for the support of the nobility; and the fourth was for the common people. Thus, the people were able to cultivate their own lands and live in peace. Furthermore, there were no fixed taxes or levies, and the people enjoyed a life of leisure and abundance. Even during times of famine, they did not suffer from hunger, and when harvests were plentiful, they did not experience surplus. There were no laws concerning punishments or rewards, and no regulations regarding the promotion or demotion of officials. The people lived in harmony, and all things flourished. This was the Way of the Great Peace (Taiping). It was because the Way of the Great Peace was practiced that the world was transformed and all things attained their proper order. Second, he assisted the chief ministers through the system of feudal enfeoffment;
third, he rewarded those of brilliant intelligence, profound learning, and eminent talent;
fourth, he established fields of merit to provide for practitioners of various religious paths.
Therefore, taxes and levies were light, and corvée labor was sparing; everyone remained secure in their ancestral occupations, each cultivating their allotted land.
When borrowing seed from royal fields, they paid one-sixth of the harvest as tax.
Merchants pursue profit as they transport goods back and forth; at ferries, roads, and frontier posts, they pass through with light taxes.
When the state undertakes construction projects, it does not impose labor services in vain; rather, it compensates the workers with their fair value once the work is successfully completed.
For garrisoning, military expeditions, and imperial residences, guards and encampments were recruited according to the requirements of each task, with rewards proclaimed to attract and retain men.
Governors, ministers, officials, and their subordinates each had their assigned territories and subsisted from their respective fiefs.
As the climates and soils differ, so too do the advantages of the land vary; thus, the flowers, grasses, fruits, and trees are of diverse species and distinct names.

These include the āmra fruit, the āmrātaka fruit, the mātuluṅga fruit, the badara fruit, the kapittha fruit, the āmalaka fruit, the ciñcā fruit, the udumbara fruit, the mocā fruit, the nālikera fruit, and the panasa fruit. Of all such varieties, it would be difficult to record them exhaustively; therefore, I have briefly mentioned those that are prized by the world.
As for dates, chestnuts, *bī* (a type of plum), and persimmons, they are unheard of in India;
fruits such as pears, crabapples, peaches, apricots, and grapes have been planted sporadically since the time of Kaśmīra;
while pomegranates and sweet oranges are grown in all countries.
As for the cultivation of fields and agricultural affairs, they sow, reap, plow, and till according to the seasons, each undertaking labor or rest as appropriate.
Among the products suited to the soil, rice and wheat are particularly abundant.
As for vegetables, there are ginger, mustard, melons, gourds, *huṇḍa* greens, and so forth;
although onions and garlic are scarce and rarely consumed, those in households who eat them are driven out of the city walls.
As for milk, curd, clarified butter, fresh butter, granulated sugar, rock honey, mustard oil, and various cakes and parched grains—these were his regular fare.
Fish, mutton, roe deer, and stag meat were served as occasional delicacies.

Cows, donkeys, elephants, horses, pigs, dogs, foxes, wolves, lions, monkeys, and apes—among all such hairy creatures, none are eaten for their flesh; those who eat them are held in contempt and shame, loathed by the multitude, and must dwell outside the city walls, rarely appearing among human beings.
As for the various grades of wine and their distinct flavors:
those made from grapes and sugarcane are for the Kṣatriyas to drink;
those made from fermented yeast and thick liquor are for the Vaiśyas and others to drink.
When śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas drink grape juice or sugarcane syrup, these are not what is meant by "alcoholic liquor.
Among those of mixed caste or low birth, there is no distinction in their consumption.
However, as for the utensils used for their sustenance, there were differences between the refined and the simple;
the various household implements were provided according to the needs of the time and lacked nothing.
Although cauldrons and pots were employed, they knew nothing of the steamer used for cooking rice.
Vessels are mostly made of unbaked clay, with few being made of red copper.

Food is served in a single vessel where various flavors are blended together; it is generally consumed using the fingers, as spoons and chopsticks are largely absent, though copper spoons are used for those who are elderly or infirm.
As for gold, silver, brass, white jade, and fire-pearls produced by the local soil and climate, they are even more abundant and accumulated in great quantities.
Exquisite treasures and various miscellaneous gems of diverse kinds and distinct names come from the coastal regions and are easily obtained for trade.
As for their currency and trade, they exchange goods for one another using gold coins, silver coins, cowrie shells, and small pearls.

Having fully set forth the boundaries of the Indian realm, the differences in its climate and soil have been roughly indicated; these general outlines have been briefly presented according to a common thread and consistent system, while the distinct administrations and diverse customs are described according to each individual kingdom.
The country of Lambā is over one thousand *li* in circuit; it has the Snow Mountains to its north and borders black mountain ranges on three sides.
The capital city of the country is over ten *li* in circuit.

For several hundred years, the royal lineage has been extinct; local heroes have vied for power, and there has been no great sovereign. Recently, the region first became a dependency of the kingdom of Kāpiśī.
It is well-suited for non-glutinous rice and abounds in sugarcane. Although forest trees are numerous, fruit is scarce.
The climate gradually becomes warm, with light frosts but no snow.

The national customs are prosperous and joyful, and the people are fond of song and verse; yet their disposition is timid and weak, and their sentiments are deceitful and crafty. They constantly deceive and mock one another, never yielding precedence to others.
Their physical stature is small and their movements are light and fickle.
They mostly wear white cotton cloth, yet their clothing is bright and ornate.
There are more than ten monasteries, with few monks, most of whom study and practice the teachings of the Mahāyāna.
There are several dozen deva temples, and those of various heterodox paths are very numerous.
From here, traveling southeast for more than a hundred li, crossing a great ridge and crossing a large river, one arrives at the kingdom of Nagarahāra, within the borders of North India.
The country of Nagarahāra is over six hundred li from east to west and two hundred and fifty or sixty li from south to north.
Mountains encircle its four borders, making it remote and perilous.
The capital city of the kingdom is more than twenty *li* in circuit.
It has no great sovereign; it is subject to the command and service of the kingdom of Kāpiśī.

Crops are abundant, flowers and fruits are plentiful, and the climate is warm and hot. The customs of the people are simple and honest; they are fierce, valiant, and heroic, regarding wealth lightly and being fond of learning.
The people revere the Buddha-dharma and have little faith in heterodox paths.
Although there are many monasteries (saṃghārāma), the monks are few in number, and the various stūpas are overgrown with weeds and in ruins.
There are five deva temples with more than one hundred followers of heterodox paths.
Two li to the east of the city is a stūpa over three hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka.

Constructed of specially hewn stone blocks and adorned with exquisite carvings, it marks the place where the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, upon meeting Dīpaṃkara Buddha, spread his deerskin garment and laid out his hair to cover the mud, thereby receiving his prediction of future Buddhahood.
Though eons have passed and the world has undergone destruction, these traces have not perished.
On certain days of fasting, the heavens rain down various flowers, and the common people vie with one another in their hearts to perform offerings.
To the west is a monastery with few monks.
To the south of it is a small stūpa, which marks the site where the earth was once covered; King Aśoka avoided the main road and consequently constructed it in this secluded spot.
Within the city, there is the ancient foundation of a great stūpa.
According to the records of former sages,
it is said that in the past there was a tooth of the Buddha, which was lofty, expansive, and magnificent.
Now that the teeth are no longer there, only the old foundations remain.
Beside them stands a stūpa over thirty feet high.
According to local tradition, its origin is unknown; it is said to have descended from the sky and come to stand upon this site.
Not being the work of human hands, it truly abounds in spiritual wonders.

About ten li to the southwest of the city is a stūpa; this is where the Tathāgata, while traveling through the air from Central India to convert beings, descended to this spot. Moved by feelings of devotion and admiration, the people of the country constructed this sacred foundation.
Not far to its east is a stūpa, where Śākyamuni Bodhisattva, in a former life, encountered Dīpaṃkara Buddha and purchased flowers here.
Twenty-odd li to the southwest of the city, one reaches a small rocky ridge where there is a monastery with lofty halls and multi-storied pavilions, constructed of piled stones.
The courtyard and buildings were silent and desolate, with no monks at all.
In their midst stood a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka.
To the southwest of the monastery, there is a deep ravine with precipitous cliffs; waterfalls cascade down, and sheer rock faces stand upright.
On the eastern cliff, within a large cave in the stone wall, dwells the Nāga Kūvara.
The entrance is narrow and small, and the cave is dark and gloomy; stalactites drip from the rocky cliffs, and the mountain path is moist with residual streams.
Formerly there was a shadow of the Buddha, as radiant as his true countenance, complete with all the marks and signs of perfection, solemn and as if he were actually present.
Since recent times, people have not seen it everywhere; even when they do see it, it is but a faint and indistinct vision.
Only those who pray with utmost sincerity and receive a response from the unseen realm can behold it clearly for a brief moment, yet even this cannot last long.
Formerly, when the Tathāgata was in the world, this dragon was a cowherd who supplied milk and curds to the king; because he failed to present them properly, he incurred the king’s reproach.

Harboring resentment in his heart, he immediately used gold coins to purchase flowers and made offerings at the stūpa where [the Buddha] received the prediction of enlightenment, vowing to become a malevolent dragon to destroy the kingdom and harm the king.
He immediately rushed toward a stone cliff and threw himself down to his death;
he then took up residence in this cave as a great dragon king, intending to emerge from his lair to fulfill his former evil vow.

As soon as this thought arose, the Tathāgata perceived it; out of compassion for the people of this land who were being harmed by the dragon, he exercised his supernatural powers and arrived from Central India.
Upon seeing the Tathāgata, the dragon’s poisonous intent ceased; he received the precept against killing and vowed to protect the True Dharma.
He then entreated the Tathāgata:
"Please dwell constantly in this cave, and let your noble disciples always receive my offerings."
The Tathāgata said:
"I shall enter parinirvāṇa; for your sake, I leave behind my shadow and dispatch five arhats to constantly receive your offerings.
Even when the True Dharma disappears, this matter shall not cease."
If you harbor a poisonous mind and give way to rage, you should contemplate my preserved image; through the power of loving-kindness and compassion, your poisonous mind shall cease.
Within this Bhadrakalpa, the future World-Honored Ones will likewise feel pity for you and all leave behind their images.

Outside the entrance of the Shadow Cave were two square stones; upon one of them was the footprint left by the Tathāgata’s tread, with the mark of the wheel faintly visible and its radiance occasionally illuminating the surroundings.
To the left and right of the Shadow Cave (Chāyā-guhā) there are many stone chambers, all of which were places where the Tathāgata’s noble disciples entered meditative concentration.
In the northwest corner of the Shadow Cave is a stūpa, marking the place where the Tathāgata walked in meditation.
Beside it is a stūpa containing the hair and nail-clippings of the Tathāgata.
Not far from this is another stūpa, which is the place where the Tathāgata expounded the true doctrine and taught upon the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and bases (āyatanas).
To the west of the Shadow Cave is a large flat rock; it is said that the Tathāgata once washed his *kāṣāya* robe upon it, and faint traces of the patterns remain visible.
About thirty li southeast of the city, one reaches the city of Hilo.
It is four or five *li* in circuit, with steep and formidable fortifications; its flower groves and ponds are bright and clear as mirrors.
The inhabitants of the city are simple in character and upright in their faith.
There was also a multi-storied pavilion with painted beams and vermilion pillars.
Within the second story was a small stūpa made of the seven precious substances, in which was enshrined the cranial bone of the Tathāgata.

The bone measured one chi and two cun in circumference; the pores of the hair were clearly visible, and its color was yellowish-white. It was contained within a jeweled casket and placed inside the stūpa.

If one wishes to discern the marks of good or evil, one mixes fragrant powder with clay and uses it to imprint the cranial bone; according to the resonance of one's merit, the patterns will manifest clearly.

Furthermore, there is a small stūpa made of the seven precious gems to enshrine the Tathāgata’s skull bone; its shape resembles a lotus leaf and its color matches that of the cranial bone, and it is likewise placed within a casket sealed and bound with jewels.

Furthermore, there is a small stūpa made of the seven precious substances containing the Tathāgata’s eye; the eye is as large as a *nālika* fruit, its radiance pure and translucent, brilliantly illuminating both its interior and exterior, and it is enshrined within a sealed casket of jewels.
The Tathāgata’s saṃghāṭī robe, made of fine cotton, was yellowish-red in color; it had been placed within a precious casket for many years, and thus it was slightly damaged.
The Tathāgata’s mendicant’s staff has rings made of white iron and a shaft of sandalwood, kept within a precious tube.
Recently, a king, hearing that these items were all personally used by the Tathāgata in the past, relied upon his military might to coerce them into submission and bring them back.

Once arrived in his own country, he placed them in his palace; yet before even a full ten days had passed, they were already missing when he sought them. Upon further investigation, they were found to have returned to their original place.
These five sacred sites abound in miraculous manifestations; the King of Kāpiśī has ordered five persons of pure conduct to attend to them with incense and flowers.
Those who come to observe and pay their respects do so in an unending succession.

Those of pure conduct, wishing to maintain a state of empty stillness yet desiring to provide for their needs—things highly valued by people—provisionally established a set of regulations to curb clamor and disorder.
Their general outline was as follows:
"All who wish to see the Tathāgata’s cranial bone shall pay a tax of one gold coin."
If one takes an impression, the tax is five gold coins;
for the remaining grades, the regulations follow in successive order.
Although the regulations are strict, those who come to observe the rites are ever more numerous.

To the northwest of the multi-storied pavilion is a stūpa, which is likewise exceedingly tall and large, and is full of miraculous wonders; when people touch it with their fingers, it immediately trembles and shakes, causing the entire foundation to sway and the bells and chimes to ring in harmony.
From here, traveling southeast through mountain valleys for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Gandhāra (formerly called Qianduo’ei, which is a corruption),
located within the borders of North India.
The country of Gandhāra is over one thousand *li* from east to west and over eight hundred *li* from south to north.
To the east it borders the Indus River.
The capital city of the country is called Puruṣapura, with a circumference of more than forty *li*.
The royal lineage having become extinct, the country was subjugated by Kapishī.
The towns and villages were desolate and deserted, with inhabitants being very few; there were only over a thousand households in one corner of the palace city.
The grain crops are abundant and the flowers and fruits are luxuriant; there is much sugarcane, from which rock honey is produced.
The climate is warm and hot, with almost no frost or snow.
The people are timid by nature and fond of practicing the classical arts; most revere heterodox paths, while few believe in the True Dharma.

Since ancient times, among the masters who composed treatises within the borders of India, there have been those such as Nārāyaṇadeva, Bodhisattva Asaṅga, Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, Dharmatrāta, Ghoṣaka, and the Venerable Pārśva, all of whom were born there.
There are over a thousand monasteries, most of which have been devastated and left in ruin; they are overgrown with weeds and lie desolate, while many of the stūpas are in a state of collapse.
There are several hundred deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
Within the city, to the northeast, there is an old foundation which was formerly the jeweled terrace for the Buddha’s almsbowl.

After the Tathāgata entered nirvāṇa, the bowl traveled to this country; after remaining there for several hundred years and being venerated according to ritual, it moved on through various lands and is now in Persia.
Eight or nine *li* to the southeast outside the city, there is a *pippala* tree over a hundred feet high, its branches and leaves spreading wide and casting a dense, thick shade.
Four Buddhas of the past have already sat beneath it, and even now there remain statues of four Buddhas seated there.
Within this Bhadrakalpa, nine hundred and ninety-six Buddhas shall all sit beneath it.
The spirits of the underworld shall provide vigilant protection, and its spiritual influence shall be subtly pervasive.
Here, beneath this tree, Śākyamuni Tathāgata sat facing south and addressed Ānanda, saying:

“Four hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a king who reigns over the world named Kaniṣka. Not far to the south of here, he shall erect a stūpa, within which the majority of the bone and flesh śarīras of my body shall be gathered.”
To the south of the Pippala tree is a stūpa built by King Kaniṣka.

Four hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, King Kaniṣka ascended the throne and ruled over Jambudvīpa; at that time, he did not believe in the retribution of sin and merit, and he held the Buddha-dharma in contempt and disparagement.
While hunting in the marshy grasslands, he encountered a white hare; the King pursued it on foot, and as they reached this spot, it suddenly vanished.
There he saw a young cowherd boy among the trees constructing a small stūpa, three feet in height.
The king asked, "What have you been doing?
The cowherd replied:
"Formerly, the noble wisdom of Śākyamuni Buddha made this prophetic declaration:
'There shall be a king who will construct a stūpa at this excellent site, and within it shall be gathered the many relics of my body.'"

"Your Majesty’s sacred virtue was cultivated in former lives, and your fame accords with ancient prophecies; your divine merit and supreme blessings truly belong to this auspicious occasion, which is why I have now first come to awaken you."
Having spoken these words, he suddenly vanished.

Upon hearing this account, the king’s heart was filled with increased joy and satisfaction; he took pride in his name being foretold by the Great Sage, and consequently gave rise to right faith, deeply revering the Buddha and the Dharma.
Beside the small stūpa of Zhouxiao, another stone stūpa was constructed with the intent that its structural power might completely cover the former.

However, for every measure of height added, the small stūpa would invariably rise three feet higher. Even when the new structure reached over four hundred feet in height, its base remained one and a half li in circumference; it possessed five tiered foundations rising to a height of one hundred and fifty feet, only then managing to cover the small stūpa.

The King, filled with joy, further erected twenty-five tiers of gilded copper *cakra* upon it, enshrining one *hu* of the Tathāgata’s relics therein and performing offerings in accordance with the ritual.
As soon as the construction was completed, a small stūpa appeared at the southeast corner of the great base, emerging halfway from the side.

The King, feeling displeased, immediately cast it away; however, it then remained fixed within the stone foundation of the second tier of the stūpa, appearing halfway up. Furthermore, another small stūpa emerged from its original location.
The King then withdrew and sighed, saying:
"Alas! Human affairs are easily deluded, yet divine power is difficult to conceal; when one is supported by the holy and numinous, what can even the most wrathful avail?"
Once filled with shame and fear, they apologized for their transgressions and returned home.

The two stūpas still exist today; those who suffer from illness and seek recovery by applying fragrant ointments and scattering flowers, while taking refuge with utmost sincerity, mostly receive healing.

On the southern side of the stone steps on the eastern face of the great stūpa, two smaller stūpas were carved in relief; one was three feet high and the other five feet high, their scale and form resembling that of the great stūpa.

Furthermore, he fashioned two Buddha statues: one four feet high and the other six feet high, both modeled after the seated cross-legged image beneath the Bodhi tree. When the sunlight shone upon them, their golden hue blazed brilliantly; as the shadows gradually shifted, the patterns on the stone appeared in deep azure.

I have heard from the elders that several hundred years ago, there were golden ants in the crevices of the stone foundation; the large ones were as big as fingers and the small ones like wheat grains. Moving together in their kind, they gnawed at the stone walls, creating patterns like carvings and inlays of golden sand, forming this image which remains visible even today.

On the southern side of the stone steps of the Great Stūpa, there is a painted image of the Buddha, sixteen feet in height. From the chest upward, it appears as two distinct bodies; from the chest downward, they merge into a single form.

I have heard from the records of former sages that, in the beginning, there was a poor man who supported himself by manual labor. Having obtained a single gold coin, he wished to commission the creation of a Buddha image.
Upon arriving at the site of a stūpa, he spoke to a painter, saying:

"I now wish to depict the wondrous marks of the Tathāgata; however, I have but a single gold coin, which is insufficient as a reward for my labor. My long-held aspiration is burdened with anxiety due to this poverty."
At that time, the painter, perceiving his utmost sincerity, did not mention the price and consented to complete the work.
Furthermore, there was another person whose circumstances were identical to those previously described; he brought a single gold coin and requested a painting of the Buddha’s image.
At that time, the painter accepted the money from the two men and sought out exquisite pigments and colors to paint a single image together.
On the same day, both men came to pay their respects; the painter then pointed to the same image for them both and said to them, "This is the Buddha image you commissioned."
The two looked at each other as if harboring some secret thought.
The painter, knowing their suspicion in his heart, said to them:
"Why do you contemplate so long?"
"Whatever material offerings are received shall not diminish by even a hair’s breadth.
If these words are not false, the image will surely manifest divine transformations.
Before his voice had even faded, the image displayed miraculous wonders: it manifested multiple bodies with interlacing reflections, its radiant features shining brilliantly.
The two men were pleased and submitted, their hearts filled with faith and joy.

More than a hundred paces to the southwest of the Great Stūpa, there is a white stone Buddha image, eighteen feet in height, standing facing north; it possesses many miraculous signs and frequently emits radiance.
At that time, some people saw the image emerge at night and circumambulate the great stūpa.

A band of thieves nearby intended to enter and commit robbery; the image came out to meet them, and the thieves fled in terror. The image then returned to its original place, standing there as before.
Consequently, the bandits reformed their ways and traveled through the towns and villages, announcing [their conversion] far and wide.
To the left and right of the great stūpa, there are hundreds of small stūpas arranged like fish scales.

The Buddha images were magnificently adorned, crafted with the utmost ingenuity and artistry; occasionally, extraordinary fragrances and marvelous sounds were perceived, and spiritual immortals and holy sages were sometimes seen circumambulating them.
Regarding this stūpa, the Tathāgata gave a prophetic prediction that it would be burned seven times and rebuilt seven times before the Buddha-dharma finally comes to an end.
An ancient record states:
"It has already undergone three cycles of completion and destruction."
Upon first arriving in this country, I happened to encounter a great fire; at that time, the construction was still not yet completed.
To the west of the Great Stūpa is an old monastery, which was established by King Kaniṣka.
With its multi-storied pavilions, tiered terraces, lofty platforms, and arched chambers, it summoned eminent monks to manifest great blessings;
though now in ruins, it is still said to be a marvel of craftsmanship.
The number of monastics has diminished, and they have collectively studied the Hīnayāna.
Since the founding of the monastery, extraordinary individuals have emerged from among them;
the pure influence of the various masters of śāstras and those who have realized the fruits of sainthood still fans like a gentle breeze, and their sublime virtues have not perished.
On the third story of the pavilion is the chamber of the Venerable Pārśva (translated into Chinese as Xié), which has long since fallen into ruin; yet a commemorative monument still stands there.
Initially, when the Venerable was a teacher of Brahmins, he was nearly eighty years old when he renounced his home and donned the dyed robes of a monk.
A youth in the city further derided him, saying:
"O foolish old man, how shallow is your wisdom!
Now, for one who has left the household life, there are two primary tasks: first, the practice of meditative concentration; second, the recitation of the scriptures."
"Now that I am decrepit and old, I have nothing further to achieve; I merely follow in the footsteps of the pure stream, knowing only how to eat my fill.
When the Venerable Pārśva heard these criticisms, he apologized to the people of his time and made this vow:

"If I do not master the principles of the Tripiṭaka, sever the desires of the three realms, attain the six supernormal powers, and possess the eight liberations, I shall never again let my side rest upon a mat!"

From that time forward, he spoke only of his own inadequacy; whether walking, sitting in meditation, standing, or reflecting, he spent his days studying the principles and teachings, and his nights in quiet contemplation and mental concentration. After three years had passed, his learning had mastered the Tripiṭaka, he had severed the desires of the three realms, and attained the wisdom of the three insights. The people of the time looked up to him with reverence and thus named him the Venerable Pārśva (The One with the Flank).

To the east of the Venerable Pārśva’s chamber was an old room where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu composed the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. People held it in high esteem and sealed it with a record of its significance.
More than fifty paces south of Vasubandhu’s chamber is a second-story pavilion, where the master Manoratha (translated into Chinese as Ruyi) composed the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
The Master was renowned during the first millennium after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
From his youth, he was fond of learning; possessed of talent and eloquence, his reputation spread far and wide, and both monastics and laypeople turned their hearts toward him.

At that time, King Vikramāditya—whose name means "Sun of Valor" in the language of Tang—ruled over Śrāvastī. His majestic influence extended far and wide, and he held sway over all of India; every day, he distributed five hundred million gold coins to provide for the poor, the destitute, the orphaned, and the solitary.
The Treasurer, fearing that the state treasury would become depleted, offered this indirect admonition:

"Your Majesty’s majesty extends to foreign lands, and your benevolence reaches even the insects; I pray you increase the five hundred million gold coins to relieve the destitution of the four quarters."

Once the treasuries are empty, taxes on landowners are increased; as heavy levies continue without end, cries of resentment resound everywhere. Thus, while the sovereign above claims the grace of universal provision, his ministers below incur the reproach of insubordination.
The King said,
"To take from those who have a surplus to provide for those who lack is not a matter of seeking personal luxury at the expense of the state's resources.
He then added fifty million more to bestow upon the poor and destitute.

Later, while on a hunting expedition, the king lost the trail of a boar he was pursuing. He issued a proclamation that anyone who could find its tracks would be rewarded with one hundred million gold coins.
Master Ruci sent a man to shave his head, and the king immediately bestowed upon him one hundred million gold coins; the chroniclers of that kingdom recorded this event accordingly.
The King was humiliated by [Yijing’s] superior reputation and his mind was constantly dissatisfied; he desired to publicly disgrace the Master of Shastras, Ruci.
He then summoned one hundred scholars of heterodox schools whose virtue and learning were profound and eminent, and issued an edict, saying:

"I wish to gather the eyes and ears of the people and travel through the realms of truth. Yet, as heterodox paths are confused and intermingled, there is no way to direct my heart toward them. Now, I shall examine their relative merits so that they may single-mindedly follow and revere the correct path."
When the time came for the debate to assemble, he issued another decree, saying:

"The non-Buddhist masters are all men of brilliance; the śramaṇas of the Dharma community should likewise be well-versed in their own tenets. If you prevail, the Buddha-dharma shall be honored; if you fail, the monks shall be executed."
Thereupon, Ruci cross-examined the various non-Buddhist practitioners; ninety-nine of them retreated and fled.
One person remained seated, regarding him with utter contempt, and proceeded to engage in a heated discussion that turned to the nature of fire and smoke.
The King and the non-Buddhist teachers all spoke clamorously, saying:
"The Master Yìrú has erred in both word and meaning!
Now, smoke precedes fire; this is the constant order of things."
Although Vasurāta wished to resolve the objections, there was no one to listen.
Shamed by this public humiliation, he bit off his own tongue and then wrote a warning to his disciple, Vasubandhu, saying:
"Among the factions that support you, do not compete for great principles."
"Amidst this mass of deluded people, there is no one to debate the orthodox doctrine.
Having finished speaking, he died.
Not long after, King Chao Ri lost his kingdom, and King Xing rose to power in accordance with destiny, honoring and exemplifying the eminent and virtuous.
The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, wishing to wipe away his former humiliation, came before the king and said:
"Your Majesty rules with sagely virtue as the sovereign lord of all sentient beings.

My former teacher, Manoratha, had mastered the profound mysteries; yet out of old resentment from a previous reign, the masses have suppressed his great reputation. Having received his guidance and instruction, I now wish to avenge that prior grievance."
The king, recognizing that Yaśomitra was a man of such wisdom, admired his refined character; he then summoned the various non-Buddhist teachers to debate with him.
Yaśomitra restated the previous arguments with great weight, whereupon the non-Buddhists, acknowledging their defeat, withdrew in apology.
Traveling over fifty li northeast from the monastery of King Kaniṣka and crossing a great river, one arrives at the city of Puṣkarāvatī.
It is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit.
The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, with residential quarters extending in continuous rows.
Outside the western gate of the city is a temple dedicated to a deity; the divine image is majestic and awe-inspiring, and miraculous manifestations have occurred there in succession.
To the east of the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, which is the very site where the four past Buddhas preached the Dharma.
In ancient times, many sages and worthies descended their spirits from Central India to guide sentient beings; this land was truly abundant with them.
Among them was Vasumitra—translated into Chinese as Shiyou (World-Friend);
the old transcription, Huixumiduō, is erroneous. This master of śāstras composed the *Abhidharma-prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* here.
Four or five *li* to the north of the city is an old monastery; its courtyards and halls are desolate, and the monks are few in number, yet they all follow and practice the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
This is where Dharmatrāta (translated into Chinese as Fajiu) resided.
Formerly called Damoduo Luo, which is a corruption; here the Śāstrin composed the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*.
Beside the monastery is a stūpa several hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka.
The carved wood and patterned stone are remarkably different from human craftsmanship.

This is where Śākyamuni Buddha, in the past when he was a king practicing the bodhisattva path, tirelessly bestowed gifts according to the desires of sentient beings, regarding the loss of his body as if discarding something trivial; in this very land, he served as king for a thousand lifetimes, and it was at this superior site that he gave away his eyes for a thousand lifetimes.
Not far to the east of the Abandonment of the Eyes, there are two stone stūpas, each over a hundred feet in height.
The one on the right was erected by Brahmā, and the one on the left was built by Śakra, Lord of the Devas; both are adorned and embellished with exquisite precious gems.
When the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa, the precious materials transformed into stone;
though its foundation has now subsided, it is still called "Sublime.

Over fifty li to the northwest of the stūpas of Brahmā and Śakra, there is another stūpa where Śākya Tathāgata converted the Mother of Ghosts (Hārītī), causing her to cease harming people. Consequently, the local custom of this country is to offer sacrifices here in order to seek offspring.

Traveling north from the Temple of the Mother of Ghosts for over fifty li, there is a stūpa. This is the site where the Bodhisattva Śaṅmaka—formerly called Śyāma, which is an erroneous transcription—reverently practiced filial care while tending to his blind parents. While he was gathering fruit here, he encountered a king out hunting; by mistake, the king’s poisoned arrow struck him.
His utmost sincerity moved the divine spirits, and the Lord of Devas applied medicinal ointment. His virtue so moved the sagely and luminous ones that he immediately revived.
Traveling more than two hundred li southeast from where the Bodhisattva Śaṅkha was martyred, one arrives at the city of Varuṣa.

To the north of the city is a stūpa; this is the place where Prince Sudāna (translated into Chinese as Shanya)—having given his father the king’s great elephant to a Brahmin—was censured and banished. As he looked back to bid farewell to the people of the country, he took his leave here upon exiting the city gate.
To the side of this monastery are more than fifty monks, all of whom study the Hīnayāna.
Formerly, the master Īśvara—translated into Chinese as Zìzài (Svatantra)—composed the *Abhidharma-pradīpa-śāstra* here.
Outside the eastern gate of the city of Varṣa, there is a monastery with more than fifty monks, all of whom study the Mahāyāna. There is also a stūpa erected by King Aśoka.
Formerly, Prince Sudāna was exiled to Mount Daṇḍaka (formerly called Mount Dantaka, which is a corruption), where a Brahmin begged for his son and daughter and sold them there.
More than twenty li to the northeast of the city of Varṣa, one reaches Mount Tāḍakā.
On the ridge of the mountain is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, where Prince Sudāna lived in seclusion.

Not far from its side is a stūpa; it was here that the Prince gave his son and daughter as alms to a Brahmin. The Brahmin beat the boy and girl, and their blood flowed until it stained the ground; even now, the grasses and trees there still bear a crimson hue.
The stone chamber among the cliffs was the place where the Prince and his consort practiced meditative concentration.
The trees in the valley hang their branches like curtains; all these were the sites where the Prince formerly dwelt and wandered.
Not far from its side was a stone hermitage, which was the dwelling place of an ancient seer.

Traveling northwest from the seer’s hermitage for over a hundred li, one crosses a small mountain and reaches a great mountain. On the southern side of this mountain is a monastery where the monks are few in number, and they all study the Mahāyāna.
Beside it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka.
This was formerly the dwelling place of the Ṛṣi Ekaśṛṅga.
Having been seduced and led astray by a courtesan, the Ṛṣi lost his supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*); the courtesan then mounted upon his shoulders and returned to the city.
More than fifty li northeast of the city of Varṣa, one reaches a lofty mountain.
On this mountain is a statue of the consort of Maheśvara made of blue stone; she is the goddess Bhīmā.
According to local tradition, it is said that this image of the deity appeared spontaneously.

As its spiritual manifestations are manifold, those who offer prayers are numerous; people from all the kingdoms of India, whether noble or humble, gather here, and those from near and far assemble together to seek blessings and fulfill their vows.

If there are those who wish to see the form of a celestial deity, provided they are sincere and single-minded, fasting for seven days, some may succeed in seeing it, and many of their prayers will be fulfilled.
At the foot of the mountain is a shrine of Maheśvara, where the ash-smearing heretics perform their ritual worship.
Traveling one hundred and fifty *li* southeast from the temple of Vaimānika, one arrives at the city of Udakhāṇḍa; it is over twenty *li* in circuit and borders the Indus River to the south.
The inhabitants live in wealth and happiness, with precious goods accumulated in abundance; rare treasures from all quarters are mostly gathered here.
Traveling twenty-odd *li* northwest from the city of Udakhāṇḍa, one reaches the village of Bharadvāja, which is the birthplace of the Ṛṣi Pāṇini, who composed the *Śabdavidyāśāstra*.

At the very beginning of remote antiquity, written characters were abundant and extensive; however, as time passed through the destruction of kalpas and the world became empty and void, the long-lived devas descended their spirits among both the clergy and the laity. For this reason, the written records came into being.
From that time forth, its source has overflowed in all directions.

Brahmā Kings and Heavenly Emperors have established models according to the times, while various immortals of divergent paths have each devised their own scripts. People have successively followed these traditions, vying with one another to practice what was transmitted; thus, students expend their efforts in vain, finding it difficult to investigate them in detail.

During the era when the human lifespan was one hundred years, there was a seer named Pārṣva, who possessed innate knowledge and vast erudition. Lamenting the decadence of his time and desiring to eliminate superficiality and falsehood while pruning away redundancy and vulgarity, he traveled abroad to seek the Way. There he encountered Īśvara, and subsequently set forth his resolve for composition.
Īśvara said: "How magnificent!
I shall grant you my protection."

The rishi accepted these instructions and withdrew; thereupon, he refined his essence and engaged in deep contemplation, collecting and selecting from various sayings to compose a book of characters consisting of a full thousand stanzas, each stanza comprising thirty-two syllables.
He investigated the ultimate principles of past and present and synthesized the essence of written expressions.

He sealed the work and presented it to the King, who held it in high esteem as something extraordinary. The King issued an edict throughout the land, ordering that it be studied and practiced by all; he promised a reward of one thousand pieces of gold to anyone who could recite it with complete fluency.
Consequently, the transmission between teacher and disciple flourished in that era.
Thus, the brahmins within this city were all men of profound learning and eminent talent, possessing vast knowledge and powerful memories.
In the city of Vālurā there is a stūpa at the place where an arhat converted the seer Parnika.

Five hundred years after the Tathāgata had passed into nirvāṇa, a great arhat traveling from the kingdom of Kaśmīra came to this location to teach and transform beings; there he saw a brahmin beating a young boy as a means of instruction.
Then the Arhat said to the brahmin,
"Why do you distress this child?
The brahmin replied:
"I have had him study the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra*, yet his progress in his studies has not been timely.
The Arhat smiled with amusement.
The elderly brahmin said:
"Generally, those who are śramaṇas take compassion as their fundamental sentiment and feel pity for all living beings.
As for what you, O Benevolent One, have just laughed at, I pray that you will explain its meaning. The Arhat said:
"It is not easy to discuss this, for I fear it may lead to deep doubts.
Have you perhaps heard that the Ṛṣi Pāṇini composed the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on Grammar) to provide instruction for the world?"
The brahmin said, "This son of this town was revered by his juniors for his virtue; his image remains established here.
The arhat said:
"This son of yours is none other than that very seer.
Yet, despite his powerful memory, he merely studies worldly scriptures and discusses heterodox doctrines, failing to investigate the ultimate truth."
Divine wisdom has been squandered and the cycle of rebirth continues without ceasing; yet, by virtue of residual merit, you have become my beloved child.
Thus, the words and rhetoric of worldly treatises merely exhaust one's efforts;
how can they compare to the Tathāgata’s holy teachings, which nourish both merit and wisdom in profound silence?
In the past, on the shores of the Southern Sea, there was a withered tree in which five hundred bats lived in their roosts.

A group of merchants halted beneath this tree; as it happened to be a time of wind and cold, everyone was hungry and frozen. They gathered firewood and kindled a fire beneath the tree, and as the smoke and flames gradually grew fierce, the withered tree subsequently caught fire.
At that time, among the caravan of merchants, there was a certain trader who, after the second watch of the night had passed, recited the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
Although those bats were distressed by the fire, they loved the sound of the Dharma and endured it without departing; they died right there.

Reborn according to their karma, they all attained human form; leaving home to practice and study, they were moved by the sound of the Dharma, and with their keen intelligence and wisdom, they together realized the fruits of sainthood, becoming fields of merit for the world.

Recently, King Kaniṣka and the Venerable Pārśva convened five hundred noble sages in the kingdom of Kaśmīra to compose the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*; these were all merely five hundred bats within a withered tree.
Although I am unworthy, I am nonetheless counted among them.
Thus, our strengths and weaknesses differ greatly, and our status as the soaring or the hidden is vastly distinct.
You, O Benevolent One, now love your son; you may grant him permission to leave the household life.
"The merit of leaving the household life cannot be fully described in words.
When the Arhat had finished speaking these words, he manifested his supernormal powers and suddenly vanished.

The Brahmin felt deep reverence and wonder, praising him for a long time; he then informed his neighbors in full and subsequently released his son to leave the household life and pursue study. Consequently, he turned his faith toward the Triple Gem and revered them with great devotion. His fellow villagers followed his example, and their practice has remained steadfast to this day.

Traveling north from the city of Udakhāṇḍa for more than six hundred li, crossing mountains and traversing rivers, one arrives at the kingdom of Udyāna (which in the language of Tang means "Garden"); it was formerly the pleasure garden of a Cakravartin King.
Formerly called Wuchang, or alternatively Wucha; both are corruptions.
It is within the borders of North India.
*Great Tang Records on the Western Regions*, Scroll II.
*The Great Tang Dynasty Record of the Western Regions*, Volume Three: Eight Countries.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree;
compiled by the Śramaṇa Bianji of Dazongchi Monastery.

The eight countries are: Udyāna, Prayāga, Takṣaśilā, Siṃhapura, Ulāśī, Kaśmīra, Pan-nu-je (Punach), and Ālaṃbura. Regarding the country of Udyāna: it is over five thousand *li* in circuit; mountains and valleys follow one another, and rivers and marshes extend across the plains.
Although grain crops are sown, the soil does not yield them in abundance.
Grapes are plentiful while sugarcane is scarce; the land produces gold and iron and is well-suited for saffron. The forests are lush and verdant, and flowers and fruits grow in profusion.
The cold and heat are temperate and harmonious, and wind and rain follow their proper seasons.
By nature the people are timid and weak, and their customs are devious and strange.
They are fond of learning but achieve no success; they regard the recitation of incantations as a professional craft.
They wear mostly white cotton cloth and have few other garments.
Although their spoken language differs, it is largely the same as that of India.
Their writing and etiquette are also considerably intertwined with those of India.
They revere the Buddha-dharma and honor and believe in the Mahāyāna.
Along both banks of the Suvāstu River, there were formerly one thousand four hundred monasteries, most of which have now fallen into ruin and desolation.
Formerly there were eighteen thousand monks, but now their numbers have gradually diminished.

They all study the Mahāyāna and take meditative concentration as their primary practice; they are skilled at reciting the texts but have not yet fathomed their profound meanings. Their observance of the precepts is pure, and they are particularly proficient in the recitation of protective mantras.
The transmission of the Vinaya precepts consists of five schools:
first, the Dharmaguptaka; second, the Mahīśāsaka; third, the Kāśyapīya; fourth, the Sarvāstivāda; and fifth, the Mahāsāṃghika.
There are more than ten deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
There are four or five strong walled cities, though the king mostly governs from the city of Mo-kie-li (Mathurā).
The city is sixteen or seventeen *li* in circuit, and its inhabitants are numerous and prosperous.

Four or five *li* to the east of the city of Mung-kie-li (Monghyer) is a stūpa that possesses many miraculous and auspicious signs; this is where the Buddha, in a former life as the Rishi Kṣāntivādin (the Immortal of Forbearance), was subjected to violence by King Kali (translated into Chinese as "Strife").
The old transcription "Golī" is erroneous; it refers to one who cuts off limbs.
Traveling two hundred and fifty or sixty li northeast from the city of Maṅgala, one enters a great mountain and reaches the Apsarāsa Dragon Spring, which is the source of the Suvāstu River.
The river flows toward the southwest; it retains ice during the spring and summer, and snow falls at dusk and evening. The falling snow displays five colors, its radiance streaming in all directions.

This dragon was born in the human realm during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha and was named Gaṅgī. He was deeply proficient in incantations and spells, using them to restrain evil dragons and prevent torrential rains. The people of the country relied upon him to store surplus grain.
The local inhabitants and the common people were grateful for his kindness and cherished his virtue; they contributed a *dou* of grain from each household as offerings.
As years passed, some failed to pay their dues.
Keng-chi harbored resentment and vowed to become a venomous dragon, unleashing violent winds and rains to damage the crops.
After his life ended, he was reborn as a dragon of this pond.
The spring flowed with white water, which damaged the local land and its resources.

Śākyamuni Tathāgata, governing the world with great compassion, took pity on these people who alone had encountered such calamity; he descended his spirit to this place, desiring to transform the violent dragon.
