The Vajrapāṇi deity struck the mountain cliff with his vajra; the dragon king was struck with terror and emerged to take refuge. Upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, his mind became pure, faithful, and awakened. The Tathāgata thereupon ordained that he must not damage the farmers' crops.

The dragon said, "In all that we eat, we rely on harvesting the fields of men; now that we have received your holy teaching, we fear it will be difficult to provide for ourselves. We pray that we may store up grain for a harvest once every twelve years."
The Tathāgata, out of compassion and concealment, granted his permission.
Therefore, every twelve years, this place suffers the calamity of white water.

More than thirty *li* to the southwest of the spring of the Āpālāla Dragon, upon a large flat rock on the northern bank of the water, there is a footprint left by the Tathāgata’s tread. Its length varies according to the power of a person's merit; it was left here when the Tathāgata, having subdued this dragon, departed.
Later generations piled stones upon this spot to form a chamber; people from near and far flocked there to offer flowers and incense as an act of devotion.
Following the current downstream for more than thirty li, one reaches the Stone where the Tathāgata Washed His Robes; the patterns on his *kāṣāya* are as brilliant as if they had been engraved.

More than four hundred *li* south of the city of Mung-kie-li, one reaches Mount Hila. There, a tributary of the valley stream branches off to the west and flows upstream toward the east. Various flowers and exotic fruits cover the ravines and line the cliffs; the peaks and crags are perilous, and the gullies and valleys wind and meander. One may hear the sound of clamorous conversation or the resonance of musical instruments.
The square stones are like stupas, appearing as if crafted by human hands; they extend and connect one after another, spread across cliffs and valleys.
These were made when the Tathāgata, in the past, for the sake of hearing half a verse—formerly called *ga*, which is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term—[bestowed his body].
Some call it *gāthā*, which is a corruption of the Sanskrit sound.
Following the correct pronunciation, it should be called *geya*.
*Geya* is translated into Chinese as "verse" (*sòng*); it is the method of composing verses consisting of thirty-two syllables, and for this [purpose], one should sacrifice body and life here.
More than two hundred *li* south of the city of Mung-kie-li (Monghyr), by the side of a great mountain, lies the Mahāvana (translated into Chinese as "Great Forest") Monastery.

This is where the Tathāgata, in former times while practicing the bodhisattva path as the king named Sarvadatta (translated into Chinese as "All-Giver"), fled his kingdom to evade his enemies and traveled in secret until he reached this place. There he encountered a poor Brahmin who had come to beg for alms.

Having lost his kingdom and position, he had nothing left with which to practice giving; he therefore allowed himself to be bound and led away as a captive to the enemy king, hoping that through the wealth of a reward he might turn it toward acts of charity.
To the northwest of the Mahāvana Monastery, after descending thirty or forty *li* from the mountain, one reaches the Māyū (in the local language, Māyu) Monastery.
There is a stūpa there, over a hundred feet in height.

On a large square stone at its side are the footprints left by the Tathāgata when he stepped upon it; it was here that the Buddha formerly trod this stone, emitting hundreds of millions of rays of light to illuminate the Mahāvana monastery and preach the accounts of his previous births for the sake of humans and devas.
At the base of this stūpa there is a stone, yellowish-white in color, which is always moist and oily.
This is where the Tathāgata, in the past while practicing the bodhisattva path, broke his own bones to write out the scriptures in order to hear the True Dharma.
Sixty or seventy *li* to the west of the Mayū vihāra, one reaches a stūpa built by King Aśoka.
This is the site where the Tathāgata, in former times while practicing the bodhisattva path, was known as King Vika (translated into Chinese as Yu).
The old [Chinese] name was King Śibi, which is an error. To seek the fruit of Buddhahood, he cut his own body here to substitute himself for a pigeon in place of a hawk.

Over two hundred li to the northwest from the place where he substituted himself for the pigeon, one enters the Sannirāja River and arrives at the Sarosaka Monastery (translated into Chinese as Shéyào Sēngqiélán).
There is a stūpa over eighty feet high.
This is where the Tathāgata, in a former life as Śakra, encountered a time of famine and the spread of pestilence; medical treatments were ineffective, and deaths occurred in rapid succession.
Śakra, moved by compassion and reflecting on how to provide salvation, transformed his form into that of a great python, lying across the mountain valleys. He proclaimed this throughout the air;
those who heard it were filled with joy and rushed there in succession. As they cut away the flesh, it grew back again, curing their hunger and healing their ailments.
Not far from its side is the great stūpa of Soma.

In the past, when the world was afflicted by an epidemic, the Tathāgata, out of compassion for all sentient beings, transformed his body into that of a Soma serpent; whoever consumed it found no one who did not become healthy and at ease.
On the northern side of the stone cliff by the Śaṇṇirāja River, there is a stūpa.
Those who visit it seeking relief from illness mostly receive healing.

In the past, when the Tathāgata was the Peacock King, he came to this place with his flock; being oppressed by heat and thirst, they sought water but could not find any. The Peacock King then pecked at the cliff with his beak, causing a spring to gush forth and flow.
It has now become a pond, where drinking from it or bathing therein cures illnesses.
On the stone, there still remain the tracks of peacocks.
Traveling sixty or seventy li southwest from the city of Maṅgala, there is a stūpa on the eastern bank of a great river, over sixty feet high, which was built by King Udayana.
Formerly, when the Tathāgata was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he addressed the great assembly:
"After my nirvāṇa, King Upariṣṭha of the kingdom of Udyāna should be granted a portion of the śarīra."
When the various kings were about to weigh the relics equally, King Upāriṣṭa arrived late, which led to some disparaging remarks.

At that time, the great assembly of devas and humans reiterated the Tathāgata’s final testament, whereupon they were granted a share of the relics; they carried them back to their own country to honorably enshrine and erect a stūpa.
Beside the stūpa, on the bank of a great river, there is a large rock shaped like an elephant.

In the past, when King Upayāja was returning with the śarīra relics carried by a great white elephant, he arrived at this place where the elephant suddenly stumbled and fell, dying on the spot; it was subsequently transformed into stone, and a stūpa was erected beside it.

More than fifty *li* west of the city of Mung-kie-li (Monghyr), one crosses a great river and arrives at the Lūhityaka (translated into Chinese as "Red") Stūpa, which is over fifty feet high and was built by King Aśoka.

In the past, when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path, he was a great king named Maitrībala (Compassionate Power). It was here that he pierced his own body to provide blood for five yakṣas (formerly called *yecha*, which is an error).
More than thirty li to the northeast of the city of Mung-kie-li, one reaches the A-pu-to (in the language of Tang, "Extraordinary") stone stūpa, which is over forty feet high.

In the past, when the Tathāgata preached the Dharma to guide all humans and devas, he did so from this very spot; after the Tathāgata’s passing, it sprang forth from the earth, and the common people have revered it with unceasing offerings of incense and flowers.

Crossing the great river to the west of the stone stūpa for thirty or forty *li*, one arrives at a vihāra. Within it is a statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (translated into Chinese as Guanzizai).
When the characters are combined and the sounds joined, the Sanskrit term is as stated above;
when the text is divided and the sounds dispersed, *avalokita* is translated as "Contemplation" (*guān*) and *īśvara* is translated as "Sovereign" (*zìzài*).
The old translations as "Guangshiyin" (Light-World-Sound), "Guanshiyin" (Contemplating-World-Sound), or "Guanshizai" (Contemplating-World-Sovereign) are all erroneous.
His majestic spirit is secretly pervasive and his divine traces are manifest; both monastics and laypeople flock to him, making offerings without ceasing.
One hundred and fifty *li* to the northwest of the image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one reaches Mount Lanpolu.
On the mountain ridge is a dragon pool, over thirty *li* in circumference; its emerald waves are vast and expansive, and its clear currents are as bright as a polished mirror.
Formerly, when King Viśvāmitra led his forces against the Śākyas, four members of the clan who resisted the army were ostracized by their kinsmen and fled in different directions.
One member of the Śākya lineage, having already departed from the capital city, grew weary from the arduous journey and halted midway.
At that time, there was a wild goose that flew toward him; as it had become tame and familiar, he mounted it.
The goose took flight and descended beside this pond.
A member of the Śākya clan was traveling abroad to a distant foreign land; lost and unable to find his way, he dozed off in the shade of a tree.

A young nāga maiden from the pond, wandering along the water’s edge, suddenly saw the Śākya man. Fearing she might not be worthy of him, she transformed herself into human form and approached to stroke and caress him.
The Śākya man woke up in alarm and apologized, saying, "I am but a weary traveler;
why do you treat me with such intimacy?
Nevertheless, he pressed his suit with great persistence and forced a union in the wilderness.
The girl said,
"My parents have given me instructions that I must reverently follow without fail.
Although I am honored by your kind attention, I have not yet received your command."
The Śākya said, "The mountains and valleys are deep and dark; where is your home?
He replied:
"I am a nāga maiden of this pond.
Having respectfully heard that the noble lineage has been wandering in exile and fleeing from calamity, I have taken the opportunity of your visit to offer you my humble consolation.
I invited you to a private banquet, yet I have not yet heard of your acceptance."
"How much more so, having accumulated calamities to receive this dragon body; that humans and beasts are of different paths is something unheard of.
The Śākya said, "If my single word is granted permission, my long-cherished heart's desire shall be fulfilled."
The nāga girl said, "I respectfully accept your command; let it be as you see fit.
Thereupon, the Śākya youth made a vow in his heart, saying:
"By the power of all the merit I possess, may this dragon girl's entire body be transformed into that of a human.
Moved by the power of this merit, the dragon subsequently changed its form; having attained a human body, she was deeply filled with joy.
He then took leave of the Śākyas, saying:
"I have accumulated a course of calamities and wandered through the evil realms.
Fortunately, by your compassionate regard and the power of your merit, this wretched body of mine, which has endured for kalpas, has been transformed in a single moment."
To repay this kindness, even the sacrifice of my body would not suffice.
My heart’s desire is to accompany you on your travels, yet I am constrained by public opinion.
I wish to inform my parents first, and thereafter prepare the necessary rites.
The dragon girl returned to the pond and said to her parents:

"While out for a stroll today, I suddenly encountered a member of the Śākya clan. Moved by the power of his merit, he transformed me into a human being; my heart desires to unite with him, and I venture to relate these facts."
The Dragon King, his heart drawn toward the human realm and his mind deeply respectful of the Noble Clan, acceded to the daughters' request.
He then emerged from the pond and, expressing his gratitude to the Śākya kin, said:

"You have not cast aside one of a different species, but have condescended to honor the lowly by descending to my humble abode; I pray you will grace my home, where I venture to offer you service and hospitality."
The Śākya having accepted the Dragon King’s invitation, he proceeded to his abode.
There, within the dragon palace, the wedding rites were performed in person; they celebrated their union with feasting and revelry, indulging to the utmost in joy and pleasure.
When the Śākyas beheld the form of the dragon, their hearts were filled with constant fear and loathing, and they wished to take their leave and depart.
The Dragon King stopped them, saying:

"Please do not abandon us from afar; dwell as our neighbors in this residence. We shall cause you to possess the territory, assume the great title, command subjects and ministers, and extend your reign through many generations."
The Śākya replied,
"These words are not to be hoped for.
The Dragon King placed a precious sword within a casket and covered it with a fine white cotton cloth.
He said to the Śākyas, "Please take this cotton cloth and present it to the king; the king will surely receive this tribute from a man from afar in person, and at that moment, you may slay him."
"Would it not be well for you to take possession of that kingdom?
Following the dragon’s instruction, the Śākya went to present the offering;
the King of Uḍḍiyāna personally lifted the woolen cloth, while the Śākya grasped his sleeve and stabbed him.
The attendants and guards clamored at the steps; the Śākyas brandished their swords and declared:
"The swords we wield were bestowed upon us by divine dragons; they are for the execution of those who remain in hiding and for the beheading of those who are disloyal."
All, fearing his divine martial prowess, proffered him the supreme throne.
Thereupon, he rectified abuses and established governance, honoring the worthy and relieving the distressed.
Subsequently, he mobilized a great multitude and prepared the imperial carriage; he proceeded to the Dragon Palace to deliver his decree and welcomed the Dragon Maiden back to the capital.
The dragon girl’s past karma was not yet exhausted, and its residual retribution still remained; whenever she attended private banquets, nine dragon heads would emerge from her head.
The Śākyas were terrified by this abomination and, knowing no other plan, waited for her to fall asleep and severed them with sharp blades.

The dragon girl was startled from her sleep and said, "This will not be beneficial for your descendants; it will not merely cause some slight injury to my life, but your progeny shall suffer from headaches."
Therefore, this nation and its clans have always suffered from this affliction; though it does not persist continuously, it occasionally flares up.
Once the Śākya clan had perished, their son ascended the throne; he was King Utrāśirṣa, which in the language of Tang means "Superior Army."
After the King of the Upper Army succeeded to the throne, his mother lost her sight.
When the Tathāgata returned from subduing the Āpālāla Dragon, he descended from the air into her palace.
The King of the Upper Army had just gone out on a hunting expedition when the Tathāgata briefly expounded the essentials of the Dharma for his mother.
Having encountered the Sage and heard the Dharma, she subsequently regained her sight.
The Tathāgata asked:
"My son, you are of my own clan; where are you now?
The mother replied, "He went out at dawn to hunt and will soon return in his carriage."
As the Tathāgata was about to set out with the great assembly, the King’s mother said:

“I am truly fortunate to have given birth to this holy lineage. Since the Tathāgata has looked upon me with compassion and personally descended here, and my son is just now returning, I pray that you will stay for a short while to wait for him.”
The World-Honored One said:
"This person is of my own kin.
He can hear the teaching and attain faith and awakening; it is not necessary to instruct him personally to arouse his resolve."
"I am now departing.
Upon my return, I shall tell them:
'The Tathāgata has gone from here to the śāla trees at Kuśinagara to enter parinirvāṇa; you should take his relics and make offerings to them yourselves.'"
The Tathāgata and the great assembly ascended into the void and departed.
King Shangjun was then out hunting; seeing from afar the brilliant and dazzling radiance within the palace, he suspected a fire had broken out, so he abandoned his hunt and returned.
He then saw that his mother’s sight had been restored;
filled with joy, he asked her, "How long has it been since I left when such an auspicious response occurred, enabling my compassionate mother to regain her sight as it was before?"
The mother said, "After you had gone out, the Tathāgata arrived here; having heard the Buddha preach the Dharma, your sight was restored.
From here, the Tathāgata will proceed to the śāla trees at Kuśinagara, where he shall enter parinirvāṇa. He summons you to come quickly so that you may receive a portion of his relics."
When the king heard this, he wailed in grief and collapsed to the ground; after a long time, he regained consciousness and ordered his carriage to hasten there.
Upon reaching the space between the twin trees, the Buddha had already entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the various kings held those from the remote borderlands in low esteem while cherishing the śarīra relics as precious treasures, and thus they were unwilling to share them.
Thereupon, the great assembly of devas and humans reiterated the Buddha’s intention; having heard this, the kings finally proceeded to distribute them equally.

To the northeast of the city of Mung-kie-li (Monghyr), one crosses mountains and valleys, traveling upstream along the Indus River. The path is perilous, with deep, dark mountain gorges; in some places one must tread upon hanging ropes, in others pull oneself along iron chains. The plank bridges overhang the void and the flying beams are precariously constructed. Treading upon wooden pegs and stepping-stones, one travels more than a thousand *li* until reaching the Darel Valley, which is the ancient capital of the kingdom of Udyāna.
It produces much gold and saffron.

Beside a great monastery in the middle of the Dārlī River stands a carved wooden image of Maitreya Bodhisattva; its golden hue is radiant and brilliant, and its spiritual perception communicates with the hidden realm. It is over one hundred feet high and was fashioned by the Arhat Madhyāntika (formerly called Madhyāndina, which is an erroneous abbreviation).

By means of his supernormal powers, the Arhat led the artisans up to Tuṣita Heaven—formerly called Doushuaituo, which is a corruption of Doushetai—to personally observe the wondrous features; after three such visits, the work was finally completed.
Since this image first appeared, the Dharma has flowed toward the East.

From here, traveling eastward, crossing ridges and valleys, and ascending the Indus River against its current, traversing suspension bridges and mountain paths while treading upon perils and braving hardships for over five hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Parvata within the borders of North India.
The country of Parvata is over four thousand *li* in circuit; it lies amidst the Great Snow Mountains, being long from east to west and narrow from south to north.
It produces much wheat and beans, and yields gold and silver; by deriving profit from its gold mines, the state's resources are abundant and prosperous.
At that time, the climate was exclusively bitter cold, and the people were fierce and violent by nature; they were deficient in benevolence and righteousness and had no knowledge of ritual propriety.
Their physical appearance was coarse and unkempt, and their clothing consisted of hair-cloth and coarse wool.
The script is largely the same as that of India.

The spoken language differs from those of other countries. There are several hundred monasteries and several thousand monks; their studies lack specialization, and their observance of the precepts is often lax.

From here he returned to the city of Udakhaṇḍa; crossing the Indus River to the south, which was three or four li wide, flowing southward, clear as a polished mirror, with its waters surging and drifting along.

Poisonous dragons and fierce beasts dwell within its caves; if those who cross it carry precious treasures, rare flowers, seeds, or the relics of the Buddha, their boat will mostly drift away and sink.
Crossing the river, he reached the kingdom of Takṣaśilā, within the borders of North India.
The kingdom of Takṣaśilā is more than two thousand li in circuit.
The capital city of the country is over ten li in circuit.
The local chieftains compete for power, and the royal lineage has become extinct. In the past, the country was subject to Kāpiśī; recently, it has become a dependency of Kaśmīra.
The soil is renowned for its fertility, and agriculture is abundant; springs and streams are numerous, and flowers and grasses flourish.
The climate is mild and pleasant, the local customs are characterized by a light-hearted vigor, and the Triple Gem is held in high esteem.
Although there are many monasteries, they are already largely overgrown with weeds; the number of monks is small, and they all study the Mahāyāna.
More than seventy *li* to the northwest of the great city is the Lake of the Naga King Elāpattra, which is over a hundred paces in circumference.
The water was clear and limpid, where lotuses of various colors flourished together in diverse hues.
This dragon was none other than the bhikṣu who had destroyed the airāvaṇa tree during the time of the Buddha Kāśyapa.

Therefore, whenever it is now requested for rain or prayed for fine weather in that land, they invariably go together with the śramaṇas to the site of the pond; there, by snapping their fingers and offering words of comfort, their wishes are invariably fulfilled.
Traveling more than thirty li southeast from the dragon pond, one enters between two mountains where there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, over a hundred feet in height.

This was the prophecy made by Śākyamuni Tathāgata that when the future World-Honored One Maitreya appears in the world, there will spontaneously arise four great treasuries of jewels; this very superior site shall be one of them.
I have heard from the records of former sages that at times when an earthquake occurs and all the mountains tremble, this stupa remains unshaken for a hundred paces around it.
Yet foolish men, acting on their delusions, attempt to excavate it; consequently, the earth shakes violently and they all fall prostrate.
Beside it is a monastery that is extremely dilapidated and has long been devoid of monks.
Twelve or thirteen *li* to the north of the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka.
On fast days, it sometimes emits brilliant light, and divine flowers and celestial music are frequently seen and heard.
According to the records of former sages:

recently, there was a woman afflicted with malignant leprosy who secretly came to the stūpa to reproach herself and perform rites of repentance. Seeing that the courtyard contained various filth and impurities, she scooped them up to clear away, swept, sprinkled water, applied fragrant pastes, scattered flowers, and gathered blue lotuses.
It was spread thickly over the ground.
His malignant illness was cured, his appearance became more beautiful, and a wondrous fragrance emanated from his body, as rich as that of the blue lotus.

This is a most excellent site where, in the past, the Tathāgata practiced the bodhisattva path as a great king named Candraprabha (translated into Chinese as Yuèguāng, "Moonlight"), who sought enlightenment with such resolve that he severed his own head as a gift of almsgiving.
If one were to practice such renunciation, it would take a thousand lifetimes.
Beside the Stūpa of the Gift of the Head is a monastery; its courtyards and buildings are desolate, and the number of monks has diminished.
In the past, the Sautrāntika master Kumāralāta (translated into Chinese as Tóngshòu) composed various treatises here.

To the southeast outside the city, on the northern side of the Southern Mountain, there is a stūpa over one hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka at the site where his son, Prince Kuṇāla, had his eyes gouged out after being falsely accused by his stepmother.
The blind who offered prayers were often restored to sight.
This Prince was born of the principal consort; his appearance was elegant and refined, and his compassion and benevolence were renowned from early on.
When the principal consort passed away, the secondary wife became lustful and, indulging her own ignorance and folly, privately coerced the Prince.
The Crown Prince wept bitterly as he took responsibility for his own failings and withdrew to offer his apologies.
Seeing him thus submissive, the stepmother’s anger increased all the more; she waited for an opportunity when the King was at leisure and spoke with deliberate calm:
"Takṣaśilā is the vital stronghold of the kingdom; how can its governance be entrusted to anyone other than a son of your own blood?"
"Now, the Crown Prince’s benevolence and filial piety are renowned; because he is close to the worthy, public opinion rests upon him.
When the King heard these words, he took pleasure in the treacherous scheme and immediately summoned the Crown Prince, admonishing him, saying:
"I have inherited the remaining legacy and am entrusted with the succession of the ancestral enterprise; I fear only that I may fail or lose it, thereby bringing shame upon the former kings."
"Takṣaśilā is the strategic gateway of the kingdom; I now command you to serve as its governor.
State affairs are weighty and human nature is devious and complex; do not act on impulse or with recklessness, lest you bring harm to the royal foundation."
"Whenever there is a summons, verify my tooth-seal.
Since the seal is upon my mouth, how could there be any error?
Thereupon, the Crown Prince received the mandate and came to govern.

Although years had passed, the secondary wife grew increasingly enraged; she forged an imperial decree, sealed it with purple clay, and while waiting for the King to fall asleep, she stealthily used his teeth as a seal. She dispatched a messenger to deliver the letter of reprimand.
The attending ministers knelt to read [the decree], looking at one another in bewilderment.
The Crown Prince asked,
"What is there to grieve?"
He said:

"By the King’s command, a letter has been sent to reprimand the Crown Prince, ordering that his two eyes be gouged out and he be banished to the mountain valleys; his wife and he are left to their own devices, to live or die as fate decrees."
"Although we have received this command, it cannot yet be relied upon.
We should now request it again, binding ourselves with our faces turned toward you to await punishment.
The Prince said:
"If my father has been sentenced to death, how could I possibly refuse?
The seal of his teeth is indeed unmistakable.
He then commanded the *caṇḍāla* to gouge out his eyes.
Having lost his sight, he sustained himself by begging; wandering from place to place, he eventually reached his father’s capital city.
His wife told him, "This is the royal city."
Alas! The suffering of hunger and cold is truly bitter!
Formerly a prince, now a beggar!
I pray that you will take heed of this and once again address my former transgressions.

Thereupon, according to this plan, he entered the inner stables of the king; during the latter part of the night, he wept facing the clear breeze, letting out long, mournful whistles and chanting with the accompaniment of a *konghou* lute and drums.
The king was atop his high tower when he heard her refined singing; as the lyrics were filled with profound resentment and sorrow, he marveled and asked:
"The sound of the kōng-hou lute and the voice of the song seem to belong to my daughter; for what reason has she come here now?"
He immediately questioned the inner stables:
"Who is singing and whistling?
Thereupon, he brought a blind man forward to answer his command.
When the King saw the Crown Prince, he spoke with suppressed grief, asking:
"Who has harmed your body to bring upon you such calamity?
Even though your beloved son has lost his sight, you yourself do not yet realize it; how can we, as commoners, investigate and examine such matters?"
"O Heaven! O Heaven! How has my virtue declined!
The Prince wept bitterly, apologized, and replied:

"Truly, because of my unfiliality, I have incurred a debt toward Heaven. On such a year, month, day, and hour, I suddenly received Your Majesty’s compassionate command; having no means to offer further words, I did not dare evade my responsibility."
The king knew in his heart that the secondary wife had acted treacherously; without further investigation, he immediately subjected her to the death penalty.

At that time, there was in the Bodhi Tree Monastery an Arhat named Ghoṣa (translated into Chinese as Miaoyin, "Wondrous Sound"), who possessed unimpeded mastery of the four analytical knowledges and was fully endowed with the three types of supernormal knowledge.
The King took his blind son with him and related the matter, saying, "I only pray that you will show compassion and restore his sight.
Having accepted the King's request, the Arhat immediately issued a proclamation to the people of the country on that very day:
"On the coming day, I wish to expound the sublime Dharma; let each person bring a vessel and come here to listen to the teaching, so as to collect their tears."
Thereupon, people from near and far flocked together, and men and women gathered like clouds.

At that time, the Arhat expounded upon the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; among all who heard the Dharma, there was none who was not moved to deep sorrow, so that they held their vessels to catch their falling tears.
Having finished preaching the Dharma, he collected all the tears and placed them upon a golden platter, then made this vow:
"Whatever I have preached is the ultimate truth of all Buddhas."
If the principle were not true and there were errors in its exposition, that would be the end of it;
but if it is otherwise, I pray that with these many tears I may wash those blind eyes, so that their vision may be restored and they may see clearly as before.
Having spoken these words, he took his tears and washed his eyes; his vision was immediately restored.
The King then reprimanded his ministers, interrogated his officials and subordinates, and demoted, banished, transferred, or executed them accordingly.
The various nobles of the secular world moved their residences to the midst of the sandy deserts to the northeast of the Snowy Mountains.
From here, traveling southeast across various mountains and valleys for more than seven hundred li, one reaches the kingdom of Saṃkapura, within the borders of North India.
The country of Siṃhapura is three thousand five or six hundred li in circuit and borders the Indus River to the west.
The capital city of the country is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit; it is built upon mountains and ridges, being firm, steep, and impregnable.
Agricultural labor requires little effort yet yields abundant harvests from the land.
The climate is cold, and the people are fierce by nature; their customs prize martial valor, and they are also largely deceitful.
The country has no sovereign ruler; it is a dependency of the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
Not far to the south of the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka.
Although its ornamental decorations have fallen into disrepair, miraculous manifestations continue to occur in succession.
Beside it is a monastery, which is now empty and devoid of monks.
Forty or fifty *li* to the southeast of the city, one reaches a stone *stūpa* built by King Aśoka, over two hundred feet in height.
There are dozens of ponds and pools reflecting off its sides, with stone embankments carved into various extraordinary shapes and forms.

The rushing waters and clear currents gush and swirl, flowing onward; dragons, fish, and aquatic creatures dwell in their caves and glide beneath the surface; four-colored lotuses spread across the limpid pools.
A hundred fruits flourish in abundance, sharing their splendor yet differing in hue; groves and ponds reflect one another, truly a place fit for recreation.
Beside it stands a monastery that has long been devoid of monks.

Not far from the side of the stūpa is the site where the original teacher of the white-robed heretics attained the principle he sought and first preached the Dharma; there is now a commemorative mark there, with a deva temple built beside it.
Their disciples practiced asceticism, exerting themselves with diligence day and night without seeking rest.

Regarding the Dharma taught by their original master, they largely plagiarized the meanings of Buddhist scriptures, establishing teachings according to various categories and imitating the formal rituals and protocols.
The elders are called *bhikṣus*, while the juniors are termed *śrāmaṇeras*.
Their deportment and observance of the precepts are largely identical to those of the monastic community.

They differ only in that they retain a small amount of hair and, moreover, go naked; though they may wear some clothing, white is used as their distinguishing mark. Based on these distinctions, they are somewhat differentiated.
The image of that Heavenly Master resembles the Tathāgata; while there are differences in their vestments, their marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa*) are no different.

From here, returning to the northern border of the kingdom of Takṣaśilā, he crossed the Indus River and traveled southeast for more than two hundred *li*. Crossing a great stone gate, this is where in the past Prince Mahāsattva threw himself to feed the starving vultures.

One hundred and forty or fifty paces to the south, there is a stone stūpa. Here, Mahāsattva, out of pity for the starving beast’s lack of strength, arrived at this spot and pierced himself with a dry bamboo splinter to feed it his blood; it was only then that the beast began to devour him.
The soil there, as well as all the grasses and trees, were tinged slightly with a crimson hue, as if stained by blood.
When people stepped upon that ground, it felt like walking on thorns; regardless of whether they were skeptical or faithful, there was none who did not feel profound sorrow and lamentation.
To the north of the place where he sacrificed his body is a stone stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka.
Its carvings are of extraordinary design, and it frequently emits a divine light.
There are small stūpas and stone niches numbering in the hundreds surrounding this precinct; those who suffer from illness are often cured by circumambulating them.
To the east of the stone stūpa is a monastery with over a hundred monks, all of whom study the Mahāyāna teachings.
From here, traveling east for more than fifty li, one reaches Mount Gu, where there is a monastery with over two hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna.
Flowers and fruits flourish in abundance, and the springs and ponds are as clear as mirrors.
Beside it stands a stūpa over two hundred feet high, which marks the place where the Tathāgata in the past converted a malevolent yakṣa, causing him to cease eating flesh.
From here, traveling southeast for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Uraśā, within the borders of North India.
The kingdom of Uraśā is over two thousand *li* in circuit; its mountains and hills are joined together, and its fields and plains are narrow and confined.
The capital city of the country is seven or eight *li* in circuit; it has no great sovereign and is subject to the kingdom of Kāśmīra.
It is suitable for sowing and reaping, but flowers and fruits are scarce.
The climate is mild, with only slight frosts and snow.
The customs lack propriety and righteousness; the people are by nature fierce and violent, frequently practicing deceit and fraud, and they do not believe in the Buddha-dharma.
Four or five *li* to the southwest of the great city is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka.
Beside it is a monastery where the monks are few in number, and all of them study the teachings of the Mahāyāna.

From here, proceeding southeast, climbing mountains and traversing perilous terrain, crossing an iron bridge and traveling over a thousand li, one arrives at the kingdom of Kaśmīra—formerly called Jibin, which is a corruption.
In the region of North India lies the kingdom of Kaśmīra. The kingdom of Kaśmīra is over seven thousand *li* in circuit.

It is surrounded on all sides by mountains that are exceedingly steep and precipitous; although there are gateways and paths, they are narrow and constricted, so that from ancient times no neighboring enemy has been able to launch an attack.
The capital city of the kingdom borders a great river to the west; it is twelve or thirteen *li* from south to north and four or five *li* from east to west.
It is suitable for sowing and reaping, abounds in flowers and fruits, and produces dragon-breed horses, saffron, fire-pearls, and medicinal herbs.
The climate is cold and biting, with much snow and little wind.
The people wear woolen garments and white cotton cloth.
The local customs are frivolous and light, and most people are timid and weak.
The kingdom is protected by dragons and has consequently become preeminent among its neighbors.
Its inhabitants possess handsome and beautiful features, yet their dispositions are deceitful.
They are fond of learning and possess extensive knowledge, believing both in heterodox and orthodox teachings alike.
There are more than one hundred monasteries with over five thousand monks.
There are four stūpas, all built by King Aśoka, each containing more than a sheng of the Tathāgata’s relics.
The *Guo-zhi* states:
"The land of this country was originally a dragon pool.

In the past, after the World-Honored Buddha had subdued the malevolent spirits in the kingdom of Udyāna and wished to return to the Middle Kingdom, he traveled through the air above this country and said to Ānanda:"
"After my parinirvāṇa, there will be an arhat named Madhyantika who shall establish a kingdom in this land to settle its people and propagate the Buddha-dharma."

Fifty years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, a disciple of Ānanda named the Arhat Madhyantika—who had attained the six supernormal powers and was endowed with the eight liberations—heard the Buddha’s prophetic prediction. Rejoicing in his heart, he came to this place and, sitting in meditative equipoise within the forest on a great mountain ridge, manifested great supernatural transformations.
The dragon, seeing this, developed deep faith and requested whatever he desired.
The Arhat said,
"I wish for you to grant me a space within the pond large enough to accommodate my knees."
The Dragon King then withdrew the water and offered it as a gift.

The Arhat used his supernatural powers to expand his body; although the Dragon King exerted all his strength to withdraw the water, the pond became empty and the water was exhausted. The Dragon then requested the land back.
The Arhat left behind a single pond here in the northwest, measuring over one hundred li in circumference;
his other kinsmen each dwell in separate small ponds.
The Dragon King said:
“I offer this entire pool and its grounds; may you accept my offerings forever.
Madhyantika replied, “I shall soon enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder; though I wish to accept your invitation, how could that be possible?”
The Dragon King requested again:
"May five hundred arhats constantly receive my offerings until the Dharma comes to an end; after the Dharma has ended, they shall return to this country to take it as their dwelling pool."
Madhyantika accepted their request.
Once the Arhat had obtained the land, he exercised his great supernormal powers and established five hundred monasteries.
In various foreign lands, they purchased and sold low-caste people (dāsas) to provide labor and serve the monastic community.

After Madhyāntika entered parinirvāṇa, those low-caste people established their own leaders; however, the neighboring kingdoms despised them for their low birth and would not form alliances with them, calling them Kṛtaka (translated into Chinese as "bought").
Nowadays, the spring waters have already overflowed in abundance.
One hundred years after the Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, King Aśoka of Magadha ascended the throne and ruled the world, his majesty extending even to foreign lands.
He placed deep faith in the Triple Gem and cherished all four classes of living beings.
At that time, there were five hundred arhat-monks and five hundred ordinary monks whom the king revered and honored with equal and undifferentiated offerings.

There was an ordinary monk named Mahādeva (translated into Chinese as Dàtiān), who was broad-minded and possessed great wisdom. He sought out the profound meaning of names and reality, and through deep reflection, he composed a treatise whose principles contradicted the holy teachings; whenever anyone heard of this, they followed him in dissenting from the orthodox view.

King Aśoka, unable to distinguish between the ordinary and the noble, followed his own inclinations and sided with those he favored; he summoned the assembly of monks to the Ganges River, intending to cast them into its deep current and execute them all.

At that time, as the Arhats were confronted with the peril of their lives, they all exercised their supernatural powers, soaring through the air and traversing the void to arrive in this country, where they dwelt among the mountains and hid in the valleys.
When King Aśoka heard of this, he was filled with fear; he came in person to apologize for his transgressions and invited them to return to his own kingdom.
Those arhats resolutely did not comply with his command.
King Aśoka built five hundred monasteries for the arhats and offered the entire kingdom as a gift to the Saṃgha.

In the kingdom of Gandhāra, King Kaniṣka, at the fourth century after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, responded to the auspicious timing to govern the realm; his royal influence spread afar, and those of different customs submitted within his domain.
In his leisure time from state affairs, he regularly studied Buddhist scriptures and invited a monk into the palace daily to preach the Dharma;
however, as various interpretations and sectarian tenets differed, the King harbored deep doubts and had no means to dispel his confusion.
At that time, the Venerable Pārśva said:

"Since the Tathāgata passed into nirvāṇa, the years have grown ever more distant; the disciples have formed various schools and held differing views as teachers and students, each relying on their own hearsay and observations, resulting in mutual contradictions."
When the King heard this, he was deeply moved; after lamenting for a long time, he said to the Venerable One:

"By the grace of my remaining merit, I have followed in the footsteps of my predecessors. Although the Sage is far removed, I still consider myself fortunate. Forgetting my own mediocrity and vulgarity, I shall propagate and honor the Dharma teachings, providing a complete commentary on the Tripiṭaka according to their respective schools."

The Venerable Pārśva said, “Great King, you have planted roots of goodness in past lives and possess abundant merit and blessings; that you set your heart upon the Buddha-dharma is precisely what we desire.
The King then issued a proclamation far and wide to assemble sages and wise men.

Thereupon, people flocked from all directions like spokes converging at the hub, traveling ten thousand *li* as swiftly as shooting stars; men of outstanding talent and wisdom gathered in full, and the sagely and enlightened assembled together.
For seven days, they were provided with the four types of offerings.
Desiring to deliberate on the Dharma, yet fearing that the assembly might become noisy and disorderly, the King expressed his thoughts to the monks, saying:
"Those who have realized the fruits of sainthood may remain; those still bound by fetters shall return."
As it was, the crowd was still large.
He then issued another proclamation:
"Those who are beyond training (aśaikṣa) may remain; those still in training (śaikṣa) shall return."
"They are still too numerous.
He then issued another order:
"Those who possess the three types of clear knowledge and are equipped with the six supernormal powers may remain; all others shall return to their respective homes."
"However, they were still too numerous.
He then issued another order:
'Those who have mastered the Tripiṭaka within and attained proficiency in the Five Sciences without shall remain; all others shall return to their respective homes.'"
Thus, four hundred and ninety-nine persons were obtained.
The King, finding his own country unbearably hot and humid, wished instead to proceed to the stone cave of Mahākāśyapa’s assembly at Rājagṛha.
The Venerable Pārśva and others deliberated, saying:
"It is not possible.
There are many non-Buddhists there, and their heterodox arguments are so entangled that one would have no leisure even to respond to them; what achievement could be made in composing a treatise?"
The hearts of those gathered here are set upon this land.

This country is surrounded by solid mountains and guarded by yakṣas; its soil is rich and fertile, its products abundant, and it is a place where the worthy and sages assemble and where holy seers dwell.
As the assembly deliberated on this matter, they all agreed, saying:
"It is most fitting.
At that time, the King, together with various arhats, arrived from that place; he established a monastery and convened a council to collect the Tripiṭaka, intending to compose the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
At that time, the Venerable Vasumitra was wearing his patched robe outside the door.
The Arhats said to Vasumitra, "Your fetters have not yet been eliminated;
your pure deliberations are erroneous. You should withdraw to a distant place and not remain here."
Vasumitra said:

"Virtuous ones, you have no doubts regarding the Dharma; acting as the Buddha’s successors to bestow transformation, you are now gathering the great principles and intend to compose an orthodox treatise.

Although I am not quick-witted, I have gained a rough understanding of the subtle words. I have also delved deeply into the profound texts of the Tripiṭaka and the ultimate truths of the five sciences, and have grasped their essential purport."
The Arhats said:
"One should not speak in such a manner.
You ought to dwell in seclusion and swiftly realize the state of no-more-learning; you may then join us here, for it will not be too late."
Vasumitra said, "In my view, the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) is like mucus or spittle; my resolve is to seek the fruit of Buddhahood, not to follow the lesser path.
Before this ball of thread has fallen to the ground, I shall surely realize the noble fruit of no-more-learning."
Then the Arhats rebuked him again, saying:
"This is what is called an 'arrogant person' (adhimānika).
One who has attained the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣaphala) is praised by all Buddhas; you ought to quickly realize it yourself to resolve the doubts of the assembly."
Thereupon, Vasumitra threw the ball of thread into the air, whereupon the devas in the sky caught it and entreated him, saying:

"You are destined to realize the fruit of Buddhahood and succeed Maitreya as his regent; you shall be the most honored in the three realms and the sole reliance for all beings born of the four modes of birth. Why, then, do you wish to realize only the lesser fruit here?"

When the arhats witnessed this event, they apologized for their faults and extolled his virtues, requesting him to serve as the senior elder (upādhyāya); whenever there were matters of doubt or debate, they all sought his decision.
These five hundred noble ones first composed the *Upadeśa-śāstra* in one hundred thousand verses—formerly called the *Youbotishe lun*, which is an erroneous transcription.
He explained the *Sūtrapiṭaka*—formerly called the *Xiuduoluo Zang*, which is an error.
Next, he composed the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* in one hundred thousand stanzas to explain the *Vinayapiṭaka*—formerly called the *Binaye Zang*, which is an error.
Later, he composed the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* in one hundred thousand stanzas to explain the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*, also known as the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*; "Abhidharma" is an abbreviation.

It comprises three hundred thousand verses and nine million six hundred thousand words, providing a comprehensive commentary on the Tripiṭaka that shall hang as a beacon for all eternity. Therein, every branch and leaf is exhausted, every depth and height investigated; the great principles are re-clarified and the subtle words are once more revealed. It has been widely proclaimed and disseminated, upon which future generations rely.
King Kaniṣka then had the treatise inscribed upon plates of red copper; these were enclosed within a stone casket, which was sealed and enshrined inside a stūpa that he erected.

He commanded yakṣa deities to guard the kingdom all around and not allow those of heterodox learning to take this treatise out; those who wished to study it were to receive instruction within its borders.
Thus, when his work was completed, he returned to his capital with his army.
Outside the western gate of this country, he knelt facing east and further offered the entire kingdom as a gift to the monastic community.
After King Kaniṣka had passed away, the Kṣatrapas again proclaimed themselves kings; they expelled the monks and destroyed the Buddha-dharma.
In the kingdom of Tukhāra, there was King Himatala (translated into Chinese as "Below the Snow Mountains"), whose ancestors were of the Śākya clan.

Six hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, he came to possess the territories and succeeded to the royal lineage; he established his mind upon the ground of Buddhahood and directed his sentiments toward the ocean of Dharma.

Having heard that Kīrti was destroying the Buddha-dharma, he gathered three thousand brave warriors from throughout the kingdom; disguised as merchants, they brought with them abundant treasures and concealed weapons, entering this country.
The ruler of this country treated him with exceptional courtesy and hospitality.

From among the merchants and travelers, he further selected and recruited five hundred men who were fierce and resourceful; each carried a sharp blade hidden in his sleeve and held precious treasures. Carrying the offerings they had personally brought, they went together to present them to the sovereign.

Then the King of Himavat beneath the Snowy Mountains removed his cap and took his seat; King Kṛtīra was struck with terror and stood at a loss, whereupon [the King of Himavat] cut off his head and addressed his subordinates, saying:
"I am the King of Himavat beneath the Snowy Mountains from the kingdom of Tu-luo."
"I am enraged that this base lineage has openly practiced tyrannical governance; therefore, I have now executed those who were guilty.
As for all you common people, it is not your fault.
Nevertheless, the state’s assisting ministers and chief officials were exiled to other regions.
Having pacified this country, he summoned the monastic community and formally established a monastery, restoring it to its former state.
Furthermore, outside the western gate of this country, he knelt facing east and offered alms to the assembly of monks.

The Kirātas have repeatedly caused the extinction of their ancestral lineages through their monastic followers; thus, resentment has accumulated for generations, and they harbor hatred toward the Buddha-dharma.
As the years passed, they once again proclaimed themselves kings.
Consequently, in this country today, there is not much veneration for Buddhism; instead, people pay particular attention to the non-Buddhist temples of the heretics.
About ten li southeast of the new city, to the north of the old city and on the southern slope of a great mountain, there is a saṃghārāma with more than three hundred monks.
Within this stūpa is a tooth of the Buddha, approximately one and a half inches in length and yellowish-white in color; it occasionally emits radiance on fast days.
Formerly, when the Kṛtya clan destroyed the Buddha-dharma, the monastic community was dispersed, and each member settled wherever their interests led.
There was a śramaṇa who traveled throughout India, visiting and paying homage to sacred sites to express his utmost sincerity.

Later, hearing that his native land had been pacified, he set out on his return journey; en route, he encountered a herd of elephants moving recklessly through the marshy grasslands, galloping about with thundering roars.
When the śramaṇa saw this, he climbed a tree to take refuge.

At that time, the herd of elephants rushed forward in a frantic charge, vying with one another to suck up the water from the pond and soak the roots of the tree; they pushed and dug at it together until the tree finally toppled over.

Having obtained the śramaṇa, he loaded him upon his back and traveled until they reached a great forest. There was a sick elephant lying down, suffering from a wound; it led the monk’s hand to the afflicted spot, which had been pierced by a withered bamboo splinter.
Thereupon, the śramaṇa pulled out bamboo splinters and applied medicinal herbs; he tore his garment and bandaged the elephant's foot.

There was another great elephant there who took a golden casket and gave it to the sick elephant; once the elephant had received it, he passed it on to the śramaṇa. When the śramaṇa opened the casket, it was a Buddha-tooth relic.
Surrounded by elephants, there was no way for the monks to exit.
The next day at mealtime, each held a different kind of fruit as their midday meal.
After they had eaten, he carried the monks out of the forest; only after traveling several hundred li did he set them down, whereupon they each knelt and prostrated themselves before departing.
When the śramaṇa reached the western border of the kingdom, he crossed a swift river; as he reached midstream, the boat was about to capsize.
Those on board the same vessel said to one another, "If this boat capsizes now, the calamity will be because of this śramaṇa."
"There must be relics of the Tathāgata within; the dragons will benefit from them.
The ship's captain inspected [the vessel] and indeed obtained a Buddha-tooth relic.
At that time, the śramaṇa held up the Buddha-tooth and, looking down, said to the dragon:
"I now entrust this to you; I shall return to collect it before long.
Thereupon, he did not cross the river but turned his boat and departed. Looking back at the river, he sighed and said:
"I lack the arts of restraint; I have been deceived by these dragon-beasts!"
He traveled to India once more to study the methods for subduing dragons.

After three years, he returned to his own country; as he reached the banks of a river and was just setting up an altar, the dragon there presented a casket containing Buddha’s tooth relic to the śramaṇa.
The śramaṇa took it back and made offerings here at this monastery.
Fourteen or fifteen *li* to the south of the monastery is a small monastery, within which stands a statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
There were those who fasted and vowed to die before they could see the Bodhisattva; for them, a body of wondrous color would emerge from within the statue.

Over thirty li to the southeast of the small monastery, one reaches a great mountain where there is an old monastery. Its architectural layout was once magnificent, but it is now utterly overgrown with weeds; currently, only a small multi-storied pavilion has been rebuilt in one corner.
There are more than thirty monks, all of whom study the Mahāyāna teachings.
Formerly, the master of śāstras Saṃghabhadra (translated into Chinese as Zhòngxián) composed the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* here.
To the left and right of the monastery are various stūpas containing the relics of great arhats.
Wild beasts and mountain monkeys gather flowers to offer them in worship, never failing through the seasons, as if following a direct command.
However, this mountain abounds in various sacred traces; in some places stone cliffs are split asunder, and in others peaks bear the marks of horses.
All such phenomena are of a wondrous and extraordinary nature, all resulting from arhats and śrāmaṇeras who, while playing in groups, drew figures with their fingers or rode horses back and forth.
Relics such as these are difficult to describe in detail.

About ten li to the east of the Buddha-tooth monastery, amidst the cliffs of the northern mountains, there is a small monastery where the great master of śāstras Saṃghabhadra once composed the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
In a small monastery there is a stone stūpa over fifty feet high, containing the bodily relics of an arhat.
Formerly, there was an arhat of immense stature whose consumption of food and drink was equal to that of an elephant.
The people of the time ridiculed him, saying:
"He knows nothing but eating his fill; how could he recognize right from wrong?
When the Arhat was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he addressed the people, saying:
"I shall soon attain the state of Nirvana without remainder; I wish to proclaim the sublime Dharma realized within myself.
When the multitude heard this, they mocked him all the more, gathering together to witness his success or failure.
Then the Arhat addressed the people, saying:
"I shall now explain for you the causal conditions of your past lives.
Prior to this life, as a karmic retribution, I received the body of an elephant in Eastern India, residing in the royal inner stable."
At that time, there was a śramaṇa in this country who traveled far to India to seek out the various sūtras and śāstras of the holy teachings.
At that moment, the king took me and bestowed me upon the śramaṇa; carrying the Buddhist scriptures, he arrived here.
Not long after this, he passed away.

By virtue of the power of his merit from carrying the scriptures, he was subsequently reborn as a human being. Furthermore, enjoying the remaining blessings of his past, he donned the dyed robes of a monk at an early age and diligently sought liberation, finding no leisure for rest. He attained the six supernormal powers and severed the desires of the three realms.
However, as for what he ate, his residual habits remained the same; he would always restrain himself, consuming only one-third of his food.
Although this was said, people still did not believe it.

He immediately ascended into the void and entered the fire-light samādhi; smoke and flames issued from his body as he entered nirvana. His remaining relics fell to the ground, and a stūpa was erected over them.

Traveling over two hundred li northwest from the royal city, one arrives at the Śāṇavana Monastery, where the master of śāstras Punyavardhana—known in the language of Tang as Wǎnmǎn—composed the *Vyākhyā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

Traveling one hundred and forty or fifty *li* west of the city, north of the Great River and south of the mountains, one reaches the monastery of the Mahāsāṃghika school, where there are over a hundred monks.
Formerly, the master of śāstras Buddhadeva composed the *Saṃyuktavastu-śāstra* (or *Mahāsāṃghika-saṃgraha-śāstra*) here.
From this point, traveling southwest across mountains and over perilous terrain for more than seven hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Paṇḍuvardhana, within the borders of North India.
The country of Ban-nu-cha (Pāṇḍuva) is over two thousand *li* in circuit.

Mountains and rivers are numerous, while the fields and ridges are narrow. Grains are sown according to the seasons, and flowers and fruits grow in profusion. There is much sugarcane, but no grapes. Fruits such as the āmra, udumbara, and mocā grow in groves planted by every household, for their flavors are prized.
The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are bold and fierce.
As for their clothing and attire, they mostly wear cotton cloth.
The people are upright by nature and have pure faith in the Triple Gem.
There are five monasteries, all of which are largely in ruins.
There is no sovereign ruler; they are subject to the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
To the north of the city, there are few monks in the monastery.
To the north of the monastery is a stone stūpa that is truly replete with miraculous manifestations.
From here, traveling southeast for more than four hundred li, one arrives at the country of Aḷasapura, within the borders of North India.
The Kingdom of Hlūśāpurā: The kingdom of Hlūśāpurā is over four thousand *li* in circuit.
Its capital city is over ten *li* in circuit.
It is extremely rugged and fortified, abounding in mountains and hills; its rivers and plains are narrow and confined, so the natural resources are not abundant.
The suitability of the soil and the sequence of the seasons are the same as those of the country of Ban-nu-cha.
The customs are fierce and the people are valiant by nature.
The country has no sovereign ruler and is subject to the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
There are ten monasteries, but the number of monks is small.
There is one deva temple, where the non-Buddhists are very numerous.

From the kingdom of Lan-p'o to this land, the physical appearance of the people is coarse and unrefined, their dispositions are vulgar and violent, their speech is common and base, and their sense of propriety is slight and frivolous; it is not the orthodox territory of India, but rather a region of frontier customs.
From here, proceeding southeast, descending a mountain and crossing a river, one travels more than seven hundred *li* to reach the kingdom of Cakka, within the borders of North India.
*Da Tang Xi Yu Ji*, Scroll Three (and Scroll Forty-five). Kingdoms.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree;
compiled by the Śramaṇa Bianji of Dazongchi Monastery.

**Chapter Fifteen: The Countries from Takka to Jalandhara.** **Takka (磔迦國):** The country of Takka is over ten thousand *li* in circuit. To the east it borders the Vipāśā River, and to the west it adjoins the Sindhu River.
The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty li in circuit.
It is suitable for growing non-glutinous rice and abounds in winter wheat; it produces gold, silver, brass, copper, and iron.
The climate is hot, and the land is subject to frequent gales and storms.
The customs are violent and cruel, and their speech is vulgar and indecent.
Their clothing is bright white, consisting of what are known as *kauśeya* (silk) garments, *cāruṣka* (morning glow) garments, and the like.
The people have little faith in the Buddha-dharma and mostly worship heavenly deities.
There are ten monasteries and several hundred deva temples.

In this country, there have long been many charitable almshouses to provide for the poor and destitute; whether by distributing medicine or providing food, travelers are never burdened for their sustenance.
Fourteen or fifteen *li* to the southwest of the great city, one reaches the old city of Śākala.
Although its walls and ramparts are ruined, the foundations remain firm;
it is more than twenty *li* in circuit.
Within it, a smaller city was further constructed, six or seven *li* in circuit, where the inhabitants were wealthy and prosperous;
this was the ancient capital of this country.
Several hundred years ago, there was a king named Mahirāja (translated into Chinese as Dazú, "Great Clan"), who ruled from this city and governed all of India.
He was possessed of talent and wisdom, and his nature was courageous and fierce; none among the neighboring kingdoms failed to submit as subjects to him.
In his leisure from state affairs, he desired to study the Buddha-dharma and ordered that an eminent and virtuous monk be selected from among the Sangha.

At that time, none of the monks dared to accept the summons; those with few desires and no worldly involvements sought neither fame nor distinction, while those who were widely learned and brilliant feared the king’s majesty.

There was, however, an old servant of the royal household who had long since donned the dyed robes of a monk; his discourse was refined and elegant, and his speech was both abundant and敏捷 (agile). The assembly collectively recommended him to accept the summons.
The king said:
"I have revered the Buddha-dharma and traveled far to seek out renowned monks; yet the assembly has recommended this slave to converse with me.
I have often thought that among the monastics, the wise and enlightened stand shoulder to shoulder, but now I know it for myself—what is there to revere?"
Thereupon, an edict was proclaimed throughout the five regions of India that the Buddha-dharma was to be utterly destroyed and the monastic community expelled until not a single person remained.

King Balāditya (translated into Chinese as Youri) of Magadha revered the Buddha-dharma and cherished his subjects; because King Mahāśakya had employed excessive punishments and tyrannical governance, he defended his own borders and failed to submit tribute.
At that time, King Mahāvaṃśa was mobilizing his army to launch a punitive expedition.
King Kumārakalpa, having learned of these reports, addressed his ministers, saying:
"Now that I hear the enemy has arrived, I cannot bear to fight their troops."
"I pray that you, my fellow officials and the common people, will pardon me and spare me from punishment, so that this humble body may withdraw to dwell in the marshes and wilds.
Having finished these words, he departed the palace and took refuge among the mountains and forests.
Moved by gratitude and longing for him, more than several tens of thousands of people followed him, taking up residence and fleeing to the islands.
King Mahāvaṃśa entrusted his army to his younger brother and sailed across the sea to wage war.

King Kaniṣka guarded the strategic passes; with light cavalry he lured the enemy into battle. At the first clash of gongs and drums, elite troops rose up from all sides, capturing Mahāvaṃśa alive and leading him away with his hands bound behind his back.
King Mahāsaṃghika, ashamed of having lost his way, covered his face with his robe.
King Kumāra, seated upon a lion throne and surrounded by his ministers, commanded an attendant to say to Mahāsaṃghika:
"Reveal your face; I have words for you."

The Great Clan replied, "When the positions of sovereign and subject are reversed and one regards the other as an enemy, there is no longer any friendly rapport; why then should we converse face-to-face?
Though he was informed repeatedly, the man ultimately refused to comply with his command.
Thereupon, he issued a proclamation enumerating their crimes, saying:
"The Triple Gem is a field of merit upon which the four modes of birth depend.
Yet you have willfully acted as jackals and wolves, destroying this supreme enterprise."
"Fortune does not protect you; you have been captured by me.
Your crime is unforgivable, and you ought to undergo the punishment of the law.
At that time, King Youthful Sun’s mother was widely learned and possessed a powerful memory; she was highly proficient in the art of divination and physiognomy.

Upon hearing that Mahāgovinda had been executed, he urgently informed King Kumārabhūta, saying, "I have often heard that Mahāgovinda possessed extraordinary features and great wisdom; I wish to see him once.
King Kumārabhūta then ordered that Mahāgovinda be brought into his mother’s palace.
The mother of Bālapaṇḍita said:
"Alas, noble family, do not feel ashamed!
The world is impermanent; honor and disgrace alternate. I am as your mother, and you are as my son; you should remove your veil and face me with a single word."
The Great Clan said:

"Formerly I was the sovereign of a rival state, but now I am a captive prisoner. Having brought ruin to the royal enterprise and extinguished my ancestral sacrifices, I am ashamed before the spirits of my ancestors above and feel humiliated before the common people below; I truly have cause for shame in my own countenance."
Looking up at heaven and down at earth, I could not bear the grief of my own loss; therefore, I have covered myself with this cloth.
The Queen Mother said, “Rising and falling follow the seasons; existence and non-existence are subject to destiny.”
If one uses the mind to align with all things, then both gain and loss are forgotten;
if one uses all things to align with the mind, then slander and praise will arise once more.
One should therefore believe in karmic retribution and adapt to the changing times; by casting aside delusion and responding appropriately to speech, one may perhaps preserve one’s life.
The Great Clan apologized, saying:

"Since I, being of no talent, have succeeded to the royal enterprise, my administration of justice and government has lost its way, leading to the extinction of the state's fortune. Even though I am now within the bonds of captivity, I still cling to the hope of life for a morning or an evening."
"I venture to receive your great favor;
I come before you in person to thank you for your profound kindness. Thereupon, she removed her veil and revealed her face.
The Queen Mother said:
"May you cherish yourself and live out your full span of life.
Having said this, he then addressed King Yòurì:
"The ancient canons contain this instruction: 'Pardon transgressions and love life.'"

"Although King Mahāvaṃśa has accumulated evil for a long time, his remaining merit is not yet exhausted. If you kill this man, for twelve years the people will look upon one another with the pallor of starvation.
However, he possesses the air of a restorer; he shall certainly not be the king of a great nation, but shall instead occupy the north and possess a small territory."

King Young-Sun, obeying the command of his compassionate mother and taking pity on the ruler who had lost his kingdom, betrothed his young daughter to him and treated him with exceptional courtesy; he gathered the king’s remaining troops and increased his escort, before they had yet departed from the island.

The younger brother of King Mahāsammata returned to his own country and established himself as king; Mahāsammata, having lost his throne, fled into the mountains and wilds and sought refuge in the north at the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
The King of Kaśmīra treated him with profound courtesy and respect, taking pity on him for his loss of the kingdom, and granted him a territory and a city as a fief.
As the years passed, he led the people of his district to treacherously assassinate the King of Kaśmīra and establish himself as sovereign.

Taking advantage of the momentum of his victory, he campaigned westward against the kingdom of Gandhāra; there, by concealing his troops and lying in ambush with armored men, he ultimately killed the king and utterly exterminated the royal clan and the great ministers.
He destroyed stūpas and demolished monasteries, numbering one thousand six hundred in total.
Beyond those killed by the military, there remained nine hundred million people, all of whom he intended to slaughter until not a single soul was left alive.
At that time, all the ministers and assistants came forward to remonstrate, saying:
"Your Majesty’s majesty has intimidated the powerful enemy; without the clash of arms, you have executed only their principal evildoers.
What fault do the common people bear?"
"I pray that you will use this humble body of mine to take the place of those who ought to die.

The King said, "You believe in the Buddha-dharma and revere the merit of the unseen realm; intending to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, you have extensively recounted your past lives—do you wish to transmit my evil deeds to future generations?"
"You should return to your proper station; do not offer further excuses.

Thereupon, he had three hundred million members of the upper class executed by throwing them into the Indus River, and three hundred million members of the middle class by drowning them in the Indus River.
Three hundred million pieces of base metal were distributed as rewards to the soldiers; thus, carrying the treasures of the fallen kingdom, they returned with their ranks arrayed.
Before even a year had passed, he soon met his end.
At that time, clouds and mist shrouded the world in darkness, the great earth shook, and violent winds broke forth.
Those who had realized the fruits of the path sighed with compassion and said:
"To have slain the innocent in vain and destroyed the Buddha-dharma is to fall into the Avīci Hell, where one will continue to transmigrate without end."
In the ancient city of Śākala, there was a monastery with more than a hundred monks, all of whom studied the Hīnayāna teachings.
It was here that the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu formerly composed the *Paramārthasatya-śāstra*.
Beside it stands a stūpa over two hundred feet high, where the four Buddhas of the past preached the Dharma.
There is also the site containing the traces of the places where those same four Buddhas performed their walking meditations.
Five or six *li* to the northwest of the monastery, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka; it is the place where the four past Buddhas preached the Dharma.

More than ten *li* to the northeast of the new capital city, one reaches a stone *stūpa* over two hundred feet high, erected by King Aśoka; it marks the place where the Tathāgata halted on his journey northward while traveling to convert sentient beings.
The *Record of India* states:
"Within this stūpa are many śarīras, and on fast days, it occasionally emits radiance.
From here, traveling eastward for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Navattha, within the borders of North India.
The Kingdom of Cinapati is over two thousand li in circuit.
Its capital city is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit.
Crops grow in great abundance, while fruit trees are sparse.
The common people live in peace and security, and the state’s resources are abundant.

The climate is warm and humid, and the customs of the people are timid and weak. Their learning encompasses both the ultimate and the conventional truths, and their faith embraces both heterodox and orthodox teachings.
There are ten monasteries and eight deva temples.

Formerly, when King Kaniṣka ruled the realm, his fame resounded throughout neighboring countries and his majesty extended to foreign lands; the tribes of the Hexi region feared his power and sent hostages.

Once King Kaniṣka had received the hostage prince, he treated him with exceptional honor and generosity, providing him with three different residences throughout the day and night and stationing the four divisions of the army as his guard.
This country was where he resided during the winter; therefore, it is called Tsinaputi, which in the language of Tang means "Han-feng" (the Han-bestowed).
The Prince resided there, and thus it became the name of the kingdom.

In this region and throughout the rest of India, there were originally no pears or peaches; because the Prince planted them, the peach was called *Cīnāratna* (in Chinese, "brought by the Han"), and the pear was called *Cīnarāja-vardhana* (in Chinese, "the Prince of Han").
Therefore, the people of this country held those from the Eastern Land (China) in deep esteem, pointing them out to one another and saying,
"He is a man from the native land of our former kings.
Traveling over five hundred li southeast from the great city, one reaches the Dharmaśūvana Monastery (translated into Chinese as Shàlín).

There are more than three hundred monks who study the Sarvāstivāda school; their communal rituals are solemn and their virtuous conduct is pure and lofty. They have particularly and extensively mastered the teachings of the Hīnayāna. It is here that the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa assemble multitudes of devas and humans to preach the profound and wondrous Dharma.

In the third century after the parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, there was the master of treatises Kātyāyanīputra—formerly called Jiànyán, which is an erroneous transcription—who composed the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* here.
Within the Jālindha Monastery is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka.
Beside it are the sites containing the traces of where the four past Buddhas sat and performed their walking meditations.

Small stūpas and various large stone caves stand in close succession, their number beyond reckoning; these are all places where various arhats who attained the fruits of sainthood entered nirvāṇa since the beginning of the kalpa. It is difficult to enumerate them all exhaustively, yet their teeth and bones still remain.
The monasteries surrounding the mountain extend for twenty li; there are hundreds of thousands of stūpas containing the Buddha’s relics, their shadows touching one another at every corner.
From here, traveling northeast for one hundred forty or fifty li, one arrives at the kingdom of Jālandhara, within the borders of North India.
The country of Jālandhara is over one thousand li from east to west and over eight hundred li from south to north.
The capital city has a circumference of twelve or thirteen li.
The soil is suitable for grain cultivation, with an abundance of non-glutinous rice; the forests are lush and the flowers and fruits are flourishing.
The climate is warm and hot, the customs are stern and fierce, the physical appearance is coarse and plain, and the households are wealthy and prosperous.
There are more than fifty monasteries with over two thousand monks, who specialize in the study of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.
There are three deva temples with more than five hundred non-Buddhists, all of whom belong to the ash-smearing sect.
The former kings of this country venerated non-Buddhist paths; however, they later encountered an arhat, heard the Dharma, and attained faith and realization.
Consequently, the King of Central India, recognizing their sincere devotion, placed the affairs of the Triple Gem throughout the five regions of India under his sole supervision.

He blended the distinction between self and others and forgot both love and hatred; he supervised the monastic community with such exquisite discernment that he thoroughly distinguished the virtuous from the depraved.
Consequently, those whose virtue and realization were renowned were revered with utmost sincerity, while those who violated their precepts and conduct were severely reprimanded and punished.
The sites of sacred traces were all marked and established, whether as stūpas or saṃghārāmas; throughout the territory of India, there was no place where they did not extend.

From here, traveling northeast across steep ridges, over mountain caves and valleys, along perilous paths and treacherous roads for more than seven hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Kuruṭa (also read as Jueju), within the borders of North India.
