The country of Kuru is more than three thousand *li* in circuit, with mountains surrounding its four borders.
The capital city of the country is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit.
The soil is rich and fertile; grains are sown in their proper seasons, flowers and fruits flourish, and plants and trees thrive.
Being adjacent to the Snow Mountains, it abounds in rare medicinal herbs and produces gold, silver, red copper, as well as fire-jewels and rain-stones.
The climate becomes increasingly cold, with light frost and snowfall.
The people’s appearance is coarse and unkempt; they suffer from goiters and elephantiasis. Their nature is fierce and violent, and they prize martial spirit and courage.
There are more than twenty monasteries with over a thousand monks, most of whom study the Mahāyāna, while few practice the various Nikāyas.
There are fifteen deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
Nestled against crags and perched upon ridges, stone chambers stand close together; some were inhabited by arhats, while others were occupied by rishis.
Within the kingdom is a stūpa built by King Aśoka.
In the past, the Tathāgata once visited this country;
having preached the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, his traces remain recorded here.
From here, traveling north for one thousand eight or nine hundred *li* along perilous roads that cross mountains and valleys, one reaches the kingdom of Lohurā.

From there, another two thousand *li* or so to the north—passing through difficult and obstructed routes where cold winds and flying snow prevail—one arrives at the kingdom of Malasa, also known as Sambhaha.

Traveling south from the kingdom of Kurughāra for more than seven hundred *li*, crossing a great mountain and crossing a large river, one arrives at the kingdom of Śatadru, within the borders of North India.
The country of Śatadru is more than two thousand *li* in circuit and borders a great river to the west.
The capital city of the country is seventeen or eighteen *li* in circuit.
The grain crops are abundant and the fruits are lush; there is much gold and silver, and precious pearls are produced there.
Their clothing and attire are bright and pure, while their garments are ornate and elegant.
The climate is hot, and the customs are simple and harmonious; the people are naturally kind and compliant, with a clear sense of order between superiors and subordinates.
They deeply believe in the Buddha-dharma and revere it with sincere hearts and genuine devotion.
Within and outside the royal city, there are ten monasteries; their courtyards and buildings are desolate, and the number of monks is very small.
Three or four *li* to the southeast of the city, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka.
Beside it are the sites containing the traces of where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation.
Proceeding again from here toward the southwest for more than eight hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Pāriyātra, within the borders of Central India.
The country of Pāriyātra is more than three thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit.
It is suitable for grain cultivation; winter wheat is abundant, and there is a special variety of rice that is harvested in sixty days.
Cattle and sheep abound, while flowers and fruits are scarce.
The climate is hot, and the customs are harsh and fierce.
The people do not esteem learning or the arts, and they follow non-Buddhist paths.
The king is of the Vaiśya caste; he is courageous and fierce by nature, and possesses great military skill.
There are eight monasteries here, most of which have fallen into severe ruin; the monks are few in number and study the Hīnayāna.
There are more than ten deva temples with over a thousand followers of heterodox paths.
Traveling east from here for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Mathurā, within the borders of Central India.
The country of Mathurā is over five thousand li in circuit.
Its capital city is more than twenty li in circuit. The soil is rich and fertile, and the people are devoted to agriculture.
In the house of this Āmra tree, it has grown into a grove; although they share the same name, there are two varieties:
the smaller kind is green when raw and turns yellow when ripe, while the larger kind remains green from beginning to end.
It produces fine cotton cloth and gold.
The climate is hot, and the customs are gentle and compliant; the people are fond of cultivating merit for the afterlife, honoring virtue, and valuing learning.
There are more than twenty monasteries with over two thousand monks, who study and practice both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles concurrently.
There are five deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
There are three stūpas, all of which were built by King Aśoka.
Relics of the four past Buddhas are very numerous here.

The reliquary stūpas containing the remains of the noble disciples of Śākyamuni Tathāgata include those of Śāriputra—formerly called Sheli-zi, and also Shelifu, which are erroneous abbreviations—and Maudgalyāyana—formerly called Mujianlian, which is an error—and Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, whose name in the language of Tang means "Son of Maitrāyaṇī."

"Mi-tuo-lo-ni-zi" (Maitrāyaṇīputra) is an abbreviation and corruption [of Maudgalyāyana]; "Ūpāli," "Ānanda," and "Luo-hu-lo" (Rāhula)—also called "Luo-yun"—are all corruptions and abbreviations; "Manjushri" translates into Chinese as "Miaojixiang" (Wondrous Auspiciousness).

Formerly called *Niu-shou* (濡首), also called *Wen-shu-shi-li* (文殊師利), or said to be *Man-zhu-shi-li* (曼殊尸利); translated as "Sublime Virtue" (*Miaode*), which is an erroneous [transliteration]. [This refers to] the stūpas and other monuments of the various bodhisattvas.

On the three long festivals of each year and during the six monthly fasts, the monastics vie with one another to lead their fellow devotees, bringing offerings and frequently procuring rare curiosities; according to their respective schools, they arrange and present ritual images.
The Abhidharma masters made offerings to Śāriputra;
those who practiced meditative concentration made offerings to Maudgalyāyana;
and those who recited and upheld the sūtras made offerings to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.
Those studying the Vinaya made offerings to Upāli;
the bhikṣuṇīs made offerings to Ānanda;
and those who had not yet received full ordination made offerings to Rāhula.
Those who study the Mahāyāna made offerings to the various bodhisattvas.

On this day, the stūpas vied with one another in their offerings: pearl banners were arrayed in rows, jeweled canopies were gathered in clusters, incense smoke rose like clouds, and flowers fell like rain, obscuring the sun and moon and shaking the mountain valleys.
The king and his ministers take the cultivation of goodness as their primary task.

Five or six *li* to the east of the city, one reaches a mountain monastery; with its cliffs serving as chambers and its valleys as gates, it was established by the Venerable Upagupta (translated into Chinese as Jìn hù, "Near Protection").
Within it is a stūpa containing the fingernails and toenails of the Tathāgata.
Between the cliffs to the north of the monastery is a stone chamber, over twenty feet high and over thirty feet wide, its interior filled with slender counting-slips four inches long.

Whenever the Venerable Upagupta preached the Dharma and converted a couple such that both attained the fruit of Arhatship, he would cast down a tally-stick; however, if they were from different households or distinct clans, even if they attained the fruit, it was not recorded.
Twenty-four or twenty-five *li* to the southeast of the stone chamber, one reaches the Great Dry Pond, beside which stands a stūpa.

In the past, when the Tathāgata was traveling through this place, there was a monkey who brought honey to offer to the Buddha; the Buddha had it mixed with water and distributed it to the entire assembly.
The monkey leaped for joy and fell into a pit where it died; by virtue of this merit, it was reborn among human beings.
Not far to the north of the pond, within a great forest, are the traces left by four past Buddhas as they walked to and fro.

Beside it are the places where one thousand two hundred and fifty great arhats, such as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, practiced meditative concentration; stupas have been erected at these sites to commemorate their traces.
During the Tathāgata’s lifetime, he frequently traveled to this country; at all the sites where he preached the Dharma, trees were planted and demarcated by boundary markers.
From here, traveling northeast for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Sthāneśvara, within the borders of Central India.
The country of Sātavāhana is more than seven thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is more than twenty *li* in circuit.
The soil is fertile and crops flourish in abundance.
The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are frivolous; households are wealthy and prosperous, vying with one another in luxury.
They are deeply skilled in the arts of illusion and highly regard extraordinary talents.
Most pursue profit while few are devoted to agriculture; consequently, rare commodities from all quarters are gathered in great abundance within this kingdom.
There are three monasteries with more than seven hundred monks, all of whom study and practice the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
There are more than a hundred deva temples, and those of various heterodox paths are very numerous.
Within a circumference of two hundred li surrounding the great city, the people of that land call it a "Land of Blessings.
According to what I have heard from the records of former sages:
In the past, two kings ruled separately over the five regions of India; their territories encroached upon one another, and the clash of arms never ceased.
The two lords conspired together, desiring to settle their superiority through military combat so as to bring peace to the common people.
The common people were all resentful and would not obey the king's commands.

The king thought to himself: "It is difficult to have the masses deliberate upon a new undertaking from the beginning; however, through the spirit one can move the masses, and through expedient means one can achieve success."

At that time, there was a brahmin who had long been known for his great talent; he secretly brought a bundle of silk and invited [the Master] into the rear garden to compose a book of Dharma, which was then concealed within mountain caves.
As time passed, the trees grew until they formed a canopy.
While seated at court, the King addressed his ministers, saying:

"Because of my lack of virtue, I have unworthily occupied this great throne. The Lord of Heaven has looked down upon me and granted me a sacred scripture in a dream; it is now located on a certain mountain, hidden within a certain ridge."
Thereupon, an order was issued to search for it, and the document was found beneath a mountain forest.
The officials celebrated its discovery, and the common people were filled with joy; it was proclaimed far and wide so that all might hear and know of it.
Its general outline states:
"Life and death have no shore, and the cycle of transmigration is without end; sentient beings are submerged and drowning, with no means by which to save themselves.
By means of my extraordinary stratagems, I shall cause them to depart from all suffering."
This royal city now spans two hundred li in circumference; it was a land of merit and blessing during the eras of former emperors.
As the years and months have passed so very long ago, the inscriptions have crumbled and vanished; living beings remain unaware of this, and thus they sink into the sea of suffering.
To see someone drowning and not rescue them—what can this be called?

You sentient beings, by facing the enemy and dying in battle, may be reborn among humans; by sparing the innocent, you receive heavenly blessings and joy; and by supporting your aged parents as dutiful grandsons and filial sons, you shall obtain inexhaustible merit upon passing through this place.
With little merit yet abundant blessings, how could one fail to gain advantage?
Once the human body is lost, the three realms of darkness lie in wait.
Therefore, all sentient beings should each strive to cultivate their practice!
Thereupon, all the men fought as soldiers, regarding death as returning home.
The king then issued an edict to recruit the brave and fierce; the two nations engaged in battle, and the accumulated corpses were like a wild thicket.
Down to the present day, skeletal remains cover the fields; as the times are ancient, the human skeletons are massive.
According to the traditions of the local customs, this place is called a "Land of Blessings."
Four or five *li* to the northwest of the city, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka.

Its bricks are all yellowish-red and exceedingly lustrous and clean. Within it are one *dou* of the Tathāgata’s relics, which occasionally emit a brilliant light; its miraculous manifestations are manifold.
Traveling more than one hundred li south of the city, one arrives at the Kukkuṭapāda Monastery.
Its multi-storied pavilions have interconnected eaves, and tiered terraces stand in alternating heights.
The monks are pure and disciplined, their deportment serene and elegant.
From here, traveling northeast for more than four hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Śrughna, within the borders of Central India.
The kingdom of Śrughna is over six thousand *li* in circuit; it borders the Gaṅgā River to the east and has a great mountain to its north, with the Yamunā River flowing through its center.
The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty li in circuit; it borders the Yamunā River to the east. Although it is extremely desolate, its foundations remain firm.
Regarding the products of the soil and the climate of the region, they are the same as those of the kingdom of Sthāneśvara.
The people are simple and honest by nature and revere and believe in non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas).
They value arts and learning, and esteem merit and wisdom.
There are five monasteries with over a thousand monks; most study the Hīnayāna, while few practice other schools.
They deliberate upon subtle words and engage in pure discourse regarding profound mysteries; eminent scholars from various regions seek out these discussions to resolve their doubts.
There are one hundred deva temples, and followers of diverse paths are exceedingly numerous.
To the southeast of the great city, west of the Yamunā River and outside the eastern gate of a large monastery, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka.
In the past, the Tathāgata once preached the Dharma and delivered sentient beings at this very spot.
Beside it is another stūpa, within which are the hair and nail-clippings of the Tathāgata.
To the left and right [of this site], there are more than several dozen stūpas containing the hair and nail relics of Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and other arhats.
After the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa, this country was led astray by various non-Buddhist teachers; they accepted false doctrines and abandoned the correct view.
As for the five monasteries existing here today, they were established because this was the site where a master of logic from another country defeated various non-Buddhists and Brahmins in debate.

Traveling eastward from the Yamunā River for more than eight hundred li, one reaches the source of the Gaṅgā River, which is three or four li wide; where it flows southeast into the sea, its width is over ten li.

The color of the water is a deep azure; its waves flow vast and expansive. Although many spirits and monsters dwell therein, they do no harm to living beings. Its taste is sweet and delicious, and fine sand drifts along with the current.
According to their secular records, it is called "Water of Merit": though one's transgressions may have accumulated, they are removed by bathing in it;
by casting one's life into it, one is reborn in heaven to receive blessings;
and by casting one's remains there after death, one does not fall into the evil realms.
As the waves surged and the currents raged, the departed souls were delivered across.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Deva from Siṃhala, who had profoundly realized the true nature of reality and attained the essence of all dharmas, came here out of compassion for the ignorant to guide and convert them.
At that time, men and women had all gathered, and people of all ages assembled by the riverbank to splash the waves and stir the swift currents.
Bodhisattva Deva joined them in the common practice of drawing water, yet he bent his head and drew the water upward in a manner that differed from the others.
A non-Buddhist practitioner said,
"Why are you so strange, my son?
Deva Bodhisattva replied:
"My parents and kinsmen are in the kingdom of Śrīlaṅkā; fearing they may suffer from hunger and thirst, I hope for their distant rescue.
The non-Buddhists said, "My son, you are mistaken!"
Never having reflected further, you have rashly carried out this matter.

The distance between our home and the state is vast, and the mountains and rivers are remote; to divert this water here in order to relieve the hunger there is like walking backward while seeking to catch up with those ahead—it is something I have never heard of.
The Bodhisattva Deva said:
"If those on the dark path who are burdened by their sins still receive the benefit of this water,
how could it not save us when the mountains and rivers, though obstructive, stand between us?"

At that time, the non-Buddhist practitioners, realizing they were defeated and unable to respond, abandoned their heterodox views and accepted the True Dharma. Reforming themselves and seeking new beginnings, they vowed to receive his instruction.
Crossing to the eastern bank of the river, they arrived at the kingdom of Mathurā within the borders of Central India.
The Kingdom of Mathurā: The kingdom of Mathurā is more than six thousand *li* in circuit.
Its capital city is over twenty *li* in circuit.
It is suitable for growing grain and wheat, and abounds in flowers and fruits.
The climate is harmonious and pleasant, and the customs are pure and simple.
The people revere learning and the arts, and are deeply proficient in incantations and esoteric techniques.
Those who believe in heterodox teachings and those who follow the orthodox path are about equal in number.
The king is of the Śūdra caste; he does not believe in the Buddha-dharma and reverently serves the heavenly deities.
There are more than ten monasteries with over eight hundred monks, most of whom study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna teachings.
There are more than fifty deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
Four or five li to the south of the great city, one reaches a small monastery with over fifty monks.
In the past, the master of śāstras Guṇaprabha—translated into Chinese as Deguang (Virtuous Light)—composed more than one hundred treatises here, such as the *Tattvasaṃdeśa* (*Bian zhen lun*).

From his youth, the master was brilliant and outstanding; as he grew, he became expansive and sagacious. He was erudite and possessed a powerful memory, being a scholar of vast learning and great renown.

Originally practicing the Mahāyāna, I had not yet exhausted its profound mysteries; however, upon reading the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, I abandoned my studies and turned to the Hīnayāna, composing dozens of treatises to undermine the fundamental principles of the Mahāyāna and establish attachments to the Hīnayāna.
Furthermore, he composed several dozen secular works that disparaged and rejected the "Discourses on the Classics" (Dian lun) written by his predecessors.
He pondered the Buddhist sutras with deep reflection; though he had not resolved ten or so points despite long and diligent study, his state of doubt remained unresolved.
At that time, there was an arhat named Devaśarman (translated into Chinese as Tiānjūn, "Celestial Army"), who traveled back and forth to the Tuṣita Heaven.
Guṇaprabha wished to see Maitreya in order to resolve his doubts and seek further instruction.
By means of his supernormal powers, Tianjun transported him up to the celestial palace.
Upon seeing Maitreya, he merely performed a long bow and did not prostrate.
Tianjun said to him:
“Maitreya Bodhisattva is next in line to succeed to the Buddha’s position; how can he be so self-important as to dare not pay his respects?
As you are about to receive instruction from him, why do you not bow?”
Guṇaprabha replied, "Venerable sir, your words are indeed instructive.

However, I am a bhikṣu who has received the full precepts and a disciple who has left the household life. Since the Bodhisattva Maitreya enjoys celestial blessings and happiness, he is not a fellow practitioner of the renunciant life; I fear it would be inappropriate for me to pay him homage."
The Bodhisattva, knowing that his pride was so firmly rooted that he was not a vessel for hearing the Dharma, went back and forth three times but could not resolve his doubts.
He requested Deva-sena once more, wishing to pay him further homage.
Devasena detested his arrogance and treated him with contempt, refusing to respond.

Since his desire was not fulfilled, Devaruci gave rise to resentment; he immediately retired to the mountain forests to cultivate the supernormal powers of meditative concentration, yet because his pride had not been eliminated, he did not realize the fruits of the Path.

Three or four li to the north of the De-guang Monastery is a large monastery with more than two hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna; this is the place where the master of śāstras Saṃghabhadra passed away.

The Master was a native of Kaśmīra; he was intelligent and widely learned, enjoying an esteemed reputation from his youth, and had conducted particularly profound research into the *Sarvāstivāda-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

At that time, there was the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, who focused his mind on the profound Way and sought understanding beyond the literal words. He refuted the tenets held by the Vaibhāṣika masters and composed the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, which is skillful in both diction and meaning, and sublime in its logical principles.
As Saṃghabhadra perused [the *Abhidharmakośa*], he eventually conceived the intent [to refute it].

Thereupon, he immersed himself in profound study and exhaustive investigation for twelve years, composing the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra-śataka-śāstra* (The Hundred-Verse Treatise on the *Kośa*) in twenty-five thousand stanzas, totaling eight hundred thousand words.
His words were profound and far-reaching, exhausting the mysteries and penetrating the subtle.
He told his disciples:
"With my exceptional talent and my orthodox arguments, I shall expel Vasubandhu and blunt his sharp edge, ensuring that this old man does not alone monopolize preeminence."
Thereupon, three or four of the most eminent disciples among the followers took the treatise they had composed and went in search of Vasubandhu.
At that time, Vasubandhu was in the city of Śākala in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā; his reputation had spread far and wide, and it was rumored that Saṃghabhadra was about to arrive.
Having heard this, Vasubandhu immediately prepared his travel gear.
His disciples, harboring doubts, came forward to remonstrate with him, saying:
"The Master’s virtue surpasses that of former sages, and your fame is preeminent in this age; there are no students, near or far, who do not pay you their respects."
"Now that we hear of Saṃghabhadra, why such alarm?
He must have been defeated; we are indeed shameless.
Vasubandhu said:
"I am now traveling far away, not to avoid this man.
Looking throughout this land, there is no longer anyone capable of presiding over the debate.
Zhongxian is but a junior scholar whose deceptive sophistry flows like a stream; I am old and decrepit, and none can uphold the argument against him."

Desiring to overturn their heterodox tenets with a single word, he led them to Central India to confront the eminent scholars there, so that the true and the false might be examined and gain and loss thoroughly scrutinized.
He immediately summoned his companions and set out on a long journey, carrying his book-case.

On the day following [Vasubandhu’s departure], the master of śāstras Saṃghabhadra arrived at this monastery; suddenly feeling his strength waning, he composed a letter to apologize to Vasubandhu, saying:

"Since the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa, his disciples have held various sectarian tenets. As they transmitted his teachings, each has specialized in their own field, favoring those of the same school and viewing other sects with hostility."

Being foolish and of meager understanding, I have nonetheless inherited the traditional teachings. Having perused the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* you composed—which refutes the great principles of the Vaibhāṣika masters—I have ventured, despite my lack of capacity, to investigate the matter deeply over many years and have thus produced this treatise to support the study of the orthodox school.
When one of small wisdom plots for great matters, death is bound to arrive.

The Bodhisattva proclaims subtle words and elevates the ultimate truth; that he did not destroy what he upheld and that his writings remain preserved is indeed fortunate—what cause for regret should there be in death?
Thereupon, he selected from among his disciples those who were eloquent and addressed them, saying:
"I am truly but a junior scholar, yet I have treated my predecessors with contempt; what can be done about such a fate?"
"I shall now pass away from this life!
You must take these letters and the treatises I have composed, offer my apologies to that Bodhisattva, and repent on my behalf.
As soon as he had finished speaking these words, he suddenly passed away.
The disciples delivered the letter to Vasubandhu and conveyed these words:
"Our teacher Saṃghabhadra has already passed away.
In his final testament, he sent this letter, reproaching himself and apologizing for his faults."
"That he should not fall from his reputation is something I did not dare to hope for.
Upon reading the letter and examining the treatise, Master Vasubandhu pondered it for a long time and said to his disciples:
"The master Saṃghabhadra is a brilliant junior; though his reasoning may be insufficient, his rhetoric is indeed abundant."
I now wish to refute the arguments of Saṃghabhadra; it would be as easy as pointing at something on one's palm.

Yet, out of regard for his final testament and the weight of his words acknowledging the difficulty of the task, I shall, for the sake of the Great Meaning, preserve his original intention—how much more so since this treatise elucidates my own school?
He then changed the title to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*.
His disciples remonstrated, saying:
"While Saṃghabhadra has not yet passed away, you have gone far away; now that you have obtained his treatise and further changed its title, how can all of us disciples bear the shame?"
The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, wishing to dispel the doubts of the assembly, spoke in verse:
"Just as the lion king flees far away from the boar, the wise should understand the victory or defeat of these two powers."
After Saṃghabhadra had died, his body was cremated and his bones collected; a stūpa was erected in an āmra grove some two hundred paces northwest of the monastery, which still exists today.
Beside the Āmra grove is a stūpa containing the remains of the master of śāstras, Vimalamitra (translated into Chinese as Wugouyou).
This master was a native of Kaśmīra and entered the monastic order within the Sarvāstivāda school.

He had extensively mastered the various sutras and investigated divergent doctrines; having traveled through the five regions of India and studied the profound texts of the Tripitaka, his reputation was established and his studies completed, and he was about to return to his native land.
Along the way, he came to the stūpa of the Master of Śāstras Saṃghabhadra; touching it, he sighed and said:

"Only this master possessed such noble magnanimity and pure loftiness, upholding the great principles. Just as he was about to subdue the heterodox schools and establish the foundation of his own school’s teachings, how tragic that his allotted years were not long!"
I, Vimalamitra, though but a humble recipient of the final teachings, have long admired his righteousness and cherished his virtue for generations.

Although Vasubandhu has passed away, his school and learning still endure; therefore, I shall exhaust all that I know to compose various treatises, so as to cause the scholars of Jambudvīpa to cease their praise of the Mahāyāna and extinguish the name of Vasubandhu. This shall be my enduring legacy, fulfilling my lifelong aspiration.
Having spoken these words, his mind became deranged; five tongues protruded from his mouth, and hot blood gushed forth.
Knowing that his life would surely end, he composed a letter of repentance, saying:
"The Mahāyāna teaching is the ultimate exposition within the Buddha-dharma."
Names and flavors have been extinguished, and the underlying principles are profound and mysterious.
Out of my own ignorance, I rashly refuted the teachings of the predecessors; as the retribution for such karma is starkly evident, it is fitting that my body be extinguished.
"I venture to inform you students: the mirror of discernment lies herein. Each of you must be cautious regarding your resolve; do not harbor doubts.
As he spoke, the great earth shook, and his life came to an end.
At the place where he died, the ground collapsed to form a pit.
His fellow travelers cremated his body, collected the remains, and erected a memorial stele.
At that time, an Arhat saw this and sighed, saying:
"Alas! What suffering!
This present master of treatises, following his own whims and clinging to his views, slanders and reviles the Mahāyāna and shall fall into the Avīci Hell."
To the northwest of the kingdom, on the eastern bank of the Gaṅgā River, lies the city of Mathurā, more than twenty li in circuit.
Its inhabitants are numerous and prosperous; it is encircled by clear, flowing waters and produces brass, crystal, and precious vessels.
Not far from the city, bordering the Gaṅgā River, there is a great temple of Mahādeva that is filled with many miraculous wonders.

Within it is a pond with stone embankments, replenished by water drawn from the Gaṅgā; the people of the five Indias call this the "Gate of the Gaṅgā," a place for generating merit and extinguishing transgressions.
There are always several hundred thousand people from distant regions who gather here to bathe.

Benevolent kings, delighting in goodness, have established houses of merit, providing rare delicacies and storing medicines; they bestow gifts upon widowers and widows and provide for the solitary and destitute.
From here, traveling north for more than three hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Brahmapura, within the borders of North India.
The kingdom of Brahmapura is over four thousand *li* in circuit, and its four boundaries are surrounded by mountains.
The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty li in circuit.
Its inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and the households are wealthy.
The soil is fertile, and crops are sown according to the seasons; it produces brass and crystal.
The climate is slightly cold, and the customs are harsh and fierce.
Few pursue the arts of learning; most chase after profit.
The nature of the people is wild and violent, and they believe in both heterodoxy and orthodoxy with equal fervor.
There are five monasteries with few monks.
There are more than ten deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
To the north of this country’s borders, within the Great Snow Mountains, lies the kingdom of Suvarṇagotra (translated into Chinese as Jīnshì, "Gold-clan").
It produces superior gold, and is thus named after it.
It is long from east to west and narrow from south to north; this is the Kingdom of the Eastern Women (Dongnüguo).
The world has designated the country by the name of its women for generations.
Its ruler is also a king who is ignorant of the affairs of government; the men concern themselves only with military expeditions and agriculture.
The soil is suitable for winter wheat, and they raise many sheep and horses.
The climate is harsh and severe, and the people are impetuous and violent by nature.
To the east it borders the kingdom of Tufan (Tibet), to the north it borders the kingdom of Yutian (Khotan), and to the west it borders the kingdom of Sambhaha.
Traveling southeast from Matipura for more than four hundred *li*, one arrives at Jābūśāna, within the territory of Central India.
The country of Goviśanā is more than two thousand *li* in circuit.

Its capital city is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit; it is lofty, steep, and strongly fortified. The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and flowering groves and ponds are interspersed here and there.
The climate and natural products are similar to those of the country of Mathurā.
The customs are simple and honest; the people are diligent in study and fond of merit.
Most believe in non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika) and seek happiness in the present life.
There are two monasteries with more than one hundred monks, all of whom study and practice the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
There are over thirty deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
Within an old monastery beside the great city, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, over two hundred feet in height.
In the past, the Tathāgata stayed here for one month and expounded the essentials of the Dharma; nearby are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas.
Beside it are two stūpas containing the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata, each over one zhang in height.
From here, traveling southeast for more than four hundred li, one arrives at the country of Ākṣaṭrā, within the borders of India.
The country of Ākṣaśītra is over three thousand *li* in circuit. Its capital city is seventeen or eighteen *li* in circuit;
it is situated upon a secure and fortified site, is suitable for growing grain and wheat, and abounds in forests and springs.
The climate is harmonious and pleasant, and the local customs are simple and sincere.
The people delight in the Way and are devoted to learning; they are many-talented and possess broad knowledge.
There are more than ten monasteries with over a thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
There are nine deva temples with more than three hundred followers of heterodox paths who worship Maheśvara; they are the ash-smearing companions (Pāśupatas).
Beside the Dragon Pond outside the city is a stūpa, built by King Aśoka.
In the past, when the Tathāgata was a dragon king, he preached the Dharma here for seven days.
Beside it are four small stūpas, which mark the sites where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation.
From here, traveling east for two hundred and sixty or seventy *li* and crossing the Gaṅgā River, one arrives southward at the kingdom of Vīraṇā, within the borders of Central India.
The kingdom of Vīraṇā (also known as Vīraśanā) is more than two thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over ten li in circuit.
Its climate and natural products are the same as those of the country of Axi Che’ta.
The customs are fierce and violent, yet the people are knowledgeable in learning and the arts.
They have great faith in non-Buddhist paths and little respect for the Buddha-dharma.
There are two monasteries with three hundred monks, all of whom study and practice the teachings of the Mahāyāna.
There are five deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
Within the old monastery in the great city, there is the foundation of a stūpa; although it has collapsed, it is still over a hundred feet high, having been built by King Aśoka.
This is the place where the Tathāgata in the past preached the *Skandhadhātvāyatanasūtra* for seven days.
Beside it are the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas; their vestiges remain here.
From here, traveling southeast for more than two hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Kāpiśī (formerly called Saṃkāśya).
It lies within the borders of Central India.
The kingdom of Kāpiśī is more than two thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty *li* in circuit.
Its climate and natural products are similar to those of the kingdom of Vīraṇā.
The customs are pure and harmonious, and the people are largely devoted to learning and the arts.
There are four monasteries with more than a thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
There are ten deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths live together, collectively worshipping Maheśvara.

More than twenty li to the west of the city is a great monastery, its construction magnificent and its craftsmanship perfected through intricate carving; the sacred forms and honored images therein are dedicated to the utmost solemnity and splendor.
There are several hundred monks who study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school.
Tens of thousands of *śrāmaṇeras* (lay attendants) reside in dwellings adjacent to it.

Within the great enclosure of the monastery are three jeweled staircases aligned north to south, descending toward the east; these are where the Tathāgata descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven upon his return.

In the past, the Tathāgata rose from the Śītavana Grove and ascended to the celestial palace, where he dwelt in the Sudharmā Hall to preach the Dharma for his mother; after three months had passed, he was about to descend.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, then exerted his supernatural power to construct jeweled stairways: the central one of gold, the left of crystal, and the right of white silver.
When the Tathāgata rose from the Hall of Good Dharma, he descended with the assembly of devas by treading upon the central stairway;
Mahābrahmā, holding a white fly-whisk, followed on the right, treading upon the silver stairway as an attendant.
Śakra, Lord of Devas, held a precious parasol and attended on the left, treading upon crystal steps;
the celestial hosts hovered in the void, scattering flowers and praising his virtues.
Several hundred years ago, these steps still existed, but by the present time, they have completely subsided and vanished.

The kings of various nations, lamenting their failure to meet [the Buddha] in person, piled up bricks and stones and adorned them with precious jewels; upon the old foundations, they modeled a jeweled staircase after the ancient one, reaching a height of over seventy feet, and erected a vihāra at its summit.

Within it is a stone image of the Buddha, with images of Śakra and Brahmā on the steps to its left and right; their forms are modeled after those of the original [statues], yet they still appear inferior in stature.
Beside it stands a stone pillar over seventy feet high, erected by King Aśoka.

The pillars are deep blue in color, lustrous, and of solid, dense grain; at their tops are carved lions crouching toward the steps, with intricate carvings of wondrous forms adorning all four sides, which manifest reflections according to the sins and merits of people within the columns.
Not far from the side of the jeweled staircase is a stūpa, which marks the site where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation.
Beside it is another stūpa, where the Tathāgata bathed in former times.
Beside it is a vihāra, which is the place where the Tathāgata entered meditative concentration.
Beside the vihāra is a large rock, fifty paces in length at its base and seven feet in height; this is the place where the Tathāgata walked in meditation.
The footprints left wherever he stepped were all marked with the pattern of lotus flowers.
To the left and right of the base, there are small stūpas, each erected by Śakra and Brahmā.
In front of the stūpa of Śakra and Brahmā is the place where the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā transformed herself into a Cakravartin King in order to be the first to see the Buddha.
When the Tathāgata was returning from the celestial palace to Jambudvīpa, there was at that time Subhūti (translated into Chinese as Shànxiàn, "Good Manifestation").
Formerly called Subhūti, or sometimes Subhadda, translated as "Good Fortune" (Śubhamati), all of which are corruptions. While sitting in meditation within a stone chamber, he thought to himself:
"Now that the Buddha has returned in descent, attended by humans and devas, what course of action is appropriate for one such as I?"
"I have heard it said that when one understands that all phenomena are empty and realizes the nature of all phenomena, this is to behold the Dharma-body with the eye of wisdom.

At that time, the Bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, wishing to be the first to see the Buddha, transformed herself into a Wheel-Turning King, preceded by the seven treasures and escorted by the fourfold army; she went to the place where the World-Honored One was and then resumed her form as a Bhikṣuṇī.
The Tathāgata said:
"It is not that you have not seen it before.
One who is truly 'Well-Appeared' (Subhūti) contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena; this is the seeing of the Dharma-body."
Within the enclosure of the holy sites, miraculous manifestations occurred in succession.
To the southeast of the Great Stūpa, there was a dragon pond that constantly guarded the sacred traces.
Since these were protected by spiritual powers, they were difficult to violate lightly; though many years passed and they decayed of their own accord, no human being could destroy them.
From here, traveling southeast for less than two hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Kanyakubja (in the language of Tang, the Kingdom of the Crooked Woman’s City).
This is within the borders of Central India.
From the *Great Tang Records on the Western Regions*, Volume IV.
*The Great Tang Dynasty Record of the Western Regions*, Volume Five: Six Kingdoms.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree;
compiled by the Śramaṇa Bianji of Dazongchi Monastery.

The six kingdoms are: the kingdom of Kanyakubja, the kingdom of Ayodhyā, the kingdom of Ajamukha, the kingdom of Prayāga, the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, and the kingdom of Viśākha. As for the kingdom of Kanyakubja, it is more than four thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom borders the Gaṅgā River to the west; it is over twenty li in length and four or five li in width.
The city walls and moats are firm and steep, with watchtowers and pavilions facing one another, while flower groves and ponds are as bright and clear as polished mirrors.
Rare goods from distant lands are gathered here in great abundance.
The inhabitants live in prosperity and joy, and their households are wealthy and well-provided for.
Flowers and fruits flourish in profusion, and crops are sown according to the seasons.
The seasonal cycles are harmonious and agreeable, and the customs are pure and simple.
The people’s countenances are beautiful and elegant, and their clothing is bright and ornate.
They are devoted to learning and the cultivation of the arts, and their discourse is refined and profound.
Between the heterodox and orthodox paths, those who follow each are roughly equal in number.
There are over a hundred monasteries with more than ten thousand monks, who study and practice both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles concurrently.
There are more than two hundred deva temples and several thousand followers of heterodox paths.
During the time when the people of Kanyakubja enjoyed long lifespans, the old royal city was called Kusumapura, which in the language of Tang means "Flower Palace."

The king was named Brahmadatta; endowed with the long-cultivated merit and wisdom of his past lives, he was fully prepared in both civil and military arts. His majesty intimidated all of Jambudvīpa, and his fame resounded throughout neighboring kingdoms.
He possessed a thousand sons, wise, brave, magnanimous, and resolute, as well as a hundred daughters of exquisite and elegant appearance.

At that time, there was a rishi dwelling on the banks of the Gaṅgā River who had settled his mind in meditative absorption for tens of thousands of years. His body was like withered wood, and migratory birds gathered to roost upon him; they dropped nyagrodha fruits onto the rishi’s shoulders, and as the seasons passed from summer to winter, the spreading shade formed a canopy several armspans wide.

Having spent many years in this state, he arose from meditative concentration; wishing to depart, he feared that removing the tree would destroy the birds' nests. The people of the time praised his virtue and called him the Great Tree Seer (Mahādruma-ṛṣi).

The rishi cast his gaze toward the riverbank and strolled through the thickets, where he saw the king’s daughters playing together. Lust arose within him and a mind of defiled attachment was born; he then went to the Flower Palace, desiring to offer his request for union.

When the king heard that the seer had arrived, he went in person to welcome him and comforted him, saying, "Great Seer, you dwell your mind beyond the mundane world; how could you have come so lightly?
The seer replied:

"I have dwelt in the forest thickets for many years; while wandering abroad after emerging from meditative concentration, I beheld the king's daughters, and a mind of defiled attachment arose within me. Therefore, I have come from afar to request [their hand]."
When the king heard these words, he was at a loss for a solution and said to the rishi,
"Please return to your dwelling and wait for an auspicious day.
Having received this command, the rishi returned to the forest retreats.
The king then questioned all his daughters one by one, but none was willing to accept his proposal.
Fearing the power of the seer, he became sorrowful and grew haggard with grief.
One of his youngest daughters, taking advantage of a lull in the king’s affairs, asked him calmly:
"The King, my father, possesses a full thousand sons and ten thousand nations admire his transformative influence; for what reason do you grieve so sorrowfully, as if fearing something?
The King replied, "The Great Tree Rishi has fortunately come to seek a marriage alliance with us, yet none among you are willing to obey his command."

The immortals possess awesome power and can bring about both calamities and auspiciousness; should their desires not be fulfilled, they will surely give rise to wrath, destroying the state, extinguishing the ancestral sacrifices, and bringing disgrace upon the former kings.
Reflecting deeply on this calamity, I am truly filled with apprehension.
The younger daughter replied,
“To leave you with such profound anxiety is our own fault.”
"I pray that with this humble body, I may prolong the destiny of the state.
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy and ordered his carriage to escort him back.
Once he arrived at the immortal’s abode, he thanked the immortal, saying:
"The Great Seer has looked beyond worldly affairs yet cast his gaze upon this world; I venture to offer my young daughter to serve as your attendant.
Upon seeing her, the Seer was displeased and said to the King, "You slight me, an old man, by matching me with one so unattractive."
The king said,
"I have questioned all the women one by one, but none was willing to obey my command.
Only this young girl wishes to serve as a handmaid."
The seer, harboring anger, uttered a malevolent curse:
"May ninety-nine daughters have their waists simultaneously become crooked; their forms thus ruined and degraded, may they remain unmarried for the rest of their lives."
The king sent messengers to investigate, and it was found that he had indeed become hunchbacked.
From that time on, the city was named Kanyākubja (Curved Woman City).
The current king is originally of the Vaiśya caste; his name is Harṣavardhana, which in the language of Tang means "Joy-Increaser."
Ruling over the land, there were two generations and three kings.

His father’s name was Prabhākaravardhana (translated into Chinese as Zuoguāngzēng, "Increasing the Light"), and his elder brother’s name was Rājyavardhana (translated into Chinese as Wángzēng, "Increasing the King").
Rājyavardhana succeeded to the throne as the eldest son and governed the realm with virtue.
At that time, King Śaśāṅka—known in the language of Tang as Yue (Moon)—of Karṇasuvarṇa (known in the language of Tang as Jinyier, or "Golden Ear") in Eastern India, frequently said to his ministers:
"To have a wise sovereign as a neighbor is a calamity for a state."
Thereupon, they invited him under false pretenses, assembled for the occasion, and murdered him.
Once the people had lost their ruler, the kingdom fell into chaos and disorder.
At that time, there was a great minister named Bāṇi (translated into Chinese as Biànliǎo), whose official rank and reputation were most eminent; he addressed his colleagues and subordinates, saying:
"The great plan of the state is settled this day.

The son of a former king and younger brother of the deceased sovereign possesses benevolence as his natural disposition and filial piety as his innate heart; being both a kinsman and a man of virtue, he is worthy to succeed to the throne."
"As for this matter,
what are your respective intentions?
The assembly, all admiring his virtue, never harbored any divergent plans.
Thereupon, the assisting ministers and officials all urged him forward, saying:
"May the Prince lend us his ear. Our late king accumulated merit and virtue, and thus brilliantly possessed the mandate of the state.
It has now passed to Your Majesty, Bimbisāra, who was expected to enjoy a long and full life; yet—"
To have served as an assistant without integrity, resulting in the loss of his life at the hands of an enemy, is a great disgrace to the state and the fault of this humble servant.
Public opinion and contemporary ballads alike point toward the Virtuous and Enlightened One as the rightful recipient of authority.

Having graced our realm with your presence, you have been able to reconcile even with one’s own enemy, wiping away the nation's shame and illuminating your father’s legacy; what achievement could be greater than this?
We pray that you will not decline our request!
The prince said, "The gravity of the succession to the throne has been difficult throughout both ancient and modern times; the position of a sovereign must be established with careful deliberation.
I am truly of meager virtue, having been abandoned by my father and elder brother; if I were to be urged to inherit the great office, would I be able to succeed?"
Public opinion deems this appropriate; how could I dare forget my own insignificance?
Now, on the banks of the Ganges, there is an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva which is renowned for its many miraculous responses; I wish to go there and request his leave.
He immediately went before the image of the Bodhisattva and fasted, offering prayers.
Moved by his sincere heart, the Bodhisattva manifested his form and asked:
"What do you seek that you are so earnest and diligent?"
The prince said:
"I alone have accumulated calamities; my compassionate father has passed away, and now, upon this further cruel punishment, my benevolent elder brother has been slain."
Reflecting upon my own meager virtue, the people of this land have honored me by enjoining me to succeed to the great throne and illuminate my father’s legacy.
Being ignorant and lacking wisdom, how could I dare hope for Your Majesty’s decree?
The Bodhisattva said:
"In a previous life, you were an aranyaka bhikṣu in this very forest, practicing with diligence and without slackening.
By the power of that merit, you have become this prince."

"Since King Suvarṇakarṇa has already destroyed the Buddha-dharma, you, upon succeeding to the throne, ought to cause it to flourish once more. Make compassion your resolve and take pity as your inner motive; before long, you shall rule over the realms of the five regions of India."
If you wish to prolong the destiny of the state, you must follow my instruction; then hidden blessings will be added in abundance, and neighboring powers shall have no formidable enemies.
Do not ascend the lion throne, and do not assume the title of Great King.

Thereupon, having received these instructions, he withdrew and immediately ascended the throne; he styled himself Prince and was known by the title Śīlāditya, which in the language of Tang means "Virtue-Sun."
Thereupon he said to his ministers:
"The vengeance for my elder brother’s enemy has not yet been taken, and neighboring states remain unsubmissive; thus, there will never be a time when a right hand may advance food to me.
You, all you officials, must be of one mind and exert your strength together."
He then mobilized the entire national army and trained his warriors.
With five thousand elephant troops, twenty thousand cavalry, and fifty thousand infantry, he marched from west to east to subjugate those who were not subject to his rule.
Without the elephants shedding their saddles and the men removing their armor, he brought the five regions of India under his臣 (vassalage) within six years.
Having expanded his territory, he further increased his troops and weaponry.
He commanded sixty thousand elephant troops and one hundred thousand cavalry.

For nearly thirty years, weapons were not raised; the administration and teachings were peaceful and harmonious. He devoted himself to practicing frugality, cultivating merit and performing good deeds, forgetting both sleep and food.
He decreed that throughout the five regions of India, no meat was to be consumed; should anyone take life, they were to be executed without pardon.
Along the banks of the Gaṅgā River, he erected several thousand stūpas, each over a hundred feet in height.

In the cities, towns, villages, lanes, and crossroads of the five regions of India, he established hermitages, stored food and drink, and provided medical supplies; he bestowed alms upon the destitute and the poor, providing for them exhaustively and without ceasing.
At these sites of sacred traces, monasteries were established in each location.

Every five years, a Great Unrestricted Assembly (Pañcavārṣika) was convened; the treasuries were completely emptied to bestow gifts upon all living beings, with the sole exception that weapons were not included among the offerings.

Once every year, śramaṇas from various kingdoms would assemble for a period of twenty-one days, where they were provided with the four requisites of support. They would adorn the Dharma seat and extensively decorate the assembly for debate, causing them to engage in mutual refutation and discussion to evaluate their relative strengths and weaknesses, praise the virtuous and censure the depraved, and demote the obscure while promoting the enlightened.
If one’s observance of the precepts is steadfast and their virtue profound, he shall be elevated to the Lion Throne, and the King will personally receive the Dharma from him.
Even if one’s precepts are pure, if his learning lacks antiquity, the King will merely offer him respectful salutations to show honor.
However, if one’s discipline is disordered and their corrupt character is manifest, they shall be driven out of the kingdom’s borders, for the King has no desire to hear or see them.

The neighboring small kings and their assisting ministers cultivate merit without ceasing and seek the good without regard for toil; thus they join hands and sit together, calling one another "virtuous friends.
Those who differ from this do not exchange words face-to-face; when there are matters to be discussed, they communicate through the sending and receiving of envoys.
He traveled through the various regions to inspect the local customs, never remaining in one place; wherever he halted, he would construct a thatched hut for his dwelling.
Only during the three months of the rainy season did he refrain from traveling due to the heavy rains.
Every day at his temporary palace, he prepared exquisite delicacies to provide meals for one thousand monastics and five hundred Brahmins.

He divided each day into three periods: during one period he attended to administrative affairs and governance; during two periods he cultivated merit and practiced virtue. He was diligent and tireless, never feeling that the day had been exhausted.
Initially, having accepted the invitation of King Kumāra, he traveled from the kingdom of Magadha to the kingdom of Kāmarūpa.
At that time, King Śīlāditya was on a tour of inspection in the kingdom of Kajughira and commanded King Kumāra, saying:
"You should have the visiting śramaṇas from Nālandā come quickly to attend the assembly."
Thereupon, he went with King Kumāra to meet him.
After King Śīlāditya had greeted him with words of comfort, he asked:
"From which country have you come, and what is it that you seek?"
He replied,
"I have come from the land of the Great Tang to seek the Buddha-dharma.
The King said:
"Where is the land of the Great Tang?
How far is it from here, and what is the route that leads there?
He replied:
"To the northeast of here, at a distance of several tens of thousands of *li*, lies the land known in India as Mahācīna. The King said,
"I have heard that in the land of Mahācīna there is the Son of Heaven, the Qin Emperor, who was spiritually perceptive in his youth and divinely martial in his maturity."

In the past, during the chaos and turmoil of former dynasties, the entire realm was fragmented and collapsed; weapons of war rose up in competition, and all living beings were subjected to bitter suffering. Yet the Son of Heaven, the King of Qin, early on conceived far-reaching strategies and gave rise to great compassion to rescue and deliver all sentient beings. He brought peace and stability to within the seas, and his moral teachings spread to distant lands while his virtuous bounty reached afar; those from strange regions and foreign domains admired his transformation and submitted as vassals.
The common people have been sustained by his nurturing care and all sing the "Qin Wang Po Zhen Le.
We have heard its refined odes for a long time now.
Is the reputation of his magnificent virtue indeed well-founded?
"Is this, perhaps, the Great Tang Kingdom?
He replied, "Indeed it is."
"Zhìnà" (Cīna) was the dynastic name of former kings;
"Dàtáng" (Great Tang) is the title of my sovereign's realm.
Formerly, before I ascended the throne, I was called the King of Qin."
Now that I have inherited the succession, I am styled the Son of Heaven.
When the mandate of former dynasties came to an end, the myriad beings were left without a ruler; weapons of war arose in chaos, bringing destruction and harm to living creatures.

The King of Qin was naturally endowed with vast magnanimity, his heart giving rise to compassion; his majestic influence spread far and wide, utterly exterminating the multitude of wicked ones, bringing tranquility to the eight directions, and causing the myriad nations to bring tribute.

He nurtured the four classes of living beings and revered the Triple Gem; he lightened taxes and reduced punishments, such that state resources were more than sufficient and the common people lived in peace. His moral influence and great transformation were too vast to be recounted in full detail.
King Śīlāditya said,
"How magnificent!
The sentient beings of that land have moved a holy sovereign by their merit."

At that time, King Śīlāditya, intending to return to the city of Kanyākubja, was holding a dharma assembly with a multitude of several hundred thousand followers on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā River.
King Kumāra, accompanied by a multitude of several tens of thousands, remained on the northern bank.
Dividing the middle of the river, they advanced both by water and land.
The two kings led the way, while the fourfold army provided a solemn guard; some floated in boats, others rode elephants, as drums were beaten, conchs blown, strings plucked, and pipes played.
After ninety days had passed, he arrived at the city of Kanyākubja, located in the Great Flower Grove on the west bank of the Gaṅgā River.

At that time, more than twenty kings from various nations, having previously received his summons, each brought with them the eminent śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of their respective countries, as well as their ministers, officials, and soldiers, and assembled for the great convocation.
The king first constructed a great monastery on the west bank of the river;
to the east of the monastery he erected a jeweled terrace over a hundred feet high, within which was a golden image of the Buddha equal in size to the king’s own body;
to the south of the terrace he built a jeweled altar for the purpose of bathing the Buddha image.
From here, fourteen or fifteen *li* to the northeast, a separate traveling palace was constructed.
At that time, it was the second month of spring;
beginning from the first day, various delicacies were served to the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas until the twenty-first day.

The royal palanquin proceeded toward the monastery, with pavilions lining both sides of the road, adorned to the utmost with every kind of precious ornament. Musicians remained in place as elegant strains were played in succession.

From the palanquin, the King brought forth a golden image, hollow within and embossed on the surface, over three feet in height; it was carried upon a great elephant and covered with a jeweled canopy.

King Śīlāditya, wearing the attire of Śakra, held a precious parasol as he attended on the left; King Kumāra, assuming the ceremonial guise of Brahmā, held a white fly-whisk as he attended on the right.

Each was surrounded by five hundred elephant troops clad in armor; before and behind the Buddha-image were one hundred great elephants each, upon which musicians rode, beating drums and performing music.
King Śīlāditya scattered pearls, various jewels, and flowers of gold and silver along his path as he proceeded to make offerings to the Triple Gem.

First, he approached the precious altar and bathed the images with fragrant water; then, carrying them himself upon his back, he ascended the western platform and made offerings of various rare treasures and hundreds of thousands of *kauśeya* silken garments.
At that time, there were only some twenty śramaṇas following as attendants, while the various kings served as guards.
Once the meal was finished, he gathered the followers of various heterodox schools to deliberate upon subtle words and to exalt the ultimate truth.
As the sun was about to set, he turned his carriage back toward the temporary palace.
Thus, the golden image was escorted day after day with the same ceremonial retinue as before, until the final day of the festival.
Suddenly, fire broke out on the great platform, and smoke and flames blazed fiercely from the gate-tower of the monastery.
The King said:

"I have exhausted the national treasures to offer them to my late sovereign and established this monastery to manifest his sublime achievements. Yet, lacking virtue and receiving no protection, such calamities and anomalies have occurred. With such omens of retribution as these, what is the use of living?"
He then burned incense and paid his respects with a formal invocation, making this vow:

"By the merit of my past good deeds, I have become king over all India; by the power of my blessings, I pray that this fire disaster may be averted and extinguished. If there is no response from the divine, I shall forfeit my life from this moment on!"
He immediately exerted himself, leaping over the threshold of the gate; it was as if the fire had been extinguished by a sudden blow, and the flames vanished along with the smoke.
Witnessing this marvel, the kings were filled with even greater awe and trepidation.
After a while, his countenance remained unmoved and his speech was as before;
he asked the kings, "Now that this calamity has suddenly occurred and my work has been consumed by fire, what is it that you harbor in your hearts, and what do you intend to say?"
The kings prostrated themselves and wept sorrowfully, responding:
"We hoped that these monuments of accomplished merit would be transmitted to future generations; how can we bear the thought of them being reduced to ashes in a single day?"
"How much more so for the various non-Buddhists, who will surely rejoice with glad hearts!
The King said,
"Judging by this, what the Tathāgata has spoken is indeed true."
The heterodox teachers and followers of other paths cling tenaciously to the view of permanence, whereas our Great Master alone teaches impermanence.

Now that my acts of giving are complete and my heart's wishes have been fulfilled, it is precisely through this transformation and cessation that I once again recognize the truth of the Tathāgata’s words; this is a great blessing, and there is no cause for profound sorrow.
Thereupon, the kings ascended the Great Stūpa from the east to ascend and survey the site.

Just as they were descending the steps, a strange man suddenly appeared carrying a blade to confront the king. The king, in a state of urgency, retreated while continuing his ascent, seized the man from below, and handed him over to the officials.
At that time, the assembled officials were terrified and did not know how to proceed with a rescue.
All the kings requested that this man be executed, but King Śīlāditya showed no sign of anger and strictly forbade the killing.
The king questioned him personally, saying,
"What have I done to you that you commit such violence and evil? He replied:
"Great King, your virtuous bounty is impartial, and both those within and without your realm are sustained by it.

Yet I, in my madness and folly, failed to deliberate upon the great plan; moved by a single word from various heterodox teachers, I have suddenly become an assassin, intending first to commit treason."
The King asked,
"For what reason have these non-Buddhists conceived such evil intent?
They replied:

"Great King, you have assembled the various nations and emptied your treasuries to provide offerings to the śramaṇas and cast images of the Buddha; yet the various non-Buddhist practitioners, though summoned from afar, have received no inquiry from you, which truly fills us with shame."
"It was only because of his madness and folly that he dared to commit such a wicked and treacherous act.
Thereupon, the king interrogated the followers of the non-Buddhist sects.

Five hundred Brahmins, all men of eminent talent, were summoned at his command. Envious that the śramaṇas had received the King’s profound honor, they launched flaming arrows to set the jeweled pavilion on fire, hoping that while the crowd scrambled in chaos to extinguish the flames, they might seize this moment to assassinate the Great King. Finding no other opportunity, they then hired this man to rush through the narrow passage and carry out the assassination.

At that time, the kings and great ministers requested the execution of the heretics; the king then punished only the principal culprits and did not penalize the rest of the faction, banishing five hundred Brahmins beyond the borders of India.
Thereupon, he returned to the capital.
To the northwest of the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka.
In the past, the Tathāgata stayed here for seven days preaching various sublime dharmas.
Beside it are the sites where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation.
There are also small stūpas containing the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata.

To the south of the Dharma-preaching stūpa, bordering the Gaṅgā River, there are three monasteries sharing a single enclosure but having separate gates. The Buddha images are magnificent and beautiful, and the monks are solemn and disciplined; more than several thousand households serve as their laborers.
Within a precious casket in the vihāra was a Buddha’s tooth, over an inch and a half in length, emitting extraordinary radiance and wondrous colors that shifted from morning to evening.
People flocked from near and far, and both officials and commoners gathered in great numbers—hundreds and thousands every day—to pay their respects and gaze upon it in veneration.
The guards, finding the crowds too numerous and noisy, established heavy taxes as a temporary measure and proclaimed far and wide:
"Those who wish to see the Buddha’s tooth must pay a large sum of gold coins.
Nevertheless, the devotees who came to pay their respects were truly numerous, and they vied with one another with joyful hearts to pay the tax of gold coins.

On every fast day, he would bring it out and place it upon a high throne; hundreds of thousands of people would burn incense and scatter flowers, yet though the flowers accumulated in abundance, they could not submerge the ivory casket.

To the left and right of the front of the monastery, there are respectively two vihāras, each over a hundred feet high, with stone foundations and brick chambers; the Buddha images within them are adorned with various precious gems, some cast in gold or silver, and others melted from brass.
In front of each of the two monasteries is a small vihāra.

Not far to the southeast of these vihāras is a great monastery with a stone foundation and brick chambers, over two hundred feet in height. Within it is a standing image of the Tathāgata, over thirty feet tall, cast of brass and adorned with various exquisite jewels.
Upon the stone walls surrounding the vihāra, the deeds performed by the Tathāgata while practicing the bodhisattva path were carved and painted in full detail.
Not far to the south of the stone vihāra is a temple dedicated to the Sun God (Sūrya).
Not far to the south of the shrine is a temple of Maheśvara.
Both are polished from blue stone and are exquisitely carved; their proportions and scale are identical to those of Buddhist vihāras.
Each [of these] was assigned a thousand households to provide for their sweeping and cleaning; drums, music, and stringed songs resounded day and night without ceasing.
Six or seven li to the southeast of the great city, on the south bank of the Gaṅgā River, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka.
In the past, the Tathāgata spent six months here preaching that the body is impermanent, suffering, empty, and impure.
Beside it are the sites where the four past Buddhas sat and practiced walking meditation.

Furthermore, there is a small stūpa containing the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata; if anyone afflicted by illness circumambulates it with utmost sincerity, they will surely be healed and receive its blessings and benefits.
Traveling southeast from the great city for more than one hundred li, one reaches the city of Navadevakula, situated on the eastern bank of the Gaṅgā River and measuring over twenty li in circuit.
The flowering groves and clear ponds reflect one another.

To the northwest of the city of Navadevakula and to the east of the Gaṅgā River, there is a celestial shrine with multi-storied pavilions and tiered terraces, constructed with extraordinary craftsmanship and unique design.

Five li to the east of the city are three monasteries sharing a single enclosure but having separate gates; they house more than five hundred monks, all of whom study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hinayana.
More than two hundred paces in front of the monastery, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka.
Although its foundations have subsided, it still stands over one hundred feet high; this is the place where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Dharma for seven days.
Within it are śarīra relics that occasionally emit a brilliant light.
Beside it are the sites where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation.
Three or four *li* to the north of the monastery, on the bank of the Gaṅgā River, stands a stūpa over two hundred feet high, erected by King Aśoka.

Formerly, when the Tathāgata was teaching the Dharma here for seven days, five hundred hungry ghosts came to where the Buddha was; upon hearing the Dharma, they attained realization, cast off their ghostly state, and were reborn in heaven.
Beside the Dharmacakra-pravartana Stūpa are the sites where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation.
Adjacent to these is another stūpa containing the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata.
From here, traveling southeast for more than six hundred *li* and crossing the Gaṅgā River, one arrives south at Ayodhyā, within the borders of Central India.
The kingdom of Ayodhyā is more than five thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty li in circuit.
Crops are abundant and flowers and fruits grow in profusion.
The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs are virtuous and harmonious; the people take pleasure in cultivating merit and are diligent in learning and the arts.
There are more than one hundred monasteries with over three thousand monks, who study and practice both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
There are ten deva temples, where followers of heterodox paths are few in number.
Within the great city is an ancient monastery, which was [the residence] of the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu—translated into Chinese as Shijinqin (世親);
formerly called Basu Pandou (婆藪盤豆), translated as Tianqin (天親).
For several decades, various treatises on both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna were composed here amidst error and confusion.

The ruins beside it are the lecture hall where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu expounded the meaning of the Dharma and preached the teachings for kings, eminent scholars from the four quarters, śramaṇas, and brahmins.
Four or five *li* north of the city, on the bank of the Ganges River, within a great monastery, stands a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka.
It was here that the Tathāgata, for the sake of the assembly of devas and humans, preached various sublime Dharmas during these three months.
Beside it is a stūpa marking the site where the four past Buddhas sat and performed their walking meditations.
Four or five *li* to the west of the monastery is a stūpa containing the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata.

North of the hair and nail relic stūpa are the ruins of a monastery where, in the past, the Sautrāntika master Śrīlāta (translated into Chinese as Shèngshòu, "Victorious Reception") composed the Sautrāntika *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

Five or six li to the southwest of the city, within a great āmra grove, there is an old monastery; this is the place where the Bodhisattva Asaṅga—translated into Chinese as Wuzhuo—sought instruction and guided ordinary beings.

At night, Bodhisattva Asaṅga ascended to the celestial palaces and received the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-bhāṣya*, the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra*, and other treatises from Bodhisattva Maitreya; by day, he expounded their sublime principles for the great assembly.
More than a hundred paces to the northwest of the Āmra grove is a stūpa containing the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata.
Beside it is an old foundation, which is the place where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu descended from Tuṣita Heaven to visit the Bodhisattva Asaṅga.

The Bodhisattva Asaṅga was a native of Gandhāra. During the millennium following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he was born with keen insight; having encountered the Dharma through its reputation, he awakened to the Way. He initially left the household life and studied under the Mahīśāsaka school, but after some time, he turned his faith toward the Mahāyāna.

His younger brother, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, entered the order and received instruction within the Sarvāstivāda school; he was widely learned, possessed a powerful memory, and had mastered the teachings while refining his intellectual faculties.
As for Asanga’s disciple Buddhasimha—translated into Chinese as Shizi Jue (Lion Awakening)—his secret practices were unfathomable and his eminent talent was renowned.
Two or three wise men frequently said to one another:

"In all our practice of the path, we vow to behold Maitreya. If any of us should first relinquish this life and succeed in fulfilling our long-cherished wish, you must inform the others so that they may know where he has gone."
Subsequently, Siṃhabuddhi passed away first, yet for three years there was no news of him.
Vasubandhu Bodhisattva soon followed by passing away; six months elapsed, and likewise there was no report of his life.

At that time, all the followers of other schools mocked them, saying that since both the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu and Siṃhabuddhi had transmigrated into evil destinies, they clearly lacked spiritual insight.

Later, during the first watch of the night, while the Bodhisattva Asaṅga was instructing his disciples in the methods of meditative concentration, the lamp light suddenly dimmed and a great radiance appeared in the sky. A celestial rishi descended through the void and, entering the courtyard, paid respectful homage to Asaṅga.
Asanga said:
"Why have you come so late?
What is your name now?"
He replied:

"From this point, having relinquished my life-span, I shall go to Tuṣita Heaven and be born within a lotus among the inner retinue of Maitreya. As soon as the lotus opens, Maitreya will praise me, saying:
'Welcome, O Vast Wisdom! Welcome, O Vast Wisdom!'"
"Once you have completed one circumambulation,
you shall immediately return to report.
Bodhisattva Asanga asked, "Where is Siṃhabuddhi now?"
He said:

"While I was circumambulating, I saw Śrīgupta among the assembly outside; he was so deeply attached to sensual pleasures that he had no leisure even to look back, so how could he have come to report?"
The Bodhisattva Asaṅga said:
"That matter is settled.
What are the characteristics of Maitreya?"
"What Dharma did he expound?
He replied,
"The marks and signs of Maitreya cannot be fully described in words."
He expounds the sublime Dharma, the meaning of which does not differ from this.
Yet the Bodhisattva’s wondrous voice is pure, resonant, harmonious, and elegant; those who hear it forget their weariness, and those who receive it never grow weary.

More than forty li to the northwest of the old foundations of the Anāthapiṇḍada Lecture Hall, one reaches the ruins of an old monastery situated on the north bank of the Gaṅgā River. Within it stands a brick stūpa over a hundred feet high, the place where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu first conceived the aspiration for the Mahāyāna.
When the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu arrived there from North India, the Bodhisattva Asaṅga commanded his disciples to go and welcome him.
Upon reaching this monastery, they encountered and met one another.
A disciple of Asaṅga was staying outside the door and windows; after midnight, he recited the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
Upon hearing this, Vasubandhu was moved to realization and felt deep remorse, thinking:
"This profound and wondrous Dharma is something I have never heard before. The transgression of slandering it originated from my tongue; the tongue is the root of sin, and I should now sever it."
He immediately seized a sharp blade, intending to cut out his own tongue.
Then he saw Wuzhuo standing before him and said:
