"The Mahāyāna teaching is the principle of ultimate truth; it is praised by all Buddhas and revered as the fundamental doctrine by all sages."
I wish to instruct you, yet you have now awakened of your own accord.
Since the time for awakening has arrived, what could be more auspicious than this?
Regarding the holy teachings of all Buddhas, even cutting out one's tongue is no cause for regret.

In the past, you used your tongue to disparage the Mahāyāna; now, you use your tongue to praise the Mahāyāna. To remedy past faults and renew yourself is still a virtue; if you were to seal your mouth and cease all speech, where would the benefit lie?
Having spoken these words, he suddenly vanished from sight.
Vasubandhu, having received this command, did not cut out his tongue.
At dawn, he went to Asaṅga to inquire about and receive the Mahāyāna teachings.
Thereupon, he refined his insights and engaged in profound contemplation, composing over one hundred Mahāyāna treatises, all of which were widely propagated.
From there, he traveled east for more than three hundred li, crossed the Gaṅgā River, and proceeded north to the kingdom of Ayodhyā within the borders of Central India.
The country of Ajamukha, Ajamukha, is two thousand four or five hundred *li* in circuit.
Its capital city borders the Gaṅgā River and is over twenty *li* in circuit.
Its climate and local products are similar to those of the country of Ayodhyā.
The people are simple and honest by nature; they are diligent in study and fond of merit.
There are five monasteries with more than a thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
There are more than ten deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.

Not far to the southeast of the city, on the bank of the Gaṅgā River, stands a stūpa built by King Aśoka, over two hundred feet in height; this is the place where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Dharma for three months.
Beside it are the sites where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation.
There is also a blue stone stūpa containing the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata.
Beside it is a monastery with more than two hundred monks; the Buddha images are magnificently adorned, their majestic presence as if they were actually there.

The terraces and pavilions are vast and magnificent, rising up in extraordinary architectural splendor. This was where the master Buddhadeva—translated into Chinese as Juéshǐ (Awakening the World)—composed the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* of the Sarvāstivāda school.

From here, traveling southeast for more than seven hundred *li*, crossing the south bank of the Gaṅgā River and the north bank of the Yamunā River, one arrives at Prayāga, within the borders of Central India.
The country of Prayāga is over five thousand *li* in circuit.
Its capital city is situated at the confluence of two rivers and is over twenty *li* in circuit.
Crops grow in abundance and fruit trees are luxuriant.
The climate is harmonious and pleasant, and the customs are virtuous and compliant.
The people are fond of learning and the arts, and they believe in non-Buddhist paths.
There are two monasteries with few monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
There are several hundred deva temples, and followers of heterodox paths are indeed numerous.
To the southwest of the great city, within a grove of *campaka* flowers, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka.
Although its foundation has collapsed and subsided, it still stands over a hundred feet high; in the past, the Tathāgata subdued non-Buddhist heretics at this very spot.
Beside it are the stūpas containing his hair and nail relics, as well as the traces of his walking meditation.

Beside the stūpas of hair and nail relics, there is an ancient monastery; this is the place where the Bodhisattva Deva—translated into Chinese as Tianshou—composed the *Śataśāstra-vyākhyā* (Extensive Hundred-Verse Treatise) to refute the Hinayana and subdue the non-Buddhists.

Formerly, when Bodhisattva Deva arrived at this monastery from South India, there was a non-Buddhist Brahmin in the city who was renowned for his lofty discourse and possessed unimpeded eloquence; he scrutinized names to demand their reality and cross-examined him until his arguments were exhausted.
Yaśas knew that Deva had extensively investigated the profound mysteries; wishing to blunt his sharp edge, he followed the convention of names and asked:
"What is your name? Deva replied:
"His name is Deva," the outsider asked.
"Who is Deva?"
Deva said, "I. The non-Buddhist said:
"Who am I? Deva replied, "A dog."
The non-Buddhist asked,
"Who is the dog? Deva replied:
"You. The non-Buddhist said, "Who are you?"
Deva replied, “Heaven.
The non-Buddhist said:
"Who is 'Heaven'? Deva replied, "It is 'I'."
The non-Buddhist asked, "Who am I? Deva replied:
"A dog," he said.
The non-Buddhist asked,
"Who is the dog?"
Deva said, "You. The non-Buddhist replied:
"Who are you? Deva replied, "A deva."
After such repeated cycles, the non-Buddhists finally attained realization.
From that time forward, they have held his character and conduct in deep reverence.
Within the city there is a temple dedicated to the gods, brilliantly adorned and magnificent, manifesting many kinds of spiritual wonders.

According to their scriptures, this place is a supreme site for sentient beings to cultivate merit; to donate even a single coin at this shrine yields a merit that surpasses the gift of a thousand pieces bestowed elsewhere.
Furthermore, they are able to disregard their own lives, offering up their lives as sacrifices within the shrine to receive the blessings and pleasures of heaven, which are vast and eternal.

Before the heavenly shrine stands a great tree with spreading branches and leaves, its shade dense and thick; there dwells a man-eating ghost who has made it his home, and thus many remains of corpses are found in its vicinity.

If people come to this shrine, there are none who do not recklessly sacrifice their lives; being both intimidated by heterodox teachings and seduced by the deity, they have practiced these errors without ceasing from antiquity until the present day.

Recently, there was a son of noble family from the Brahmin caste, who was broad-minded and possessed great wisdom, being both quick-witted and highly talented. He came to the sacrificial hall and said to the assembly:
"The vulgar minds of common folk are difficult to guide and convert; I shall first associate with them, and only then lead them toward transformation."
Having ascended there, he looked down and said to his companion, "I am about to die.

What I previously called deceptive and false is now proven true: celestial music and musicians are welcoming me through the air from this sublime realm; I shall cast off this wretched body to follow them."
He immediately desired to cast himself down to bring about his own death; though his friends and relatives exhorted him with gentle words, his resolve did not waver.
He then spread out his robes beneath a tree, and when he threw himself down, he preserved his life.
After a long while, he awoke and said, "I saw only the various devas in the sky summoning me; this was led by a malevolent deity and was not the music of the heavens.
To the east of the great city, two rivers converge; it is over ten li wide, the terrain is high and dry, and fine sand spreads everywhere.
From antiquity to the present, whenever kings and noble clans have made offerings, they have all come here; providing for all without regard for cost, it is known as the "Field of Great Almsgiving."

Now, King Śīlāditya has continued the legacy of his predecessors and is deeply committed to the practice of giving; having accumulated wealth over five years, he has bestowed it all at once, gathering a vast quantity of rare treasures at his site of almsgiving.
On the first day, a great Buddha image was installed, adorned with various precious gems; immediately, he offered the finest and most rare treasures as a gift to it,
followed by the resident monks,
and then to the assembly before him.
Next were those of lofty talent and profound learning, who were well-versed in the world and possessed many skills;
next were the disciples of non-Buddhist paths, who lived in seclusion and retired from the world;
and finally were the widowers, widows, orphans, and the destitute beggars.
She exhausted her most precious curiosities and the finest delicacies, providing for them in every grade of excellence without exception.

Once her treasury was emptied and her garments and ornaments were completely spent, she gave away in succession the bright pearl from her hair-knot and all the jeweled necklaces upon her body, never once feeling regret.
Having completed the act of giving, he exclaimed: "How joyful!
Whatever I possessed has now entered the adamantine, indestructible treasury."
From that time forward, the kings of various nations each presented precious garments.
Before even ten days had passed, the treasuries were filled to overflowing.
At the confluence of rivers to the east of the Great Field of Almsgiving, several hundred people drowned themselves every day.

The local people believe that those who wish to be reborn in heaven should fast and drown themselves at this site; by bathing in the middle of the stream, their karmic defilements will be extinguished.
Consequently, people from distant lands and foreign countries flock here one after another, abstaining from food for seven days before ending their lives.
As for the mountain apes and wild deer, they wandered in groups along the riverbanks; some returned after bathing in the current, while others died of starvation.

During King Śīlāditya’s great almsgiving, there was a macaque living on the riverbank who remained alone beneath a tree, withdrawing from his tracks and abstaining from food. After several days, he died of self-starvation.

Therefore, those non-Buddhist practitioners who cultivate asceticism plant tall pillars in the middle of rivers; as dawn approaches, they immediately ascend them, grasping the top of the pillar with one hand and one foot while treading upon side pegs, with the other hand and foot suspended and extended outward. Remaining poised over the void without bending, they stretch their necks and open their eyes, gazing at the sun as they rotate to the right, only descending once the evening twilight has arrived.
Those who follow this path number in the dozens; they hope that through such diligent toil they may transcend birth and death, never slackening for even several decades.
From here, one enters a great forest to the southwest, where ferocious beasts and wild elephants roam in packs and harass travelers; it is difficult to traverse without a large company.
After traveling more than five hundred *li*, he arrived at the kingdom of Kauśāmbī (formerly called Jushanmi, which is an erroneous transcription).
It is within the borders of Central India.
The kingdom of Kauśāmbī is more than six thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over thirty li in circuit.
The soil is renowned for its fertility, and the land yields abundant crops; there is much non-glutinous rice and luxuriant sugarcane.
The climate is hot, and the customs of the people are fierce and impetuous.
They are fond of studying the classics and arts, and they cultivate merit and goodness.
There are more than ten monasteries, which have fallen into ruin and overgrown with weeds; there are over three hundred monks who study the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
There are more than fifty deva temples, and non-Buddhists are indeed numerous.

Within the old palace in the city is a great vihāra, over sixty feet in height, containing a sandalwood image of the Buddha with a stone canopy suspended above it; this was made by King Udayana (translated into Chinese as Chū-ài, "One Who Gives Love").
The former claim that it was made by King Udayana is an error.
Its sacred features manifest from time to time, and its divine radiance shines forth occasionally.
When the kings of various nations, relying on their strength, sought to lift it, although they gathered a great multitude of people, none were able to move it.
They subsequently commissioned a representation for veneration, both claiming it was the true image; when its origins and history were related, it was revealed that this was indeed the very statue.
Initially, after the Tathāgata had attained perfect enlightenment, he ascended to the celestial palaces to preach the Dharma for his mother, remaining there for three months without returning.
The king, longing with deep admiration, wished to have an image of him depicted.

He then invited the Venerable Maudgalyāyana, who by means of his supernormal powers transported artisans to the celestial palace so that they might personally observe the wondrous marks and carve them into sandalwood.
When the Tathāgata returned from the celestial palace, the sandalwood image rose to welcome the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One comforted it, saying:
"Are you weary from the toil of teaching and transforming?
To guide and lead those of the final age—this is indeed my hope."
More than a hundred paces to the east of the vihāra is the site containing the traces of where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation.
Not far from its side are the Tathāgata’s well and bathing chamber; the well is still used for drawing water, while the chamber has fallen into ruin.

In the southeast corner of the city, there are the ruins of an old residence; this was the former home of the elder Kuśira (formerly transcribed as Qiūshīluó, which is an error). Within it are a Buddhist vihāra and a stūpa containing hair and nail relics.
Furthermore, there is an old foundation, which was the bathing hall of the Tathāgata.
Not far to the southeast of the city, there is an old monastery, which was the former garden of the householder Sudatta.
Within it stands a stūpa erected by King Aśoka, over two hundred feet in height.
It was here that the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for several years.
Beside it are the sites containing the traces of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas, as well as a stūpa for the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata.

On the upper story of the multi-storied pavilion to the southeast of the monastery is an old brick chamber where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu once resided; it was here that he composed the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) to refute the Hinayana schools and challenge various non-Buddhist outsiders.
To the east of the monastery, within the Āmra grove, there is an old foundation where the Bodhisattva Asaṅga composed the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.
Eight or nine li to the southwest of the city is the stone cave of the venomous dragon.
In the past, the Tathāgata subdued this venomous dragon and left behind his shadow within it; although this is recorded in traditional accounts, it cannot be seen today.
Beside it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, over two hundred feet in height.
Beside it are the traces of the Tathāgata’s walking meditation as well as stūpas containing his hair and nail clippings; those afflicted by illness often find recovery through their prayers here.

As this country is the last to remain when the Dharma of Śākya is exhausted, everyone from the sovereign above to the commoners below feels a natural sense of grief upon entering its borders; none fail to drink in tears and return home sighing with sorrow.

Traveling more than seven hundred *li* through the great forest northeast of the Dragon Cave, one crosses the Gaṅgā River and reaches the city of Kāśapura to the north; it is over ten *li* in circuit, and its inhabitants are wealthy and happy.
Beside the city is an old monastery, of which only the foundations remain; this is the place where the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla formerly subdued the non-Buddhists.
The former kings of this country supported heterodox doctrines, wishing to destroy the Buddha-dharma and showing great veneration for the non-Buddhists.

From among the assembly of non-Buddhists (tīrthika), he summoned a master of debate who was intelligent, brilliant, and adept at penetrating the most subtle points. This master composed a spurious and heterodox treatise of one thousand stanzas, totaling thirty-two thousand words, which slandered the Buddha-dharma while purporting to uphold his own orthodox school.
Thereupon, he summoned the assembly of monks and ordered them to engage in a debate. He declared:
"If the non-Buddhists prevail, the Buddha-dharma shall be destroyed;
if the monastic community suffers no defeat, their tongues shall be cut off as an apology."
At that time, the monastic community feared defeat and gathered to deliberate, saying:
"The Sun of Wisdom has already set, and the Bridge of Dharma is about to collapse; how can we hope to withstand the king’s faction and the heretics?"
"The situation is such as this; what course of action do you propose?
The assembly remained silent, with none daring to offer a proposal.

The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla, though young in years, was possessed of great eloquence, wisdom, and extensive learning, and his character was noble and far-reaching. Standing amidst the great multitude, he spoke up in praise, saying:
"Though I am dull-witted, I beg to set forth its outline briefly.
It is truly fitting that I respond to Your Majesty’s command with my illness.
If these lofty arguments prevail, it shall be due to divine protection; "
"To raise an objection and then fail in the debate is merely the error of youth.
Thus, having grounds for both advancing and withdrawing, neither the Dharma nor the Sangha is at fault.
All agreed, saying:
“Very well,” he replied,
in accordance with their plan.
He then obeyed the King’s command and immediately ascended the seat of debate.
The non-Buddhist then raised the mainstay of his arguments and elevated the significance of his rhetoric, reciting what he held to be true while awaiting the opponent's rebuttal.
The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla accepted his words and said with a smile, "I have won!"
"Will you recite it by reversing the order,
or will you recite it with the words scrambled?
The non-Buddhist was taken aback and said:
"Do not be conceited, my son.
To be able to grasp the words completely is itself a victory; first receive the text as it is, and later explain its meaning.
Dharmapāla then followed the rhythm of his voice, recounting the text and its meaning with no error in word or principle, and no deviation in its tone or resonance.
Upon hearing this, the non-Buddhists wished to cut out their own tongues.
Dharmapāla said, "Cutting out one's tongue is not an apology; changing one's adherence is true repentance."
He immediately preached the Dharma for him, and the king’s heart was filled with faith and his mind attained awakening.
The king abandoned heterodox paths and reverently followed the True Dharma.
To the side of where he subdued the heretics while protecting the Dharma, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; although its foundation has subsided, it still stands over two hundred feet high.
This is where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Dharma for six months.
Nearby are the traces of his walking meditation as well as a stūpa containing his hair and nail relics.
From here, traveling north for one hundred and seventy or eighty *li*, one arrives at Mount Viśākha in the kingdom of Kanyakubja, within the borders of Central India.
The country of Vīṣaka is more than four thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the country is sixteen *li* in circuit.
Cereals grow in great abundance, and flowers and fruits are both numerous and flourishing.
The seasonal cycles are harmonious and pleasant, and the local customs are simple and sincere.
The people are fond of learning without weariness and seek blessings with unwavering devotion.
There are more than twenty monasteries with over three thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
There are more than fifty deva temples, and the non-Buddhists are very numerous.
To the left of the road south of the city, there is a great monastery.
In the past, the Arhat Devaśarman composed the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* here, propounding the doctrine of no-self and no-person.
The Arhat Gopā composed the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (The Treatise on the Reality of the Essential Teachings), in which he asserted the existence of a self and a person (*pudgala*).
Because of this attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*), intense disputes ensued.
Furthermore, during these seven days, the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla defeated one hundred masters of the Hīnayāna.
Beside the monastery is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka.
In the past, the Tathāgata stayed here for six years, preaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings.

Beside the place where he preached the Dharma, there is a marvelous tree, six or seven feet high, which remains constant without increase or decrease through the alternating seasons of spring and autumn.
This is because the Tathāgata once used it to clean his teeth and discarded the remaining branch; it subsequently took root and has flourished until the present day.
Various people with false views and hosts of non-Buddhists came vying with one another to ravage and cut it down, yet it grew back as before.
Not far from its side is the site containing the traces where the four past Buddhas sat and practiced walking meditation.
There is also a stūpa containing the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata;
its sacred foundations extend to the corners, with groves and ponds reflecting one another.
From here, traveling northeast for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Śrāvastī (formerly called She-wei, which is an error).
Within the borders of Central India.
*Great Tang Records on the Western Regions*, Scroll Five;
*Great Tang Records on the Western Regions*, Scroll Six: Four Kingdoms.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree;
compiled by the Śramaṇa Bianji of Dazongchi Monastery.

The Four Countries: 1. Śrāvastī Country (Śrāvastī); 2. Kapilavastu Country (Kapilavastu); 3. Rāmagrāma Country (Rāmagrāma); 4. Kuśinagara Country (Kuśinagara). Śrāvastī Country: Located in Śrāvastī, it is over six thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city was desolate and dilapidated, and the boundaries of the fields were no longer demarcated.
The old foundations of the palace city measured over twenty li in circumference; although much of it lay in ruins, there were still inhabitants remaining.
Crops are abundant and the seasons are harmonious.
The local customs are simple and honest; the people are devoted to learning and fond of merit.
There are several hundred monasteries, many of which are in ruin; the monks are few in number and study the Saṃmitīya school.
There are one hundred deva temples, and the non-Buddhists are very numerous.
This was the place where, during the time the Tathāgata was in the world, King Prasenajit (translated into Chinese as Shengjun, "Victorious Army") resided.
Formerly called Po-si-ni (Prasenajit), which is a corruption and abbreviation [of the original name], it was the capital city where he governed.
Within the old palace city, there are ancient foundations, which are the remaining traces of King Vijitasena’s hall.
Not far to the east, there is an old foundation upon which a small stūpa has been erected; this was the great Dharma hall formerly built by King Jayasena for the Tathāgata.

Not far from the side of the Dharma Hall, there is a stūpa upon the remains of an old foundation; this was the bhikṣuṇī vihāra of the Buddha’s maternal aunt, Prajāpatī (translated into Chinese as Shengzhu;
the former term, Poshajboti, is a corruption), which was established by King Jayasena.
Next, to the east, is a stūpa which is the former residence of Sudatta—translated into Chinese as Shanshi (Good Giver).
The old transcription "Xuda" is erroneous.
Beside the house of the elder Sudatta is a large stūpa, which is [the site] of Aṅgulimāla—translated into Chinese as Zhiman (Finger-Garland).
The former name, Aṅgulimāla, is a corruption. It is the place where he abandoned his heterodoxy; as for Aṅgulimāra, he was a malefactor from Śrāvastī.
He brought harm to living beings and acted with violence toward cities and states; he killed men to take their fingers, wearing them as a garland upon his head.
Now, wishing to kill his own mother to complete the required number of fingers, he was about to do so.
The World-Honored One, moved by compassion, was proceeding to guide and transform sentient beings.
Seeing the World-Honored One from afar, he thought to himself with secret joy:
"It is certain that I shall now be reborn in heaven."
"My former teacher had this instruction, and his final words remain here: 'One who harms the Buddha and kills his mother shall be reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
He said to his mother, 'Mother, stop for now; first we must harm that great śramaṇa.'"
He immediately took up his sword and went to confront the World-Honored One.
The Tathāgata then withdrew with a slow gait, while the murderous Aṅgulimāla rushed forward in haste but could not catch him.
The World-Honored One said to him:
"Why do you cling to your base resolve, abandoning the roots of goodness and inciting the source of evil?

At that time, Angulimāla, having heard this instruction, realized the error of his conduct; he immediately took refuge and sought entry into the Dharma, practicing with diligent perseverance until he realized the fruit of Arhatship.
Five or six *li* south of the city is the Jetavana—translated into Chinese as "Victorious Forest" (*Shenglín*).
The old name "Jita" is a corruption; it is the Anāthapiṇḍika Garden.
A great minister of King Prasenajit, Sudatta, built a vihāra for the Buddha here. It was formerly a monastery, but is now in ruins.

To the left and right of the eastern gate stand stone pillars, each over seventy feet high; the left pillar is carved with a wheel at its summit, while the right pillar bears the figure of an ox upon it—both were erected by King Aśoka.
The buildings have crumbled and collapsed, leaving only their old foundations; only a single brick chamber stands tall and solitary, containing a Buddha image within.

Formerly, after the Tathāgata ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother, King Jayasena, having heard that King Udayana had carved a sandalwood image of the Buddha, then commissioned this image.

The Elder Sudatta was benevolent and sagacious; he accumulated wealth yet was able to disperse it, rescuing the destitute and aiding the poor, showing compassion for orphans and providing relief to the elderly. At that time, people praised his virtue and called him "Givaka," meaning "He Who Provides for the Lonely."
Upon hearing of the Buddha’s merits, he conceived a profound sense of reverence and wished to construct a vihāra, inviting the Buddha to descend there.
The World-Honored One commanded Śāriputra to accompany him to survey the site; however, only the grounds of Prince Jeta’s garden were fresh, elevated, and pure.
He immediately went to the Prince and informed him of his situation in detail.
The Prince said jokingly,
"I will sell it once gold covers the entire ground."
Upon hearing this, Shan-shi’s mind was suddenly cleared; he immediately brought forth gold from his treasury and spread it upon the ground as requested.
When there was a small amount remaining and the ground was not yet fully covered, the Prince asked him to stop, saying:
“The Buddha is truly a fertile field; one ought to sow the seeds of goodness therein.”
He immediately established a vihāra on that open ground.
The World-Honored One went there and addressed Ānanda, saying:
"The site of the garden was purchased by Sudatta, and the grove of trees was gifted by Jeta; with one heart, these two have together accomplished this meritorious work."
"From this day forward, this place shall be called the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
To the northeast of Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park is a stūpa, which marks the place where the Tathāgata washed a sick bhikṣu.
Formerly, when the Tathāgata was in the world, there was a sick bhikṣu who remained alone, harboring suffering within.
The World-Honored One saw him and asked,
"What is it that pains you?"
"Why do you dwell alone?
He replied, "By nature I am indolent and cannot endure nursing the sick; therefore, now that I am stricken with illness, there is no one to look after me."
At that time, the Tathāgata, out of compassion, said to him:
"Good son, I shall now attend to you.
He stroked him with his hand, and all his suffering from illness was completely healed.
He was helped outside to change his bedding, personally bathed, and dressed in new clothes.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"You should exert yourselves with diligence."
Having heard these instructions, he felt gratitude and was joyful in heart and at ease in body.
To the northwest of the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden is a small stūpa, marking the place where Maudgalyāyana, employing his supernormal powers, attempted to lift Śāriputra’s sash but could not move it.
Formerly, when the Buddha was at Lake Anavatapta, humans and devas had all gathered together, yet Śāriputra alone did not attend the assembly from time to time.
The Buddha commanded Maudgalyāyana to go and summon him to the gathering.
Maudgalyāyana accepted the command and departed, while Śāriputra mended his dharma robes.
Maudgalyāyana said, "The World-Honored One is currently at Lake Anavatapta; he has commanded me to summon you."
Śāriputra said, "Wait;
let me finish mending it first, and then I shall go with you.
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"If you do not depart quickly, I shall exercise my supernormal power to lift this stone chamber of yours and carry it to the site of the great assembly.
Thereupon, Śāriputra untied his waistband, placed it on the ground, and said,
"If you can lift this band, perhaps my body might move."
At that time, Maudgalyāyana exercised his great supernormal powers, yet he could not lift the belt; the earth shook because of it.
Thereupon, by means of his psychic power, he returned to the place where the Buddha was, only to see Śāriputra already seated in the assembly.
Maudgalyāyana bowed his head and sighed, saying,
"Only now do I understand that the power of supernatural faculties is not equal to the power of wisdom.
Not far from the side of the stūpa, there was a well.
While the Tathāgata was in the world, this place served his needs.
Beside it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, containing the relics of the Tathāgata.
At the sites where he walked in meditation and the places where he preached the Dharma, memorial markers were erected and *stūpas* were constructed.

Deities of the underworld provided vigilant protection, and auspicious omens appeared at intervals: sometimes celestial music resounded, and sometimes divine fragrances were perceived. Such portents of sublime blessings are difficult to recount in full detail.
Not far behind the monastery is the place where a non-Buddhist brahmin killed a courtesan in order to slander the Buddha.
The Tathāgata possesses the ten powers and fearlessness, the knowledge of all modes; he is venerated by devas and humans, and revered by sages and worthies.
At that time, the various non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas) deliberated among themselves, saying:
"We should employ deceit to slander and humiliate him before the assembly.

They then enticed and hired a courtesan to feign listening to the Dharma; once she was known by the public, they killed her in secret, buried her body beside a tree, and went to the king to lodge a complaint of grievance.
The King ordered a search, and his corpse was found in the Jeta Grove.
At that time, the non-Buddhist heretics cried out in a loud voice:
"The Great Śramaṇa Gautama always proclaims morality and patience; yet now he has secretly violated this woman and killed her to silence her."
"Since you have already committed lust and murder, what precepts or forbearance can you possibly possess?
The devas in the sky followed these words, shouting:
"These are merely the slanders of a wicked heretic!"
More than a hundred paces to the east of the monastery is a large, deep pit; this is the place where Devadatta, wishing to harm the Buddha with poison, fell alive into hell.
Devadatta, whose name means "Heaven-Conferred" in the language of Tang, was the son of King Droṇodana.
After twelve years of diligent application, he had already mastered and recited the eighty thousand dharma-piṭakas.
Later, for the sake of gain, he sought to learn supernatural powers and associated with evil friends. They consulted together, saying:
"Our marks are thirty, only slightly fewer than the Buddha's;
surrounded by a great assembly, how are we different from the Tathāgata?"
Having reflected thus, he proceeded to cause a schism in the Saṃgha.

Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, having received the Buddha’s instructions and sustained by his majestic spiritual power, preached the Dharma and offered exhortations, whereby the Saṃgha was once again reconciled.
Devadatta, harboring an evil mind that he could not relinquish, placed a potent poison under his fingernails, intending to harm the Buddha while prostrating before him.
Just as he was carrying out this plot, traveling from afar and arriving at this spot, the earth suddenly split open, and he fell alive into hell.
To the south of that, there is another great pit; it was here that the bhikṣu Kokālika slandered the Tathāgata and fell into hell alive.
More than eight hundred paces to the south of the pit where Kokālika fell is a large, deep pit; this is the place where the brahmin woman Cañcā slandered the Tathāgata and fell into hell alive.

While the Buddha was expounding the essentials of the Dharma for the sake of humans and devas, a disciple of a non-Buddhist sect saw from afar that the World-Honored One was being venerated by a great assembly. He then thought to himself:
"Today I must humiliate Gautama and destroy his good reputation, so that my own teacher alone may enjoy this glorious fame."
She then tucked a wooden bowl against her body and went to the Anāthapiṇḍika Garden, where she cried out in a loud voice amidst the great assembly:
"The speaker of the Dharma had illicit relations with me; the child within my womb is of the Śākya clan."
Those with wrong views all believed it to be true, while those of steadfast integrity knew it to be slander.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, wishing to dispel their doubts, transformed himself into a white mouse and gnawed through the cord of the bowl. When the cord was severed, the sound caused the great assembly to tremble; all who saw or heard it felt an even deeper joy.
One person among the crowd rose, took up a wooden bowl, and showed it to the woman, asking, "Is this your son?
At that moment, the earth spontaneously split open; her entire body fell into the abyss and entered the Avīci Hell, where she underwent the full retribution of her misdeeds.
These three pits are all bottomless and shoreless; though the ditches and ponds overflow during the rains of autumn and summer, these deep pits never hold water.
Sixty or seventy paces to the east of the monastery, there is a vihāra over sixty feet high, containing a Buddha image seated facing east.
In the past, the Tathāgata held debates with various non-Buddhists at this very spot.
Next to the east is a devakula (temple to the gods), equal in size to the vihāra.
When the sun first sheds its light, the shadow of the devakula does not obscure the vihāra;
when the sun is about to set, the shade of the vihāra then covers the devakula.
Three or four *li* to the east of the Jeta Grove Monastery, there is a stūpa at the site where the Venerable Śāriputra debated with the non-Buddhists.
Initially, the elder Sudatta purchased Prince Jeta’s grove, intending to establish a monastery for the Tathāgata.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra followed the elder’s lead to observe the situation; the six heretical teachers sought to compete in supernatural powers, and Śāriputra, according to the circumstances, gathered and transformed them, subduing them in accordance with their dispositions.
To the side of this vihāra, a stūpa has been erected; it was here that the Tathāgata defeated the various non-Buddhists and also accepted the invitation of the mother Viśākhā.

South of the stūpa marking the site where he accepted her invitation is the place where King Virūḍhaka—formerly called Pilili, which is a corruption—raised his armies to slaughter the Śākya clan, but upon arriving here, beheld the Buddha and withdrew his troops.

After King Vairocana Śākya ascended the throne, he harbored resentment for his former humiliation; he mobilized his armed forces and assembled his great host. Having completed the deployment, he issued his commands and set forth.
At that time, a bhikṣu heard of this and informed the Buddha. Thereupon, the World-Honored One sat beneath a withered tree.
King Virūḍhaka Śākya saw the World-Honored One from afar; he dismounted from his carriage to pay his respects and, standing back, said:
"The lush trees are so verdant and spreading—why do you not sit beneath them?"
"How can you dwell and rest upon a withered trunk and rotten sprout?
The World-Honored One replied,
"One's kinsmen are the branches and leaves."
"The branches and leaves are about to wither; where will there be shelter and shade?
The King said, "The World-Honored One is my kinsman; you may turn back your carriage."
Thereupon, beholding the holy one and moved by deep emotion, he turned his army back and returned to his kingdom.
Beside the place where the army was turned back, there is a stūpa; this is the spot where the Śākya maiden was executed.
King Vairocana Śākya defeated Śakraka and selected five hundred women from his clan to fill his palace.
The Śākya women were filled with resentment and indignation; they spoke insolent words of complaint and reviled their king, saying:
"He is but the son of a commoner!"
Upon hearing this, the king was incensed and ordered their execution.
The enforcers, carrying out the king’s command, lopped off their hands and feet and cast them into a pit.

At that time, the Śākya women, harboring their suffering, called upon the Buddha. The World-Honored One, with his holy discernment, perceived their bitter agony and commanded the bhikṣus to gather their robes and go there. For the sake of the Śākya women, he preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma, namely: the entanglements of the five desires, wandering through the three miserable realms, the separation from those one loves, and the long duration of birth and death.

At that time, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, the Śākya women were freed from dust and defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye; they passed away simultaneously and were all reborn in the heavens.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, manifested as a brahmin, collected their remains, and performed a cremation, which was later recorded by people.
Not far from the side of the Stūpa of the Execution of Śākya, there is a large dried-up pool; this is the place where King Virūḍhaka fell into hell.
After the World-Honored One had observed the Śākya maiden, he returned to the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden and addressed the bhikṣus: "Seven days from now, King Virūḍhaka shall be consumed by fire."
Upon hearing the Buddha’s prophecy, the king was filled with great trepidation.
When the seventh day arrived, however, he remained peaceful and free from peril.
Overjoyed, the king commanded his palace women to go to the riverbank to enjoy themselves with music, play, and drink.
Still fearing that fire might break out, he beat his oars upon the clear waters and drifted with the waves.
Suddenly, a fierce flame burst forth, incinerating the light boat and causing the King’s body to fall into the Avīci Hell, where he underwent every kind of suffering.
Three or four *li* to the northwest of the monastery, one reaches the Forest of Regained Sight (*Cakṣur-lābha-vana*).
There are traces where the Tathāgata walked and places where various sages practiced meditative concentration; these sites have all been marked by tree enclosures and stūpas have been erected there.
Formerly, five hundred bandits in this kingdom roamed wantonly through the villages and towns, acting with utter defiance toward the city and the state.
King Jayasena captured them, gouged out their eyes, and cast them away in a deep forest.
Harassed and oppressed by a band of robbers, he cried out in distress, invoking the name of the Buddha.

At that time, the Tathāgata was at the Jetavana Monastery; hearing his piteous cry, He gave rise to a heart of compassion. A pure and gentle breeze blew from the Snowy Mountains, carrying medicinal herbs to fill his eyes, whereupon his sight was immediately restored.
There he saw the World-Honored One standing before him; he resolved his mind on Bodhi, prostrated himself with joy, cast away his staff, and departed, whereupon the staff took root.
Over sixty li to the northwest of the great city lies an old city, which was the birthplace of Kāśyapa Buddha during the Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years.
To the south of the city is a stūpa, the place where he first beheld his father after attaining perfect enlightenment.
To the north of the city is a stūpa containing the entire bodily relics of Kāśyapa Buddha.
It was not built by King Aśoka.
From here, traveling southeast for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Kapilavastu (formerly called Jiālówèi, which is an erroneous transcription).
Within the borders of Central India lies the kingdom of Kapilavastu. The kingdom of Kapilavastu is over four thousand *li* in circuit.
There are some dozen empty cities, which have become exceedingly desolate and overgrown.
The royal city is in ruins, and its circumference is not clearly known.
Its inner palace city measures fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit; it is constructed of piled bricks, and its foundations are lofty and solid.
Long abandoned and desolate, its human settlements were sparse and remote.
Lacking a sovereign ruler, each city established its own leader.
The soil was fertile and rich, and crops were sown according to the seasons.
The seasons proceed without deviation, and the local customs are harmonious and pleasant.

There are more than a thousand old foundations of monasteries (*saṃghārāma*); among them, by the side of the palace city, there is one monastery with over three thousand monks who study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
There are two deva temples where followers of different paths dwell together.
Within the palace city, there are old foundations which were the main hall of King Śuddhodana;
a vihāra has been constructed above them, with an image of the king placed within.
Not far from its side is an old foundation, which was the sleeping palace of Mahāmāyā—translated into Chinese as Dàshù (Great Skill) Fūrén (Lady).
A vihāra has been erected above it, and within it is fashioned an image of the Lady.
Beside it is a vihāra, which is the place where Śākyamuni Bodhisattva descended into his mother’s womb; inside is an image of the Bodhisattva’s descent.

According to the Sthavira school, the Bodhisattva descended into his mother’s womb on the night of the thirtieth day of the month of Uttarāṣāḍhā, which corresponds here to the fifteenth day of the fifth month;
according to other schools, he descended into his mother’s womb on the night of the twenty-third day of that same month, corresponding here to the eighth day of the fifth month.
To the northeast, where the Bodhisattva descended into his mother’s womb, there is a stūpa marking the place where the seer Asita prophesied concerning the Prince.
On the day the Bodhisattva was born, auspicious omens converged from all directions.
At that time, King Śuddhodana summoned the various physiognomists and addressed them, saying:
"Now that this son has been born, what are his auspicious or inauspicious traits?
You should examine them thoroughly and respond with clear and honest words."
He said:

"According to the records of former sages and examining the signs of auspiciousness, if he remains at home he will become a Wheel-Turning Sage King; if he leaves the household life, he will surely attain Equal and Perfect Enlightenment."
At that time, the seer Asita arrived from afar and knocked at the gate, requesting an audience.
The king was greatly delighted; he personally went out to welcome him with reverence, invited him to take a precious throne, and said:
"I did not expect the Great Seer to deign to visit me today."
The seer said:
"While I was dwelling in meditative seclusion within the celestial palace, I suddenly saw the hosts of devas dancing and frolicking. I then asked them:
'Why are you so exceedingly joyful?'"
He said:

"Great Seer, you should know that in Jambudvīpa, the first queen of King Śuddhodana of the Śākya clan has now given birth to a prince who shall realize *samyak-saṃbodhi* and perfect the wisdom of omniscience."
"Having heard these words, I have come to gaze upon you in reverence.
Alas, that my decrepit old age prevents me from encountering your holy transformation.
To the south of the city gate is a stūpa, which marks the place where the Prince contended with the Śākyas in a contest of strength and hurled an elephant.
The Crown Prince was versatile in the arts and excelled beyond his peers.
As King Śuddhodana, filled with joy, was about to return, the charioteer was driving the elephant and was just about to exit the city.
Devadatta, who had long possessed great strength, entered from outside and asked the charioteer,
"Who wishes to mount this elephant that has been thus caparisoned?"
He replied, "The Prince is about to return, so I am going to drive the elephant for him.

Devadatta, filled with indignation, pulled at the elephant, struck its forehead, and kicked its chest; it fell prostrate, blocking the road and cutting off all passage. No one was able to move it, and the crowd became completely congested.
Nanda arrived later and asked him,
"Who killed this elephant?
He replied:
“Devadatta,” he said,
and immediately dragged him aside to clear the path.
When the Prince arrived, he asked again:
"Who has done this unwholesome deed of harming this elephant?
They replied,
"Devadatta harmed it to block the path, while Nanda led it away to clear the way."

The Prince then lifted the elephant and hurled it high, leaping over the city moat; when the elephant fell to the ground, it formed a great deep pit, which local tradition calls "the Pit where the Elephant Fell."
In a vihāra beside it is an image of the Prince.
Beside that is another vihāra, which is the bedchamber of the Prince’s consort; within it is an image of Yaśodharā, together with an image of Rāhula.
Beside the palace is a vihāra containing an image of him receiving his lessons; this is the site of the former foundation of the Prince’s schoolhouse.
At the southeastern corner of the city is a vihāra, within which is an image of the Prince riding a white horse as he ascends into the void; this is the place where he passed beyond the city walls.
Outside each of the four gates of the city, there was a shrine containing images of an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a śramaṇa.

As the Prince went out on his excursion, he beheld these sights and his feelings were deepened; filled with profound weariness toward worldly life, he was moved to realization at that moment and commanded his servant to turn the carriage back.

Traveling more than fifty li south of the city, one arrives at an old city where there is a stūpa; this was the birthplace of Krakucchanda Buddha during the Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was sixty thousand years.
Not far to the south of the city is a stūpa at the place where he beheld his father after attaining perfect enlightenment.
To the southeast of the city is a stūpa containing the relics of that Tathāgata’s physical remains.
In front stands a stone pillar over thirty feet high, upon which is carved the image of a lion; its sides record the events of his parinirvāṇa. It was erected by King Aśoka.

Traveling more than thirty li northeast from the city of Krakucchanda Buddha, one arrives at an old great city. Within it is a stūpa; this was the birthplace of Kanakamuni Buddha during the *bhadrakalpa* when the human lifespan was forty thousand years.
Not far to the northeast is a stūpa at the place where he attained perfect enlightenment and converted his father.

To the north of that is another stūpa containing the bodily relics of the Tathāgata; in front of it stands a stone pillar over twenty feet high, topped with an image of a lion and inscribed on its side with an account of his parinirvāṇa, which was erected by King Aśoka.

More than forty li to the northeast of the city, there is a stūpa; this is where the Prince sat in the shade of a tree, observing the plowing of the fields, and practiced meditative concentration here, thereby attaining freedom from desire.

When King Śuddhodana saw the Prince sitting in the shade of a tree, having entered into meditative absorption, the sunlight shone brightly while the shadow of the tree did not shift; knowing in his heart that he was a holy sage, the King’s profound reverence increased all the more.
To the northwest of the great city, there are several hundred thousand stūpas at the site where the Śākyas were slaughtered.

After King Virūḍhaka had conquered the Śākyas and captured their clansmen—numbering nine million nine hundred and ninety thousand—he put them all to death; the corpses were piled as high as a wild thicket, and the flowing blood formed a lake.
The gods alerted the people's hearts, and they collected the remains to bury them.
To the southwest of the execution site, there are four small stūpas, marking the places where the four Śākya clans resisted the army.
Initially, when King Vijaya ascended the throne, he sought a marriage alliance with the Śākya clan.
The Śākyas, deeming him of an inferior class, mistakenly bestowed upon him the daughter of a family member and formally betrothed her to him with great ceremony.
King Vijaya installed her as his chief queen, and she gave birth to a son, who became King Vīrasena Śākya.

Vilāsa Śākya, wishing to seek instruction and receive a formal education from his maternal uncle, arrived at the southern city wall; seeing a newly constructed lecture hall there, he halted his carriage to rest within it.
When the Śākyas heard of this, they pursued him and reviled him, saying:
"You low-born son of a slave-girl, how dare you occupy this chamber!"
"This chamber was built by the Śākyas to serve as a residence for the Buddha.
After Vairocana-Śākya succeeded to the throne, he sought to avenge the previous humiliation and mobilized his troops, stationing them here.
The four members of the Śākya clan were personally plowing the fields when they immediately resisted; the invading troops retreated and dispersed, whereupon they entered the city.

Their kinsmen, considering them to be the heirs of the lineage of the Wheel-Turning Kings and the primary sons of the Dharma Kings, deemed it intolerable that they would dare to commit such atrocities and endure the taking of life, thereby defiling their noble house; thus, they banished them to a distant land.

The four men were driven out and headed north toward the Snow Mountains; one became the king of Udyāna, one the king of Bāmiyāna, one the king of Himatala, and one the king of Śāmbī. They transmitted their hereditary rule through successive generations, and their descendants have never ceased.
Three or four *li* south of the city is a grove of *nyagrodha* trees where there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka.
This is the place where Śākyamuni Tathāgata, having attained perfect enlightenment, returned to his kingdom to see his father, the king, and preached the Dharma for him.

When King Śuddhodana learned that the Tathāgata had already subdued the armies of Māra and was traveling about to convert and guide beings, he felt a deep longing and yearning, wishing to pay his respects.
He then dispatched a messenger to invite the Tathāgata, saying:
"In the past, you vowed that upon attaining Buddhahood, you would return to your native land."
"These words are still ringing in my ears; it is time for you to come here.
When the messenger arrived at the Buddha's dwelling, he fully conveyed the King's intention.
The Tathāgata replied:
"Seven days hence, he shall return to his birthplace.

When the envoy returned and reported this to the King, King Śuddhodana issued a command to his ministers and subjects to sprinkle and sweep the roads, to stockpile flowers and incense, and to wait with the various officials forty *li* outside the city to escort him upon his arrival.

At that time, the Tathāgata was together with the great assembly; the eight Vajrapāṇis surrounded him on all sides, the Four Heavenly Kings led the way, Śakra and the gods of the desire realm attended on his left, Brahmā and the gods of the form realm attended on his right, and the community of bhikṣus followed behind him.

The Buddha was among the assembly like the moon reflected among the stars; his majestic spiritual power stirred the three realms, and his radiance surpassed the seven luminaries. Treading through the void, he arrived at the land of his birth.
After the king and his retinue had completed their salutations, they returned together to the kingdom and stayed at the Nyagrodha Monastery.
Not far from its side was a stūpa, marking the place where the Tathāgata sat facing east beneath a great tree and accepted the gold-threaded kāṣāya robe from his maternal aunt.
Next to this stūpa is where the Tathāgata converted the eight princes and five hundred members of the Śākya clan.
To the left of the road inside the eastern gate of the city is a stūpa; it was here in the past that Prince Sarvārthasiddha practiced the various arts and crafts.

Outside the gate was a temple of Maheśvara; within the temple was a stone image of the deity standing in a towering, majestic posture. This was the very temple where the Prince had entered while still in his swaddling clothes.
When King Śuddhodana was returning from the country of Lumbinī with the Crown Prince, they passed by a celestial shrine along the way.

The King said, "This celestial shrine possesses many miraculous responses; whenever the young Śākya children seek its protection, their prayers are invariably efficacious. It would be fitting to take the Crown Prince there to pay his respects."
At that time, the foster mother carried him into the shrine, where the stone image of the deity rose up to welcome the Prince.
Once the Prince had departed, the divine image sat back down.
To the left of the road outside the southern city gate, there is a stūpa marking the place where the Prince competed in martial arts with the Śākyas and shot at an iron drum.

From here, traveling more than thirty li to the southeast, there is a small stūpa. Beside it is a spring whose flowing water is as clear as a mirror. This is where the Prince, together with the Śākyas, competed in strength and skill; having drawn his bow and released his arrow, it pierced the drum and passed through the target, continuing until its feathers submerged in the pool. Thereupon, a clear stream gushed forth. According to local tradition, it is called the Arrow Spring.
Now, those who suffer from illness often find great relief through drinking or bathing [in the clay].

People from distant regions carry the mud back with them; according to their specific ailment, they soak it and apply it to their foreheads. Thus, the spiritual deities provide secret protection, and many receive complete recovery.

Traveling eighty or ninety *li* northeast from Arrow Spring, one reaches the Lavaṇī Forest, where there is a bathing pool belonging to the Śākya clan; its waters are clear and bright as a mirror, and various flowers cover its surface.
Twenty-four or twenty-five paces to its north stands a *aśoka* flower tree, which is now withered; this is the place where the Bodhisattva manifested his spiritual birth.
According to the [Sarvāstivāda] tradition, it was on the eighth day of the second half of the month of Vaiśākha, corresponding to the eighth day of the third month;
according to the Sthavira school, however, it was on the fifteenth day of the second half of the month of Vaiśākha, corresponding to the fifteenth day of the third month.
Next is the stūpa to the east, built by King Aśoka at the site where two nāgas bathed the Prince.
After the Bodhisattva was born, he walked unaided for seven paces in each of the four directions and declared:
"In the heavens above and the world below, I alone am the most honored."
"From this moment forth, my life's portion is exhausted.
As his feet stepped, great lotus flowers emerged from the ground.
Two dragons leaped forth, staying suspended in the air, each spouting water—one cold and one warm—to bathe the Prince.
To the east of the stūpa marking the place where the Prince was bathed, there are two clear springs; beside them stand two stūpas, which mark the spot where two nāgas emerged from the earth.
Once the Bodhisattva was born, his kinsmen and relatives all rushed forward to seek water for his ablution.
Before the Lady’s presence, two springs gushed forth—one cold and one warm—and with these she bathed him.
To the south is a stūpa, the place where Śakra, Lord of the Devas, received the Bodhisattva in his hands.
When the Bodhisattva first emerged from the womb, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knelt and received the Bodhisattva with a sublime celestial robe.
Next are four stūpas, which mark the places where the Four Heavenly Kings received the Bodhisattva in their arms.
After the Bodhisattva was born from the right side, the Four Great Heavenly Kings took him up with golden cotton garments and placed him upon a golden table.
He went before his mother and said, "It is truly a cause for joy and celebration that you, noble lady, have given birth to this blessed son.
Even the devas rejoice; how much more so the people of the world!"
Not far from the side of the stūpa enshrining the Prince, whom the Four Heavenly Kings supported, there is a great stone pillar topped with the image of a horse; it was erected by King Aśoka.
Later, struck by a thunderbolt from an evil dragon, the pillar snapped in the middle and fell to the ground.
Beside it flows a small river toward the southeast, which the local custom calls the Oil River.

After Lady Māyā had given birth, the devas transformed this pond, making it radiant, moist, clear, and pure, so that the lady might take its water for a bath to dispel the wind and weakness resulting from childbirth.
Now it has transformed into water, its current still oily.
From here, traveling eastward through a vast wilderness and desolate forest for more than two hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Rāma, within the borders of Central India.
The Kingdom of Rāmagrāma: Having been desolate for many years, its borders are no longer demarcated; its cities and towns are in ruins, and the inhabitants are sparse and few.
To the southeast of the old city stands a brick stūpa, less than one hundred feet in height.

In the past, after the Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa, the former kings of this country each obtained a portion of his relics. They brought them back to their own lands and erected stūpas in accordance with the sacred rites; since then, miraculous wonders have arisen from time to time, and divine radiance has frequently illuminated the surroundings.

Beside the stūpa is a clear pool where a dragon frequently comes to play; transforming its form into that of a serpent, it coils and winds to the right, circling the stūpa. Herds of wild elephants also pass by, gathering flowers to scatter as offerings. Through the power of the unseen, this vigilance continues without interruption.

Formerly, when King Aśoka divided and established the stūpas, those built in seven kingdoms had all already been opened; however, as he was now about to undertake the work in this country, the dragon of this lake, fearing it would be usurped, transformed himself into a Brahmin and approached the elephant, saying:
"The Great King’s heart flows toward the Buddha-dharma, and you are extensively planting fields of merit. I venture to request that you deign to turn your carriage and descend to my abode."
The king asked, "Where is your home? Is it near or far?
The brahmin replied:
"I am the dragon king of this lake.
Having learned that Your Majesty intends to establish supreme merit, I have ventured here to pay my respects.
The king accepted his invitation and entered the dragon palace.
After sitting for a long time, the dragon approached and said:

"I have received this dragon body solely due to my evil karma; by making offerings to the śarīra, I hope to extinguish my transgressions. I pray that Your Majesty will go in person to behold and pay homage to it."
When King Aśoka saw this, he was struck with awe and said,
"All these articles for making offerings are not of human origin.
The nāga replied:
"If that is so, I pray you do not destroy it.
King Aśoka, judging his own power to be no match for theirs, ultimately did not excavate it.
The place where he exited the pond still bears a commemorative seal.
Not far from the side of the stūpa, there is a monastery where the monastic community is small; it is pure and serene, and the śrāmaṇeras manage all the communal affairs.
When monks arrive from afar, they are received with exceptional honor; they are invariably detained for three days and provided with the four requisites of monastic life.
According to the records of former sages, there was once a bhikṣu who, invited by a fellow practitioner, traveled from a great distance to pay homage at the stūpa.
He saw herds of elephants moving back and forth, some using their tusks to clear away grass, others using their trunks to sprinkle water, each holding various flowers to perform offerings together.
When the assembly saw this, they sighed with grief and were moved by deep emotion.
A certain bhikṣu then renounced his full ordination, wishing to remain to provide offerings, and addressed the assembly, saying:
"I alone possess great merit, yet I have occupied a place among the Sangha unworthily; the years and months have passed rapidly, while my conduct and practice have remained without discipline."
This stūpa contains the relics of the Buddha; his sacred virtue communicates with the unseen world, such that a herd of elephants comes to water it.
Having left his body here, he was content to join their company; that he may complete the remainder of his life among them is truly a blessing.
The assembly said to him:
"This is a magnificent undertaking.
Our defilements are heavy and our wisdom insufficient; we were not capable of planning this."
"Love yourself at all times and do not let your superior practice decline.
Having thus departed from the community, he reaffirmed his sincere vows; dwelling alone with joy, he resolved to remain there until the end of his days.
Thereupon, he thatched a hut with rushes, diverted a stream to form a pond, gathered seasonal flowers, and swept the precincts of the burial site.
As the years passed, his devotion never faltered.

The kings of neighboring countries heard of this and held it in high esteem; they vied with one another to donate wealth and treasures to jointly construct monasteries. Consequently, they entreated him to deign to oversee monastic affairs.
From that time forward, this tradition was passed down in succession so as not to let his original merit perish, and thus śrāmaṇeras were appointed to preside over all monastic matters.
To the east of the Śrāmaṇera monastery, traveling over a hundred li through a great forest, one reaches a large stūpa built by King Aśoka.
This is the place where the Prince, having crossed the city walls and arrived here, took off his precious robes, removed his jeweled necklaces, and commanded his servant to return home.
At midnight, the Prince leaped over the city wall and arrived here at the break of dawn; having fulfilled his long-held aspiration, he spoke these words:
"This is the place where I have finally emerged from the cage and enclosure, cast off my fetters and chains, and unyoked my chariot for the last time."
He untied a maṇi jewel from his celestial crown and commanded his attendant, saying:
"Take this jewel and return to inform our father, the King: 'I have now fled far away not out of a desire for mere separation, but because I wish to sever impermanence and cut off all outflows.'"
Chandaka (formerly transcribed as Che-ni, which is erroneous) said,
"What heart could there be to return empty-handed after driving [the horse]?
The Prince comforted him with kind words, and he returned with a sense of realization.
Turning the carriage eastward toward the stūpa, there was a Jambū tree; although its branches and leaves had withered, the gnarled trunk still remained.
Beside it was another small stūpa, the place where the Prince exchanged his remaining precious robes for a deer-skin garment.
Once the Prince had cut his hair and changed his clothes, although he had removed his jeweled necklaces, he still wore celestial robes.
He said, "These garments are too extravagant; how can they be changed?"
At that time, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven transformed himself into a hunter, wearing a deer-skin robe, holding a bow, and carrying a quiver of arrows on his back.
The Prince lifted up his garment and said to him, "I wish to trade with you;
I hope you will grant me this request."
The hunter said,
"Excellent.
The Prince removed his upper garment and bestowed it upon the hunter.
Having obtained them, the hunter returned to his celestial body and, carrying the garments he had acquired, departed soaring through the air.
Not far from where the Prince changed his clothes, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; this is the place where the Prince shaved his hair.
The Prince took a sword from Channaka and cut off his own hair; Śakra, Lord of the Devas, received it and ascended to the celestial palace to offer it as an act of worship.
At that time, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven transformed himself into a barber, holding a sharp razor, and approached with measured steps.
The Prince said to him:
"Can you shave my hair?
I would be grateful if you would cleanse me of it."
The transformed person received his command and subsequently shaved his hair.

The time he leaped over the city walls to renounce the world was also uncertain: some say the Bodhisattva was nineteen years old, while others say twenty-nine; he leaped over the walls on the eighth day of the latter half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the eighth day of the third lunar month, though some say it was the fifteenth day of the latter half of Vaiśākha, corresponding to the fifteenth day of the third lunar month.

To the southeast of the Stūpa of the Prince’s Shaving of His Hair, after traveling one hundred and eighty or ninety li through the wilderness, one reaches the Nyagrodha Grove, where there is a stūpa over thirty feet high.
Formerly, when the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa and his relics had already been distributed, the brahmins obtained nothing at the *nirvāpaṇa*—which in the language of Tang means "cremation."

The old term "jiaowei" (cremation) is a corruption. [The monks] collected the remaining ashes and charcoal from the site and brought them back to their own country, where they established this sacred foundation and performed offerings.
From that time until now, miraculous events have occurred in succession; those suffering from illness are often cured through prayer and petition.
Beside the Ash-Charcoal Stūpa, within an old monastery, there are sites containing the traces of where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation.
To the left and right of this old monastery, there are several hundred stūpas.
The largest of these was built by King Aśoka; although its lofty foundation has subsided, it still stands over a hundred feet high.

From here, traveling northeast through a great forest, the path is arduous and perilous, with dangerous obstacles along the way. Mountain oxen, wild elephants, bands of robbers, and hunters lie in wait for travelers, inflicting harm without ceasing.
Having emerged from this forest, he arrived at the kingdom of Kuśinagara, within the borders of Central India.
In the kingdom of Kuśinagara, the city walls were in ruins and the towns and villages were desolate.
The brick foundations of the old city walls extend for more than ten *li* in circumference.
The inhabitants are sparse and few, and the lanes and alleys are overgrown and desolate.
In the northeastern corner of the city stands a *stūpa*, built by King Aśoka; it marks the site of the former residence of Cunda (formerly called Chun-tuo, which is an error).
In the residence there was a well; when they were about to prepare offerings, they then dug it.
Although many years have passed, the water remains clear and delicious.
Three or four *li* to the northwest of the city, one crosses the Ajitavatī River—translated into Chinese as Wusheng (Invincible), which is the common name used by the world.
The old transcription "A-li-lo-bo-ti River" is erroneous.
According to the authoritative texts, it is called the Śīrṣavatī River, which translates as "The River with Gold.
Not far from its western bank, one reaches the Sāla forest.
The trees resemble the *hu* tree, with bark that is greenish-white and leaves that are exceptionally glossy.
Four of these trees are particularly tall; they are the site where the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa.
Within the great brick vihāra, there is an image of the Tathāgata in the posture of nirvāṇa, lying with his head toward the north.
Beside it stands a stūpa built by King Aśoka; although its foundations have subsided, it still rises over two hundred feet high.
In front of it was erected a stone pillar to record the events of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa; though the inscription remains, the date—both day and month—is not recorded.

I have heard from ancient records that the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa at the age of eighty on the fifteenth day of the second half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the third lunar month here.
According to the Sarvāstivādins, the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa on the eighth day of the second half of the month of Kārttika, which corresponds to the eighth day of the ninth month.

Since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, various schools have held differing opinions: some say more than one thousand two hundred years; some say more than one thousand three hundred years; some say more than one thousand five hundred years; and others say that nine hundred years have already passed, but the millennium has not yet been completed.
Not far from the side of the vihāra, there is a stūpa at the place where the Tathāgata, while practicing the bodhisattva path, acted as a king of pheasants to extinguish a fire.
In the past, there was a vast and lush forest in this location, where various beasts and birds dwelt in nests and burrows.
A startling wind rose from all sides, and fierce flames blazed with violent speed.
At that time, there was a pheasant who, moved by compassion, plunged into the clear stream and flew into the air, vigorously splashing water.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, looked down and said:
"Why do you persist in such folly and exhaust your wings in vain?
A great fire is breaking out, consuming the forests and wilds; how could your tiny body possibly extinguish it?"
The pheasant asked,
"Who was it that spoke?
He replied:
"I am Śakra, Lord of the Devas," he replied.

The pheasant said, "Now, Your Majesty Śakra possesses great power of merit; there is no desire you do not fulfill. To rescue from calamity and save from distress is as easy for you as pointing at something in the palm of your hand. Yet, when questioned, you claim to have achieved no merit—where, then, does the fault lie?"
"The fierce fire is now blazing; there is no time for further words!
He then immediately took flight and went toward the flowing water.

Śakra, Lord of Devas, subsequently scooped up water in his palms and sprinkled it over the forest; the fire was extinguished and the smoke vanished, and all living beings were saved from death. For this reason, it is now called the Fire-Quelling Stūpa.
Not far from where the pheasant rescued the fire is a stūpa; this is the place where the Tathāgata, while practicing the bodhisattva path, saved the lives of deer.

In the distant past, there was a great forest here; when a conflagration broke out in the wilds, the birds and beasts were driven to desperation. Ahead lay the peril of a swift-flowing torrent, and behind them was the hardship of a fierce blaze; none failed to drown or lose their lives.
The deer felt compassion and, though his body was pinned against the rushing current with skin pierced and bones broken, he exerted himself to rescue the drowning one.
When the lame hare arrived later, he endured the exhaustion and suffering to bring him across as well.
His strength being utterly exhausted, he drowned and died.
The devas collected his remains and erected a stūpa.
Not far to the west of the place where the deer rescued him from drowning, there is a stūpa; this is [the site of] Subhadra (translated into Chinese as Shanxian).
Formerly called Subhadra, which is a corruption; this is the place where he entered parinirvāṇa.
The Venerable Subhadra was originally a teacher of the Brahmins;
he was one hundred and twenty years old, venerable and possessed of great wisdom.
Hearing that the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, he went to the space between the twin trees and asked Ānanda:
"The World-Honored Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa; I have lingering doubts and hesitations, and wish to inquire about them."
Ānanda said, "The Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa; pray do not cause him disturbance.
He replied:
"I have heard that a Buddha appears in the world but rarely, and the True Dharma is difficult to encounter. I harbor deep doubts and fear there may be no one to whom I can address them.
Subhadra then entered and first asked the Buddha:

"There are various other assemblies who claim themselves to be teachers; each possesses distinct doctrines by which they instruct and guide the laity. Does Gautama [formerly called *Gautama*, corrupted to *Jo-dha-mo*] know them all thoroughly?"
The Buddha said,
"I have thoroughly investigated all things," and then he expounded it for them.
Having heard this, Subhadra’s mind was filled with pure faith and understanding; he sought entry into the Dharma and requested the full ordination.
The Tathāgata said to him:
"Are you truly capable?"

When those of external paths and different schools who practice the holy life (brahmacarya) wish to join, they shall undergo a four-year probationary period; their conduct must be observed and their nature examined. If their deportment is tranquil and their speech is truthful, they may then purify the holy life within my Dharma.
"If it were merely a matter of human hearing, what difficulty would there be!
Suvīra said, "The World-Honored One is compassionate and bestows grace upon all without partiality; after four years of study and practice, my three karmas have finally become harmonious."
The Buddha said, "I have already stated before that it depends on the person's own practice!
Thereupon, Subhadra went forth and immediately received full ordination; he applied himself with diligence to his cultivation, his body and mind being courageous and resolute.
Thereafter, he became free from doubt regarding the Dharma and realized it through his own direct experience.
Before long during the night, he attained the fruit of Arhatship; all taints were exhausted, and the holy life was established.

Unable to bear seeing the Buddha enter Great Parinirvāṇa, he immediately entered the fire-samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*) amidst the assembly, manifested miraculous powers, and passed into extinction first.
He was the final disciple of the Tathāgata to attain parinirvāṇa; he was none other than the lame hare who crossed last in a previous life.
Beside the site of Subhadra’s parinirvāṇa is a stūpa, which marks the place where Vajrapāṇi fell to the ground.

The World-Honored One of Great Compassion, having benefited beings according to their capacities and completed his work of transformation, entered the bliss of parinirvāṇa, lying between the twin śāla trees with his head to the north.
When the Vajrapāṇi deity, Guhyapada Malla, saw that the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, he cried out in bitter grief:
"The Tathāgata has abandoned me and entered Great Nirvana! I have no refuge and no protection; the poisonous arrow has pierced deep, and the fire of sorrow blazes fiercely!"
He cast down his vajra, fell to the ground in a swoon, and after a long time rose again.
In deep sorrow and longing, he said to the others:
"In the great ocean of birth and death, who shall serve as our boat and oars?"
"In the long night of ignorance, who shall serve as the lamp?
Beside where Vajrapāṇi fell to the ground, there is a stūpa; this is the place where offerings were made for seven days after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa.
When the Tathāgata was about to enter parinirvāṇa, his radiance shone everywhere; humans and devas gathered together, all of whom were moved by grief and said to one another:
"The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One is now about to enter parinirvāṇa; the merit of sentient beings is exhausted, and the world will be without refuge."
The Tathāgata lay on his right side upon the lion-bed and addressed the great assembly:
"Do not say that the Tathāgata has entered ultimate extinction; the Dharma-body is eternally abiding and free from all change. You should cast off indolence and seek liberation without delay."
The bhikṣus sobbed and were overcome with grief.
Then Aniruddha—formerly called Anarudha, which is an error—addressed the bhikṣus:
"Cease, cease! Do not grieve!"
"The devas are mocking and finding it strange.
At that time, when the Malla assembly had finished their offerings and wished to lift the golden coffin to proceed to the place of the *nirvāṇa*,
Aniruddha addressed them, saying:
“Cease for now!
The devas wish to remain for seven days to offer worship.
Thereupon, the host of devas, holding exquisite celestial flowers, traveled through the void, extolling the holy virtues, each exhausting their sincere hearts as they collectively raised offerings.
Beside where the coffin was halted stands a stūpa; this is the place where Lady Mahāmāyā wept for the Buddha.
When the Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa and the enshrouding in the coffin was completed, Aniruddha ascended to the celestial palace and informed Lady Mahāmāyā, saying:
"The Great Sage, the Dharma King, has now entered parinirvāṇa."

Upon hearing this, Māyā was choked with grief and fainted; she went with the assembly of devas to the space between the twin trees. Seeing the saṃghāṭī robe, the alms bowl, and the mendicant’s staff, she stroked them and wailed aloud, fainting again and then regaining her senses, saying:
"The merit of humans and devas is exhausted! The Eye of the World has been extinguished!"
"Now these various objects are empty and have no owner.
