By the holy power of the Tathāgata, the golden coffin opened of its own accord; emitting radiance, he sat with palms joined and comforted his compassionate mother, saying:
"You have come down from afar!"
"It is the natural law of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); I pray that you do not grieve too deeply.
Ānanda, suppressing his sorrow, petitioned the Buddha, saying:
"If those of future generations question me, with what shall I answer them?"
He replied:

"The Buddha has already entered nirvana; his compassionate mother, Māyā, descended from the celestial palace and arrived between the twin trees. For the sake of all unfilial sentient beings, the Tathāgata rose from the golden coffin, joined his palms, and preached the Dharma."
More than three hundred paces north of the city wall, across the river, there is a stūpa at the place where the Tathāgata cremated his body.
The ground is now yellowish-black, the soil being mixed with ashes and charcoal; if one makes a sincere supplication, one may perhaps obtain śarīra relics.

When the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa, humans and devas were moved by grief. A coffin was made of the seven precious gems, and his body was wrapped in a thousand layers of fine cotton cloth. Incense and flowers were offered, and banners and canopies were erected. The Malla multitude carried the bier in a funeral procession, with attendants leading and following before and behind. They crossed the Hiranyavati River to the north, filled it with fragrant oil, piled up much fragrant wood, and set fire to it; yet two layers of cloth did not burn—one that directly touched the body, and one that covered the outermost layer.
For the sake of all sentient beings, his relics were distributed; only his hair and nails remained intact and undamaged.
Beside the site where his body was cremated is a stūpa, marking the place where the Tathāgata manifested his two feet for Mahākāśyapa.
When the Tathāgata’s golden coffin had been lowered and the fragrant wood piled up, the fire would not ignite,
and the assembly was filled with alarm and wonder. Aniruddha said,
"We must wait for Kāśyapa."
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, together with five hundred disciples, came from the mountain forests to the city of Kuśinagara and asked Ānanda:
"Is it possible to see the body of the World-Honored One?"
Ānanda said:
"A thousand layers of fine cotton cloth have been wrapped around him, the heavy coffin has been fully encased, and the fragrant wood has already been piled up;
the cremation is about to take place. At that moment, the Buddha extended his two feet from within the coffin; upon the wheels of his feet (the *cakrāṅka*), a strange color was seen.
He asked Ānanda,
"Why is this so? He replied:
“The Buddha has just entered parinirvāṇa; humans and devas are struck with grief and lamentation, and their tears have fallen and stained [the wood], resulting in these extraordinary colors.
Kāśyapa prostrated himself, circumambulated the pyre while offering praises, and the fragrant wood ignited spontaneously as a great fire blazed forth.
Therefore, when the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa, he emerged from the coffin three times:
first, he extended his arm and asked Ānanda to prepare the road;
next, he sat up and preached the Dharma for his mother.
Afterwards, he manifested his two feet to show them to Mahākāśyapa.
Beside the manifestation of the feet is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; this is the place where the eight kings divided the śarīra relics.
A stone pillar was erected beforehand, inscribed with an account of these events.

After the Buddha entered *nirvāṇa* and the *nirvāṇa-pariṣad* had concluded, the kings of the eight kingdoms arrived with their fourfold armies. They dispatched the Brahmin Ajita to address the Mallas of Kuśinagara, saying:
"The Teacher of gods and humans has attained parinirvāṇa in this kingdom; therefore, we have come from afar to request a portion of his relics."
The Malla said:
"The Tathāgata has humbled his majesty to descend to this inferior land; he has extinguished the world’s enlightened guide and lost the compassionate father of sentient beings.
As for the Tathāgata’s relics, we shall naturally offer them worship ourselves; it would be in vain to exhaust yourselves on the road, for you will ultimately gain nothing."
At that time, the great kings used humble words to entreat him; yet, as their request was not granted, they spoke to him again, saying:
"If you do not comply with our formal invitation, military force will not be far behind."
The Brahmin Ṛjusarva raised his voice and said:

"Take heed! The World-Honored One, the Greatly Compassionate One, has cultivated merit and goodness through the endurance of countless kalpas; this is surely what you have heard. Now that you wish to insult him, it is not fitting."
"Now that the śarīra are here, they should be divided equally into eight portions so that each may receive their share for veneration; why go so far as to raise an army?
Following these words, the Mallas immediately measured them out, intending to divide them into eight parts.
Śakra addressed the kings, saying, "The heavens shall have their own portions; do not rely on force to compete.
The Naga Kings Anavatapta, Mucilinda, and Elāpattra then made this proposal:
"Do not leave us behind.
If you rely on strength alone, the multitude shall be no match for you.
The Brahmin Ṛjuka replied:
"Do not quarrel; you should divide it among yourselves.
He then divided it into three portions: one for the devas, one for the nāgas, and one to remain in the human world, which was subsequently divided among the eight kingdoms.
The devas, nāgas, and kings of men were all moved by grief.
Traveling more than two hundred li southwest from the stūpa containing the divided relics, one arrives at a large town.
There was a brāhmaṇa of noble lineage and immense wealth, steadfast and pure in conduct, who had mastered the five sciences and revered the Triple Gem.

Beside his residence, he constructed a monastery, exhausting all resources and providing it with every kind of precious ornament. Whenever monks passed along the road, he would earnestly invite them to stay, making offerings with a sincere heart for one night or even up to seven days.

Subsequently, King Śatavāhana destroyed the Buddha-dharma, and the community of monks was left without companions; as the years and months passed rapidly by, the Brahmins were constantly filled with sincere compassion.
While walking for exercise, he saw a śramaṇa with thick eyebrows and white hair approaching, leaning on a *khakkhara* staff.
The brāhmaṇa hurried forward to meet him and asked where he had come from; he invited him into the monastery and prepared various offerings, serving him a gruel cooked with pure milk at dawn.
Having accepted it, the śramaṇa took but a single bite with his teeth, then immediately set down the bowl, sighing deeply and reflecting in silence.
The brāhmaṇa, holding the food, knelt and asked:
"Venerable One, you who possess wisdom and benefit others according to conditions, have deigned to visit us; is it that you are uneasy at evening?"
"Is the congee not flavorful?
The śramaṇa said with compassion, "I grieve that the merit and blessings of sentient beings are gradually diminishing; let us set this aside for now and speak once you have finished eating."
When the śramaṇa had finished eating and adjusted his robes, he immediately spoke.
The brāhmaṇa said, "You previously promised to speak; why do you now remain silent?"
The śramaṇa replied, “It is not that I have forgotten.
Such discourse is not undertaken lightly; the matter may give rise to doubt.”
If you truly desire to hear it, I shall now speak briefly.
What I sighed over just now was not that your porridge was poor;
rather, for several hundred years, I have not tasted such a flavor.

In the past, when the Tathāgata was in the world, I was among those who followed him. While at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha, I would stoop by the clear stream to wash my vessels, using them for rinsing the mouth or for bathing.
"Alas! The pure milk of today does not equal the plain water of antiquity; this is brought about by the exhaustion of the merit of humans and devas.
The Brahmin said:
"In that case, Venerable Sir, did you personally see the Buddha?
The śramaṇa replied, "Indeed."
"Did you not hear that the Buddha’s son Rāhula was none other than my own self?
It is for the sake of protecting the True Dharma that I have not yet entered parinirvāṇa.
Having spoken these words, he suddenly vanished.

The Brahmin then prepared the room where [the Master] had stayed, anointing it with fragrant ointments and sweeping it clean; he arranged the images with solemn ritual, honoring them as if they were truly present.

Furthermore, traveling more than five hundred *li* through the great forest, he reached the kingdom of Vārāṇasī (formerly called Bālúnàiguó, which is a corruption). The term "nǚ" (女) is a phonetic transcription of the character "xué" (黠), while "sī" (斯) is a phonetic transcription of the character "sī" (斯). Thus, it is the old kingdom of Vārāṇasī. This is an error [in the original transcription].
Within the borders of Central India.
*The Great Tang Dynasty Record of the Western Regions*, Scroll Six;
*The Great Tang Dynasty Record of the Western Regions*, Scroll Seven: Five Kingdoms.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree;
compiled by the Śramaṇa Bianji of Dazongchi Monastery.

The Five Kingdoms: the Kingdom of Vārāṇasī (the "V" in Vārāṇasī is pronounced as *xiá* [反]), the Kingdom of Yaśodharā, the Kingdom of Vaiśālī, the Kingdom of Pṛṣṭhāpura, and the Kingdom of Nepal. Regarding the Kingdom of Vārāṇasī: it is more than four thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom borders the Gaṅgā River to the west; it is eighteen or nineteen *li* in length and five or six *li* in width.

The residential quarters are as dense as the teeth of a comb, and the inhabitants are numerous and prosperous; every household accumulates tens of millions of wealth, and every chamber is filled with rare treasures.
The people are gentle and respectful by nature, and their customs value diligent study; many believe in non-Buddhist paths while few revere the Buddha-dharma.
The climate is mild, grain crops flourish, fruit trees grow in lush profusion, and the thick grasses sway gently in the breeze.
There are more than thirty monasteries with over three thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.

There are more than one hundred deva temples with over ten thousand non-Buddhists; most of them worship Maheśvara, some shaving their heads, others wearing their hair in topknots, some remaining naked without clothing, and others smearing their bodies with ashes, diligently practicing asceticism in their quest for liberation from birth and death.

Within the great city, there are twenty deva temples. Their multi-storied terraces and shrines feature carved stone and ornate woodwork; they are shaded by dense forests and encircled by clear, flowing streams. The brass statues of the deities measure nearly one hundred feet in height; their majesty is solemn and awe-inspiring, as if they were truly present.
To the northeast of the great city, west of the Vārāṇasī River, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, over one hundred feet in height.
In front of it stands a stone pillar, as clear and fresh as a mirror, with a lustrous sheen that appears to flow; within it, the image of the Tathāgata constantly manifests.

Traveling northeast from the Varanasi River for over ten li, one arrives at the Deer Park Monastery (Mṛgadāva-vihāra). Its precincts are divided into eight sections, enclosed by continuous walls and ramparts; its tiered eaves and multi-storied pavilions reach the pinnacle of architectural elegance.
There are fifteen hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.

Within the great enclosure is a vihāra over two hundred feet high; its summit features an embossed mango fruit made of gold. The foundation and steps are made of stone, while the tiered niches are constructed of brick, encircling the structure on all four sides. There are hundreds of such tiers, each containing an embossed golden image of the Buddha. Inside the vihāra is a brass image of the Buddha, equal in size to the body of the Tathāgata, depicted in the posture of turning the Wheel of Dharma.
To the southwest of the vihāra is a stone stūpa built by King Aśoka; although its foundation has subsided, it still stands over one hundred feet high.
In front of it stands a stone pillar, more than seventy feet tall.

The stone possesses the luster of jade; its clarity reflects and penetrates all things. Through earnest supplication, the images of various forms appear as reflections, and those who behold them occasionally perceive the signs of both good and evil.
This is the place where the Tathāgata, having attained perfect enlightenment, first turned the Wheel of Dharma.

Not far from its side is a stūpa; this is where Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya and the others, seeing that the Bodhisattva had abandoned his ascetic practices and thus no longer attended upon him, came here to practice meditative concentration on their own.
Beside it is a stūpa marking the place where five hundred pratyekabuddhas entered nirvāṇa together.
Furthermore, there are three stūpas at the sites of the past three Buddhas’ sitting and walking meditation.

To the side of where the three Buddhas performed their walking meditation (caṅkrama) is a stūpa; this is the place where Maitreya—whose name in the language of Tang means "Compassionate" (and whose surname is likewise)—received the prediction of his future Buddhahood.
The older transcription "Mile" is a corruption and abbreviation. This is the site where the Bodhisattva received the prophecy of his attainment of Buddhahood.
In the past, while the Tathāgata was at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"In a future age, when the lands of this Jambudvīpa are level and even, and the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, there will be a son of a brāhmaṇa named Maitreya. His body will be of true golden color, radiant and luminous; he shall leave the household life to attain perfect enlightenment and extensively preach the Dharma for sentient beings in three assemblies."
Those who are delivered and saved are all sentient beings who have planted blessings within my bequeathed Dharma.

Whether they are laypeople or monastics, those who uphold the precepts or those who violate them—provided they possess deep reverence for the Triple Gem and a single-minded devotion—they shall all receive my transformative guidance, realize the fruits of the path, and attain liberation.

"Among the three assemblies where the Dharma is preached, I shall deliver those disciples of my bequeathed teaching, and only thereafter will I transform those virtuous friends with whom I share a common affinity.
At that time, having heard these words of the Buddha, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"May I become that World-Honored One, Maitreya."
The Tathāgata said:
"As you have spoken, you shall realize this fruit.
All that has been described above constitutes the ritual of your teaching and transformation."
To the west of the stūpa where Maitreya Bodhisattva received his prediction is the site where Śākyamuni Bodhisattva received his prediction.

During the Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, Kāśyapa Buddha appeared in the world; he turned the sublime wheel of Dharma and enlightened sentient beings, bestowing a prediction upon the Bodhisattva Guṇaprabha (Huming), saying:
"In a future age, when the lifespan of sentient beings is one hundred years, this bodhisattva shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni."

Not far to the south of where the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni received his prediction, there is a footprint left by four past Buddhas during their walking meditation. It is over fifty paces long and about seven feet high, constructed from stacked blue stones. Upon it is fashioned an image of a Tathāgata in the act of walking; the form of the image is extraordinary, its majestic presence solemn and awe-inspiring. From above the *uṣṇīṣa*, hair and beard protrude prominently; no sacred mark is hidden, and its divine manifestation is clearly evidenced.

Within its enclosure, sacred sites are truly numerous; there are several hundred monasteries and stūpas, of which I shall briefly mention two or three, as it is impossible to describe them all in detail.
To the west of the monastery wall is a clear pond, over two hundred paces in circumference, where the Tathāgata once bathed.
To the west of that is a large pond, one hundred and eighty paces in circumference, where the Tathāgata once washed his utensils.
To the north of this is a pond, one hundred and fifty paces in circumference, where the Tathāgata once washed his robes.
In all three of these ponds, dragons reside.
Their waters are deep and sweet, clear and pristine, remaining constant without increase or decrease.
If those with arrogant minds bathe in this pool, the *kumbhīra* (crocodile) spirits often cause them harm;
yet if one approaches with deep reverence, one may draw water from it without fear.

On a large flat stone beside the washing-pool, there are traces of the Tathāgata’s *kāṣāya* (monastic robe); the patterns are clearly visible and as brilliant as if they were carved or engraved, and those of pure faith come here frequently to make offerings.
If heretics or wicked men should lightly step upon this stone, the dragon king within the pond will immediately raise wind and rain.

Not far from the side of the pond is a stūpa, which marks the place where the Tathāgata, while practicing the bodhisattva path, was a six-tusked elephant king. A hunter, coveting its tusks, falsely donned a *kāṣāya* robe and waited in ambush with a drawn bow. Out of reverence for the *kāṣāya*, the elephant king then broke off his tusks and presented them to him.

Not far from Līcchavi, there is a stūpa where, when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path, he took pity on the world’s lack of propriety and manifested himself as a bird. There, together with a monkey and a white elephant, they inquired of one another who had first seen this nyagrodha tree; each recounted their own experiences, whereby the order of seniority was established. Thus, the teachings gradually spread from near to far, and people came to understand the distinction between superior and inferior, leading both monastics and laity to take refuge.
Not far from its side, within a great forest, there is a stūpa at the place where the Tathāgata and Devadatta, both formerly serving as kings of deer, once settled a dispute.
Long ago, in this very place within a great forest, there were two herds of deer, each numbering more than five hundred.
At that time, as the King was hunting in the marshlands, the Bodhisattva, the Deer King, stepped forward and addressed the King, saying:

"Great King, as you range through the central plains for sport, setting fires and loosing flying arrows, all my followers will lose their lives this morning; before long they will rot and stink, leaving nothing to serve as provisions for your meal."
"I pray that you will grant me a turn in the rotation to provide one deer daily.
Thus, Your Majesty may have fresh meat for your meals, and I may prolong my life for a day or two.
The King approved of his words and turned his carriage back.
Two herds of deer took turns surrendering their lives one after another.
In Deva’s herd, there was a pregnant doe whose turn it was to die;
she said to her king, "Though my body should die, my child has not yet reached its turn."
The deer king said in anger,
"Who would not treasure their life!
The doe sighed and said:
"Our king is unrighteous; his death is imminent.
They then appealed for help to the Bodhisattva Deer King.
The Deer King said:
"How tragic is the heart of a compassionate mother, whose kindness extends even to an unborn child!
I shall now take your place.
Having said this, he proceeded to the king's gate.
People on the road raised their voices in proclamation, crying out:
"That great deer king is now entering the town!
The people of the capital, both officials and commoners, all rushed to see him.
When the king heard this, he considered it to be untrue.
The gatekeeper informed the king, and the king then believed it to be so,
saying:
"Why has the Deer King come in such haste?
The deer replied, "There is a doe who is due to die, yet her fetus has not yet been born; my heart cannot bear this, so I venture to offer my own body as a substitute."
Upon hearing this, the king sighed and said, "I am a human being in the body of a deer; you are a deer in the body of a human.

Thereupon, he released all the deer and no longer required them to pay tribute. He then made that forest a sanctuary for the deer, and thus it came to be called the Deer Park of Almsgiving (Mṛgadāva).
The name "Deer Park" originated from this point.

Two or three *li* to the southwest of the monastery is a stūpa over three hundred feet high; its foundation is broad and imposing, adorned with rare and precious jewels. It lacks tiered niches, and a bowl-shaped canopy is placed directly upon it. Although a pillar has been erected, it is without the wheel or the bell.
Beside it is a small stūpa, which marks the place where the five men, including Ajñāta-kauṇḍinya, abandoned their rules to welcome the Buddha.
Initially, he was named Sarvārthasiddha, which in the language of Tang means "One Who Has Accomplished All Aims."

Formerly called Siddhārtha, this is a corruption and abbreviation. After the Prince had leaped over the city walls, he dwelt among the mountains and hid in the valleys, forgetting his own person to devote himself to the Dharma.
King Śuddhodana then commanded three members of the royal clan and two from his maternal kin, saying:

"My son Sarvārthasiddha has abandoned his home to practice and study; he wanders alone through the mountains and marshes, dwelling solitary in the forests and thickets. Therefore, I command you all to follow him and learn where he resides."

"Internally, he is my paternal uncle and maternal uncle; externally, he is both my sovereign and my minister. In all his movements and stillnesses, he ought to know when to advance and when to desist.
The five men, bearing this mandate, kept watch over one another as they provided protection; they then diligently sought an opportunity, hoping to bring about his escape.
Every time they spoke to one another, they would say:
"Now, for one who cultivates the Way, is it realized through suffering or through joy?"
The two said,
"Peace and happiness constitute the Way.
The third said:
"Exerting oneself through ascetic toil is the way to the Path.
As these two views conflicted and neither could be clearly proven, the Prince contemplated the ultimate truth;
to subdue the non-Buddhist practitioners of self-mortification, he restricted his intake of hemp and rice to sustain his body.
The two men saw him and said:
"The conduct of the Prince is not the true Dharma.
As for the Way, it is to be realized through joy; now he undergoes such toil and suffering—he is not one of our kind."
He abandoned them and fled far away to contemplate the realization of the fruit.

After the Prince had practiced austerities for six years without attaining Bodhi, he realized that such asceticism was not the true path; thus, he accepted the milk-rice offering and attained the fruit of enlightenment.
When these three men heard this, they sighed and said:
"The merit was nearly complete, yet now it shall be abandoned.
Six years of ascetic practice, and in a single day, the merit is discarded!"
Thereupon, they sought out and found one another; having met, they sat upright and engaged in lofty discourse, further deliberating with one another:

"In the past, we saw Prince Sarvārthasiddha leave the royal palace for the desolate valleys, cast off precious garments, and don deerskins. With diligent application and resolute intent, he cultivated his heart with steadfast virtue, seeking the profound and wondrous Dharma and aspiring toward the unsurpassed fruit."
"Now you have accepted the milk-rice from the cowherd girl; I knew then that you would fail in the Way and let your resolve decline—you are truly powerless.
The two men said, "How late was your realization?"
This man is merely one who has gone mad.

Dwelling in the deep palace and abiding in such exalted honor, he was unable to quiet his will to seek seclusion in the mountain forests; instead, he abandoned the rank of a Wheel-Turning King to act like a lowly and base person—how can this be worthy of consideration?
"I speak only out of great compassion!

Having bathed in the Nairañjanā River and sat beneath the Bodhi tree, the Bodhisattva attained perfect enlightenment and was hailed as the Teacher of Gods and Humans. Remaining in tranquil silence, he contemplated those who were ready to be delivered, saying:
"That Udraka Rāmaputra has realized the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; he is capable of receiving the sublime Dharma."
The devas in the sky immediately replied to his voice, saying,
"Since Udraka Rāmaputra passed away, seven days have now elapsed.
The Tathāgata sighed with regret:
"How is it that we did not encounter him sooner? Having heard the sublime Dharma, he has already passed away through transformation.

Observing once more and searching throughout the world, [the Buddha] saw that Ārāḍa Kālāma had attained the meditative concentration of the sphere of nothingness and was capable of being entrusted with the ultimate truth.
The devas spoke again, saying:
"It has already been five days.
The Tathāgata sighed once more, pitying their meager merit.
Furthermore, he observed with keen discernment: "Who should receive my teaching?
Only the five men in the Deer Park should be guided first.

At that time, the Tathāgata rose from beneath the Bodhi tree and proceeded toward the Deer Park. His deportment was serene and his divine radiance shone brilliantly; the tuft of hair between his brows possessed the luster of jade, and his body was the color of pure gold. He advanced with tranquil composure, leading those five men.
When these five men saw the Tathāgata from afar, they said to one another: "Sarvārthasiddha is coming;
it has been many years since he failed to realize the holy fruit, and his resolve having faltered, he now seeks us out."
"You should each remain silent and not rise to offer greetings.

As the Tathāgata drew near, his majestic spiritual power moved their hearts; the five men forgot their injunctions, prostrating themselves to welcome him and inquire after his well-being, attending upon him according to the proper ritual.
The Tathāgata gradually guided him and revealed the subtle principles; only after completing the two periods of the rainy season retreat did he attain the realization of the fruit.

Two or three *li* to the east of the Deer Park, one reaches a stūpa beside which lies a dried-up pond, eighty-odd paces in circumference; it is called "Saving Life" and is also known as the "Pond of the Hero."

I have heard from the records of former sages that several hundred years ago, there was a recluse who built a hut by this pond to withdraw from the world. He extensively studied various arts and techniques and investigated the ultimate mysteries of the spirit, such that he could transform tiles and rubble into treasures and change the forms of humans and animals; yet, he was still unable to command the winds and clouds to accompany the chariots of the immortals.
He examined ancient diagrams and sought further the arts of the immortals.
Their method stated:
"The so-called 'gods and immortals' refers to the art of eternal life."
Those who wish to seek cultivation must first resolve their will. They should construct an altar-platform, more than ten feet in circumference.
They shall command a valiant hero of proven courage and integrity to stand at a corner of the altar holding a long sword, holding his breath and remaining silent from dusk until dawn.

The seeker of immortality shall sit in the center of the altar, pressing his hand upon the long sword and reciting the divine mantra with focused vision and inward listening; thus, at the break of dawn, he ascends to immortality.

The sharp sword he held transformed into a precious blade; traversing the void and treading upon the air, he became the sovereign of all the assembly of seers. Wielding his sword to direct them, everything he desired was fulfilled; he was subject neither to decay nor old age, neither to illness nor death.
Having obtained the immortal’s formula, this man traveled about in search of a heroic man, seeking him for many years without fulfilling his heart's desire.
Later, in the city, he encountered a man who was wailing and crying out as he followed the road.
The hermit beheld his appearance and was deeply moved with joy; he immediately approached him to offer consolation, asking, "Why have you come to such grief and sorrow?
He replied:
"Being poor and destitute, I supported myself by hiring out my labor.
My master took notice of me and placed exceptional trust in me; when the five-year term is complete, he shall grant me a generous reward."
Thereupon, he endured toil and hardship, forgetting his own suffering.
As the five years were drawing to a close, he was suddenly dismissed; having already suffered the humiliation of the cane, he now obtained nothing at all.
"Taking this as your core concern, who will pity you in your grief?

The hermit invited him to travel with him and arrived at a thatched cottage. By the power of his arts, he conjured a full spread of delicacies; thereafter, he had him bathe in a pond and dress in new clothes, and further bestowed five hundred gold coins upon him, saying, "Come back for all of this when the time is right;
do not hesitate to seek it."
From that time forward, he repeatedly presented heavy bribes and secretly performed acts of benevolence to move the man's heart.
The knightly hero sought many times to offer his life in service to repay his benefactor.

The hermit said, "I have sought a man of heroic resolve for many years; fortunately, I have now encountered one whose extraordinary appearance accords with the ancient diagrams. It is for no other reason than this that I wish for you to remain silent for a single night."
The knight said, "I do not even shrink from death; how could I merely hold my breath?
Thereupon, he established an altar and received the methods of the immortals; following the prescribed rites, he sat and awaited the setting of the sun.
After dusk, each attended to his duties: the hermit recited divine mantras, while the knight gripped his sharp blade.
As dawn was about to break, he suddenly let out a cry.
At that time, fire descended from the sky, with smoke and flames billowing like clouds. The hermit quickly led the man away and into a pond to seek refuge.
Afterward, he asked him, "I cautioned you not to make a sound; why did you cry out so alarmingly?"
The knight said:
"After receiving my orders, when the night had reached its midpoint, I was dazed as if in a dream, and further strange transformations arose.
I saw my former master come in person to console and thank me; moved by his profound kindness, I restrained myself from responding to him."
That man, filled with violent rage, subsequently killed him.

Having received an intermediate state body (*antarābhava*), he looked upon the corpse and lamented; he vowed that throughout successive lifetimes he would remain silent as a way to repay his profound kindness.

He was then seen to take birth in the family of a great Brahmin in South India; from his conception and emergence from the womb, he underwent all manner of hardships and calamities, yet out of gratitude for their kindness and virtue, he never uttered a sound.

Upon reaching the stages of receiving instruction, capping, marriage, mourning for relatives, and the birth of children, he constantly recalled his former kindness; he endured his circumstances and remained silent, to the point that all his kinsmen and relatives regarded him with wonder and strangeness.
When I was sixty-five years old, my wife said to me:
"You must speak! If you do not speak, I shall kill your son."
At that time, I reflected that many lifetimes had already passed; seeing myself grown old and frail, I stopped my wife from killing this young child for his sake alone.
"It was I who uttered this sound," the hermit said.
"It was my fault!"
"This was merely the harassment of a demon.
The hero, grateful for the kindness shown yet grieving that his mission had failed, died in a fit of indignation and rage.
Because he was spared from the disaster of fire, it is called "Saving One's Life."
It is called the Pond of the Martyrs (Kṣatriya-tīrtha), as those who died with gratitude were also termed "martyrs.
To the west of the Pond of the Martyrs is a stūpa of the Three Animals; this is the place where the Tathāgata, while practicing the bodhisattva path, performed self-immolation.
At the beginning of the kalpa, in this forest wilderness, there lived a fox, a rabbit, and a monkey who took pleasure in one another despite their different species.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, wishing to test those practicing the bodhisattva path, descended as a spirit and manifested as an old man. He said to the three animals:
"Are you all well and at peace, my children?"
"Are you free from fear and anxiety?
He replied, "Wandering through lush grass and roaming in verdant forests, I share joy with all different species; I am both secure and happy."
The old man said, "I have heard that you gentlemen’s feelings are deep and your intentions sincere; forgetting my own decrepitude, I have come from afar to seek you out.
Now I am precisely hungry and exhausted—how can you provide me with food?"
He replied, "I would be grateful if you would stay here for a short while; I shall go in person to seek him out.
Thereupon, they united in purpose and humbled themselves, parting ways to search for him.

A fox, following along the water's edge, carried a fresh carp in its mouth; a monkey, amidst the forest trees, gathered exotic flowers and fruits; both arrived together and presented them to the old man.
They merely avoided returning empty-handed and frolicked about his left and right.
The old man said to them,
"As I observe you, it appears that you are not yet in harmony."
The monkeys and the foxes shared a common purpose and were each able to exert their minds; only the rabbit returned empty-handed, alone receiving no gift.
From this, one can truly understand the truth of the matter.
Hearing this censure, the hare said to the fox and the monkey, "Gather a great quantity of firewood; we are about to perform a task.
The fox and the monkey raced against each other, carrying grass in their mouths and dragging timber, until they had piled it high and the fierce flames were about to blaze up.
The rabbit said, "O Benevolent One, my body is lowly and insignificant, yet it is difficult for me to fulfill your request; I venture to offer my humble self to satisfy this single meal.
Having finished his speech, he entered the fire and immediately perished.
At that time, the old man resumed his form as Śakra, extinguished the embers, gathered the remains, and after lamenting for a long while, he said to the fox and the monkey,
"How could things have come to this!"
"I was moved by his heart and did not wish to let his traces vanish; I have entrusted them to the lunar disc to be transmitted to future generations.
Thus, they all say that the hare within the moon has existed since that time.
Later generations erected a stūpa at this site.
Following the course of the Gaṅgā River from here and traveling east for over three hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Yodheya within the borders of India.
The kingdom of Yodheya (War-Lord) is over two thousand *li* in circuit; its capital city borders the Gaṅgā River and is over ten *li* in circuit.
The inhabitants live in abundance and happiness, with towns and villages situated close together.
The soil is rich and fertile, and crops are sown according to the seasons.
The climate is harmonious and pleasant, and the customs are simple and honest; yet the people are fierce by nature, believing both in heterodoxy and orthodoxy.
There are more than ten monasteries with fewer than a thousand monks,
all of whom follow and study the teachings of the Hinayana.
There are twenty deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
In a monastery to the northwest of the great city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka.
The *Record of India* states:
"Within this [stūpa] is one *dōu* of the Tathāgata’s relics."
"In the past, the World-Honored One once stayed at this very spot for seven days, expounding the sublime Dharma for the multitudes of devas and humans.
Beside it are the sites where the three past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation."

Adjacent to this is a statue of Maitreya Bodhisattva; although its physical dimensions are small, its majestic spirit is imposing. Its divine discernment communicates in secret, and miraculous events arise from time to time.
Traveling east from the great city for more than two hundred *li*, one arrives at the Avītagartā Monastery (translated into Chinese as *Bùchuān'ěr*, "Unpierced Ears").

Its surrounding walls are not extensive, yet its carvings and decorations are most exquisite; flower ponds reflect one another, and the pavilions and galleries have interconnected eaves. The monks are solemn and reverent, and the various rituals are conducted with dignified order.

I have heard from the records of former sages that, in the past, there were śramaṇas fond of study in the kingdom of Tukhāra to the north of the Great Snow Mountains. When these two or three like-minded companions had finished their ritual recitations and were at leisure, they would often say to one another:
"The subtle principles are profound and mysterious; they cannot be fully exhausted through mere discourse."
"The sacred traces are so clearly manifest that they may be sought by the tip of one's foot.
You should consult with those who are in perfect harmony and personally behold these holy sites.
Thereupon, two or three friends took up their staffs and traveled together.
Having arrived in India, he stayed at various monasteries; however, they held him in low regard as a man from a remote borderland and none would grant him shelter.
Harassed by wind and dew without and burdened by the struggle for food and drink within, his complexion grew haggard and his physical form became withered and emaciated.
At that time, the king went out on an excursion to the outskirts and saw several visiting monks; marveling at them, he asked:
"From what direction have you mendicants come?
For what reason have you arrived?"
"Since my ears have not been pierced and my robes are moreover soiled and tattered," the śramaṇa replied,
"I am a man from the country of Tukhāra."
Reverently upholding the bequeathed teachings, we have transcended the mundane dust and led those of like inclination to observe the sacred traces of the Sage.
Alas, due to our meager merit, we were collectively abandoned; the śramaṇas of India took no notice of us as weary travelers.
"I wish to return to my native land, yet my pilgrimage has not yet been completed; though pressed by hardship and toil, my heart will not cease until the end.
When the King heard these words, his grief increased all the more. Thereupon, at this most excellent site, he established a monastery and inscribed upon white cotton cloth a decree, saying:
"I consider that my exalted station above the world and my supreme nobility among men are entirely due to the spiritual protection of the Triple Gem."
Having become a king of men and received the Buddha’s entrustment, I shall provide relief and succor to all those who wear the dyed robes.
I have established this monastery to welcome travelers from afar.
"From this day forward, no monks who have pierced their ears shall be permitted to dwell in this monastery.
It was for this reason that it was named accordingly.

Traveling southeast from the Avīta-kalana monastery for more than a hundred li, and crossing the Ganges River to the south, one arrives at the town of Mahāśālā; its inhabitants are all of the Brahmin caste and do not follow the Buddha-dharma.
However, upon seeing a śramaṇa, he first inquired about his studies; only when he knew him to be of keen intellect would he pay him deep respect.
To the north of the Ganges River, there was a temple dedicated to the deity Nārāyaṇa.
The multi-storied pavilions and tiered terraces are magnificent and exquisitely adorned.
The images of the various devas are carved from stone; their craftsmanship reaches the pinnacle of human ingenuity, and their spiritual efficacy is difficult to fathom.
Traveling more than thirty li east from the temple of Nārāyaṇa, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, of which more than half has subsided into the ground.
In front stands a stone pillar over twenty feet high, topped with the image of a lion, inscribed with a record of the subduing of the demon.

Formerly, there was at this place a wilderness spirit who, relying on his great power, devoured the flesh and blood of men and brought calamity upon living beings, unleashing his demonic influence to the utmost.

The Tathāgata, out of compassion for sentient beings who do not meet their deaths in a timely manner, employs his supernormal powers to entice and transform the various ghosts, leading them with the reverence of taking refuge and unifying them with the precept of non-killing.
The spirits, receiving these instructions, attended upon him with diligence.
Thereupon, they lifted the stone and requested that the Buddha take his seat, vowing to hear the True Dharma and to maintain it with mindful care.
From that time forward, groups of faithless people vied with one another to move the stone from its pedestal; though numbering in the thousands, none were able to shift it.
Lush forests and clear ponds surround its foundations on all sides; whenever anyone approaches them, they cannot help but feel dread in their hearts.
Not far from where the ghosts lurk, there are several monasteries; although many have fallen into ruin, there are still monks remaining, all of whom follow and practice the teachings of the Mahāyāna.
From here, traveling southeast for more than a hundred *li*, one arrives at a *stūpa* whose foundation has already collapsed, though it still stands several *zhang* high.

In the past, after the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa, the great kings of the eight kingdoms divided his relics. A Brahmin, measuring the relics, smeared the inside of a jar with honey and distributed them to the various kings; he then took the jar back home. Having obtained the relics that had adhered to the jar, he subsequently erected this *stūpa* and placed both the relics and the jar within it, and thus it was named accordingly.
Later, King Aśoka opened the śarīra jar and reconstructed it as a great stūpa; on fast days, it occasionally emits a brilliant light.
From here, traveling northeast across the Gaṅgā River for one hundred forty or fifty *li*, one reaches the country of Vaiśālī (formerly called Bisheli, which is a corruption).
Within the borders of Central India lies the kingdom of Vaiśālī. The kingdom of Vaiśālī is over five thousand *li* in circuit.
Its soil is rich and fertile, and its flowers and fruits grow in abundance; both the *āmra* (mango) and *mocā* (plantain) fruits are plentiful and highly prized.
The climate is harmonious and pleasant, and the local customs are simple and honest. The people cherish merit and value learning, though they hold a mixture of heterodox and orthodox beliefs.
There are several hundred monasteries, most of which have fallen into ruin; only three or five remain, and the monks are few in number.
There are several dozen deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together; those who practice "naked asceticism" are particularly numerous among them.

The city of Vaiśālī is already in a state of extreme decay; its old foundations extend sixty or seventy *li* in circumference, while the palace city is four or five *li* around, with very few inhabitants.
Five or six *li* to the northwest of the palace city, one arrives at a monastery where the monks are few in number and study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
Beside it stands a stūpa, the site where the Tathāgata in the past preached the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra and where the merchant’s son Ratnākara and others offered precious parasols.
To its east is a stūpa where Śāriputra and others realized the fruit of arhatship.
To the southeast of the stūpa marking Śāriputra’s realization of the fruit is another stūpa, which was built by King Vaiśālī.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the former kings of this country obtained a portion of his relics and constructed [stūpas] to enshrine them in honor.
The *Record of India* states:
"In this place there was originally one hu of the Tathāgata’s relics; King Aśoka opened it and took nine dou, leaving only one dou behind."
Later, another king desired to open it and take [the relics] away; just as he was about to undertake the work, the earth shook, so that he did not dare to open it.
To the northwest stands a stūpa, built by King Aśoka.
Beside it stands a stone pillar, fifty or sixty feet high, topped with the image of a lion.
To the south of the pillar is a pond, which was excavated by a troop of monkeys for the Buddha.
In the past, the Tathāgata once dwelt here.
Not far to the west of the pond is a stūpa, the place where the monkeys took the Tathāgata’s bowl up into a tree to fetch honey;
not far to the south of the pond is a stūpa, the place where the monkeys offered the honey to the Buddha.
In the northwest corner of the pond, there is still an image of a monkey.
Three li to the northeast of the monastery is a stūpa; this is the site of Vimalakīrti (translated into Chinese as Wǔgòuchēng, "Stainless Renown").

Formerly it was called Jingming (Pure Name); however, "pure" implies being free from defilement, while "name" refers to a designation. Although the meanings are taken as identical, the names themselves differ.
The former name, Weimojie (Vimalakīrti), is a corruption and abbreviation. The foundations of his former residence abound with spiritual wonders.
Not far from here is a shrine, constructed of piled bricks—tradition says of accumulated stones—which is the place where the Elder Vimalakīrti manifested illness and preached the Dharma.
Not far from here is a stūpa, the former residence of the elder’s son Ratnākara.
Not far from here is another stūpa, the former residence of the woman Āmrapālī, where the Buddha’s maternal aunt and other bhikṣuṇīs attained parinirvāṇa.

Three or four *li* to the north of the monastery is a stūpa, which marks the place where the Tathāgata, on his way to the kingdom of Kuśinagara to enter parinirvāṇa, was followed by humans and non-humans who stood waiting here upon reaching this spot.
Not far to the northwest is a stūpa, where the Buddha made his final observation of the city of Vaiśālī.
Not far to its south is a vihāra with a stūpa erected in front; this was the garden of the lady Āmrapālī, which she offered as a gift to the Buddha.
Beside the Āmra Garden is a stūpa, which marks the place where the Tathāgata announced his nirvāṇa.
In the past, the Buddha was here when he said to Ānanda:
"One who has attained the four bases of supernatural power can remain for the duration of a kalpa."
"How long shall the Tathāgata’s lifespan now be?
Thus he asked a second and a third time, yet Ānanda did not respond, for he was bewildered by a celestial Māra.
Ānanda rose from his seat and remained in silent meditation within the grove.
At that time, Māra came to request of the Buddha, saying:

"The Tathāgata has been in the world teaching and transforming for a long time; those who have received his salvation from the cycle of transmigration are as numerous as dust motes and grains of sand. The time for the bliss of parinirvāṇa has now arrived."
The World-Honored One placed a small amount of soil on his fingernail and said to Māra:
"Which is more: the soil of the earth, or the soil on my nail?"
He replied, "The soil is vast.
The Buddha said:
"Those who have been delivered are like the soil on a fingernail, while those yet to be delivered are like the soil of the great earth.
In three months' time, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Upon hearing this, Māra rejoiced and withdrew.
In the Ānanda Grove, Ānanda suddenly experienced a strange dream and came to inform the Buddha, saying:
"While I was in the grove, I dreamed of a great tree with lush branches and leaves, its shade dense and thick; suddenly a fierce wind arose, tearing it apart until nothing remained."
"Is it not that the World-Honored One intends to enter parinirvāṇa?
My heart is filled with fear, and for this reason I have come to inquire.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"I previously informed you that you were obscured by Māra and did not request that I remain at this time.
The King of Māras urged me to enter parinirvāṇa early, and I have already granted the appointed date; this dream is of that very matter."
He said, "Not far from where he announced the time of his parinirvāṇa, there is a stūpa at the place where the thousand sons saw their parents.

Long ago, there was a rishi who lived in seclusion among the rocky valleys. In the second month of spring, while he was bathing in a clear stream, a doe followed him to drink; she conceived and gave birth to a girl whose beauty surpassed that of ordinary humans, though her feet resembled those of a deer. Upon seeing her, the rishi took her in and raised her."
Thereafter, he was commanded to seek fire; upon reaching the hermitage of another rishi, wherever his feet trod the ground, lotus flowers appeared as footprints.
When that rishi saw this, he marveled at it deeply and ordered him to circumambulate the hermitage before he would grant him the fire.
The Deer Woman followed these instructions, obtained fire, and returned.
At that time, King Brahmadatta, while out hunting, saw the flowers; he followed their tracks to find them and, delighted by their extraordinary nature, took her back with him in his carriage.
The physiognomist’s divination stated that she would give birth to a thousand sons.
Upon hearing this, the other wives all devised schemes.
When her months were complete, she gave birth to a lotus flower with a thousand petals, and upon each petal sat a son.
The other wives, out of deceit and falsehood, all claimed it was an ill omen; they cast him into the Ganges River, where he drifted along with the waves.

King Uggayana, while traveling for recreation downstream, saw a yellow cloud-canopy coming upon the waves. He took it up and opened it to look inside, finding a thousand sons. They were nurtured and raised until they grew up, possessing great strength.
Relying on his thousand sons, he expanded his territory in all four directions; with his military might emboldened by successive victories, he was about to reach this kingdom.
When King Brahmadatta heard of this, he was seized with great trepidation; unable to match the enemy's forces, he found no way out.
At that time, the Deer Woman knew in her heart that it was her son;

she then said to the King, "Now that the enemy hordes have approached our borders and the hearts of high and low are divided, this humble servant, through my simple loyalty, can defeat the powerful foe."
The king did not yet believe her and was filled with profound anxiety and fear.
The Deer Woman then ascended the city tower to await the arrival of the invaders.
When the thousand sons led their army and had completely surrounded the city, the Deer Woman addressed them, saying:
"Do not act in opposition!
I am your mother; you are my son.
The thousand sons said to her:
"What absurdity is this?
The Deer Woman pressed her two breasts with her hands, and milk flowed forth in a thousand streams; moved by their innate nature, [the men] all drank from them.
Thereupon, they cast off their armor to return to their kin and laid down their weapons to rejoin their clans. The two nations shared mutual joy, and the common people lived in peace and happiness.
Not far from the place where the thousand sons returned to their father is a stūpa, marking the site of an ancient trace where the Tathāgata once walked. Pointing it out to the assembly, he said:
"In the past, it was here that I returned to my father and saw my kin."
"If you wish to know who these thousand sons are, they are none other than the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.

To the east of the site where this account of his past lives was told, there is an ancient foundation upon which a stūpa has been erected; its radiance frequently illuminates the surroundings, and prayers offered here are often fulfilled. This is the remaining site of the multi-storied lecture hall where the Tathāgata preached the *Samantamukha-dhāraṇī* and other sūtras.
Not far from the side of the lecture hall is a stūpa containing half of Ānanda’s śarīra.

Not far from here are several hundred stūpas; though one wishes to determine their exact number, it has not yet been possible to know it for certain—this is the place where a thousand pratyekabuddhas entered parinirvāṇa.
The inner and outer moats surrounding the city of Vaiśālī abound in sacred sites, making it difficult to enumerate them all.

These sites of ancient excellence stand like fish scales in close succession; yet, as the years have swiftly changed and the seasons have rapidly shifted, the forests have been ravaged and the ponds have dried up. Only withered stumps and lingering traces remain for detailed inspection.
Traveling fifty or sixty *li* northwest from the great city, one arrives at a large stūpa, the site where the Licchavi (formerly called "Li-che-zi," which is an error) paid homage to the Tathāgata.

As the Tathāgata proceeded from the city of Vaiśālī toward the kingdom of Kuśinagara, the Licchavis, hearing that the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, followed him one after another, wailing in grief as they escorted him.

The World-Honored One, seeing that their grief and longing were beyond the reach of words, immediately employed his supernormal powers to manifest a great river with precipitous banks and a torrential current. The Licchavis were so overcome with sorrow that they stopped there; the Tathāgata left behind his almsbowl as a memorial for them to reflect upon.
Two hundred li to the northwest of the city of Vaiśālī lies an ancient city that has been desolate for many years, with its inhabitants sparse and few.

Within it stands a stūpa, which marks the site where the Buddha, in the past, for the great assembly of bodhisattvas, humans, and devas, recounted his previous births (*jātaka*) and his cultivation of the bodhisattva path; it was here in this city that he was once a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), named Mahādeva (translated into Chinese as Dàtiān, "Great Deva").

Possessing the seven treasures as his regalia, he ruled over the four quarters of the world; yet, beholding the signs of decay and transformation and realizing the principle of impermanence, he withdrew in profound contemplation and relinquished his attachment to the great throne. He abdicated the kingdom to leave the household life, donned the dyed robes of a monk, and devoted himself to study and practice.
Traveling fourteen or fifteen *li* southeast from the city, one arrives at a great *stūpa*, which is the site where seven hundred noble ones held a second council.
One hundred and ten years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there were certain bhikṣus in the city of Vaiśālī who had distanced themselves from the Buddha-dharma and practiced the precepts erroneously.

At that time, the Elder Yaśoda resided in the kingdom of Kośala; the Elder Subhūti resided in the kingdom of Mathurā; the Elder Revata resided in the kingdom of Kanyākubja; the Elder Śāradvatīputra resided in the kingdom of Vaiśālī; and the Elder Puṣyamitra resided in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.

These great arhats had attained mastery over their minds, upheld the Tripitaka, and acquired the three types of supernormal knowledge; they possessed great renown and were well-known to all, being all disciples of the Venerable Ānanda.
At that time, Yaśoda dispatched messengers to inform the various worthy sages that they should all assemble in the city of Vaiśālī.
There was still one person short, such that the number did not yet reach seven hundred.
At that moment, Puṣyamitra, using his divine eye, saw the great worthy sages gathering to deliberate on matters of the Dharma; he then exercised his supernormal powers and arrived at the assembly.
Then Tripuṭa, in the midst of the great assembly, bared his right shoulder, knelt down, and proclaimed:
"Be silent, all of you! Reverence! Be mindful!"
In the past, when the Great Sage, the Dharma King, entered parinirvāṇa through his skillful means, although many years have passed, his verbal teachings still remain.
In the city of Vaiśālī, indolent bhikṣus became errant regarding the Vinaya; ten matters emerged that contravened the teachings of the One of Ten Powers.

"Now these worthy ones clearly understand what is upheld and what is transgressed; having both received the instructions of the Venerable Ānanda, they shall mindfully repay the Buddha’s kindness and re-proclaim the holy intent.

At that time, the entire great assembly was moved by grief. They immediately convened all the bhikṣus and, in accordance with the Vinaya, rebuked and prohibited [the errors], expunged the erroneous teachings, and proclaimed the clarity of the holy doctrine.

Traveling eighty or ninety *li* south from the place where the seven hundred noble ones held the council, one arrives at the Śvetapura Monastery. Its tiered terraces shine brilliantly and its multi-storied pavilions soar like soaring pheasants; the monastic community is pure and disciplined, and all study the Mahāyāna.
Beside it are the sites where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation;
at its side is a stūpa built by King Aśoka.
This is the site where the Tathāgata, while formerly traveling south toward the kingdom of Magadha and looking back north toward the city of Vaiśālī, rested midway.

Traveling southeast from the Śvetapura Monastery for more than thirty *li*, there is a stūpa on each of the northern and southern banks of the Gaṅgā River; these are the places where the Venerable Ānanda divided his body to bestow [relics] upon the two kingdoms.

Ānanda was the younger half-brother of the Tathāgata’s paternal uncle; he possessed vast learning and the power of dhāraṇī, was erudite and possessed a powerful memory. After the Buddha passed into nirvāṇa, he succeeded Mahākāśyapa in upholding the True Dharma and guided the students in their progress.
While walking in meditation in a forest within the kingdom of Magadha, he saw a novice reciting a Buddhist scripture with errors in its phrases and a disordered arrangement of its characters.
Having heard this, Ānanda was moved with deep longing; he slowly approached him, intending to rouse his attention and give him instruction.
The śrāmaṇera laughed and said, "Venerable sir, you are old; what you say is erroneous!"
"My teacher is of lofty wisdom and in the prime of his years; having received his personal instructions, I am truly without error.
Ānanda remained silent, then withdrew and sighed, saying:
"Though my years have advanced, for the sake of all sentient beings, I wish to dwell long in this world to uphold the True Dharma."
"However, sentient beings are heavily defiled and difficult to instruct; there is no benefit in remaining for long, so they may be swiftly brought to parinirvāṇa.
Thereupon, he departed from the kingdom of Magadha and proceeded toward the city of Vaiśālī; crossing the Gaṅgā River, he sailed upon its midstream.

When the King of Magadha heard that Ānanda had departed, his heart was deeply moved by devotion to the Master's virtue; he immediately prepared his chariots and horses and pursued him in haste to invite him back, while several hundred thousand followers established their camp on the southern bank.

When King Vaiśālī heard that Ānanda had arrived, his heart was filled with both grief and joy; he likewise mobilized his troops and galloped forth to welcome him, as hundreds of thousands of people gathered on the northern bank.
As the two armies faced one another, their banners and standards obscured the sun.

Fearing that his soldiers would engage in combat and slaughter one another, Ānanda rose from within the boat and ascended into the void, manifesting supernatural transformations. He then entered parinirvāṇa, whereupon fire issued forth to cremate his remains. The remains were split in two: one half fell upon the southern bank, and the other half fell upon the northern bank.
Thereupon, each of the two kings received one portion; the entire army wailed in grief, and they all returned to their respective countries to erect stūpas and perform offerings.

From here, traveling northeast for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Vṛji (also called the country of Baisi by those to the north), which is said to have been the country of the three generations of the Śākyas.
In the region of North India lies the kingdom of Vṛji. The kingdom of Vṛji is over four thousand li in circuit; it is long from east to west and narrow from south to north.
The soil is fertile, and flowers and fruits grow in abundance.
The climate is slightly cold, and the people are by nature impetuous; they mostly revere non-Buddhist paths and have little faith in the Buddha-dharma.
There are over ten monasteries with fewer than a thousand monks, who study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles concurrently.
There are several dozen deva temples, and the followers of external paths are indeed numerous.
The capital city of the kingdom is called Jāguda; most of it has already fallen into ruin.
Within the old palace city, there are still more than three thousand households, forming what are essentially villages and towns.
To the northeast of the great river is a monastery with few monks, whose studies are pure and lofty.

Traveling west from here along the riverbank, there is a stūpa over three zhang in height, situated beside a long flowing stream; this is the place where the World-Honored One of Great Compassion delivered the fishermen.

During the time of the Buddha, five hundred fishermen formed a guild and joined as a faction to fish for aquatic creatures. While fishing in this river, they caught a large fish with eighteen heads, each head having two eyes.

Just as the fishermen were about to harm him, the Tathāgata, while staying in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, perceived this with his divine eye. Moved by compassion, he seized the opportune moment to guide them and, according to their spiritual capacity, awakened them, addressing the great assembly:
"In the kingdom of Vṛji there is a great fish; I wish to guide it in order to awaken these fishermen. You should know that the time has come."
Then, surrounded by the great assembly, he ascended into the air by means of his supernormal power and arrived at the riverbank, where he spread out his seat as usual.
He then addressed the fishermen:
"Do not kill the fish."

By means of his supernormal powers, he opened the gate of skillful means; his majestic influence reached the great fish, causing it to know its past lives, enabling it to speak the language of humans, and allowing it to thoroughly understand human sentiments.
At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, said:
"In your previous life, what transgression did you commit such that you have wandered through the evil realms and received this wretched body?"
The fish said:
"In the past, by virtue of accumulated merit and blessings, I was born into a noble clan; I am that great Brahmin named Kapitha.
Relying on my lineage, I looked down upon and despised human relations; relying on my vast learning, I held the sutras and the Dharma in contempt."

With a mind of contempt, they slandered the Buddhas; with foul and wicked speech, they reviled the Saṃgha, drawing comparisons and likening them to various ugly forms, such as camels, donkeys, elephants, and horses.
Due to these evil karmas, he received this wretched body;
yet, sustained by his past merit, he was born into the age of a Buddha, beheld the holy transformations with his own eyes, and personally received the sacred teachings.
Thereupon, they offered repentance and thanked [the Buddha], regretting their past deeds.
The Tathāgata, according to their capacities, gathered and transformed them, providing guidance as was appropriate.
Having heard the Dharma, the fish then passed away.
By virtue of this merit, he was reborn in a celestial palace.
Thereupon, he observed his own body and wondered by what cause he had been born here.

Having realized his past lives, he resolved to repay the Buddha's kindness; accompanied by the assembly of devas, he arrived one after another. Once the preliminary prostrations were completed, they circumambulated him to the right and withdrew to stand aside, offering celestial precious incense and flowers as an act of worship.

The World-Honored One pointed out the fishermen and preached the sublime Dharma for them; they were immediately enlightened and moved to realization, offering their sincere devotion through prostrations and repentance. They tore their nets and burned their boats, returning to the truth and receiving the Dharma.
Having donned the dyed robes and heard the supreme teaching, they all emerged from the dust and defilement and together realized the fruits of sainthood.

To the northeast of the ferry crossing, after traveling over a hundred li, there is a stūpa to the west of an old city built by King Aśoka, standing over a hundred feet high. This is where the Buddha in the past preached the Dharma for six months, delivering many devas and humans.
One hundred and forty or fifty paces to the north of this place is a small stūpa; it was here that the Tathāgata formerly established the precepts for the bhikṣus.
Not far to the west is a stūpa containing the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata.
In the past, at this place, people from nearby and distant towns flocked together, burning incense and scattering flowers, with lamps and torches never ceasing.
From here, traveling northwest for one thousand four or five hundred li, crossing mountains and entering valleys, one reaches Nepal, which is within the borders of Central India.
The kingdom of Nepal is over four thousand li in circuit and is situated amidst the Snow Mountains.
The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty li in circuit.
The mountains and rivers are interconnected; the land is suitable for grain cultivation and abounds in flowers and fruits. It produces red copper, yak oxen, and jīvaṃjīvaka birds.
Red copper coins are used as currency.
The climate is bitterly cold, and the customs are treacherous and perverse. The people are by nature fierce and unruly, and their sense of honor and trustworthiness is slight.
They possess no scholarly arts, yet they are skilled in crafts.
Their physical appearance is ugly and wretched, and they believe both in heterodoxy and orthodoxy.
Monasteries and deva temples stand side by side, their walls meeting at every corner.
There are more than two thousand monks who study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles with equal diligence.
The number of non-Buddhist heterodox practitioners is not precisely known.
The King is of the Kṣatriya Licchavi lineage.
He is dedicated to learning and is pure and lofty in character, possessing sincere faith in the Buddha-dharma.
In recent times, there was a king named Aṅśuvarma, which in the language of Tang means "Guangzhou" (Radiant Armor).
A man of great learning and keen intelligence, he composed his own treatise on *śabda-vidyā* (phonetics and grammar). His reverence for learning and virtue was renowned far and wide.

To the southeast of the capital city, there is a small pond; if one throws fire into it, the water immediately bursts into flames, and even when other objects are thrown in, they likewise transform into fire.

From there he returned once more to the kingdom of Vaiśālī, crossed the Gaṅgā River to the south, and arrived at the kingdom of Magadha—formerly called Mojieduo (Magadha) or Mojieti (Majjadda), both of which are corruptions.
Within the borders of Central India.
*The Great Tang Dynasty Record of the Western Regions*, Scroll Seven;
*The Great Tang Dynasty Record of the Western Regions*, Scroll Eight: One Kingdom.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree;
compiled by the Śramaṇa Bianji of Dazongchi Monastery.
Part One: The Kingdom of Magadha. The kingdom of Magadha is over five thousand *li* in circuit.
The city has few inhabitants, while the surrounding villages have many registered households.

The soil is fertile and rich, producing abundant crops; there is a distinctive variety of rice with grains that are coarse and large, possessing an exceptionally superior fragrance and flavor, and a particularly brilliant color. The local people call it "rice for Great Beings."

The land is low and damp, while the inhabited villages are situated on high plateaus; from the end of the first month of summer until the middle of the eighth month, flowing waters run through the plains, making it possible to travel by boat.
The local customs are simple and honest, and the climate is warm and humid.
The people hold learning in high esteem and revere the Buddha-dharma.
There are more than fifty monasteries with over ten thousand monks, most of whom follow and study the Mahāyāna teachings.
There are several dozen deva temples, and followers of heterodox paths are indeed numerous.
To the south of the Gaṅgā River lies an old city, more than seventy li in circuit; although it has long been desolate and overgrown, its foundations still remain.
In the past, when the human lifespan was immeasurable years, this place was called the City of Kusumapura (in the language of Tang, "Fragrant Flower Palace City").
It was so named because the royal palace abounded in flowers.
When the human lifespan reached several thousand years, the city was renamed Pāṭaliputra; its former name, Bāliñfúyì (Pāṭaliputra), was a corruption.
Initially, there was a Brāhmaṇa of eminent talent and vast learning who had several thousand disciples who transmitted his teachings to him.
As the various disciples were traveling together for sightseeing, there was one scholar who lingered behind, looking on with sorrowful longing.
His companions said to him,
"What is it that you grieve over?"
He said: "When I was young and full of vigor, I wandered abroad, treading in my own shadow; yet as the years have accumulated, I have achieved nothing in the arts or learning.
Reflecting on this, my anxiety grows ever more intense."
Thereupon, the disciples joked with him, saying:
"Now we shall seek a marriage alliance for you.

They then arbitrarily established two men as the father and mother of the groom and two women as the father and mother of the bride, and they sat beneath a Pāṭalī tree—which is called the "Maiden's Voice Tree."
Gathering seasonal fruits and drawing from the clear stream, he recounted the history of their marriage alliance and requested the date for their union.
At that time, the bride’s father took hold of a flowering branch and presented it to the young scholar, saying:
"This is a most auspicious match; I pray you do not decline it."
The scholar’s heart was filled with joy and contentment; as evening fell, he spoke of returning home, but out of lingering attachment, he stopped.
His student said, “What I said earlier was merely in jest!”
"It would be fortunate for us to return together;
I fear the fierce beasts in the forest might harm one another.
The scholar then remained behind, coming and going by the side of the tree.
After evening fell, a strange light illuminated the fields; the music of pipes and strings was refined and elegant, and curtains and canopies were arrayed.

Suddenly, an old man appeared, leaning on a staff to offer his greetings. He was followed by an old woman leading a young girl, with a retinue of attendants filling the road, all dressed in magnificent garments as music was played.
The old man then pointed to the young woman and said, "This is your wife.
They indulged in songs and feasting for seven days.

The disciples suspected he had been harmed by a wild beast and went to search for him; they found him sitting alone in the shade of a tree as if conversing with a distinguished guest. They invited him to return with them, but he declined and would not obey their command.
Later, he entered the city himself to pay his respects to his relatives and old friends, recounting the beginning and end of these events.

Those who heard him were struck with amazement; together with several friends, they went to the grove and all saw that the flowering trees had become a grand mansion. Servants and attendants were busy running back and forth, while the old man received them with composure, setting out food and playing music, with every courtesy between host and guest fully observed.
The friends returned to the city and reported the matter in detail to everyone near and far.
After one year had passed, a son was born to him.
He said to his wife:
"I now wish to return home, yet I cannot bear to part with you;
yet if I remain here for long, I shall be left to dwell in the open air, exposed to the elements.
When his wife heard this, she reported it all to her father.
The old man said to the scholar, "In the life of a man, one seeks pleasure; why must it necessarily be in one's native land?
I am now about to build a house for you; you should have no other intention."
Thereupon, the laborers completed their work in no time at all.
Fragrant flowers adorned the old city as the capital was moved to this town.
Because of that son, the deity constructed the city; from that time forward, it was named Pāṭaliputra City.
To the north of the King’s former palace stands a stone pillar several tens of feet high; this is the site where King Aśoka established a hell.
One hundred years after the parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, there was one named Aśoka (translated into Chinese as Wuyou).
The former name "Aśoka" is a corruption. This king was Bindusāra (translated into Chinese as Yǐngjiān);

the former name "Pínpósuō" is a corruption. He was the great-grandson of the previous king and moved the capital from Rājagṛha to Pāṭaliputra, where he constructed an outer wall surrounding the old city.
As the ages have passed, only the old foundations remain.
Of the monasteries, deva-temples, and stūpas, there are hundreds of ruins, of which only two or three still stand.
To the north of the former palace, bordering the Ganges River, there is a small city with more than a thousand households.
Initially, after King Aśoka succeeded to the throne, his conduct was harsh and tyrannical; he established a hell and committed atrocities against living beings.

The surrounding walls stand high and steep, with watchtowers rising prominently at each corner; there are fierce flames and great furnaces, along with sharp points and keen blades—all manner of instruments of suffering are prepared, simulating the dark paths of the underworld. Wicked men are recruited and appointed as the masters of this prison.
Initially, all offenders within the kingdom, regardless of the gravity of their crimes, were collectively cast into the "paint and charcoal" (tú-tàn) pits.
Later, as he traveled past the site of the prison, they would seize and execute anyone who encountered him; thus, everyone who arrived there was killed, and the matter was silenced.

At that time, there was a śramaṇa who had recently entered the community of the Dharma. While wandering through the streets to beg for food, he happened upon the gate of a prison. A cruel jailer seized him, intending to harm him.
The śramaṇa was terrified and pleaded to be permitted to perform prostrations and repentance.

Suddenly, he saw a man being led into the prison in shackles; his hands and feet were severed and his body torn apart, so that in the space of a single glance, his limbs and members were reduced to a pulp.
Upon seeing this, the śramaṇa’s sorrow deepened; he cultivated the contemplation of impermanence and realized the fruit of arhatship.
The wardens said, "He may now die."

Since the śramaṇa had realized the fruit of sainthood, his mind was equanimous toward birth and death; though he entered the boiling cauldron, it was like a clear pool for him, where a great lotus flower served as his seat.
The jailer was struck with alarm and dispatched a messenger to inform the king. The king then went to observe it in person and deeply praised the miraculous efficacy.
The jailer said, "Your Majesty is destined to die."
The King asked, “What? He replied:

"The King previously issued an edict ordering that those overseeing the prisons must execute everyone who reaches the prison walls; it was not stated that the King himself would enter and alone be spared from death.
The King said:
"The law has already been established; there is no principle for it to change twice."
"I previously issued a decree; how could it have been intended to spare your life?
That you have lived here for so long under false pretenses is my own fault.
He then commanded the jailers to cast him into a great furnace.
Once the jailer was dead, the King was finally able to escape; thereupon he leveled the walls, filled in the moats, abolished the prisons, and mitigated punishments.

Not far to the south of the hell is a stūpa whose foundations have collapsed and subsided, leaving only the shape of an inverted bowl. Adorned with jewels and featuring stone railings, it is one of the eighty-four thousand [stūpas].

King Aśoka constructed a palace there through human labor; within it were one *dou* of the Tathāgata’s relics, which occasionally manifested spiritual visions and were frequently illuminated by divine light.
After King Aśoka had abolished the prisons, he encountered the great arhat Upagupta, who skillfully guided him through expedient means and transformed him according to his capacity.
The king said to the arhat:
"By virtue of my past merit, I have attained this position of human sovereignty; yet I lament these karmic obstructions that prevented me from encountering the Buddha’s transformation."
"Now that the Tathāgata has left behind his bodily relics, we wish to rebuild various stūpas.

The arhat said, "Your Majesty, by the power of your merit you employ the hundred spirits, and with a heart of great vows you protect and uphold the Triple Gem; this is precisely what was desired, and now is the time for it."
Because the Tathāgata extensively explained the causes for offering the land and prophesied the merit of its construction, King Aśoka heard this and was filled with joy.
He summoned the spirits and deities and commanded them, saying:
