"The Dharma King guides and benefits all beings, bringing celebration to every living soul. Through my past roots of goodness, I have attained the highest honor among men."
The Tathāgata has left behind his physical remains for you to rebuild and revere; now, you spirits and deities, exert yourselves with one mind!
Throughout the entire realm of Jambudvīpa, filling its millions of households, raise stūpas for the Buddha’s śarīra.
The aspiration originated with me, but the accomplishment was achieved through you.
As for the benefits of this supreme merit, I do not wish to possess them alone.
It is fitting that we each contribute to its construction, awaiting further instructions from the future.
The spirits and deities received the command and performed the meritorious work wherever it was required. Once the work was completed, they all came to request instructions.
After King Aśoka had opened the various stūpas erected by the eight kingdoms and divided the śarīra relics, he entrusted them to the spirits and deities and said to the arhats:
"It is my wish that the śarīras be enshrined simultaneously in all locations."
"Though the heart harbors this hope, the matter has not yet followed one's desires.
The Arhat said,
"When the King commands the spirits and ghosts to arrive on the appointed day, if the sun is obscured by something shaped like a hand— at that moment, you should deposit the śarīra."
The King, having received this instruction, proclaimed it to the spirits and deities.

When the appointed day arrived, King Aśoka observed the signs; at the moment the sun reached its zenith, the Arhat used his supernormal powers to stretch out his hand and shield the sun from view. As all those present looked on with reverence, the construction works were simultaneously completed.

Not far from the side of the stūpa, within a vihāra, there is a large stone upon which the Tathāgata walked; his two footprints still remain, measuring one foot and eight inches in length and slightly more than six inches in breadth.
Both footprints bear the mark of the wheel, and all ten toes are adorned with floral patterns; the figures of fish emerge in relief, and a brilliant light shines forth from time to time.

Formerly, when the Tathāgata was about to enter parinirvāṇa and was proceeding north toward the city of Kuśinagara, he looked south toward the kingdom of Magadha and, treading upon this stone, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"I now leave behind these final footprints as I am about to enter parinirvāṇa, looking back upon Magadha."
"A hundred years hence, King Aśoka shall appear in the world to rule; he will establish his capital here, protect and uphold the Triple Gem, and command the hundred deities.

When King Aśoka succeeded to the throne, he moved the capital and built a city there, covering over the stone traces of the [previous] Zhou dynasty. Being close to the palace city, he constantly made offerings in person.
Later, various kings vied with one another to lift it back; although the stone was not large, none were able to turn it.

Recently, King Śaśāṅka, who persecuted the Buddha-dharma, went to the site of the stone intending to destroy the holy traces; yet after he had carved away at it, the surface returned to its original state, its patterns remaining as before. Thereupon, he abandoned it in the Ganges River, whereupon it soon returned to its original place.
Beside it is a stūpa, which marks the site where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation.
Not far from the side of the Buddha’s footprint vihāra is a large stone pillar over thirty feet high; its inscription is incomplete, but its general purport states:

"King Aśoka, whose roots of faith were firm and steadfast, thrice offered the continent of Jambudvīpa to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, and thrice ransomed it back with various precious treasures."
The inscription therein states, in brief, that to the north of the palace there is a great stone chamber;
its exterior resembles a lofty mountain, while its interior is several *zhang* wide. This was constructed by King Aśoka for his ordained younger brother to employ spirits and ghosts.
Formerly, King Aśoka had a half-brother named Mahendrāditya (translated into Chinese as Dàdì, "Great Emperor").
Born of a noble lineage, he usurped royal prerogatives and was extravagant, licentious, and tyrannical; thus, the common people harbored resentment against him.
A senior minister of state advanced to offer this counsel to the king:
"Your arrogant younger brother’s exercise of power has already become excessive.
Now, when governance is impartial, the state is orderly; when the people are harmonious, the ruler is secure. This is the ancient maxim, a principle that has endured for a long time."
"I pray that you will preserve the national statutes and hand him over to those who administer the law.
King Aśoka wept and said to his younger brother, "I have inherited the throne and protected all living beings; how could I ever forget my kindness and affection toward you, my own brother?"
"Without first providing guidance and correction, they have already fallen into the net of legal punishment.
Above, he fears his ancestors; below, he is constrained by public opinion.
Mahendrarāja bowed his head and apologized, saying:
"Having failed to exercise self-restraint in my conduct, I have dared to violate the laws of the state; I pray for the gift of a second life, with an extension of seven days.
Thereupon, he was placed in a secluded chamber under strict guard, and was provided with delicacies and choice foods without fail.
The guard announced:
"One day has already passed; six days remain.

When the sixth day arrived, being deeply filled with anxiety and fear, he further exerted his body and mind, whereupon he attained the realization of the fruit, ascended into the void, displayed divine miracles, and soon departed from the mundane world to dwell far away in mountain crags and valleys.
King Aśoka went in person and said to him,
"Formerly, constrained by the laws of the state, I intended to inflict severe punishment upon you.
Who would have thought that you would ascend so purely as to realize the fruit of sainthood?"
"Since you are no longer entangled by worldly attachments, you may return to your kingdom.
His younger brother said:
"Formerly, bound by the net of affection, my heart raced after fame and beauty; now that I have emerged from this perilous city, my will finds joy in the mountain valleys."
"I wish to abandon the human world and dwell forever among hills and ravines.
The King said,
"If you desire to still the mind and its deliberations, why must it necessarily be in secluded crags?"
"I shall follow your wish and establish a monument for you.
He then summoned the ghosts and spirits and addressed them, saying:
"On a day to come, I shall prepare a vast array of delicacies; you all should lead one another to gather at my assembly, each bringing a large stone to serve as your own seat."
The deities received their command and assembled in full at the appointed time.
Once the assembly had gathered, the King said to the deities:
"The stone seats are scattered here and there; you should stack them together."
"By means of this merit, we shall not labor, but shall construct a hollow chamber.
The various deities received the command, and it was completed in less than a day.
King Aśoka went in person to invite him, and he resided in this mountain hermitage.

To the north of the old palace and to the south of the hell, there is a large stone trough. This vessel was fashioned through the divine craftsmanship of King Aśoka’s artisans; it was used to store food when providing meals for the saṃgha.

To the southwest of the former palace, there is a small rocky mountain; throughout its cliffs and valleys, there are dozens of stone chambers, which King Aśoka established for the Arhats such as Upagupta by employing spirits and deities.
Beside it stands an old terrace, its remaining foundations a mound of piled stones;

the ponds and marshes ripple with waves, their clear currents so transparent as to reflect everything. People from neighboring lands and distant regions call this "Holy Water," believing that if one drinks from or bathes in it, their sins and defilements will be extinguished.

To the southwest of the mountain are five stūpas; their lofty foundations have already subsided, yet the remaining mounds are still high. Viewed from afar, they appear as dense, verdant hills. Each side measures several hundred paces, and later generations have constructed smaller stūpas upon them.
The *Record of India* states:

"In the past, after King Aśoka had constructed eighty-four thousand stūpas, there remained five pecks of śarīra. Therefore, he separately erected five stūpas, their construction more marvelous than those elsewhere, with spiritual wonders arising from time to time, to represent the Tathāgata’s fivefold Dharma-body."

Those of shallow faith secretly discussed among themselves, saying that this was a treasury built in the past by King Nanda to store the seven precious gems. Later, there was a king who was not particularly pure in his faith;

hearing these prior rumors, he gave rein to his greedy desires and mobilized his military forces. He personally arrived to excavate the site, whereupon the earth shook, the mountains tilted, clouds darkened the sky, and the sun was obscured. Within the stūpa, a great sound thundered like a clap of lightning, causing the soldiers to fall prostrate and the elephants and horses to bolt in terror.
"From this point forward, none shall dare to covet [the throne].
Someone said:
"Though there are many opinions among the multitude, they do not constitute a definitive argument."
"Following ancient records, I believe I have obtained the truth.
To the southeast of the old city is the Kukkuṭārāma (in the Tang language, "Chicken Garden") Monastery, which was established by King Aśoka.

When King Aśoka first placed faith in the Buddha-dharma, he respectfully established monasteries and cultivated the seeds of goodness; he summoned a thousand monks from both the ordinary and holy assemblies, providing them with the four types of requisites and supplying all their daily necessities.
It has been in ruins for a long time, though the foundations still remain.
Beside the monastery is a great stūpa named Āmalaka,
which is the name of an Indian medicinal fruit.
King Aśoka fell ill and, as his condition became critical, knew that his life would not be sustained.
Desiring to relinquish his precious treasures to cultivate fields of merit, the regent ministers who held power cautioned him against following his wishes.
Later, while eating, he left behind an āmalaka fruit; as he toyed with it until it was half-rotten, he grasped the fruit and sighed deeply, then asked his ministers:
"Who is now the lord of Jambudvīpa?"
The ministers replied,
"Only Your Majesty. The King said:
"Not so. I am not the master now;
I have sovereignty only over this half-fruit."
Alas! The wealth and nobility of this world are as precarious as a candle in the wind.

Though one may occupy a position encompassing the realm and possess a name of lofty renown, at the moment of death one faces destitution and is beset by powerful ministers; the world is no longer one's own, yet half a fruit remains!
He then commanded his attendant minister and told him:
"Take this half-fruit and go to that Kukkutārāma monastery; offer it to the assembly of monks and speak thus:
'Formerly the lord of Jambudvīpa, now the King of Half-Amalaka, bows his head before the Venerable Saṃgha and prays that you accept this final offering.'"
Of all that I once possessed, everything has been lost; only this half-fruit remains, over which I have a modicum of mastery.
May it bring compassion to the poor and destitute, and cause the seeds of merit to increase.
In the midst of the Sangha, the Elder spoke thus:

"The Great King Aśoka, whose long-standing vow was for vast salvation, now suffers from malaria while a treacherous minister usurps his authority. Though he has accumulated treasures beyond measure, they are no longer his own; yet he offers even half a fruit as a gift."
"Accepting the King's command, I shall offer it universally to the assembly of monks.
He immediately summoned the administrative officers and boiled everything together in the broth.
He collected the fruit pits and erected a stūpa over them.
Having received such profound kindness, I have thus commemorated his final testament.
To the northwest of the Āmalaka Stūpa, within the ruins of a former monastery, there is a stūpa known as the "Place Where the Gandhī-wood Ghaṇṭā Was Struck."

Originally, there were hundreds of monasteries within this city; the monks were solemn and dignified, and their studies were pure and lofty, such that the followers of external paths silenced themselves and remained mute.
Thereafter, the monastic disciples passed away one after another, and none among the later generations succeeded the former masters.

Meanwhile, the teachers and disciples of the non-Buddhists transmitted their instructions and perfected their arts; they then summoned their peers and companions by the thousands and tens of thousands, who gathered at the monasteries, proclaiming aloud:
"Strike the *gandi* to assemble the students!"
The multitude of fools dwelling together engaged in fallacious debate.
They subsequently informed the King, requesting a contest to determine their relative superiority.
The non-Buddhist masters were of eminent talent and profound learning, whereas although the monastic community was numerous, their arguments were superficial.
The non-Buddhist said,
"My argument has prevailed.
From this day forward, no monasteries shall strike the *ghanṭī* to assemble the community."
The king granted his request and acted according to the previously established rule.
The monastic community, having suffered this humiliation, withdrew while enduring the insults; for twelve years, they did not strike the *gandī* gong.
At that time, there was the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna of South India—translated into Chinese as Longmeng (Dragon Fierce);

the old translation "Longshu" (Dragon Tree) is incorrect. Having enjoyed a reputation for refinement from his youth and attained a preeminent fame in his maturity, he renounced sensual desire to leave the household life and engage in study; he profoundly investigated the subtle principles and ascended to the first bhūmi.
He had a great disciple named Deva, who was brilliant in wisdom and possessed a keen and alert mind. He addressed his teacher, saying:
"The scholars of the city of Pāṭaliputra have been silenced by the non-Buddhists; the *gandī* has not been struck for twelve years now, as the days and months have swiftly passed."
"I venture to wish to demolish the mountain of false views and kindle the torch of the True Dharma.
Nāgārjuna said, "The non-Buddhists outside the city of Pāṭaliputra are deeply learned; you are not their equal. I shall go there now."
Deva said, "To destroy withered grass, why must one overturn a mountain?
I venture to accept your instruction and shall refute all heterodox teachings."
"The Great Master established the doctrines of the non-Buddhists, and I followed the text to analyze and refute them, examining their relative strengths and weaknesses before deciding how to proceed.
Nāgārjuna then supported and established the non-Buddhist tenets, while Āryadeva followed by refuting his reasoning. After seven days, Nāgārjuna lost his position and sighed, saying:
"Erroneous words are easily lost; false doctrines are difficult to support."
"Go forth! You shall surely crush them!
Deva Bodhisattva had long enjoyed a high reputation; when the non-Buddhists outside the city of Pāṭaliputra heard of this, they immediately assembled and hurried to inform the King, saying:
"Great King, in the past you deigned to grant an audience and issued a decree that the śramaṇas were not permitted to strike the *gandī*."

"I pray that you deign to issue an edict, ordering the gatekeepers not to allow monks from neighboring regions to enter the city. I fear they might form alliances and lightly alter our established regulations.
The King granted his request and strictly ordered the gatekeepers to keep watch.
When Deva arrived, he was not permitted to enter the city.

Upon hearing of the prohibition, he changed his clothes, folded his saṃghāṭī robe, placed it inside a bundle of straw, tucked up his robes, hurried on foot, and entered carrying the load upon his back.
Having arrived within the city, he discarded the grass and donned his robes; reaching this monastery, he sought a place to rest.
Finding few people there, no one offered him lodging, so he ended up spending the night atop the *gandhī* platform.
At dawn, he struck it with great force.
When the community heard it and investigated, they found it was a visiting bhikṣu.
The news spread through all the monasteries like an echo.
When the king heard this and investigated the matter, he could find no one who preceded them; upon arriving at this monastery, everyone pointed to Deva.
Deva said, "As for the *gandī*, it is struck to assemble the multitude."
"If it exists but is not used, what is the purpose of hanging it there?
The royal official replied, "Previously, when the monastic community was defeated in debate, it was decreed that they must not strike it; twelve years have already passed."
Deva said: "Is that so?
On this very day, I shall once again sound the drum of the Dharma."
The messenger reported to the king, saying,
"There is a certain śramaṇa who wishes to wipe away his former humiliation.
The king then summoned the scholars and established a formal decree, saying:
"Should I lose my original thesis in debate, I shall sacrifice my life to atone for it.
Thereupon, the non-Buddhists vied with one another to display their banners and drums, clamoring with divergent doctrines, each flashing the sharp edge of their rhetoric.

Once Bodhisattva Deva ascended the seat of debate, he listened to their preliminary arguments and then proceeded to dismantle them point by point according to their meaning; in less than a single day, he crushed all the heterodox schools.
The king and his ministers were all filled with joy, and they established this sacred foundation to commemorate his supreme virtue.
To the north of the *stūpa* where Jian struck the *ghanṭā*, there is an old foundation; this was the dwelling place of the Brahmin Guibian in the past.
Initially, there was a Brahmin in this city who built his hut in a desolate thicket and did not mingle with the world. He sacrificed to spirits to seek blessings, living in the company of *piśācas*.
In his lofty discourses and profound conversations, elegant words responded like echoes; whenever someone posed a provocative challenge, he would respond from behind a lowered curtain.
Among those of established learning and eminent talent, none could surpass him. Both officials and commoners were unanimously moved by him, looking up to him as if he were a sage.
There was a Bodhisattva named Aśvaghoṣa (translated into Chinese as Maming), whose wisdom encompassed all things and whose Way spread through the Three Vehicles. He would often say to others:

"This Brahmin has not learned through formal instruction, nor does his artistry rest upon ancient precedents. Yet he dwells in secluded solitude and alone enjoys a lofty reputation; could this not be because he relies on spirits and ghosts, or is possessed by demons and phantoms? How else could he be such as this?"

Now, this man’s eloquence is granted by the spirits; his words do not accord with those of men, and once his discourse is heard, no one can recount it again. I shall now go to him to observe his conduct.
He then went directly to his hermitage and said to him:
"I have long admired your magnificent virtue from afar.
I venture to request that you lift your curtain so that I may express my long-held aspiration."
The Brahmin, however, remained haughty and aloof; he responded from behind a curtain and would never speak face-to-face.
Aśvaghoṣa knew in his heart that this was a demonic spirit, yet he felt deeply confident in himself. Having finished his discourse, he withdrew and said to the people:
"I already know him; I shall surely defeat him."
He immediately went to inform the king, saying,
"I only pray that you will grant me permission to engage in a vigorous debate with that householder.
Upon hearing this, the king was startled and said:
"Who is this person!
Unless he has realized the three types of clear knowledge and perfected the six supernormal powers, how could he be able to debate with him?
He ordered his carriage and went in person to observe the debate in detail.

At that time, Aśvaghoṣa expounded the subtle words of the Tripiṭaka masters and set forth the great principles of the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*); his wondrous eloquence was unrestrained and his lofty discourse was pure and far-reaching.
Once the Brahmin had finished his exposition, Aśvaghoṣa spoke again:
"You have missed my intended meaning; you ought to restate it."
At that time, the brahmin remained silent and speechless. Aśvaghoṣa rebuked him, saying:
"Why do you not resolve this difficulty?
You who serve a malevolent spirit should quickly provide an answer!"
He quickly pulled back the curtain and looked to examine the anomaly.
The Brahmin said in a state of panic: "Stop!
"Stop!
Aśvaghoṣa withdrew and said, "This youth has lost his reputation this very morning; it is said that empty fame does not endure for long."
The King said:
"Were it not for one of such profound virtue, who could have discerned this heterodox path?
His wisdom in judging men is truly peerless; according to the established laws of the state, his eminent achievements ought to be commemorated."
More than two hundred *li* to the southwest of the city, there are the remains of a monastery.

Beside it stands a stūpa that occasionally illuminates the surroundings with divine light and manifests auspicious omens from time to time. All people from near and far offer prayers here; it is the site where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation.
Going southwest from the monastery for more than one hundred *li*, one arrives at the Ti-lo-shi-ka Monastery.

Its courtyards consist of four enclosures, with pavilions and galleries on three tiers; its lofty terraces rise several *ren* high, and its double gates stand wide open. It was built by the last descendant of King Bimbisāra.

He summoned those of eminent talent and widely invited men of superior virtue; scholars from distant lands and elites from afar flocked together, following one another shoulder-to-shoulder as they arrived.
The monastic community numbered in the thousands, all of whom studied the Mahāyāna.

At the central gate facing the road were three vihāras; atop them were placed wheel symbols (cakra) with bells suspended in the air, while below they were built upon tiered foundations with railings arranged all around. The doors, windows, beams, rafters, walls, and steps were adorned with raised patterns of gold and copper, interspersed with various forms of ornamentation.
In the Central Refectory stands a statue of the Buddha three zhang in height; to its left is a statue of Tārā Bodhisattva, and to its right is a statue of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
These three statues were all cast from brass; their majestic spirit is solemn and awe-inspiring, and their spiritual discernment reaches far into the unseen realm.
Within each of the viharas there is one *śarīra* (relic) of one *sheng*; spiritual radiance occasionally shines forth, and auspicious omens arise from time to time.

More than ninety *li* to the southwest of the Ti-lo-shi-ka monastery, one reaches a great mountain where the clouds and rocks are dark and luxuriant, a dwelling place for numinous immortals. Venomous snakes and fierce dragons nest in its thickets, while wild beasts and birds of prey perch within its forests.
On the summit of the mountain is a large flat rock upon which a stūpa has been erected, over ten feet in height; this is the place where the Buddha entered meditative concentration.
In the past, when the Tathāgata descended as an incarnation, he stayed here and sat upon this flat rock to enter the samādhi of cessation, remaining there for the duration of one night.
The devas, spirits, and sages made offerings to the Tathāgata, beating celestial drums and raining down celestial flowers.
When the Tathāgata emerged from meditative absorption, the devas were moved by devotion and constructed a stūpa out of precious gold and silver.
As the distance from the Sage grew ever more remote, the precious relics transformed into stone.
From antiquity until the present, no human has ever reached them.

Gazing afar at the high mountain, one beholds extraordinary sights: long serpents and fierce beasts follow in a clockwise procession, while celestial immortals and holy sages follow shoulder to shoulder in praise and worship.
On a peak of Mount Shandong is a stūpa, marking the place where the Tathāgata once stood gazing toward the territory he had traversed in Magadha.
More than thirty li to the northwest of the mountain, at its base, is a monastery with a lofty foundation backed by the ridge and pavilions rising from the precipitous cliffs.
There are more than fifty monks, all of whom study the Mahāyāna teachings.
This is the place where the Bodhisattva Guṇamati (translated into Chinese as Dèhuì) subdued the non-Buddhists.
Originally, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Māṭhara on this mountain who followed the teachings of the Sāṃkhya school to cultivate the Way.

His learning was exhaustive regarding both internal and external doctrines, and his discourse reached the ultimate depths of emptiness and existence; his reputation stood foremost among his peers, and his virtue was held in high esteem by his contemporaries.
The sovereign held him in high esteem and regarded him as a national treasure; the ministers and commoners looked up to him with devotion, all calling him their family teacher.
Scholars from neighboring states followed his influence and admired his virtue, regarding him as a senior master; he was truly one of vast erudition and profound insight.
He was granted two cities as his fief and lived surrounded by his feudal estates.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇamati of South India was precocious and highly intelligent; from an early age he excelled in subtle matters, mastered the Tripitaka, and thoroughly penetrated the principles of the Four Noble Truths.
Having heard that Māṭhava’s discourse was profoundly subtle and profound, he harbored a desire to blunt his opponent's sharpness and commanded a disciple to draft a letter, saying:
"I respectfully inquire after Māṭhava; I hope you are well and at ease."
"You should forget your weariness and toil, and diligently practice your former studies; after three years, I shall destroy your fine reputation.
Thus, during the second and third years, he sent messengers to report [the progress] each time.
As he was about to set out on his journey, he again composed a letter, saying:
"The allotted span of years has reached its limit; what progress have you made in your studies?
I am now arriving; you should be aware of this."
Māṭhava was filled with great trepidation and instructed his disciples and the households of the village:
"From this day forward, you must not allow śramaṇas or followers of other paths to reside here. Proclaim this to one another and ensure that no one violates it."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇamati arrived at the town of Māṭhava, carrying his staff. Because the people were bound by their agreement, no one would give him lodging.
The Brahmins further reviled him, saying:
"With your shorn hair and strange attire, what kind of odd person are you?"
"You should depart at once; do not remain here!
Bodhisattva Guṇamati, wishing to refute the heterodox paths and hoping to stay overnight in that town, spoke with a compassionate heart and humble words:

"Your practice is the purity of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while my practice is the purity of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Since our purities are the same, why do you refuse me?"
The brahmin, refusing to speak with him, merely pursued him;
he was driven out of the town and entered a great forest.

In that forest, a pack of fierce beasts roamed about committing violence. A person of pure faith, fearing that the Bodhisattva would be harmed by the beasts, bound up a bundle of firewood, took up a weapon, and said to the Bodhisattva:

"It is reported from afar that the Bodhisattva Guṇamati of South India intends to come here for debate; therefore, the lord of this city, fearing that his good reputation might be tarnished, has strictly renewed his prohibitions against allowing śramaṇas to stay."
"Fearing that you would be harmed by external things, I have come to assist you.
Go now and be at ease; harbor no other anxieties. Dehui said:
"I am indeed that very person, Viśuddhaśraddhā, whom you, Guṇamati, have described.
Having heard this, Viśuddhaśraddhā felt even deeper reverence and said to Guṇamati, "It is exactly as you have told me;
we should proceed with haste."
He immediately emerged from the deep forest and rested in a desolate marsh.
With pure faith, he set fire to the surroundings and, holding his bow, patrolled on all sides. When the night had ended, he said to Guṇamati, "We may now proceed;
I fear others have learned of our presence and will come to plot our harm."
Guṇamati declined, saying,
"I dare not forget your kindness.
Thereupon, he set out.
Upon arriving at the royal palace, he said to the gatekeeper:
"There is now a śramaṇa who has come from afar; I pray that Your Majesty will deign to grant him permission to debate with Māṭhara."
Upon hearing this, the king said in astonishment,
"This is merely a liar.
He immediately ordered an envoy to go to Māṭhava’s residence and proclaim the king's decree, saying:

"A certain śramaṇa has come seeking debate; now that the arena for discussion has been swept and purified, we have proclaimed it far and wide and await his arrival. We pray that you will deign to grace us with your presence."
Māṭhava asked the king’s messenger,
"Is this not the Master of Śāstras Guṇamati from South India?
He replied:
"So be it. Upon hearing this, Māṭhara was deeply displeased; yet, as the matter could not be avoided, he eventually arrived at the site of debate.
The king, ministers, officials, commoners, and nobility all assembled there, desiring to listen to the lofty discourse.

Guṇamati first established his thesis; by the time the sun had set, Mādhava excused himself on the grounds that he was advanced in years and his intellect was dimmed in rapid debate, requesting to return to a quiet place for reflection before responding to the challenge.
Every time he spoke of returning home, when he ascended the seat at dawn, there was ultimately no dissenting opinion.
On the sixth day, he spat blood and died.
As he was about to pass away, he looked toward his wife and gave her his final instructions, saying:
"You possess great talent; do not forget your sense of shame!
After Māṭhara died, [Vasubandhu] concealed his death and did not announce the mourning; instead, he dressed himself in fresh, elegant garments and came to the debating assembly.

The assembly was filled with clamor as they said to one another, "Māṭhara prides himself on his superior talent and was ashamed to face Guṇamati; therefore, he has sent his wife instead, and thus the relative superiority and inferiority are made clear."
The Bodhisattva Guṇamati said to his wife,
"He who could restrain you, I have already restrained him.
Knowing she was in the face of difficulty, Mātṛceṭā’s wife withdrew.
The King asked,
"Why did he remain silent when you spoke so cryptically? Dehui replied:
"How lamentable! Māṭhara has died!
His wife wished to come here to debate with me.
The King said:
"How do you know this?
We pray that you will deign to instruct us.
Guṇamati replied:

"When his wife arrived, her face bore the expression of one who has suffered death or mourning, and her speech was filled with the sound of grief and resentment; for this reason, I knew that Tapasa had died."
"He who can subdue you is none other than your husband.
The King ordered a messenger to go and observe, and it was indeed as they had discussed.
The King then apologized, saying:

"The Buddha-dharma is profound and subtle; eminent sages have followed in its footsteps. By maintaining the Way through non-action, all sentient beings have been moistened by its transformation. Relying on the ancient statutes of our state, the honoring of virtue has been constant."
Guṇamati said:

"If one who is indeed ignorant yet embodies the Way and dwells in integrity, whose rectitude is sufficient for the purpose of aiding sentient beings, intends to broaden the path of guidance by first subduing arrogance and employing skillful means to gather and transform others, now is the time."

I only pray that Your Majesty will grant the descendants of the inhabitants of the village of Māṭhapa for a thousand generations to serve perpetually as monastics of this saṃghārāma; by thus issuing an edict for future generations, you shall spread an inexhaustible legacy of merit.

"Only those with pure faith who witness this protection shall see their merit extend throughout the world; their food and clothing shall be shared with the monastic community, so as to encourage the lay faithful and to praise profound virtue.
Thereupon, he established this monastery to commemorate this eminent site.

Initially, after Māṭhava’s defeat in debate, about ten practitioners of pure conduct fled to a neighboring country to report the matter of their humiliation to the various non-Buddhist teachers. They recruited men of outstanding talent to come and wipe away their former disgrace.
The King, having come to cherish and revere his virtue and wisdom, went in person to invite him, saying:

"Now these various non-Buddhists, failing to measure their own strength, have banded together in groups and dared to beat the drum of debate; I only pray that the Great Master will subdue these heterodox paths."
Guṇamati said,
"It is fitting that we assemble the debaters.
Thereupon, the followers of the non-Buddhist schools joyfully comforted one another.
"We shall surely be victorious today.
At that time, as the various non-Buddhists were expounding their doctrines, Bodhisattva Guṇamati said:
"Now these non-Buddhists have fled in fear and traveled far away; according to the King's prior decree, they are all low-born men. How can I now engage in debate with them?"
Dehui had a seat-attendant who had long heard his discourses and was somewhat familiar with their subtle meanings;
he stood by the side listening to the lofty conversation. Dehui patted the seat and said, "Seat, you may speak."
The assembly was all struck with awe and marveled at his command.
At that moment, the pillar who carried the throne immediately posed a challenge; profound meanings gushed forth like a spring, and Qingbian’s responses echoed like thunder.
After he had repeated this three times, the non-Buddhists lost their core doctrine; their momentum was severely blunted and their wings were broken once more.
From the time they were defeated in debate, the site was established as a monastic community with its own residential households.

More than twenty li to the southwest of the Guṇamati Monastery, one reaches a solitary mountain where there is a monastery. It was built by Śīlabhadra—the Tang translation of which is Jiexian (Virtuous Precepts)—after he had won a debate on doctrine and offered up a village as a donation.
A single perilous peak rises loftily like a stūpa, containing the śarīra of the Buddha.
The Master was of royal lineage from the kingdom of Samataṭa and was born into the Brahmin caste.
From his youth, he was fond of learning and possessed noble character; he traveled throughout India seeking out sages and philosophers.
Upon arriving at the Nālandā Monastery in this country, he encountered the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla, heard the Dharma, and attained faith and realization.

He requested to don the dyed robes of a monk, consulting him on the ultimate goal and inquiring about the path to liberation; having exhausted the most profound principles and investigated the subtle words, his fame prevailed in his own time and his reputation resounded across distant lands.

In South India, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner who explored the profound and sought out the hidden, penetrating the obscure and fathoming the subtle. Having heard of Dharmapāla’s great reputation, he gave rise to deep jealousy born of pride and, undeterred by mountains or rivers, beat the drum to seek debate, saying:
"I am a man from South India."
"I hear that there is a great master of treatises within Your Majesty’s realm; though I am not clever, I wish to deliberate with him in detail.
The King said, "There is one, and it is indeed as you propose."
He then commanded an envoy to invite Dharmapāla, saying:

"There is a non-Buddhist from South India who has traveled more than a thousand li to seek a debate; we only pray that you will deign to descend to our presence and attend the assembly for discussion."
Upon hearing this, Dharmapāla gathered his robes and was about to depart.
His disciple Śīlabhadra, a preeminent talent among the junior monks, stepped forward and requested,
"Why do you hasten to leave?"
Dharmapāla said:

"Since the sun of wisdom has set its radiance and the lamp of transmission has shone in silence, heretics have swarmed like ants and heterodox scholars have flown in like bees; therefore, I shall now destroy their arguments."
Śīlabhadra said,
"Having respectfully heard your further discourse, I venture to refute the heterodox paths.
Dharmapāla, recognizing his brilliance, granted him permission.
At that time, Śīlabhadra was only thirty years old; the assembly looked down upon him for his youth, fearing he would be unable to shoulder the task alone.
Knowing the dissatisfaction of the multitude, Dharmapāla sought to resolve their concerns, saying:
"We value noble brilliance rather than speaking of age; judging by what we see now, he will certainly defeat them."
When the day for the assembly arrived, people flocked from far and near, both young and old gathering together.
The non-Buddhists expounded their great principles, exhausting their subtle refinements;
Śīlabhadra followed the logic and examined the facts, reaching the utmost depths of the profound and mysterious.
The non-Buddhist teacher, his arguments exhausted, withdrew in shame.
The King, wishing to reward his virtue, offered him this city-state as a fief.
The Master declined, saying:
"A man who has dyed his robes relies on contentment and maintains himself in purity; what need has he for a city?
The King replied, "The Dharma King has hidden his traces and the boat of wisdom has sunk. Without a distinguished marker, there will be no way to encourage future students."
"To propagate the True Dharma, we pray that you will deign to accept us with compassion.

The Master of Śāstras, having no choice but to decline, accepted the village; he then constructed a monastery, exhausting every architectural rule, and surrendered the households of the village to provide for its offerings.
Traveling forty or fifty *li* southwest from the Śīlabhadra Monastery and crossing the Nairañjanā River, one arrives at the city of Gayā.

It is very rugged and secure, with few inhabitants; there are only over a thousand households of Brahmins, the descendants of the Great Sage, who do not acknowledge the King’s suzerainty and are all revered by the multitude.

More than thirty li to the north of the city, there is a clear spring; according to Indian tradition, it is called "Holy Water," and whoever drinks from or washes in it will have their sins and defilements eliminated.
Five or six *li* to the southwest of the city, one reaches Gayā Mountain.

Its gullies and valleys are profound and dark, and its peaks and crags are perilous; according to the local customs of India, it is called the "Numinous Mountain" (*Lingshan*). Since antiquity, whenever kings have governed the realm and inherited the succession, their civilizing influence has reached distant peoples and their virtue has surpassed previous dynasties; there were none who did not ascend this peak to announce the successful completion of their achievements.

On the summit of the mountain stands a stone stūpa over a hundred feet high, erected by King Aśoka; its spiritual influence is subtly pervasive, and divine light occasionally illuminates it. In the past, the Tathāgata preached the *Ratnamegha* and other sūtras at this site.
To the southeast of Mount Gayā is a stūpa; it is the birthplace of Kāśyapa.
To the south of that are two stūpas, which belong to Gayākāśyapa and Nadīkāśyapa (formerly called Nadi-Kāśyapa, which is a corruption).
As for the various Kāśyapas, they likewise lack the character "p'o" (波), which is an abbreviation for the place where they served the sacrificial fire.

To the east of Gayākāśyapa’s site for serving the fire, one crosses a great river and reaches Mount Prāgbodhi (in the language of Tang, "Formerly Enlightened"). Because the Tathāgata ascended this mountain first when he was about to realize perfect enlightenment, it is called "Formerly Enlightened."

The Tathāgata sought diligently for six years without yet attaining perfect enlightenment; subsequently, he abandoned his ascetic practices and accepted the milk gruel. Traveling from the northeast, he gazed upon this mountain, and finding it profound and secluded, he desired to realize perfect enlightenment there.
As he ascended from the northeastern ridge to the summit, the earth shook and the mountain trembled and tilted.
Terrified, the mountain deity addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"This mountain is not a blessed site for attaining perfect enlightenment."
"If you stop here, the earth shall quake and sink, and the mountains shall also collapse. The Bodhisattva descended from the southwest;

halfway down a mountain cliff, facing a stream with his back to a rock, there was a great stone cave. The Bodhisattva went there and sat cross-legged within it. Again the earth shook, and the mountain once more tilted and swayed.
At that time, the Śuddhāvāsa devas proclaimed from the sky:
"This is not the place where the Tathāgata shall attain perfect enlightenment.

To the southwest of here, fourteen or fifteen *li* away, not far from the site of his ascetic practices, there is a *piyāla* tree; beneath it lies the Vajrāsana. All Buddhas of the past and future have attained perfect enlightenment upon this very seat; we pray that you proceed thither."
Just as the Bodhisattva was about to rise, the nāga within the chamber said:
"This chamber is pure and sublime, fit for the realization of holiness; I pray only that you will show compassion and not abandon it."

The Bodhisattva, knowing that this was not the place to attain realization, departed after leaving a shadow to fulfill the dragon's wish. This shadow remains as it was in the past, visible to both the wise and the foolish;
even unto the present day, some are still able to behold it.
Led by the various devas, he proceeded toward the Bodhi tree.

During the reign of King Aśoka, sites marking the traces of the Bodhisattva’s ascent and descent of the mountain were all distinguished with monuments, and stūpas were erected; though their dimensions varied, their miraculous responses were no different—sometimes celestial flowers rained down from the sky, and sometimes light illuminated the deep valleys.
Every year on the day the summer retreat (varṣā) concludes, monastics and laypeople from various regions ascend the mountain to present offerings, staying for two nights before returning.
Traveling fourteen or fifteen *li* southwest from Mount Prāgbodhi, one arrives at the Bodhi tree.
The surrounding walls were built of brick, lofty, steep, and secure.
They were long from east to west and narrow from south to north, measuring over five hundred paces in circumference.
Exotic trees and famous flowers cast continuous shade and joined their shadows together.
Fine sands and diverse grasses spread across the ground, covered in lush green.

The main gate opens to the east, facing the Nairañjanā River; the southern gate adjoins a great flower pond; the western side is secured by a formidable and steep barrier; and the northern gate leads to a great monastery.

Within the area enclosed by the perimeter wall, sacred sites are situated close together; there are both stūpas and vihāras, all erected as records by the kings, ministers, and noble families of various nations throughout Jambudvīpa, who revered the bequeathed teachings.
In the very center of the enclosure of the Bodhi tree is the Vajrāsana.

It was formed at the beginning of the present Bhadrakalpa and arose simultaneously with the great earth. Situated within the trichiliocosm, it extends downward to the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanacakravāḷa*) and upward to the surface of the earth. Composed of diamond, it measures over a hundred paces in circumference. Because the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa sit upon it to enter the Diamond Samādhi (*vajrasamādhi*), it is called the Vajrāsana.
The place where the Noble Path was realized is also called the Bodhimaṇḍa; when the great earth shook, this alone remained unshaken.

Therefore, as the Tathāgata was about to realize perfect enlightenment, he traversed these four corners and the ground everywhere trembled, but upon arriving at this spot, it became peaceful and did not shake.
Since the entry into the final kalpa, the True Dharma has gradually declined; buried beneath sand and soil, it can no longer be seen.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the kings of various nations, having heard accounts of the dimensions of the Vajrāsana as spoken by the Buddha, subsequently used two statues of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to mark the boundaries of north and south, with the figures seated facing east.
I have heard from the elders that:
"When this Bodhisattva image sinks and disappears, the Buddha-dharma shall come to an end.
Now, in the southern corner, the Bodhisattva has already sunk past the chest.
The Bodhi tree upon the Vajrāsana is the Pippala tree.
Formerly, when the Buddha was in the world, it stood several hundred feet high; though it has been repeatedly cut down, it still remains four or five zhang in height.
The Buddha sat beneath it and attained perfect enlightenment; therefore, it is called the Bodhi tree.
Its trunk is yellowish-white, and its branches and leaves are lush green; they do not wither in winter or summer, remaining radiant and unchanged throughout the seasons.
Every year on the anniversary of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, all the leaves wither and fall; after a short while, they return to their former state.

On this day, kings from various kingdoms and multitudes of monastics and laypeople from diverse regions, numbering in the tens of millions, gather without being summoned. They drench and wash [the tree] with scented water and fragrant milk, while music is performed, incense and flowers are arrayed, and lamps and torches burn continuously like the sun, as they compete to offer their worship.

After the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa, during the reign of King Aśoka’s first successor, he believed in and followed false paths; he destroyed the relics left by the Buddha and mobilized his troops, personally arriving to carry out the destruction.

The roots, stems, branches, and leaves were cut into pieces of an inch or so and piled up some dozens of paces to the west; they were then set on fire by a fire-worshipping Brahmin to offer as a sacrifice to the gods. While the smoke and flames had not yet subsided, two trees suddenly sprang forth from amidst the fierce fire, their lush leaves shimmering with emerald green. Consequently, they were called the Ash-Bodhi Trees.
King Aśoka, beholding this marvel, repented his transgression; he irrigated the remaining roots with fragrant milk, and as dawn approached, the tree grew back to its original state.
Witnessing this spiritual wonder, the king was moved by profound joy and celebration; he personally performed offerings, so absorbed in his delight that he forgot to return home.
The Queen, who had long placed her faith in non-Buddhist teachers, secretly dispatched messengers after midnight to cut down the tree once more.

When King Aśoka went to pay his respects the following morning, he saw only the stumps; filled with profound grief and lamentation, he prayed with utmost sincerity and irrigated the site with fragrant milk, whereupon the tree sprouted again within a few days.
The King, deeply revering and marveling at this, built a stone wall around it over ten feet high, which remains visible even today.

As for the recent King Śaśāṅka, he believed in and followed non-Buddhist paths; out of malice toward the Buddha-dharma, he destroyed monasteries and felled the Bodhi tree. He dug down until he reached the spring water, yet failing to exhaust its roots, he set fire to it and doused it with sugarcane juice, wishing to char and rot it so as to utterly extinguish any remaining sprouts.
Several months later, King Pūrṇavarman—whose name means "Full Armor" in the language of Tang and who was a descendant in the final generation of King Aśoka—hearing of these events, sighed and said:
"The Sun of Wisdom has already set; only the Bodhi tree remains, yet now it too is being ravaged. What shall living beings behold!"
He threw his entire body to the ground, his grief so moving that it affected all living beings.
He had several thousand cows milked and used the milk to irrigate the tree; by nightfall, the tree had grown back, reaching over ten feet in height.
Fearing that it might later be cut down, he constructed a stone wall around it, two zhang and four chi in height;
thus, the present Bodhi tree is now hidden by the stone wall, with only a little more than one zhang protruding from it.

To the east of the Bodhi tree is a vihāra, one hundred and sixty to seventy feet in height. Its foundation at the base measures over twenty paces across and is constructed of blue bricks and plastered with lime. Each tiered niche contains a golden image, and the four walls are carved with exquisite designs—some in the shape of linked pearls, others depicting celestial beings. Atop it is placed a gilded copper *āmala* fruit, also called a "jewel vase" (*ratnaghaṭa*), further referred to as a "jewel terrace."

On its eastern side, it was joined by a multi-storied pavilion, its eaves and halls rising in three tiers; its rafters, pillars, beams, doors, and windows were adorned with gold and silver carvings and inlaid with interspersed pearls and jade. Its inner chambers and deep halls featured triple-layered, interconnected doorways.

On the left and right of the outer gate, there are respective niches; the one on the left contains an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and the one on the right contains an image of Maitreya Bodhisattva, both cast from white silver and standing over ten feet high.
This was the site of an old monastery. Originally, King Aśoka first constructed a small vihāra here, which was later expanded by a brāhmaṇa.

Initially, there was a brāhmaṇa who did not believe in the Buddha-dharma and worshipped Maheśvara. Having heard that the deity resided in the Snowy Mountains, he went with his younger brother to seek a boon from him.
The deva said:
"All requests and aspirations bear fruit only when there is merit.
This is not something you can pray for, nor am I able to fulfill it."
The brahmin asked,
"What merit must one cultivate to fulfill such a wish?
The deva replied:
"If you wish to plant the seeds of goodness and seek the supreme field of merit, the Bodhi tree is the place where the fruit of Buddhahood is realized.
You should return at once; go to the Bodhi tree, construct a great vihāra, dig a large pond, and perform various offerings, and your aspirations shall surely be fulfilled."

Having received this divine mandate, the brahmins conceived great faith and returned together. The elder brother constructed a vihāra, while the younger brother dug a pond; thereupon they extensively cultivated offerings and diligently sought the fulfillment of their aspirations. Later, both achieved their goals and became ministers to the king. Whatever stipends and rewards they received, they dedicated entirely to almsgiving.
Once the vihāra was completed, he recruited artisans, intending to depict an image of the Tathāgata as he first attained enlightenment.
Time passed, yet no one responded to the summons.
After a long while, a brāhmaṇa came and addressed the assembly, saying:
"I am skilled at painting the sublime features of the Tathāgata.
The assembly asked,
"Now that we are about to create an image, what will you require?"
He replied, "It is merely fragrant clay.
It should be placed within a vihāra and illuminated by a single lamp; once I have entered, you must close the door firmly, and only after six months may the door be opened."
At that time, the assembly of monks all complied with his command.
With four days remaining and the six months not yet complete, the multitude was struck with wonder and opened [the stupa] to observe it.

Within the vihāra, he beheld the Buddha image solemnly seated in the full lotus posture; with the right foot placed above the left, the left hand drawn in and the right hand hanging down, it sat facing east, appearing as if truly present in its dignified stillness.

The height of the pedestal is four chi and two cun; its width is one zhang, two chi, and five cun. The height of the image is one zhang, one chi, and five cun; the distance between the two knees is eight chi and eight cun; the distance between the two shoulders is six chi and two cun. It is fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks of perfection, and its compassionate countenance appears as if truly alive, except that the carving and polishing of the right breast are not yet complete.
Since no human being was seen, it was proven that divine discernment was at work; the assembly all sighed with sorrow and earnestly requested to know more.
There was a śramaṇa whose long-standing mind was pure and sincere, who was moved to have a dream in which he saw the former brahmin saying to him:
"I am Maitreya Bodhisattva. Fearing that the artisans' thoughts might fail to fathom the holy countenance, I have come in person to paint this Buddha image."

As for the hanging of the right hand: in the past, when the Tathāgata was about to realize the fruit of Buddhahood, the celestial Māra came to harass him. The Earth Deity announced his arrival, and one of her manifestations first emerged to assist the Buddha in subduing the Māra.
The Tathāgata told her: "Do not be anxious or afraid; by the power of my forbearance, I shall surely subdue him."
The Māra King asked,
"Who shall serve as witness? Thereupon,
the Tathāgata extended his hand and pointed toward the earth, saying:
"There is evidence of this.
At that time, the earth deity of the second stage leaped forth to bear witness; therefore, the hands of the image today imitate those ancient ones by hanging downward.
Knowing that the spirit thus perceived them, there were none who were not moved with grief.
Thereupon, before the milk had even finished flowing, he filled the niche with various jewels, pearl necklaces, and precious crowns, all exquisitely adorned.

After King Śaṅkara had felled the Bodhi tree, he intended to destroy this image; however, upon beholding its compassionate countenance, his heart could not bear it. He turned his carriage to return and commanded his chief minister, saying:
"You should remove this Buddhist image and install the form of Maheśvara."
The minister received the decree and, filled with fear, sighed and said:

"To destroy Buddha images would bring calamity for kalpas; to disobey the King's command would lead to the loss of one's life and the extinction of one's clan. In such a dilemma, what course of action is appropriate?"

He then summoned those with faith to serve as laborers; they subsequently built a wall of bricks across the front of the image. Feeling ashamed of the darkness, he further placed a bright lamp there, and before the brick wall, he painted the deity Maheśvara.

When he completed his task and returned with the report, the King heard it and was struck with fear; blisters broke out over his entire body, and his skin was torn and split, so that before long, he passed away.
The ministers galloped back, demolished the partition walls, and although many days had passed, the lamp still did not go out.
The image remains to this day, its divine craftsmanship unimpaired.

Since he was situated in a secluded chamber with lamps and torches lit one after another, there was no means by which to clearly examine his compassionate countenance; one must wait until the early morning, holding a large bright mirror to reflect the light inward, and only then behold his numinous features.
Indeed, those who behold this are moved by an increasing sense of sorrow.
It was on the eighth day of the latter half of the month of Vaiśākha in India that the Tathāgata attained Perfect Enlightenment; this corresponds to the eighth day of the third month here.

According to the Theravāda tradition, the Buddha attained perfect enlightenment on the fifteenth day of the second half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the third lunar month.
At that time, the Tathāgata was thirty years of age.
Some say it is thirty-five years since [the Buddha’s passing].
To the north of the Bodhi tree is the place where the Buddha walked;
after the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment, he remained seated without rising for seven days in meditative concentration.

Upon his arising, he went to the north of the Bodhi tree and practiced walking meditation for seven days, pacing back and forth from east to west for more than ten paces; at every step, eighteen extraordinary lotuses appeared following his tracks.
Later generations built a brick foundation upon this mound, over three feet high.
According to the records of former sages, it says:

"This is the foundation of a sacred site that manifests the length or brevity of human life; if one first makes a sincere vow and subsequently measures [the height], the number will increase or decrease according to the duration of one's lifespan."
To the north of the walking path (caṅkrama), on the right side of the road, upon a flat rock within a great vihāra, there is a Buddha image with its eyes gazing upward.
In the past, the Tathāgata stayed here for seven days beholding the Bodhi tree, his eyes never turning away for even a moment.
To repay the kindness of the Bodhi tree, I gaze upon it from this place.
Not far to the west of the Bodhi tree, within a great vihāra, there is a brass Buddha image adorned with rare jewels, standing facing the east.

In front there is a blue stone of extraordinary patterns and wondrous luster; this is where, in the past, when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, Brahmā King erected a hall of seven treasures and Śakra Devendra constructed a throne of seven treasures. Upon it, the Buddha sat for seven days in contemplation, emitting a marvelous radiance that illuminated the Bodhi tree.
The Sage having departed long ago, the precious [relics] have turned to stone.
Not far to the south of the Bodhi tree, there is a stūpa over one hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka.
Having bathed in the Nairañjanā River, as the Bodhisattva was about to proceed toward the Bodhi tree, he reflected in private upon what should serve as his seat;
he then perceived for himself that he would require pure grass.
Śakra, Lord of Devas, transformed his body into that of a grass-cutter and carried [the grass] along the road.
The Bodhisattva said to him,
"Would you be so kind as to give me the grass you are carrying?"
Having heard these instructions, the emanated being respectfully presented the grass. The Bodhisattva accepted it and proceeded forward holding it.

Not far to the northeast of where he received the grass, there is a stūpa; this is the place where, as the Bodhisattva was about to realize the fruit of Buddhahood, blue sparrows and a herd of deer manifested auspicious omens.

These are auspicious omens from India and signs of sublime response; thus, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven followed the ways of the world, flying about in a great procession to manifest their spiritual power and reveal their sanctity.
To the east of the Bodhi tree, on both sides of the main road, there are two stūpas each, which mark the places where Māra attempted to harass the Bodhisattva.

As the Bodhisattva was about to realize the fruit of Buddhahood, the Māra King exhorted him to accept the status of a Wheel-Turning King; when his exhortations proved ineffective, the Māra returned in deep distress.

The daughters of the Māra King requested to go and seduce him, but through the Bodhisattva’s majestic spiritual power, their beautiful forms were transformed into states of decay; leaning on staffs for support, they withdrew together in a state of frailty.
To the northwest of the Bodhi tree, within a vihāra, there is a statue of Kāśyapa Buddha. It is renowned for its spiritual sanctity and frequently emits a brilliant light.
According to ancient records:
"If a person with sincere devotion circumambulates it seven times, they shall attain the knowledge of past lives in whatever place they are born."
In the two brick chambers to the northwest of Kāśyapa Buddha’s vihāra, there are images of earth deities (*pṛthivī-devatā*) respectively.
Formerly, when the Tathāgata was about to attain perfect enlightenment, one [deity] arrived to report to Māra, while the other served as a witness for the Buddha.
Later generations, mindful of his merit, depicted his image to commemorate his virtue.

Not far to the west of the enclosure of the Bodhi tree, there is a stūpa known as the Saffron (Kunkuma) Stūpa; it is over forty feet high and was built by a merchant chief from the kingdom of Tsaukuta.

In the past, there was a great merchant leader in the kingdom of Śroṇāparāntaka who worshipped celestial deities, seeking blessings and profit through sacrifices; he held the Buddha-dharma in contempt and did not believe in cause and effect.

Subsequently, leading a caravan of merchants, he traded goods for what they lacked and sailed upon the South Sea. There, they encountered a storm and lost their way; tossed by the waves and drifting on the billows for three years, their provisions were completely exhausted and they could not even sustain themselves.

Those who share the same boat cannot plan for tomorrow when facing the morning; though they exert their strength with a common purpose and contemplate the Heaven they serve, their mental anxieties are already exhausted, yet their hidden merits do not bring salvation.
Suddenly they saw a great mountain with lofty cliffs and steep ridges; two suns appeared together, their double radiance shining brightly.
At that time, the merchants comforted one another, saying:
"We are fortunate to have passed this great mountain; we should halt here, for it will bring us peace and happiness."
The merchant leader said,
"It is not a mountain, but rather a makara fish;
its lofty cliffs and steep peaks are its whiskers and fins."
"The two suns shining together in tandem—this is the light of his eyes!
Before these words had even faded, the sails of the ships converged and drifted together.
Thereupon, the merchant leader addressed his companions, saying:
"I have heard that the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara is able to bestow peace and happiness upon those in peril and distress; we should each, with utmost sincerity, invoke his name.
Thereupon, they all invoked him in unison, taking refuge and reciting his name.
Once the lofty mountains had hidden [the sun] and the two disks of the sun had also set, he suddenly beheld a śramaṇa whose dignified bearing was composed and orderly;
carrying his *khakkhara* staff, he traversed the void to come rescue those drowning, arriving in his home country before long.

Consequently, his faith became firm and steadfast; seeking merit without turning back, he constructed a stūpa to perform offerings, coating its upper and lower surfaces all around with saffron-scented clay.
Having already conceived faith, he led his companions to personally pay homage at the sacred sites and behold the Bodhi tree.
Before they had even had time to speak of returning home, months had already passed.
The merchants were traveling together when they said to one another:
"The mountains and rivers lie vast and wide, and our native lands are far away. As for the stūpas we previously erected, we are here now; who will sweep and maintain them?"

Having finished speaking, he circumambulated until he arrived there, where he suddenly saw a stūpa. Astonished by its presence, he proceeded forward to examine it and found that it was the very stūpa built in his own country.
For this reason, India is now named after the saffron flower (*kuṅkuma*).
To the southeast of the enclosure wall of the Bodhi tree, beside a *nyagrodha* tree and adjacent to a stūpa, there is a vihāra containing a seated image of the Buddha.
In the past, when the Tathāgata first realized the fruit of Buddhahood, the Great Brahmā King exhorted him here to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma.
Within the enclosure of the Bodhi tree, there is a great stūpa at each of the four corners.

In the past, after the Tathāgata had accepted the auspicious *kuśa* grass, he proceeded toward the Bodhi tree; first traversing the four quarters, the great earth shook violently, and only upon reaching the Vajrāsana did it become calm and still.
Within the enclosure of the Bodhi tree, sacred sites are arranged in dense succession, making it difficult to enumerate them all.
Outside the enclosure of the Bodhi tree, to the southwest, is a stūpa marking the former residence of the two milkmaids who offered the milk gruel.
Beside it is a stūpa where a cowherd woman cooked gruel.
Next to this stūpa is the place where the Tathāgata received the gruel.

Outside the southern gate of the enclosure wall of the Bodhi tree is a large pond, over seven hundred paces in circumference; its clear waves are as limpid as a mirror, and dragons and fish dwell therein in concealment. It was excavated by two Brahmin brothers under the command of Maheśvara.

Next to the south is a pond; in the past, when the Tathāgata had first attained perfect enlightenment and was about to wash his robes, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, transformed it into a pond for the Buddha.
To the west is a large rock; after the Buddha had finished washing his robes and was about to dry them in the sun, Śakra brought it from the Great Snowy Mountains.
Beside it is a stūpa where the Tathāgata accepted old clothes.
Further south, in the forest, is a stūpa at the place where the Tathāgata received old clothes offered by a poor old woman.
To the east of the pond manifested by Śakra, there is the pond of the Nāga King Mucilinda within a grove; its water is clear and dark, and its taste is sweet and delicious.
On the western bank is a small vihāra, in which a Buddha image has been fashioned.
In the past, when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, he sat here in meditative seclusion for seven days, remaining in samādhi.

At that time, this dragon king guarded the Tathāgata by encircling the Buddha’s body seven times with his own coils and manifesting many heads that hung down like a canopy; thus, there is his dwelling on the eastern bank of the pond.
To the east of the Mucilinda Dragon Pond, within a grove, there is a vihāra containing an image of the Buddha emaciated from illness.
Beside it is a place for walking meditation (caṅkrama), over seventy paces in length, with a *pippala* tree at each end, north and south.
Therefore, according to local custom today, whenever anyone contracts an illness, they apply fragrant oil to the image [of the Bodhisattva], and many are thereby granted recovery.
This is the place where the Bodhisattva practiced austerities.

To subdue the non-Buddhists and at the request of Māra, the Tathāgata further engaged in asceticism for six years, consuming only one sesame seed and one grain of wheat per day. His appearance became haggard and his body emaciated; when he walked back and forth, he had to lean against a tree to rise again.
Beside the Pippala tree, there is a stūpa marking the site where the Bodhisattva practiced austerities; this was the dwelling place of the five companions, Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the others.

Initially, when the Prince had renounced his home and was wandering through mountains and marshes, taking refuge among groves and springs, King Śuddhodana commanded these five men to follow him and attend to his needs.
Once the Prince had undertaken ascetic practices, Kauṇḍinya and the others also diligently sought [the path].
To the southeast of the place where Kauṇḍinya and the others resided, there is a stūpa marking the spot where the Bodhisattva entered the Nairañjanā River to bathe.
Not far from the riverbank, it was here that the Bodhisattva accepted the milk-rice offering.
Beside it is a stūpa marking the place where two elders presented him with parched grain and honey.

Seated beneath a tree in the full lotus posture, the Buddha remained in profound silence and stillness, experiencing the bliss of liberation; only after seven days had passed did he arise from his meditative concentration.
At that time, as the two merchant leaders were traveling outside the forest, the deity of that forest addressed them, saying:

"The Prince of the Śākya clan is now within this place; having first realized the fruit of Buddhahood, his mind is concentrated in profound stillness. For forty-nine days he has not yet consumed any food. Whoever offers him sustenance will obtain great and excellent merit."
At that time, the two merchant leaders each offered their travel provisions of parched grain and honey, which the World-Honored One accepted.
There is a stūpa at the place where the elder presented the parched grain, marking the spot where the Four Heavenly Kings offered their alms bowls.
Once the merchant leader had offered the parched grain and honey, the World-Honored One considered what vessel he should use to receive them.
At that moment, the Four Heavenly Kings arrived from the four directions, each holding a golden bowl, which they presented to him.
The World-Honored One remained silent and did not accept them, considering that renunciation was not suitable for such vessels.

The Four Heavenly Kings set aside their golden bowls and offered silver bowls, and even bowls made of crystal, lapis lazuli, agate, musaragalva, and pearl; yet the World-Honored One likewise did not accept any of them.
The Four Heavenly Kings each returned to their palaces, where they reverently held the stone bowls—azure in color and translucent—and presented them once more as offerings.

Because the World-Honored One had severed the distinction between self and other, he accepted them all together; he stacked them one upon another and pressed them into a single bowl, which is why there are four protrusions on its exterior.
Not far from where the Four Heavenly Kings presented the alms bowl, there is a stūpa at the place where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for his mother.

Once the Tathāgata had attained perfect enlightenment and was hailed as the Teacher of Gods and Humans, his mother Māyā descended from the celestial palace to this spot; there, the World-Honored One, according to her capacity, provided instruction and brought her joy.
Beside it, on the bank of a dried-up pool, is a stūpa at the place where, in the past, the Tathāgata manifested various divine transformations for those with whom he had a karmic connection.
Beside the site of these manifested miracles is another stūpa, marking the place where the Tathāgata converted the three brothers, including Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, along with their thousand disciples.
As the Tathāgata was now bestowing the path of goodness and subduing beings according to their needs, Upatiṣya Kāśyapa and his five hundred disciples requested to receive the Buddha’s teaching.
Kāśyapa said, "I too shall return with you from the path of delusion."
Thereupon, they followed one another to where the Buddha was.
The Tathāgata addressed them, saying:
"Cast off your deer-skin garments and abandon your fire-offering implements."
At that time, the brahmins respectfully followed the holy teaching and cast their ritual implements into the Nairañjanā River.

When Nadī-Kāśyapa saw the sacrificial vessels floating down the current, he went with his disciples to observe his elder brother’s movements; seeing that he had changed his course, he too donned the dyed robes.
When the two hundred disciples of Gayākāśyapa heard that their elder brother had abandoned the Dharma, they also went to the Buddha’s dwelling, vowing to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
To the northwest of the stūpa where the brothers Kāśyapa were ordained is the site where the Tathāgata subdued the fire-worshiping dragon attended by Kāśyapa.
As the Tathāgata was about to convert that man and subdue the object of his devotion, he stayed in the chamber of a brahmin’s fire-dragon.

After midnight, the dragon spat forth smoke and flames; the Buddha, having entered meditative concentration, likewise produced a fiery light, so that the chamber became brilliantly illuminated and ablaze with fierce, blazing flames.
The various Brahmin teachers, fearing that the fire would harm the Buddha, all rushed toward him, wailing in grief and lamenting with compassion.
Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa said to his disciples, "Judging by what we see now, this is surely not fire; it must be the śramaṇa subduing the dragon of fire."
The Tathāgata then placed the fire-dragon within his almsbowl and, at dawn, brought it forth to show to the followers of the non-Buddhist teachers.
Beside that spot is a stūpa, the place where five hundred pratyekabuddhas entered nirvāṇa together.
To the south of the Mucilinda Dragon Pond is a stūpa, the place where Kāśyapa rescued the Tathāgata from drowning.
At that time, the Kāśyapa brothers were renowned for their supernatural powers; their virtue was venerated far and wide, and the common people turned their hearts toward them in devotion.

The World-Honored One, guiding those who are deluded through his great sovereign power to transform and gather them in, raised dense clouds and sent down torrential rain everywhere except for the place where the Buddha resided, leaving him alone without water.
At that time, seeing this cloud and rain, Kāśyapa said to his disciples, "Will the dwelling place of the śramaṇa not be swept away by the flood?
He rowed a boat to rescue him, only to see the World-Honored One walking upon the water as if on land; as he stepped into the middle of the river, the waters parted and the sand was revealed.
Having seen this, Kāśyapa submitted in his heart and withdrew.
Two or three *li* outside the eastern gate of the enclosure of the Bodhi tree, there is the abode of a blind dragon.
This dragon, having accumulated misfortune over many lifetimes, received the retribution of being born blind.

As the Tathāgata was proceeding from Mount Prāgbodhi toward the Bodhi tree, he passed by the side of the Nāga’s dwelling. Suddenly, the Nāga’s eyes became clear, and seeing that the Bodhisattva was about to approach the Tree of Enlightenment, he said to him:
“Virtuous One, you shall soon attain perfect enlightenment.”
My eyes have been blind and obscured for a very long time; whenever a Buddha appears in the world, my eyes immediately become clear.
During the present Bhadrakalpa, when the three past Buddhas appeared in the world, I already attained the power of clear vision.
"Now that you, O Benevolent One, have arrived here, my eyes have suddenly opened; for this reason I know that you shall surely attain Buddhahood.
To the side of the eastern gate of the enclosure of the Bodhi tree, there is a stūpa marking the place where Māra terrified the Bodhisattva.

Initially, when the Mara King learned that the Bodhisattva was about to achieve perfect enlightenment, his attempts to seduce and distract him failed. Distraught and helpless, he assembled the various hosts of spirits and arrayed his demonic army; he marshaled his troops and raised his banners, intending to intimidate the Bodhisattva.

Thereupon wind and rain poured down, thunder and lightning shrouded the world in darkness; fires were set ablaze with soaring smoke, while sand was flung and stones were hurled; they prepared every kind of spear and shield, and brought to the utmost the use of bowstrings and arrows.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva entered the samādhi of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), whereby all his weapons were transformed into lotus flowers.
The army of Māra was struck with terror and fled in disarray.
Not far from that spot are two stūpas, erected by Śakra and Brahmā.
To the north of the gate outside the Bodhi tree is the Mahābodhi Saṃghārāma, which was originally established by King Siṃhala.

It consists of six courtyards and three-storied pavilions; its surrounding walls are thirty to forty *zhang* high, representing the pinnacle of artisanal skill and the ultimate expression of decorative painting.
As for the Buddha images, they are cast in gold and silver; all their adornments are inlaid with precious gems.
The various stūpas are high, vast, and exquisitely decorated, containing the relics of the Tathāgata within; these bone relics are as large as the joints of a finger.
It is lustrous, fresh white, and translucent both within and without.
Its flesh-relics are like large pearls, colored with a reddish-purple tint.

Every year, on the day the moon is full during the month of the Tathāgata’s Great Miraculous Transformation—namely the thirtieth day of the twelfth month in India, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the first month here—it is displayed to the public.
At this time, there were occasions when light was emitted or flowers rained down.

The monastic community numbered fewer than a thousand, who studied the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and the Sthavira schools; their discipline was pure and solemn, and their observance of the precepts was upright and luminous.
In the past, in the kingdom of Siṃhala in the southern sea, its king was naturally endowed with pure faith in the Buddha-dharma.

He had a cousin who had left the household life; desiring to visit the sacred traces of the Buddha, he traveled far to India and stayed in various monasteries, where everyone treated him with contempt as a mere man from the borderlands.
Thereupon, he returned to his native country; the king went out in person from afar to welcome him, while the śramaṇa was so overcome with grief and distress that he seemed unable to speak.
The king said, "What burden do you carry that you are so deeply sorrowful?"
The śramaṇa said:

"Relying upon the majesty of your kingdom, I have traveled abroad to seek the Way; wandering through foreign lands, I have endured both cold and heat, frequently encountered insults, and been subjected to derision in speech."
