"Bearing such grief and shame, how could one find a joyful heart?
He asked, "What do you mean by this?"
He said:

"I truly wish that Your Majesty would set your mind upon the field of merit; by establishing monasteries throughout India, you will both commemorate sacred sites and enjoy a lofty reputation. This merit shall support your late majesty, and its grace shall extend to your descendants."
He said, "This matter is most excellent; why did I hear of it so late?
Thereupon, he presented the treasures of his kingdom to the King of India.
Having received the tribute, the King, out of a sense of benevolence toward those from afar, said to the envoy:
"What shall I now bring as a return gift for your mission?
The envoy replied:
"King Siṃhala bows his head to the Great Auspicious King of India!

Your majestic power resounds afar and your benevolent grace extends to distant lands. A śramaṇa from these lower realms, admiring your reputation and longing for your transformation, dared to travel to this superior kingdom to pay homage at the sacred sites. Finding no lodging within the monasteries and reaching the utmost exhaustion, he has returned home with deep shame."

Secretly planning for the distant future and establishing a model for posterity, he constructed this monastery in India so that wandering mendicants from afar might find a place to rest their burdens; thus, the two countries may share mutual joy and the flow of envoys may never cease.
The King said, "The Tathāgata has transformed beings through his hidden influence, yet his enduring legacy remains here; as for these sites of sacred traces, you may choose whichever one you prefer.
The messenger took his leave and reported this back to the King. The ministers prostrated themselves in celebration and subsequently assembled all the śramaṇas to deliberate upon the construction.
The śramaṇa said:
"As for the Bodhi tree, all Buddhas of the past and future have realized holiness beneath it; examining various dissenting views, none surpass this plan.
Thereupon, he renounced the kingdom's treasures and built this monastery, providing offerings through the monks of that country, and then engraved a record upon copper, saying:
"Indeed, universal charity without partiality is the ultimate teaching of the Buddhas;
the wise salvation of those with whom one has affinity is the clear instruction of the former sages.

Now I, this humble youth, grandly inherit the royal enterprise and accordingly establish a *vihāra* to commemorate these sacred traces, so that merit may assist my ancestors and grace may be extended to the common people."
"Only the monks of our kingdom shall attain autonomy, and the local people shall likewise follow the precedents of the monks.
This tradition shall be transmitted to future generations, enduring forever without end.
For this reason, the monasteries here are mostly occupied by monks from Siṃhala (Sri Lanka).
More than ten *li* to the south of the Bodhi tree, sacred sites lie adjacent to one another, making it difficult to enumerate them all.

Every year, when the monks conclude their summer retreat (*varṣā*), hundreds of thousands of monastics and laypeople from the four quarters come for seven days and seven nights, carrying incense and flowers and playing music, to travel throughout the grove to pay homage and make offerings.

The Indian monastics, relying on the holy teachings of the Buddha, all enter the two-month summer retreat (*varṣā*) on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, which corresponds here to the sixteenth day of the fifth lunar month;
they conclude the two-month summer retreat on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, which corresponds here to the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month.
The names of the months in India are established according to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*); they have remained unchanged from antiquity to the present and do not differ across various schools.

It is simply because local dialects have not been harmonized and errors occurred during transmission and translation that the calculation of time and months has led to such discrepancies. Therefore, the retreat (*varṣā*) begins on the sixteenth day of the fourth month and concludes on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
