Draviḍa (Da-luo-pi-tuo) 17. Mahārāṣṭra (Mo-luo-ju-tuo) Ilāṃvarta (I-lan-na-po-fa-duo): This country is more than three thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom lies to the north, bordering the Gaṅgā River; it is more than twenty li in circuit.
Crops grow in abundance, and flowers and fruits are plentiful.
The climate is mild and pleasant, and the local customs are simple and honest.
There are more than ten monasteries with over four thousand monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
There are more than twenty deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
Recently, a neighboring king deposed his own sovereign and offered the capital city as a gift to the assembly of monks.
Within this city, he constructed two monasteries, each housing nearly a thousand monks, both of whom study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna teachings.

Beside the great city, overlooking the Gaṅgā River, lies Mount Ilāṃtaka; it exhales and inhales mists and clouds, obscuring both sun and moon. From ancient times to the present, seers and sages have followed one another to dwell there in spiritual retreat; today, a deva temple still adheres to their traditional practices.
In the past, the Tathāgata also resided here, extensively expounding the sublime Dharma for the sake of devas and humans.
To the south of the great city is a stūpa, where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for three months.
Beside it are the sites where the three past Buddhas sat and performed their walking meditations.
Not far to the west of where those three Buddhas walked is a stūpa; this is the site of Śrutas-tavati-koṭi (translated into Chinese as Wén Èrbǎiyì).
The old translation calls him "Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa," which is erroneous; it refers to the birthplace of this bhikṣu.

Formerly, there was a householder in this city who was noble, eminent, and immensely wealthy. When he finally had a successor, anyone who reported the news was immediately granted two hundred koṭis of gold coins; consequently, the son was named Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa ("Hearing Two Hundred Koṭis").
By the time he reached maturity, he had never set foot upon the ground; consequently, the hair on the soles of his feet was over a foot long, lustrous, fine, and soft, with a color like refined gold.

Cherishing this son, he provided him with every kind of plaything and luxury. From his own residence to the Snowy Mountains, way-stations were linked at every corner and servants lined the roads. Whenever a rare medicine was required, word would be passed along from one station to the next until it was delivered; it never took more than a moment. Such was his wealth and power.
The World-Honored One, knowing that the roots of goodness [in him] were about to sprout, commanded Maudgalyāyana to go and transform him.
Having arrived at the gate, he had no means to announce himself.
The householder worshipped the sun deity at his domestic shrine, bowing toward the east every morning.
At that time, by means of his supernormal powers, the Venerable One descended from the solar disk and stood before him.
The son of the elder suspected him to be the Sun God; having offered him fragrant rice, he returned home, and the fragrance of that rice pervaded the entire city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, King Bimbisāra, astonished by its extraordinary scent, ordered messengers to investigate. They discovered that it had been brought from the elder’s house by Maudgalyāyana of the Veṇuvana Monastery. Upon learning that the elder’s son possessed such a marvelous quality, the king then sent for him.
The elder received the command and pondered how he might proceed with ease:
to travel by boat, rowing through the waves, would entail the peril of wind and billows;
to ride in a carriage or upon an elephant, he feared the calamity of stumbling or falling.

Thereupon, from his own residence to the city of Rājagṛha, he dug a canal for irrigation, filling it with mustard seeds so that the boat could float steadily; then, using a long rope, he drew it along.
Upon arriving at Rājagṛha, he first paid homage to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said to him:
“King Bimbisāra has sent a messenger to summon you; his purpose is nothing other than a desire to see the hair on your feet.”
"If Your Majesty wishes to see him, he ought to sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
To extend one's feet toward the King is, by the laws of the land, punishable by death.
Having received these instructions, the son of the elder went and was ushered into the court for an audience.
When the king wished to examine the hair, he sat cross-legged; the king, appreciating his decorum, held him in especially high esteem.
Having returned home, he went back to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma and offered instruction; having heard it, he was moved to realization and immediately went forth from the household life.
Thereupon, he practiced with diligent effort, seeking the realization of the fruits of the path; he practiced walking meditation without ceasing until his feet began to bleed.
The World-Honored One asked,
"Good son, when you were living at home, did you know how to play the lute?
He replied:
"I understand.
"If that is so, let me provide an analogy for this.

If the strings are too tight, the sounds will not accord with the rhythm; if the strings are too loose, the tones will not be harmonious or elegant. Only when they are neither too tight nor too loose will the sound be in harmony."
"It is the same for those who practice cultivation:
if one is too hurried, the body becomes exhausted and the mind weary; if one is too relaxed, the emotions become loose and the will indolent.
Following the Buddha’s instruction and carrying it out with diligence, before long, he attained the realization of the fruit.

To the west of the kingdom, south of the Ganges River, reaching the Small Solitary Mountain, where steep peaks rise in layered heights, the Buddha formerly observed the three-month rains retreat here and subdued the yakṣa Bakula.

Beneath a cliff on the southeastern side of the mountain, upon a large rock, there are the footprints of the Buddha, indented into the stone by more than one inch; they are five chi and two cun long and two chi and one cun wide, and a stūpa has been erected above them.
Next, upon a stone to the south, there is a mark where the Buddha placed a kuṇḍika—that is, a water flask (formerly called *junchi*, which is a corruption and abbreviation).
The trace is over an inch deep and features an eight-petaled floral design.

Not far to the southeast of where the Buddha sat, there are the footprints of the yakṣa Bakula, measuring five or six inches in length, seven or eight inches in width, and less than two inches in depth.
Behind the Yakṣa’s footprint is a stone image of a seated Buddha, six or seven feet in height.
Not far to the west is the place where the Buddha walked.
On the summit of this mountain is the old dwelling of a Yakṣa.
To the north of this is a footprint of the Buddha, one foot eight inches long and over six inches wide, with a depth of about half an inch; atop this footprint stands a stūpa.
In the past, the Tathāgata subdued a yakṣa, commanding him not to kill humans or eat their flesh; the yakṣa respectfully accepted the Buddha’s precepts and later attained rebirth in heaven.
To the west of here are six or seven hot springs, the water of which is extremely hot.
In the great mountain forests on the southern border of the kingdom, there are many wild elephants of immense stature.
From here, traveling eastward along the southern bank of the Ganges for more than three hundred li, one reaches the kingdom of Campā within the borders of India.
The country of Campā is over four thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the country lies with its northern side facing the Gaṅgā River and is over forty *li* in circuit.
The soil is low and damp, and the cultivation of crops is abundant.
The climate is warm and humid, and the customs are simple and honest.
There are several dozen monasteries, many of which are in ruins; there are over two hundred monks who study the teachings of the Hinayana.
There are more than twenty deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
The city walls are constructed of brick, reaching several *zhang* in height; their foundations are lofty and steep, and the battlements for repelling enemies are high and formidable.
In the past, at the beginning of the kalpa, when human beings first emerged, they dwelt in the wilds and lived in caves, as they were not yet acquainted with palatial dwellings.
Later, a celestial maiden descended among men; she went to the Ganges River to bathe and adorn herself, and having been moved by its spiritual power, she conceived and gave birth to four sons.

Jambudvīpa was divided, with each region asserting its own domain; capitals were established and cities built, boundaries were demarcated, and territories were defined. This was the capital of the son’s kingdom, marking the beginning of all the cities in Jambudvīpa.

One hundred and forty or fifty *li* to the east of the city, south of the Gaṅgā River, there is a solitary island surrounded by water. Its cliffs and peaks are lofty and steep, and upon it stands a deva temple where the deity manifests many miraculous responses.

Caves were excavated from the cliffs to serve as chambers, and water was channeled to form ponds; with flowering groves, rare trees, massive boulders, and perilous peaks, this became the dwelling place of those possessing both benevolence and wisdom, such that visitors would forget to return home.
In the mountain forests along the southern border of the kingdom, thousands of wild elephants and fierce beasts roam in herds.
Traveling east from here for more than four hundred li, one reaches the country of Kajangala (also known locally as Kajangera).
Within the borders of Central India lies the kingdom of Kajuṅghira. The kingdom of Kajuṅghira is over two thousand li in circuit.
The land is damp and the soil is fertile, yielding abundant crops; the climate is warm, and the customs are mild.
They esteem high talent and honor learning and the arts.
There are six or seven monasteries with more than three hundred monks.
There are ten deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.

For several hundred years, the royal lineage has been extinct, and the kingdom has been subject to neighboring states; consequently, the city walls have fallen into ruin, and most people reside in villages and towns.

Thus, when King Śīlāditya traveled through Eastern India, he constructed a palace here to administer state affairs; upon his arrival, he would thatch it with straw, and upon his departure, he would set fire to it and burn it down.
In the southern borders of the kingdom, wild elephants abound.

Not far from the northern border, near the Gaṅgā River, there is a great high terrace constructed by piling up bricks and stones. Its foundations are vast and towering, adorned with exquisite carvings; on all its sides, images of various sages are engraved, with the forms of the Buddha and the devas depicted separately.
From here, crossing the Gaṅgā River to the east and traveling more than six hundred li, he arrived at the kingdom of Puṇḍravardhana, within the borders of Central India.
The kingdom of Puṇḍravardhana is more than four thousand li in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over thirty li in circuit.
Its inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, with ponds, pavilions, flowers, and groves interspersed here and there.
The soil is low and damp, yet the crops grow in great abundance.

The *pānasa* fruit is both abundant and precious; it is as large as a winter melon and turns yellowish-red when ripe. When split open, there are several dozen small fruits inside, each about the size of a crane's egg. Breaking these further reveals a yellowish-red juice that is sweet and delicious in taste.
Some are on the branches of trees, like clusters of fruits forming; others are at the roots of trees, like *fuling* fungi in the soil.
The seasons are harmonious and pleasant, and the local customs favor learning.
There are more than twenty monasteries with over three thousand monks, who study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles concurrently.
There are one hundred deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together; the naked Nirgranthas are particularly numerous among them.
More than twenty li to the west of the city is the Vatsīputra Monastery.
Its courtyards and halls are spacious and grand, and its terraces and pavilions are lofty and high.
There are more than seven hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna; many renowned and learned monks from the regions of East India reside here.
Not far from its side is a stūpa built by King Aśoka.
This is the place where, in the past, the Tathāgata stayed for three months to preach the Dharma for devas and humans; on fast days, it occasionally emits a brilliant light.
Beside it are the sites where four Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation.

Not far from here is another vihāra containing an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; its divine discernment leaves nothing hidden, and its spiritual responses are attested by signs, such that people from near and far abstain from grain and offer prayers there.
From here, traveling east for more than nine hundred *li* and crossing a great river, one arrives at the kingdom of Kāmarūpa, within the borders of East India.
The kingdom of Kāmarūpa is over ten thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over thirty li in circuit.
The soil is damp and rich with springs, and crops are sown according to the seasons.
Although trees bearing *pānasa* (jackfruit) and *nālikera* (coconut) fruits are numerous, they are nonetheless exceedingly precious.
Rivers, lakes, and ponds wind through and surround its cities and towns.
The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs are simple and honest.
The people are short of stature and their complexions are dark.
Their language differs slightly from that of Central India.
By nature they are extremely fierce and violent, yet they are dedicated to intensive study.
They worship celestial deities and do not believe in the Buddha-dharma.
Therefore, from the time the Buddha appeared until the present day, no monasteries have yet been established nor any monks assembled there.
Those among the faithful who possess pure belief can do nothing but think of it in secret.
There are several hundred deva temples and tens of thousands of followers of heterodox paths.

The present king is a descendant of the lineage of Nārāyaṇa Deva and belongs to the Brāhmaṇa caste; his name is Vāsukalavarman (translated into Chinese as Rìzhòu, "Sun-Scion"), and he is titled Kumāra (translated into Chinese as Tóngzǐ, "Child").
Having occupied this territory, they have ruled for generations, and by the time of the current king, a thousand generations have passed.

The sovereign is fond of learning, and the masses follow his transformation; men of high talent from distant lands come as guests, admiring his righteousness. Although they do not purely believe in the Buddha-dharma, they nevertheless revere and honor learned śramaṇas.

Initially, he heard that there was a śramaṇa from the country of Cīna residing at the Nālandā Monastery in Magadha, who had come from afar to study the profound teachings of the Buddha; though he went back and forth with earnest entreaties two or three times, the man did not accept his invitation.
At that time, the master Śīlabhadra said:
"To repay the Buddha’s kindness, one must propagate the True Dharma; you, my son, should go forth and do not let the long journey deter you."

"King Kumāra has traditionally followed the non-Buddhist paths throughout his reign; that he now invites śramaṇas is a most auspicious thing. By this means, he shall change his course, and the resulting benefit will be vast and far-reaching.

In the past, you conceived a magnanimous mind and made a great vow, wishing to travel alone to foreign lands and sacrifice your life to seek the Dharma for the universal salvation of all sentient beings—how could this concern merely your own native land?"

You should forget gain and loss, and not be constrained by honor or disgrace; propagate the holy teachings and guide the deluded masses, putting others' welfare before your own person and forgetting your reputation to spread the Dharma.
Thereupon, as he could not decline the invitation, he set out with the envoy and had an audience with him.
King Kumāra said:
"Although I am without talent, I have always admired those of lofty learning. Having heard of your noble reputation, I venture to extend this invitation."
He replied, "I am of little ability and narrow wisdom; I have presumptuously troubled Your Majesty’s hearing.
King Kumāra said:
"Excellent! You cherish the Dharma and delight in learning; regarding your own person as if it were floating on water, you have braved perilous obstacles to travel far to a foreign land.
This is precisely how the King’s transformation spreads, and how the national ethos prizes scholarship."

"I have long heard that in many kingdoms of India there are songs praising the 'Qinwang Po-zhen-le' (The King of Qin’s Victory) of the Great Cīna country; could this be the home country of the Venerable One?"
He replied, "Indeed;
this song praises the virtue of our sovereign.
King Kumāra said:

"I did not expect that you, Great Virtue, would be a native of this land. I have long admired its customs and culture, gazing toward the east for a great while; yet, because the mountains, rivers, and roads were so obstructed, there was no way for me to come here myself."

He replied, "The sagely virtue of our Great Lord reaches far and wide, and his benevolent transformation extends to distant lands; many from foreign customs and remote regions prostrate themselves at the palace gate and declare themselves subjects.
King Kumāra said:
"Under such a sovereign who covers and sustains all, my heart hopes for tribute from the various states.

Now King Śīlāditya is in the kingdom of Kajuṅghira; he intends to perform a great act of charity (*mahādāna*) to cultivate merit and wisdom, and there is no śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa among the learned in the five regions of India who has not been summoned."
"Now I have sent an envoy to invite you; I hope you will go with me.
Thereupon, he departed.

This country has mountain ridges connected to its eastern borders and lacks a large capital city; its territory borders the Southwest Barbarians (Sannan Yi), and thus its people resemble the Man and Liao tribes.

Upon detailed inquiry regarding the local customs, it was found that the journey would take about two months to reach the southwestern borders of Shu; however, the mountains and rivers were perilous and obstructed, the mountain ranges were shrouded in pestilential vapors, and venomous snakes and poisonous plants caused extreme harm.
In the southeastern wilds of this country, herds of wild elephants cause havoc; consequently, elephant troops are particularly numerous within this kingdom.
Traveling south from here for one thousand two hundred or three hundred li, one arrives at the country of Samataṭa, which lies within the borders of East India.
The country of Samataṭa is more than three thousand *li* in circuit.
Bordering the great ocean, its terrain is low-lying and damp.
The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty *li* in circuit.
Cultivation and planting flourish, and flowers and fruits grow in profusion.
The seasons are harmonious and the customs are compliant.

The people are by nature stern and fierce; they are short in stature and dark in complexion. They are fond of learning and diligent in their efforts, believing in both heterodox and orthodox teachings.
There are more than thirty monasteries with over two thousand monks, all of whom follow and study the teachings of the Sthavira school.
There are one hundred deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together; among them, the naked Nirgranthas are particularly numerous.
Not far from the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka.
In the past, the Tathāgata preached the profound and wondrous Dharma here for seven days for the sake of devas and humans.
Beside it are the sites where four Buddhas sat and performed walking meditations.

Not far from here, within a monastery, there is a statue of the Buddha made of green jade; it is eight feet high, its marks and signs are perfectly complete, and it manifests spiritual responses from time to time.
From here, in the mountains and valleys along the northeastern coast of the great ocean, lies the country of Śrīkṣetra.
Next, at the southeastern corner of the great ocean, is the country of Kāmarūpa.
Next to the east is the country of Drābhaṭi;
next to the east is the country of Īśānapura;
next to the east is the country of Mahācampā, which is here called Lin-yi.
Next, to the southwest, there is the kingdom of Yamunā.

In these six kingdoms, the mountains, rivers, and roads are so obstructed that one does not enter their territories; nevertheless, their customs and the nature of their lands can be known through reports.
Traveling westward from the kingdom of Samataṭa for over nine hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Tâmralipti, which lies within the borders of East India.
The kingdom of Tâmralipti is approximately fourteen or fifteen hundred li in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over ten li in circuit.
Bordering the edge of the sea, the land is low-lying and damp.
Crops are sown according to the seasons, and flowers and fruits grow in abundance.
The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are impetuous and fierce.
By nature, the people are bold and courageous, placing equal faith in both heterodoxy and orthodoxy.
There are more than ten monasteries with over a thousand monks.
There are more than fifty deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
Situated at a coastal corner where land and sea routes converge, rare treasures and exotic gems are largely gathered in this country; thus, its people are for the most part prosperous and wealthy.
Beside the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka;
adjacent to it are the sites containing the traces of the sitting and walking meditations of the four past Buddhas.
From here, traveling northwest for more than seven hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Karṇasuvarṇa, within the borders of East India.
The kingdom of Karṇasuvarṇa is four thousand four or five hundred li in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty li in circuit.
Its inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and their households are wealthy and well-provided.
The soil is low and damp; crops are sown according to the seasons, various flowers flourish profusely, and rare fruits grow in abundance.
The climate is harmonious and pleasant, and the local customs are pure and gentle.
The people are fond of learning and the arts, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings.
There are more than ten monasteries with over two thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
There are more than fifty deva temples, and followers of heterodox paths are truly numerous.
Separately, there are three monasteries that do not consume milk or curd, adhering to the bequeathed instructions of Devadatta.
Beside the great city was the Lokottaravādin Saṃghārāma (translated into Chinese as Chini).
Its courtyards and halls were spacious and grand, and its terraces and pavilions were lofty and imposing.

The men of high talent and profound learning, those of keen intelligence and renown within the kingdom, all gathered there; they admonished one another and mutually perfected their practice, refining themselves in the Way and its Virtue.

Formerly, when this country had not yet placed its faith in the Buddha-dharma, there was a non-Buddhist from South India who arrived in this city. He had his abdomen bound with copper plates and carried a bright torch upon his head; leaning on a staff, he strode with great confidence and beat the drum of debate, seeking an opportunity for discussion.
Or someone might ask:
"What is the difference between the head and the belly?
He replied:
"I have studied many arts and possess many skills; I fear my belly might burst.
It is out of compassion for those who are ignorant and deluded that I carry this lamp.
After ten days had passed, no one came to inquire after him; though he sought out the eminent and the wise, there was no extraordinary person to be found.
The King said,
"Within these borders, are there no men of wisdom and sagacity?
To fail to answer the guest's challenge would be a profound disgrace to the state."
"It would be fitting to seek him out further and inquire among those dwelling in seclusion.
Someone said:

"In the Great Forest there is an extraordinary man who calls himself a śramaṇa. He applies himself strenuously to these tasks and has long since retired to live in quietude; were it not for one who embodies the Dharma and accords with virtue, how could he be such as this?"
When the king heard this, he went in person to invite him.
The śramaṇa replied, "I am a man from South India who has come here as a traveler; my learning is shallow, and I fear I may fail to do justice to what I have heard."
Daring to accept your command, I shall no longer decline.
My arguments have been without fault; I request that you establish a monastery to assemble monks and gloriously propagate the Buddha-dharma.
The King said,
"I have respectfully heard this and shall not dare forget your virtue.
Having accepted the invitation, the śramaṇa proceeded to the site of the debate.
Thereupon, the non-Buddhist recited the fundamental tenets of his school, consisting of more than thirty thousand words.
Their meaning was profound and their phrasing concise; they encompassed all names and characteristics, and cast a net over all that can be seen and heard.

Upon hearing it once, the śramaṇa examined it thoroughly; his words and meanings were without error, and he explained it with eloquence using only a few hundred words. He then inquired about its fundamental tenets.
The non-Buddhist was left speechless and exhausted in reasoning, unable to offer a reply.
Having had his reputation shattered, he withdrew in shame.
The King, deeply revering his virtue, established this monastery; from that time onward, the teachings of the Dharma were propagated.
Not far from the side of the monastery is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; it was here in the past that the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for seven days to provide guidance and instruction.
Beside it is a monastery, the site where the traces of the sitting and walking meditation of the four past Buddhas remain.
There are several stūpas, all built by King Aśoka at places where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma.
From here, traveling southwest for more than seven hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Oḍra, within the borders of East India.
The kingdom of Oḍra is more than seven thousand li in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty li in circuit.

The soil is rich and fertile, and the crops grow in abundance. All varieties of fruit are considerably larger than those found in other countries, and its exotic grasses and famous flowers are difficult to describe in full.
The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are fierce and violent.
The people are stalwart in appearance, with dark and sallow complexions.
Their speech and intonation differ from those of Central India.

They are fond of learning and tireless in their studies; many believe in the Buddha-dharma. There are over one hundred monasteries with more than ten thousand monks, all of whom study and practice the teachings of the Mahayana.
There are fifty deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
There are more than ten stūpas in total, all of which mark places where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma and were constructed by King Aśoka.

In the great mountains on the southwestern border of the kingdom, there is the Puṣpagiri Monastery; its stone stūpas are exceedingly miraculous, for on fast days they occasionally emit a brilliant light.
Therefore, those of pure faith from both near and far gathered together, holding exquisite flower-canopies and vying with one another to perform offerings.
Beneath the dew-receiving basin and atop the inverted-bowl shape, they placed the shafts of the flower-canopies, and they remained fixed in place as if a magnet were attracting a needle.
To the northwest of this mountain, within a monastery, there is a stūpa; its particulars are the same as those mentioned previously.
These two stūpas were erected by spirits and ghosts, and their miraculous wonders are such as these.
On the southeastern border of the kingdom, bordering the great ocean, lies the city of Caritra (translated into Chinese as Chūfāng, "Setting Out").
It is twenty-odd *li* in circuit and serves as a resting place for merchants traveling by sea and travelers from distant lands who come and go.
The city is solid and lofty, abounding in various rare treasures.
Outside the city, there are five monasteries arranged in succession; their pavilions and towers are towering, and the sacred images are exquisitely crafted.

Traveling south for more than twenty thousand *li* from this country, one reaches Siṃhala. On a clear night, looking afar, one can see the radiance of the precious jewels atop the Buddha-tooth stūpa of that kingdom.
It was as bright as a torch suspended in the air.
From here, traveling southwest through a great forest for more than twelve hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Koṅgoda, within the borders of East India.
The Kingdom of Koṅ-yü-to (Koṅgoda) is over one thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city is over twenty *li* in circuit.
Situated near the edge of the sea, it is characterized by undulating hills and low-lying terrain; the soil is damp and moist, and crops are sown according to the seasons.
The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are bold and fierce.
Their stature is imposing, and their complexion is dark.
They possess a rudimentary sense of propriety and righteousness, and are not particularly prone to deceit.
As for their written script, it is the same as that of Central India; however, their spoken language and literary style differ considerably.
They revere non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas) and do not believe in the Buddha-dharma.
There are more than a hundred deva temples with over ten thousand followers of heterodox paths.

Within the borders of the kingdom are several dozen small cities that border mountain ridges and occupy strategic points at sea crossings; these cities are both fortified and steep, and their soldiers are bold and courageous. Their prestige dominates the neighboring regions, such that no powerful enemy exists.
The country borders the seacoast and abounds in rare treasures; conch shells, pearls, and gems serve as its currency.
It produces large dark-blue elephants capable of carrying riders to great distances.

From here, proceeding southwest into a vast wilderness of deep forests and massive trees that pierce the sky and obscure the sun, one travels one thousand four or five hundred *li* to reach the kingdom of Karṇasuvarṇa, within the borders of South India.
The Kingdom of Kāmarūpa: The kingdom of Kāmarūpa is more than five thousand *li* in circuit.
Its capital city is over twenty *li* in circuit.
Crops are sown according to the seasons, and flowers and fruits abound; forests and marshes stretch continuously for several hundred *li*.
It produces blue wild elephants, which are regarded as rare wonders by neighboring countries.
The climate is hot and the customs are impetuous; the people are generally fierce and unruly by nature, yet they place great store in integrity and honor.
The language is light and agile, the tonal modulations are pure and correct, and the style of its diction differs somewhat from that of Central India.

Few believe in the True Dharma, while most follow non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas). There are more than ten monasteries with over five hundred monks, who study the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school.
There are more than a hundred deva temples, and followers of heterodox paths are very numerous; most of them belong to the sect of the Nirgranthas.

In former times, when the kingdom of Kalinga was at its height, the populace was so dense that people jostled shoulder to shoulder and axle to axle, and their raised sleeves formed a continuous canopy.

There was a rishi possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) who dwelt upon a cliff to cultivate his essential nature. Whenever anyone insulted or provoked him, he would lose his supernatural powers and, employing malevolent incantations, brought ruin upon the people of the land, leaving no survivors among the young or old, and causing both the wise and the foolish to perish.
Human habitation had been severed for many years; although people have gradually migrated here, they have not yet filled the area, and thus the population of this country remains small today.
Not far to the south of the city is a stūpa over one hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka.
Beside it are the sites where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation.

At the northern frontier of the kingdom, atop a great mountain ridge, there is a stone stūpa over one hundred feet high; this is where a Pratyekabuddha entered parinirvāṇa during the kalpa when the human lifespan was immeasurable.
From here, traveling northwest through mountains and forests for over one thousand eight hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Kośala within the borders of India.
The kingdom of Kośala is over six thousand li in circuit; its frontiers are surrounded by mountain ridges, and forests and marshes extend continuously across the land.
The capital city of the kingdom is over forty li in circuit.
The soil is rich and fertile, and the products of the land are abundant.
Villages and towns face one another, and the households are prosperous and well-off.
Their stature is imposing and their complexion is dark.
Their customs are stern and fierce, and their nature is courageous and intense.
They believe in both heterodoxy and orthodoxy, and they are highly proficient in learning and the arts.
The king is a Kṣatriya.
He reveres and honors the Buddha-dharma, and his benevolence is profound and far-reaching.
There are more than one hundred monasteries with fewer than ten thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna.
There are more than seventy deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
Not far to the south of the city is an old monastery, beside which stands a stūpa built by King Aśoka.
In the past, the Tathāgata once manifested great supernormal powers at this very spot to subdue the non-Buddhists.
Later, when the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna resided in this monastery, the king of this land was named Śatavāhana (translated into Chinese as Yǐnzhèng, "Leading the Right").
They held Nāgārjuna in high esteem and surrounded his dwelling with a protective guard.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Āryadeva arrived from Siṃhala Island seeking to debate;
he said to the gatekeeper, "Please announce my arrival."
The gatekeeper then reported this.
Nāgārjuna, who already knew his reputation well, filled his alms bowl with water and commanded his disciple, saying:
"Take this water and show it to that Deva."
When Deva saw the water, he silently dropped a needle into it.
The disciple returned with the bowl, filled with doubt.
Nāgārjuna said:
"What words did he use?
He replied, "He remained silent and said nothing; he merely cast a needle into the water."
Nāgārjuna said:
"How wise is such a man! To know the subtle movements of events is divine;
to perceive the minute is the mark of one nearly equal to a sage. With such profound virtue as this, he ought to be summoned to enter at once."
He replied: "What do you mean?
Is it this 'subtle eloquence that is beyond words'?"

He said: "As for water, it conforms to the squareness or roundness of its vessel and follows the clarity or turbidity of its surroundings; it spreads everywhere without interval, and its profound stillness is unfathomable.
To show it when full is to compare it to the pervasive wisdom of one who has mastered the learning."
He then threw in a needle and thus reached the very limit [of the water].
"This is no ordinary man; you should summon him here at once.
Thus, the majestic bearing of Nāgārjuna was so awe-inspiring that all who spoke with him bowed their heads in submission.

Deva had long admired his virtuous reputation and had hoped for an opportunity to seek instruction; now that he was about to receive teachings, he first exercised his intellectual acumen. Fearing his majestic dignity, he ascended the hall and sat to one side, discussing profound mysteries throughout the day with refined and lofty diction and meaning.
Nāgārjuna said:

"Your learning surpasses the world and your subtle eloquence outshines those who came before. I am merely old and decrepit; that I have encountered such a brilliant talent is truly like finding a vessel to which one may entrust the contents of a jar, ensuring that the lamp of the Dharma is transmitted without interruption. It is upon such a person as you that the propagation of the teachings relies."
"I am fortunate to have been granted this front-row seat to engage in refined discourse upon the profound mysteries.

Upon hearing these words, Deva felt a sense of self-assurance within his heart; intending to open the treasury of doctrine, he first roamed the garden of debate, raising the opening points of his argument and looking up to question the meaning of the principles.

Suddenly beholding his majestic countenance, [Nāgārjuna] was struck speechless and silenced; he withdrew from his seat to take responsibility for his own faults and then requested to receive instruction.
Nāgārjuna said, "Sit down again;
I shall now impart to you the ultimate, wondrous principle, the sincere teaching of the Dharma King."
Devaputra prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and, with single-minded devotion, took refuge, saying:
"From this day forward, I shall respectfully obey your instructions.

The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna was highly skilled in the arts of medicine; by ingesting medicinal elixirs to sustain life, he lived for several hundred years, yet his will and appearance showed no signs of decline.
Having obtained the wondrous medicine, King Yinzheng lived for several hundred years.
The king had a young son who said to his mother,
"When shall I succeed to the royal throne?"
The mother said,
"Judging by the present circumstances, there is no certainty.
Your father the King has already lived for several hundred years, and his sons and grandsons who have reached old age and passed away are indeed many."
All of this is due to the empowerment of Nāgārjuna’s merit and the efficacy of his medicinal arts.
Once the Bodhisattva has entered into parinirvāṇa, the King will surely pass away.
Indeed, the wisdom of the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna is vast and profound, and his compassion is deep; he provides for all living beings, regarding even his own body and life as if they were discarded.
"You should go there and attempt to beg for his head; if you succeed in this endeavor, you shall surely fulfill your wish.
The prince respectfully obeyed his mother’s command and went to the monastery; the gatekeeper, filled with reverence and trepidation, allowed him to enter.
At that time, while the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna was engaged in walking meditation and reciting the scriptures, he suddenly saw the prince.
He stood still and said to him, "For what reason have you come to this monastery tonight? Why do you appear so distressed and fearful, arriving here in such haste?"
He replied,

"I have inherited the remaining discourses of my compassionate mother, and when she spoke of those who practice renunciation, she held that for all living beings, whose lives are a precious treasure, there is no scriptural maxim that permits one to lightly abandon the retribution-body to bestow it upon those driven by desire."
My compassionate mother said:

"It is not so. From the time the Sugatas of the ten directions and the Tathāgatas of the three periods first resolved their minds until they attained the fruit of enlightenment, they diligently sought the Buddha-way and practiced precepts and patience."

Some threw themselves to feed predatory beasts; some cut their own flesh to save a dove; King Candraprabha gave his head to a Brahmin; and King Maitrībala drank his own blood for a hungry yakṣa. Instances such as these are too numerous to be fully enumerated.
"Seeking those who have attained prior awakening—what age has not produced such persons?
Now, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna is devoted to this lofty resolve; I have a need for a human head, yet though I have sought one for many years, none have ever offered it."
If you were to commit violent robbery and murder, the accumulation of sin would be even greater; you would cruelly harm the innocent, and your defiled virtue would become manifest to all.

Now, as a Bodhisattva who cultivates the holy path and looks toward the fruit of Buddhahood in the distant future, your compassion extends to all sentient beings and your benefits reach the infinite. You regard life as light as a floating gossamer and your body as worthless as rotten wood. Do not violate your original vow, but graciously grant this request!
Nāgārjuna said: "Yes, these words are indeed true! I seek the holy fruit of Buddhahood;

I study the Buddha’s ability to renounce. This body is like an echo, this body is like a bubble; it wanders through the four modes of birth and comes and goes among the six realms of existence. Having long ago entered into a great vow, I do not oppose the desires of sentient beings."
However, Prince!
There is one thing that cannot be; what will you do about it?
Once my life has ended and your father has also passed away, considering this matter, who will be able to save us?

Nāgārjuna paced back and forth, looking about for something to end his life; he used dry *mārga* grass to sever his own neck, which was like being cut by a sharp sword, so that his body and head were separated from one another.
Upon seeing this, the prince fled in terror.
The gatekeeper reported the matter in full detail from beginning to end; when the king heard it, he was moved by grief and subsequently passed away as well.
More than three hundred li to the southwest of the capital, one reaches Mount Balaramagiri (translated into Chinese as "Black Bee").
It rises prominently and loftily, with steep and perilous peaks and cliffs; being devoid of precipices or valleys, it appears as if it were a single, solid rock.
King Udayana excavated this mountain for the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna and established a monastery there.
Several tens of li from the mountain, he carved out a tunnel; directly beneath the mountain, he excavated upward, chiseling away the rock.

Within it were long corridors with eaves for walking, lofty terraces, and multi-storied pavilions; each pavilion had five stories, and each story contained four courtyards, where vihāras were constructed side by side. In each, a golden image was cast, equal in size to the body of the Buddha, its exquisite craftsmanship reaching the pinnacle of artistry. All other adornments were embellished solely with gold and precious gems.
From the high peaks of the mountain, flying springs cascade down, flowing around the multi-storied pavilions and winding through the corridors and porticos.
Sparse windows open outward like cavities, while bright light illuminates the central halls.
Initially, when King Yingzheng founded this monastery, his human resources were exhausted and his treasuries were empty; yet the work was still not half-finished, leaving him deeply distressed.
Nāgārjuna said to him,
"Great King, why do you appear to be burdened by anxiety?
The king replied:
"I have repeatedly stirred my great resolve and ventured to plant these supreme merits, hoping they would endure forever until the arrival of Maitreya.
Yet, before the work was completed, my resources were already exhausted; harboring this regret, I sit and wait for the break of dawn."
Nāgārjuna said, "Do not worry.
When one honors merit and supreme goodness, its benefits are inexhaustible; if one gives rise to a vast aspiration, there is no concern that it will not be fulfilled."

Today we shall return to the palace and enjoy ourselves to the fullest; tomorrow morning we will go out on an excursion to survey the mountains and fields, and upon our return here, we shall deliberate on the construction.
Having received this instruction, the King honored it by putting it into practice.
The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna used a divine and wondrous medicine to drip upon various large stones, and they were all transformed into gold.
While the King was out hunting, he saw gold; his heart and mouth rejoiced together, and he turned his carriage toward the abode of Nāgārjuna, saying:
"Today, while on a hunting excursion, I was deluded by spirits and ghosts; amidst the mountains and forests, I frequently beheld clusters of gold."
Nāgārjuna said:
"This is not a delusion caused by spirits.
It is a response to your utmost sincerity that this gold has appeared; you should take it at once to complete your sublime undertaking."
He then proceeded with the construction, and upon its completion, there was still a surplus.
Thereupon, within each of the five stories, he cast four great golden images; the remaining materials were still abundant and filled the various treasuries.
He summoned a thousand monks to reside there and perform liturgical recitations.

Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva then collected and categorized the teachings of the Dharma as proclaimed by Śākyamuni Buddha and the treatises expounded by various bodhisattvas, and stored them within that place.

Therefore, the uppermost first layer contains only Buddha images and various scriptures and treatises; the lower fifth layer houses lay attendants, assets, and utensils; and the three middle layers serve as the residences for the monastic community.
According to the records of former scholars,

once King Yinzheng had completed the construction, it was calculated that the cost of salt consumed by the laborers amounted to nine *koṭi*— where *koṭi* is translated into Chinese as "hundred million"— of gold coins.
Subsequently, the monastics fell into angry dispute and went to the king to seek a resolution.
At that time, the *śrāmaṇeras* said to one another:
"The monastics have broken into contention and their arguments are at odds; wicked men will watch for an opening to destroy the monastery."
Thereupon, the multi-storied pavilion was turned inward to bar the monks;
from that time forward, there have been no more members of the Saṃgha.
Gazing afar at the mountain crags, one knows not the path to the entrance.
At that time, he summoned skilled physicians to enter and treat his illness; they entered and exited with their faces veiled, so that no one could recognize the path they took.
From this great forest, he traveled south for over nine hundred *li* and reached the kingdom of Andhra, within the borders of South India.
The country of Andhra is over three thousand li in circuit.
Its capital city is over twenty li in circuit and is called Bhṛgukaccha.
The soil is fertile and rich, and the harvests are abundant.
The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are fierce and violent.
The language and its intonations differ from those of Central India, but as for the script, the rules and forms are largely the same.
There are more than twenty *saṃghārāmas* with over three thousand monks.
There are more than thirty deva temples, and followers of heterodox paths are indeed numerous.

Not far from the side of the city of Piṅgila, there is a great *saṃghārāma* with multi-storied pavilions and tiered terraces; its construction reaches the limits of artistic engraving, and the sacred countenances of the Buddha images are the pinnacle of exquisite craftsmanship.
In front of the monastery is a stone stūpa several hundred feet high, which was erected by the Arhat Ajita (translated into Chinese as Suoxing, "One Who Acts").

Not far to the southwest of the Arhat’s Monastery where he practiced is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; it was here that the Tathāgata in the past preached the Dharma, manifested great supernatural powers, and delivered immeasurable multitudes.

Traveling twenty-odd *li* southwest from the Arhat’s Monastery, one reaches an isolated mountain. On the ridge of this mountain is a stone *stūpa*, where Dignāga (translated into Chinese as Shou)—a Bodhisattva—composed the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*.
As for the Bodhisattva Dignāga, after the Buddha had passed into nirvana, he received the Dharma and donned the saffron robes.
His wisdom and vows were vast and great, and his power of insight was deep and firm; out of compassion for a world left without refuge, he resolved to propagate the holy teachings.

He considered that the treatises on *hetuvidyā* (logic) were profound in expression and vast in principle, such that students would expend their efforts in vain and find it difficult to achieve mastery; he therefore withdrew his traces into secluded crags and settled his spirit in tranquil concentration, observing the merits and defects of composition and examining the complexity or conciseness of the phrasing and meaning.
At that time, the cliffs and valleys resounded, and the smoke and clouds shifted their colors. A mountain deity lifted the Bodhisattva several hundred feet into the air and proclaimed these words:

"In the past, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, skillfully guided sentient beings through his compassionate heart, preaching the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on Logic), which encompasses sublime principles and profoundly investigates subtle teachings."
The Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, and the great purpose [of his teaching] has vanished.

Now, the Bodhisattva Dignāga, whose merit and wisdom are vast and profound, has deeply penetrated the sacred intent; thus, on this day, his treatise on *hetuvidyā* (Logic) is once again widely propagated.
The Bodhisattva then emitted a great radiance that illuminated the darkness.

At that time, the king of this land conceived a profound sense of reverence; seeing these signs of light, he suspected the Bodhisattva had entered the Vajra-samādhi, and thus requested the Bodhisattva to realize the fruit of non-arising.
Dignāga said, "I have entered meditative absorption to contemplate and wish to explain the profound sutras; my heart aspires to perfect enlightenment, not to the fruit of non-arising.
The King said:

"The fruit of non-arising is that which all sages admire and look up to; it severs the desires of the three realms and penetrates the wisdom of the three insights—this is a magnificent achievement, and I pray you realize it swiftly."
At that time, Dharmakīrti was delighted by the King’s invitation and was just about to realize the fruit of arhatship, the state of no-more-learning.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, knowing this and feeling pity for him, wished to warn him; he snapped his fingers to awaken him and said, "What a pity!"
Why abandon such a vast mind for a narrow and inferior resolve? Why follow the inclination toward solitary self-cultivation and forsake the vow of universal salvation?
If you wish to perform deeds of benefit, you should widely propagate the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* composed by Maitreya Bodhisattva; to guide and inspire future students will bring immense benefit.
The Bodhisattva Dignāga respectfully received these instructions and carried them out accordingly.
Thereupon, he engaged in profound reflection and intensive study, extensively elaborating upon the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*.

Fearing that students might be intimidated by its subtle phrasing and concise expressions, he extracted its essential meanings and synthesized its profound words, composing the *Hetumukha-śāstra* to guide future generations.
From this point onward, he extensively propagated the Yoga system; his eminent disciples became renowned in their time.
From here, traveling south through forests and wilds for more than a thousand *li*, he reached the kingdom of Dhānakaṭaka, also known as the Great Andhra kingdom.
In the region of South India lies the kingdom of Dhānakataka. The kingdom of Dhānakataka is over six thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over forty *li* in circuit.
The soil is rich and fertile, and agricultural production is abundant.
Wild lands are extensive, while inhabited settlements are few.
The climate is warm and humid, and the people have dark complexions.
The people are by nature fierce, yet they take pleasure in learning the arts.
The monasteries stand in successive rows, though most have fallen into ruin; some twenty-odd remain, with over a thousand monks, the majority of whom study the doctrines of the Mahāsāṃghika school.
There are more than a hundred deva temples, and followers of heterodox paths are indeed numerous.

To the east of the city, situated against a mountain, is the Puṣpavatsa (translated into Chinese as "East Mountain") Monastery; to the west of the city, also situated against a mountain, is the Aparavatsa (translated into Chinese as "West Mountain") Monastery. These were built for the Buddha by a former king of this country.

The streams are dammed to form pathways, and terraced cliffs support towering pavilions; long corridors with eaves extend along the ridges, resting upon crags and connecting to peaks, where numinous spirits provide guard and holy sages come to stroll and rest.

Since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, within the first millennium, every year a thousand ordinary monks (*pṛthagjana-bhikṣu*) would enter the summer retreat together; on the day they concluded their retreat, they all realized arhatship and departed through the air by means of their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
After the millennium, ordinary beings and sages lived together;

for more than a hundred years now, there have been no longer any monastics. The mountain deities have changed their forms, appearing sometimes as jackals and wolves, or as monkeys and langurs, terrifying travelers; for this reason, the place has become desolate and empty, with no community of monks remaining.

Not far to the south of the city is a great mountain cliff, the place where the master of treatises, Bhāviveka—known in the language of Tang as Qingbian—resided in the palace of the Asuras while awaiting the appearance of Maitreya Bodhisattva upon his attainment of Buddhahood.
The Master was of noble and vast character, his supreme virtue profound; outwardly he wore the robes of the Sāṃkhya, yet inwardly he propagated the teachings of Nāgārjuna.

Hearing that the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla in the kingdom of Magadha was proclaiming the Dharma with several thousand disciples, he felt a desire to engage him in discussion and traveled there, staff in hand.
Upon arriving at the city of Pāṭaliputra, he learned that the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla was at the Bodhi tree. The Master of Treatises then commanded his disciple, saying:
"Go to the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla at the Bodhi tree and speak these words on my behalf:
'The Bodhisattva has proclaimed the Bequeathed Teachings and guided those who are deluded; we have long looked up to your virtue with a humble mind.'"
However, because my long-held vow has not yet been fulfilled, I have failed to pay my respects.
As for the Bodhi tree, I have sworn that I shall not look upon it in vain; when I see it, there shall be realization, and I shall be called the Teacher of Gods and Men.
The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla said to the messenger:
"Human existence is like an illusion and life is as fleeting as a bubble; I have been diligently devoted day after day and have had no leisure for conversation."
The messenger went back and forth several times, yet they never met.
Once the Master of Treatises had returned to his native land, he reflected in stillness, saying:
"If not when Maitreya attains Buddhahood, who else shall resolve my doubts?"
Before an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, he recited the *Cittamanī-dhāraṇī*, abstaining from grains and subsisting only on water for a period of three years.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva then manifested a wondrous physical form and said to the master:
"What is your aspiration?"
He replied,
"I wish to remain in this body until I may behold Maitreya.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva said:

"Human life is precarious and fragile; the world is fleeting and illusory. You should cultivate supreme wholesome vows to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven, where you may still have the opportunity to pay homage and behold him with speed."
The Master of Treatises said:
"One's resolve cannot be taken away, and one's mind cannot be divided.
The Bodhisattva said:

"If that is so, you should go to the Vajrapāṇi deity at the southern mountain cliff of the city of Dhānakaṭaka; there, by reciting and upholding the *Vajrapāṇi-dhāraṇī* with utmost sincerity, this vow shall be fulfilled."
The Master of Treatises then went there and recited [the scriptures].
After three years had passed, a deity said to him:
"What is your aspiration that you exert yourself so diligently?"
The Master of Treatises said:
"I wish to preserve this body until I may behold Maitreya.
That Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva has sent me here with this request—will he not fulfill my vow through his divine power?"
The deity then bestowed upon him a secret formula and said to him:

"Within this rocky cliff lies the palace of the Asuras; if you perform the invocation according to the rite, the stone wall shall open. Once it has opened, enter within, and you shall be able to wait and behold them."
The Master of Treatises said:
"Dwelling in seclusion and seeing nothing, how could one know that a Buddha has arisen?
Vajrapāṇi replied:
"When Maitreya appears in the world, I shall repay you," the Master of Treatises was thus instructed.

He devoted himself with single-minded diligence to reciting and upholding [the teachings], and after another three years had passed without a single distracting thought, he used incanted mustard seeds to strike a rock; the cliff wall suddenly split open to reveal a cavernous passage.
At that time, hundreds of thousands of people watched in such rapture that they forgot to return home. The Master of Treatises stepped across the threshold and addressed the multitude, saying:

"I have long prayed and waited to behold Maitreya. Now that the holy spirit has granted its protection and my great vow is fulfilled, you should enter here together to witness the manifestation of the Buddha."
Those who heard this were struck with terror and dared not even step upon the threshold, deeming it a den of venomous snakes and fearing for their lives.
Although he entreated them repeatedly, only six people followed him inside.

The Master of Treatises looked back and took leave of the assembly, entering with composed grace; once he had entered, the stone wall closed back together, and the multitude all lamented in sorrow, regretting the error of their previous words.
From here, traveling southwest for more than a thousand *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Culya, within the borders of South India.
The kingdom of Culya is two thousand four or five hundred *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over ten li in circuit.
The land and wilds are vast and desolate, and the marshes and wetlands are overgrown and neglected.
The resident households are few, and banditry is practiced openly.
The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are characterized by craftiness and villainy.
The people are fierce and violent by nature, and they revere and believe in non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas).
The monasteries are dilapidated, though there are a few monks remaining.
There are several dozen deva temples, mostly belonging to naked heretics.
Not far to the southeast of the city is a stūpa, built by King Aśoka.
In the past, the Tathāgata once manifested great supernatural powers at this very spot, preaching the profound and wondrous Dharma, subduing the non-Buddhists, and delivering gods and humans.
Not far to the west of the city is an old monastery, the place where the Bodhisattva Deva engaged in debate with an Arhat.

Initially, when the Bodhisattva Deva heard that there was an Uttara—anuttara, or "Superior" in the language of Tang—who was an arhat possessing the six supernatural powers and endowed with the eight liberations within this monastery, he traveled from afar to seek him out and observe his exemplary conduct.
Having arrived at the monastery, he sought lodging with an Arhat.
The Arhat, possessing few desires and being content, had provided only a single bed.
When Deva arrived, there was no place for him to sit; the Arhat therefore gathered fallen leaves and bade him take his seat upon them.
The Arhat entered meditative absorption and did not emerge until the middle of the night.

Deva then presented his doubts and requested a resolution; the Arhat explained each point according to the questions raised. As Deva followed up on each statement with further inquiries, by the seventh turn, the Arhat remained silent and could no longer respond. Secretly employing his supernormal powers, he went to Tuṣita Heaven to consult Maitreya.
Maitreya, acting as his interpreter, then said to him:
"That Deva has practiced the path for vast eons; within this Bhadrakalpa, he shall succeed to the rank of Buddha. This is not something you can fathom; you ought to pay him deep reverence."
In the time it takes to snap one's fingers, he returned to his original seat and once again expounded upon the sublime meanings and analyzed the subtle words.
Deva said to him, "This is the interpretation of the noble wisdom of Maitreya Bodhisattva; how could you, O worthy one, have been able to investigate it in such detail?"
The Arhat said, "So be it;
this is the intent of the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, he rose from his seat to pay his respects and offer thanks, expressing profound reverence and admiration.
From here, traveling south through forests and wilds for fifteen or sixteen hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Draviḍa, within the borders of South India.
The country of Draviḍa is more than six thousand *li* in circuit; its capital city is called Tāmraparṇī, which is over thirty *li* in circuit.
The soil is fertile, and the cultivation of crops is abundant; flowers and fruits are plentiful, and precious objects are produced there.
The climate is warm and hot, and the customs of the people are bold and fierce.

They are deeply devoted to good faith and righteousness, and they hold learning and broad knowledge in high esteem; however, their spoken language and written characters differ slightly from those of Central India.
There are more than one hundred monasteries with over ten thousand monks, all of whom follow and study the teachings of the Sthavira school.
There are more than eighty deva temples, where most are naked ascetics.
While the Tathāgata was in the world, he frequently traveled to this country to preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings; thus, King Aśoka erected stūpas at all the sacred sites.
The city of Takṣaśilā is the birthplace of the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (translated into Chinese as Hùfǎ, "Dharma-Protector").
The Bodhisattva was the eldest son of the chief minister of this kingdom.
In his youth he possessed a noble magnanimity, and as he grew, his aspirations became vast and far-reaching.
Just reaching the age of twenty, he was married to a princess of the royal house.
On the evening of the ritual banquet, his heart was filled with sorrow and distress; before the Buddha image, he offered earnest and fervent prayers.
Moved by the sincerity of his devotion, the deity fled far away, traveling several hundred li from this place to a mountain monastery, where he sat within the Buddha hall.
A monk opened the door and, seeing this youth, suspected him of being a thief; he further interrogated him, whereupon the Bodhisattva fully explained his circumstances and requested ordination.
The multitude were all struck with wonder and astonishment, and thus they granted his wish.
The King then issued a decree to search far and wide; he learned that the Bodhisattva’s spiritual power transcended the mundane world.
Upon this knowledge, the King’s profound respect and admiration increased even further.
Since donning the dyed robes, he has been steadfast in his studies and diligent in his efforts; his reputation and exemplary conduct have been recorded in the preceding account.
Not far to the south of the city is a great monastery where the wise and learned of the realm have gathered together.
There is a stūpa over one hundred feet high, erected by King Aśoka.
In the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here, subduing the non-Buddhists and extensively delivering humans and devas.
Beside it are the sites where the four past Buddhas sat and practiced walking meditation.
From here, traveling south for more than three thousand *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Mathurā, also known as the kingdom of Jīmūta.
In the region of South India lies the kingdom of Malakūṭa. The kingdom of Malakūṭa is over five thousand li in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over forty li in circuit.
The soil is saline and barren, so the fertility of the land does not flourish;
however, various treasures from the islands of the sea are mostly gathered in this country.
The climate is hot, and most of the people have dark complexions.
Their dispositions are stern and fierce, honoring both the heterodox and the orthodox.
They do not prize the pursuit of arts, but excel only in seeking profit.
Of the old foundations of monasteries, there remain many ruins; those still existing are few, and the monks are likewise scarce.
There are several hundred deva temples with a great multitude of non-Buddhists, many of whom are naked ascetics.

Not far to the east of the city is an old monastery; its courtyards and buildings are overgrown with weeds, though the foundations still remain. It was built by the Great Emperor, the younger brother of King Aśoka.
To its east is a stūpa whose lofty foundation has already subsided, though the inverted-bowl-shaped dome still remains; it was erected by King Aśoka.
In the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here and manifested great supernatural powers to deliver immeasurable multitudes. To commemorate this sacred trace, this monument was established.
As the years passed, his spiritual power grew ever more profound, and his prayers were often fulfilled.
To the south of the kingdom, bordering the sea, lies Mount Malaya, with its lofty cliffs and steep ridges, and its deep caves and mountain torrents.
Among them were white sandalwood trees and *candana-nīpa* trees.

These trees resembled white sandalwood so closely that they could not be distinguished; one could only identify them by climbing to a high vantage point during the height of summer and observing from afar those entwined with large serpents.
Because the nature of this wood is cool and cold, snakes coil around it.
Once it has been spotted from afar, an arrow is shot at it as a marker; only after the winter hibernation has ended is it felled.

The *karpūra* tree has a trunk like that of a pine but different leaves; its flowers and fruits are likewise distinct. When first harvested, it is moist and does not yet possess fragrance. Only after the wood has dried and is split along the grain is the fragrance revealed within; it resembles mica in appearance and snow or ice in color—this is what is called *nāgakesara* (camphor).

To the east of Mount Malaya lies Mount Potalaka. The mountain paths are perilous and the cliffs and valleys are steep and precipitous. At the summit of the mountain is a lake, its waters as clear as a mirror; from it flows a great river that winds around the mountain twenty times before entering the Southern Ocean.
Beside the pond is a stone celestial palace, which serves as a dwelling for the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara to come and go.

Those who wish to see the Bodhisattva disregard their own bodies and lives, braving the waters and climbing the mountains, forgetting all hardships and perils; yet those who are able to reach it are indeed few.

The inhabitants living at the foot of the mountain prayed with sincere hearts to see him; he would manifest in the form of Maheśvara or as an ash-smearing heretic to comfort and console them, thereby fulfilling their wishes.
From here, on the coast of Beihai (the Northern Sea) in Shandong, there is a city that serves as the route to the kingdom of Siṃhala in South India.
According to local tradition,

one enters the sea from here and travels southeast for more than three thousand *li* to reach the kingdom of Siṃhala— which in the language of Tang means "Lion-Holder"— which is not part of the territory of India.

[Records of] Twenty-three Kingdoms. Sengqialuo (Siṃhala) Kingdom: Although not a kingdom of India, it is appended here as it lies along the route.
Dujiananabuluo (Tukkhārapura) Kingdom. Molalata (Mahārāṣṭra) Kingdom. Balujietiepo (Vallabhī) Kingdom. Malaluo (Maru) Kingdom.
The country of Vāhīka, the country of Aṭali, the country of Kheṭa, the country of Varṇu, the country of Ānandapura,
the country of Surāṣṭra, the country of Kukkuṭa, the country of Ujjayinī, the country of Tiṣya, the country of Maheśvarapura,
the country of Sindhu, the country of Mūlasthāna, the country of Pārvatīya, and the country of Āndhra.
The kingdoms of Cīna, Langala, and Pārasīka, though not Indian lands, are included here as they lie along the route.
[The kingdom] formerly called Bīṭaśīla (Persia); the kingdom of Avanda; the kingdom of Varanā;
and the kingdom of Siṃhala. The kingdom of Siṃhala is more than seven thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over forty li in circuit.
The soil is rich and fertile, and the climate is warm and hot; crops are sown according to the seasons, and flowers and fruits abound.
The population is dense and prosperous, and the household wealth is abundant.
Their physical stature is short and their complexions are dark; their nature is fierce and impetuous.
They are fond of learning and esteem virtue, honoring goodness and diligently cultivating merit.
This country was originally a precious island, abounding in rare treasures and inhabited by spirits and deities.

Later, there was a king in South India whose daughter was being married off to a neighboring kingdom. On the auspicious day of her departure, she encountered a lion on the road; her attendants abandoned her to flee for their lives, leaving her in the palanquin with a heart resigned to losing her life.

Then the lion king took his daughter away and entered the deep mountains, dwelling in a secluded valley. He hunted deer and gathered fruit to provide for her from time to time; as months and years passed, she eventually gave birth to a son and a daughter whose physical appearance was human, yet whose nature and lineage were those of beasts.
As the boy gradually grew up, his strength was such that he could wrestle wild beasts.
When he reached the age of twenty, his human intelligence began to develop, and he said to his mother, "What am I called?"
"The father is a wild beast and the mother is a human; since you are not of the same species, how can you be a mate?
The mother then recounted the events of the past to her son, saying, "Humans and beasts follow different paths; you should flee at once."
The mother said, "I fled previously, but I could not save myself. Thereafter,
her son pursued his lion father, climbing mountains and crossing ridges to observe his movements and resting places, so that he might escape the danger.
Once her father had departed, she took up her mother and sister and hurried down toward a human settlement.
Her mother said, "We must each be careful and discreet; do not speak of the origin of these matters. If people were to hear of it, they would look upon us with contempt."
Thereupon, they arrived at their father’s native country; however, the kingdom was no longer under the family's control, as the ancestral line had already been extinguished.
They sought refuge with the local inhabitants, who asked them, "From what country do you people hail?"
She said, "I am originally from this country; having been scattered to a foreign land, mother and daughter have now come together to return to our native home.
Everyone felt pity for her and joined in providing her with sustenance.

When the lion king returned and saw nothing, his longing for his son and daughter gave way to a surge of fury. He emerged from the mountain valley and roamed through the villages and towns, roaring and bellowing with such force that he violently harmed people and things, cruelly destroying all living beings. Whenever the villagers came out, he would seize and kill them.
They beat drums and blew conchs, carrying crossbows and spears, with their followers forming a vast host; only then were they spared from harm.
Fearing that his benevolent transformation had not yet reached all corners, the king then released the hunters, setting them the task of capturing [the deer].
The king personally led the fourfold army, numbering in the tens of thousands, to surround the forests and thickets and span across the mountains and valleys.
As the lions let out a thunderous roar, both humans and beasts fled in terror.

Since he could not be captured, they immediately issued a recruitment notice: "To anyone who captures this lion and eliminates this scourge upon our land, a generous reward shall be granted to honor their distinguished achievement."
When the son heard the king’s decree, he said to his mother:
“Our hunger and cold are extreme; we should respond to the recruitment. If we might obtain something thereby, it could be used to support and nourish us.”
The mother said, "You must not speak thus!
Although he is but a beast, he is still called 'father'; how could you, on account of such hardships, give rise to such rebellion and harm?"
The Master said:
"Humans and beasts belong to different species; where, then, are ritual propriety and righteousness to be found?
Since we are already separated by such barriers, what hope can there be for this heart?"
He then tucked a small knife in his sleeve and went forth to respond to the recruitment.
At that time, thousands of men and tens of thousands of horsemen gathered like clouds and mist; yet the Lion sat crouching in the forest, and no one dared to approach him.

The son went before him, and the father immediately became docile and submissive; thus, out of affection, he forgot his anger and allowed the blade to be plunged into his belly. Even as he was being cut open, he still harbored loving-kindness and felt no malice or resentment, until his abdomen was ripped open and he died in agony.
The king asked, "Who is this person, that he is so extraordinary?

He enticed him with the prospect of benefit and fortune, and intimidated him with threats of punishment and calamity; only then did [the man] fully recount the beginning and end of his story, detailing his circumstances and feelings in their entirety.
The king said:
"How perverse! If one may even harm one's own father, how much more so those who are not kin?"
Beasts are difficult to tame by nature, and their ferocious instincts are easily provoked.
While his merit in eliminating the harm to the people was great,
his act of taking his father’s life was a violation of the natural heart.
"To reward their merit with heavy rewards and to punish their rebellion by banishing them afar;
thus the national statutes shall not be violated, and the King’s word shall remain consistent.
Thereupon, two large ships were prepared and stocked with abundant provisions.
The mother remained in the kingdom to provide for and reward those who had served her, while her sons and daughters each boarded a separate boat and drifted with the waves.
The son’s vessel sailed across the sea until it reached this Treasure Isle; seeing its abundance of rare gems and treasures, he settled there.
Subsequently, merchants seeking treasures returned to the island and killed their leader, keeping his sons and daughters.

Thus they multiplied, and as their descendants became numerous, they established a system of lords and ministers to distinguish ranks of high and low. They built capitals and towns, taking possession of a defined territory; because their ancestors had captured and subdued lions, they commemorated this great achievement by adopting it as the name of their kingdom.

As for that woman’s boat, it drifted westward to Persia; she was possessed by spirits and demons who caused her to give birth to a multitude of daughters, which is why the present-day Great Country of Women in the West is so named.

Therefore, the people of Siṃhala are short of stature and dark-complexioned, with square jaws and broad foreheads; their temperament is fierce and violent, and they endure even lethal poisons. They are descendants of the lineage of wild beasts, which is why these people are mostly courageous and robust.
This is one account.
According to the records of the Buddha’s Dharma, it is said:
"In the past, within this great iron city on this precious island, there resided five hundred rākṣasī women."

Upon the city towers, two tall banners were erected to signify the omens of good or ill fortune: when auspicious events occurred, the banner of good fortune would move; when calamitous events occurred, the banner of misfortune would move.

They constantly waited for merchants arriving at the Treasure Isle, transforming themselves into beautiful women who carried fragrant flowers and played music to welcome and greet them. Having enticed them into the Iron City and enjoyed banquets with them, they would then cast them into iron prisons and gradually devour them.
At that time, there was a great merchant leader in Jambudvīpa named Saṃgha; his son was named Saṃghala.

When the father grew old, the son took over the management of the household affairs. Together with five hundred merchants, he entered the sea to gather treasures, but was tossed about by wind and waves until they reached a continent of precious jewels.
At that time, seeing the auspicious banner move, the rākṣasīs brought incense and flowers, played music, and escorted one another to welcome them, luring them into the iron city.

Thereupon, the merchant leader enjoyed himself in pleasure with the queen of the rākṣasīs, while the rest of the merchants each coupled with their respective partners; as years passed, they all gave birth to a son.

The rākṣasīs, having grown cold toward their former companion and wishing to confine him in an iron prison while seeking out other merchant caravans, were at that time visited by a nightmare during the night.
Gaṅgā, sensing it was not auspicious, secretly sought a way back home; upon reaching the iron prison, she heard the sound of piteous wailing.
She then climbed a tall tree and asked, "Who has bound you here, and why do you lament so bitterly?"
He said, "Do you not know?
The women in the city are all rākṣasīs; in the past, they enticed us into the city for their amusement."
