"Now that you are about to arrive, we shall be imprisoned in a dark dungeon and gradually served as food; already more than half have been consumed, and before long you too shall meet this calamity.
Siṃhala asked, "What plan should we devise to escape this peril?"
He replied, "I have heard that there is a divine horse on the seashore; if you pray with utmost sincerity, it will surely ferry you across.
Upon hearing this, Siṃhala secretly informed his fellow merchants, and they all went together to the seashore, focusing their minds single-mindedly to seek deliverance.
At that time, the divine horse addressed the people, saying:
"Each of you must grasp my mane; provided you do not look back, I shall deliver you all across the sea to escape this calamity, reaching Jambudvīpa and arriving safely in your own lands."

Following the instructions given by the merchants, they focused their minds with single-minded devotion; grasping the horse's fine mane, the celestial steed then leaped and galloped along the path of the clouds, crossing over the seacoast.
The rākṣasī women suddenly realized their husbands had fled; they informed one another and marveled at their departure. Each taking her young child, they soared through the air, coming and going.
Learning that the merchants were about to set sail along the seashore, they summoned one another and flew far to search for them.

Not long after, he encountered a group of traveling merchants; grief and joy welled up within him simultaneously as their tears flowed together. Each covered his face in weeping and said: "I am moved by our meeting and fortunate to have encountered this good man.

My household has been blessed with celebration, and our affection has endured for a long time. Now that you abandon me from afar, leaving my wife and children orphaned and destitute—how could anyone endure such a lingering sorrow?"
"I pray that you will deign to stay and accompany me back to the city.

However, the merchants' hearts were not yet inclined to change their course; the rākṣasīs' attempts at persuasion proved fruitless, so they unleashed their seductive charms and employed every artifice of deception.
The merchant caravan was filled with longing and their emotions were unbearable; their minds wavered between staying and departing, and their bodies all began to falter.
The rākṣasī women congratulated one another and led the merchants away, carrying them with them.
Saṃgharakṣita was of profound and firm wisdom, his mind free from obstruction or attachment; thus he was able to cross the great ocean and escape this perilous danger.
At that time, the Rākṣasī queen returned empty-handed to the Iron City, and her daughters said to her:
"You lack wisdom and strategy, and have been abandoned by your husband; since you possess no skill or talent, you should not remain here."
At that time, the Rākṣasī queen took her son and flew before Saṃgharakṣita, employing every means of seduction to entice him to return with her.
Saṃgharakṣita recited divine mantras from his mouth and brandished a sharp sword in his hand, rebuking her and saying:
"You are a rākṣasī and I am a human; humans and ghosts follow different paths, so we are not a match for one another."
"If you press me with such suffering, I shall take your life.
Knowing that her attempts at seduction had failed, the rākṣasī vanished into the air and went to the house of Saṃgharakṣita. She feigned herself his father, Saṃgha, and said to him:
"I am the daughter of a certain king; Saṃgharakṣita took me as his wife and begot a son. Now, carrying precious goods, I have come to return to my native land."
While crossing the sea, we encountered a storm and our vessel was swept away; only my mother and I, along with Saṃgharakṣita, narrowly escaped drowning.

With mountains and rivers obstructing our path, we suffered the hardships of cold and hunger. For a single word that offended his will, he abandoned us, using insolent insults and reviling us as rākṣasīs.
"To return, my home and country are far away; to stay, I am left alone like a stray traveler.
Having no support whether advancing or retreating, I venture to present my circumstances. Saṃgha said:
“As you have said, it is fitting that you enter the chamber at once.
Not long after he had settled there, Saṃgharakṣita arrived.
His father said to him:
"Why do you value wealth and treasures so highly,
while holding your wife and children in such low regard? Siṃhala replied, "These are rākṣasīs."
He then reported the preceding events in detail to his parents, but his kinsmen and relatives all conspired to drive him away.
At that time, the rākṣasī woman subsequently appealed to the king, who wished to punish Saṃgharakṣita.
Saṅgharāja said,
"The rākṣasī women are full of seductive charms.
The king considered this to be untrue, yet he was captivated by her beauty and said to Saṅgharāja:
"You must abandon this woman and keep her now in the inner palace.
Siṃhala said, "I fear she will bring about calamity."
Since she was a rākṣasī, her sole sustenance was flesh and blood.
The king did not heed Saṃgharakṣita’s words and eventually took her as his wife.

Later, during the night, she flew back to the Jewel Island and summoned the other five hundred rākṣasī-demons to the royal palace together with her. There, using malevolent incantations and sorcery, they ravaged the palace; all humans and animals were devoured for their flesh and their blood was drunk. Taking the remaining corpses, they returned to the Jewel Island.
On the following morning, when the ministers gathered for court, the palace gates remained closed and did not open. After waiting and listening for a long time, they heard no sound of human speech.

Thereupon, they pushed against the doors and threw them open; proceeding together in haste, they reached the palace courtyard, which was silent and devoid of people, containing nothing but skeletal remains.
The assembly of officials and subordinates looked at one another, lost for what to do; they wailed and wept bitterly, unable to fathom the source of this calamity.
Saṃgharakṣita related the beginning and end of the matter in detail, and the ministers and commoners believed it to be true: the disaster was self-invited.

Thereupon, the state ministers, elder officials, various functionaries, and veteran generals inquired after those of illustrious virtue and, based on their merits, recommended the most exalted. All looked up with reverence to the merit and wisdom of Saṃgharāja, whereupon they deliberated together, saying:
"Is he who rules over men to be chosen merely by chance?"

First he accumulated merit and wisdom, and subsequently realized sagacity and brilliance; for without merit and wisdom one cannot enjoy a precious throne, and without sagacity and brilliance how could one manage the affairs of state?
Śrīghoṣa was precisely such a person.
Discerning the omens of calamity within his dreams, he was moved by the divine steed; loyal in admonishing his sovereign, he possessed the wisdom to secure his own person.
As the mandate of destiny now rests here, a new era is celebrated in song.
The common people joyfully urged him forward, honoring and establishing him as king.
Saṃgharāja declined, but could not avoid their request; he accepted the office with moderation, bowed respectfully to the assembled officials, and then ascended the throne.
Thereupon, he rectified former abuses and honored the virtuous and worthy.
He then issued an edict, saying:
"My former merchant companions are in the land of the rākṣasas; their fate—whether they live or die—is unknown, and their merits or faults cannot be distinguished."
Now, as we are about to rescue those in distress, it is fitting to prepare our armor and weapons;
to save the endangered and alleviate suffering brings blessing to the state, while gathering up stores and treasures brings profit to the state.
Thereupon, he marshaled his troops and set sail across the sea.

At that time, the ominous banners atop the Iron City began to stir; seeing this, the rākṣasīs were struck with terror, yet they immediately unleashed their seductive charms, coming forth to welcome, entice, and deceive him.
The King, who had long been aware of their deception, commanded his soldiers to recite divine mantras with their mouths while brandishing martial prowess with their bodies.
The rākṣasīs were thrown into disarray and defeated; some fled to hide on solitary islands, while others drowned in the surging currents.
Thereupon, he destroyed the iron city and shattered the iron prison, rescuing the merchants and acquiring a great quantity of precious jewels.
He recruited the common people and led them to relocate to the Jewel Island, where they established a capital and built towns; thus, a kingdom was founded.
The kingdom was named after the king's own name.
As for "Siṃhala," it refers to the Jātaka tales of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
Formerly, the kingdom of Siṃhala followed only the worship of licentious deities.

One hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Mahendraka, the younger brother of King Aśoka, renounced sensual desires and resolved to seek the holy fruit. Having attained the six supernormal powers and perfected the eight liberations, he traveled through the air to this kingdom to propagate the True Dharma and disseminate the Bequeathed Teachings.
From that time until now, the local customs have been pure and sincere.
There are several hundred monasteries with more than twenty thousand monks, who follow the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school.
More than two hundred years after the arrival of Buddhism, various schools specialized in their own domains and split into two divisions:
the first was called the Mahāvihāravāsin school, which rejected the Mahāyāna and practiced the Hīnayāna teachings.
The second is the Abhayagirivāsin school, whose studies encompass both vehicles and who propagate the Tripiṭaka.

Their monastic followers are pure and upright in their observance of the precepts, concentrated and luminous in meditative concentration and wisdom, and their conduct serves as a model for others; they appear in great numbers, majestic and harmonious.
Beside the royal palace stood a Tooth Relic Shrine (Dantadhātu-vihāra), several hundred feet in height, adorned with pearls and gems and embellished with rare treasures.

Atop the shrine was erected a pillar, upon which was placed a great *padmarāga* gem; its radiance blazed forth, casting a continuous brilliance that shone afar, appearing as bright as a brilliant star whether viewed by day or night.

The King bathes the Buddha’s tooth relic three times daily with perfumed water and aromatic powders, sometimes washing it and sometimes burning them as incense; he strives for the utmost rarity in his offerings to cultivate this worship.
Beside the Buddha-tooth vihāra is a small vihāra, likewise adorned and embellished with various precious gems.
Within it is a golden image of the Buddha, cast to the exact size of a former king of this country; its *uṣṇīṣa* (crown protuberance) is adorned with precious jewels.
Later, there was a thief who watched for an opportunity to steal it, but the gates were heavy and the railings were complete, and the guards maintained strict watch.
The thief then bored a passage through the wall, entered the vihāra, and began to dig; as he sought to take the treasure, the image gradually rose higher and further away.
Since the thief failed to obtain it, he withdrew and sighed, saying:

"In the past, when the Tathāgata cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva, he gave rise to a vast mind and made great vows. From his own life above down to his kingdom and cities below, he took pity on the four types of birth and provided for all beings."
"Now, why does this relic image begrudge its treasure?
To reflect silently upon this, one cannot but wonder at its past deeds.
Thereupon, the image bowed its head and bestowed the treasure upon him.
Having stolen it, he immediately took it to sell; anyone who saw him said, "This treasure is the crest-jewel from atop the head of the former king’s golden Buddha image."
"From where did you obtain this, that you have come here to sell it?
He was then seized and presented to the king.
When the king asked where he had obtained it, the thief replied:
"The Buddha gave it to me himself; I did not steal it.
The king, considering this to be insincere, ordered an envoy to investigate and verify the matter, yet the statue still had its head bowed.

Upon beholding the holy spirit, the king’s faith became firm and steadfast; he did not punish the man, but instead ransomed the treasure with great value and used it to adorn the topknot of the image, placing it back upon the crown.
Because of this image, [the king] has kept his head bowed down until the present day.
A great kitchen was established beside the royal palace, where eighteen thousand meals for the monks were prepared daily.
When the time for the meal arrived, the monks would take their bowls to receive the food; having received their portions, they each returned to their respective quarters.
Since the arrival of the Buddha's teachings, this act of offering was established; descendants have inherited the lineage and continued the tradition until the present day.
However, over the past decade or so, the country has suffered from political turmoil and lacked a settled ruler, leading to the suspension of these practices.

The kingdom borders the sea, and its soil produces rare treasures. When the king personally performs sacrifices, the deities present him with extraordinary goods. The citizens and their children come and go to seek and gather them; according to their karmic rewards, what they obtain differs.
Pearls and gems were obtained according to their yield, and taxes were levied accordingly.

In the southeastern corner of the kingdom lies Mount Laṅkā (formerly called Lángjiā, which is an error), its cliffs and valleys deep and steep, where spirits and ghosts dwell. In the past, the Tathāgata preached the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* here (formerly called the *Léngqié jīng*, which is a corruption).
Sailing several thousand li by sea to the south of the country, one reaches the island of Nalakaṅkara.

The people of this island are short and small, standing no more than three feet tall; they have human bodies with bird-like beaks. As they possess no cultivated crops, they subsist solely on coconuts.

To the west of Nalakīra Island, after sailing several thousand *li* across the sea, there is a solitary island. On its eastern cliff stands a stone Buddha image, over one hundred feet in height, seated facing east. Its *uṣṇīṣa* (cranial protuberance) is made of *candrakānta* (moon-lover) jewels; when the moon is about to turn and shine upon it, water flows down in suspension, cascading over the cliffs and ridges and pouring into the gullies and ravines below.

At that time, there was a caravan of merchants who, encountering a storm, were driven by the waves and tossed about until they reached a solitary island. The seawater was salty and could not be drunk; thus, they suffered from thirst for a long time.

At that time, it was the fifteenth day of the month; water flowed from the top of the image's head, and the multitude all obtained salvation. They considered this to be a response moved by their utmost sincerity, as the divine and holy had rescued them.
They remained there for several days; every month, it would disappear into a high cliff, and its waters would no longer flow.
At that time, the merchant leader said:
"It is not necessarily the case that the water flows only to provide for us."
"I have heard that when the moonlight shines upon the *candrakānta* jewel (moon-loved pearl), water flows forth from it; could it be that this treasure is atop the head of the Buddha image?
He then climbed the cliff to look, and found that the *candrakānta* jewel had been used for the *uṣṇīṣa* (fleshly protuberance) of the image.
When you see that person, tell them the beginning and end of this matter.
Several thousand li by sea to the west of the kingdom, one reaches a Great Treasure Island where no humans dwell; it is solely the abode where spirits reside.
Gazing afar on a tranquil night, the light illuminated the mountains and rivers.
Many merchants had traveled there, yet none returned with anything gained.
To the north of the country of Draviḍa, one enters a forested wilderness; passing solitary cities and small towns, bandits join in gangs to inflict harm upon travelers.
After traveling more than two thousand *li*, he reached the kingdom of Tāmraliptī in the territory of South India.
The kingdom of Tāmraliptī is over five thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over thirty li in circuit.
The soil is rich and fertile, and crops flourish in abundance.
The climate is warm and hot, and the customs of the people are impetuous and fierce.
Their physical appearance is dark-complexioned, and their temperament is fierce and violent.
They are fond of learning and value virtue and the arts.
There are more than one hundred monasteries with over ten thousand monks, who study and practice both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles concurrently.
There are several hundred deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
Beside the royal palace in the city is a great monastery with more than three hundred monks, all of whom are truly men of eminent talent.

The great vihāra of that monastery is over one hundred feet high; within it is the precious crown of Prince Sarvārthasiddha, less than two feet in height, adorned with rare jewels and kept within a precious casket.
Whenever the day of the fast arrives, it is brought out and placed upon a high throne, where it is venerated with incense and flowers; at such times, it emits a brilliant light.

Within a great monastery by the city wall there is a shrine over fifty feet high, containing a sandalwood image of Maitreya Bodhisattva over ten feet tall. On fast days, divine light shines forth from it; this was the work of the Arhat Śravaṇa Dvibhūtika.

Not far to the north of the city is a grove of *tāla* trees, over thirty li in circumference; their leaves are long and broad, and their color is lustrous and glossy, such that no country for writing employs them more than this one.
In the forest there is a stūpa, which marks the site where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation.
Beside it is the stūpa containing the bodily relics of the Arhat Śravaṇabhūti.
Not far to the east of the city is a stūpa whose foundations have collapsed, leaving a remaining height of three *zhang*.
According to the records of former sages, it contains relics of the Tathāgata;
on fast days, it occasionally illuminates the surroundings with a divine light.
In the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here, manifesting supernatural powers to deliver all living beings.
Not far to the southwest of the city is a stūpa over one hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka.
This is where the Arhat Śrutaviṃśatikoṭi manifested great supernatural powers to transform and deliver sentient beings.
Beside it is a monastery, of which only the foundations remain; it was built by that very Arhat.
From here, traveling northwest into a vast wilderness, one encounters fierce beasts that cause violent harm and bands of bandits who are cruel and savage.
After traveling two thousand four or five hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Mahārāṣṭra, within the borders of South India.
The country of Mahārāṣṭra is more than six thousand li in circuit.
The capital city of the country borders a great river to its west and is over thirty li in circuit.
The soil is fertile and rich, and the cultivation of crops is abundant.
The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are simple and honest.

The people are physically imposing and by nature haughty and unrestrained; they invariably repay kindness and surely seek revenge for grievances. If someone insults or humbles them, they will risk their lives to avenge it; if they are in distress, they will join forces with others, forgetting their own bodies to come to their rescue.
When intending to retaliate against an enemy, one must first inform them; only after both sides have donned sturdy armor do they engage at the sharp of the spearhead.
When pursuing a defeated foe on the battlefield, one does not kill those who have already surrendered.
When the soldiers and generals suffered defeat, they were not subjected to punishment; instead, they were granted women’s garments, and moved by this indignation, they committed suicide.

The state maintained several hundred brave warriors; whenever it was time for a decisive battle, they would drink until they were thoroughly intoxicated, and with one man leading the charge, the sharpness of ten thousand men was blunted.
Whenever they encountered people, they would inflict harm upon them without the state's legal system being applied; every time they went out on a procession, drums were beaten to lead the way.

Furthermore, they kept several hundred head of violent elephants; when they were about to engage in battle, these elephants were also first made to drink wine, after which they would charge and trample forward, with no enemy able to withstand them.
Relying upon these men and elephants, that king treated neighboring states with contempt.
The king was of the Kṣatriya caste and was named Purāṃjaya.
His strategic planning was far-reaching and his benevolence extended widely; his ministers served him with the utmost loyalty.

Now, Great King Śīlāditya has campaigned eastward and westward; those far away have become guests of his court and those nearby are in awe. Yet, only the people of this land alone have not submitted as subjects. He has repeatedly led the armored troops of the five Indias and summoned the fierce generals of various nations, personally going forth to subdue them, yet he has still not achieved victory.
Such are its military forces, and such are its customs.
The people are known for their fondness for learning, honoring both the heterodox and the orthodox.
There are over a hundred monasteries with more than five thousand monks, who practice both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles, mastering them in equal measure.
There are hundreds of deva temples and many followers of heterodox paths.
Within and without the great city, there are five stūpas, all of which mark the sites where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation; they were built by King Aśoka.
As for the remaining stone bricks and various stūpas, they are so numerous that it is difficult to enumerate them all.

Not far to the south of the city is an old monastery, within which is a stone image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; its spiritual influence is subtly pervasive, and those who pray to it receive many blessings.
On the eastern border of the kingdom there is a great mountain, with overlapping ridges forming continuous barriers and layered peaks rising in steep precipices.

There stands a monastery founded in a secluded valley; its lofty halls and deep chambers are carved into the cliffs and rest against the mountain summits. With its multi-storied pavilions and tiered terraces, it faces the river while its back leans against the rock. It was built by the Arhat Ācāra (in the language of Tang, "One Who Practices").

The Arhat was a native of Western India. After his mother passed away, he observed her rebirth and saw that she had received a female body in this country. The Arhat then came here, intending to guide and transform her, and to bring her under his spiritual influence according to her capacity.

Entering the village to beg for alms, he arrived at his mother’s natal home; when a young woman came forward with food to offer him, milk flowed from her breasts. Upon seeing this, his relatives considered it an ill omen.
The Arhat recounted the original causes and conditions, whereupon the woman immediately realized the fruits of sainthood.
Moved by the kindness of her parents and mindful of the workings of karmic conditions, he sought to repay their profound virtue and established this monastery.
The great vihāra of the monastery is over one hundred feet high, containing within it a stone Buddha image seventy-odd feet tall.
Above it are seven tiers of stone canopies, suspended in mid-air without any attachments; the distance between each canopy is approximately three feet.
I have heard from the records of former sages that this is sustained by the power of the vows of an Arhat;
others say it is the power of supernatural faculties (ṛddhi).
Some say this is the efficacy of medicinal arts;
yet, upon examining the authentic records, the cause remains unclear.
The stone walls surrounding the vihāra are carved and engraved with scenes depicting the various causal-ground deeds performed by the Tathāgata in the past while practicing the bodhisattva path.
The auspicious signs of realizing the fruits of sagehood and the spiritual responses of entering nirvana—both great and small—are recorded here without omission, all fully engraved and carved.
Outside the monastery gate, there is one stone elephant each to the south, north, left, and right.
According to local tradition,
it is said that whenever this elephant lets out a great roar, the earth trembles.
In the past, the Bodhisattva Dignāga frequently resided in this monastery.
From here, traveling west for more than a thousand *li* and crossing the Narmadā River, one arrives at the kingdom of Valabhī (also known as Changye), within the borders of South India.
The kingdom of Valabhī is approximately two thousand four or five hundred *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty li in circuit.
The soil is saline and alkaline, and vegetation is sparse.
They produce salt by boiling seawater and make their livelihood from the sea.
The climate is hot, with whirlwinds rising frequently.
The local customs are frivolous and superficial, and the people are deceitful by nature.
They are ignorant of learning and the arts, believing both in heterodoxy and orthodoxy.
There are more than ten monasteries with over three hundred monks, who study the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school.
There are more than ten deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths live together.
From here, traveling northwest for more than two thousand *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Mālava, also known as Southern Lāṭa.
It is within the borders of South India.
The kingdom of Mālava is more than six thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over thirty li in circuit and is situated to the southeast of the Mahī River.

The soil is rich and fertile, and agricultural production is abundant; vegetation flourishes, and flowers and fruits grow in profusion. It is particularly well-suited for winter wheat, and the inhabitants mostly eat cakes and parched grain.
The people are by nature gentle and compliant; for the most part, they are intelligent and quick-witted, their speech is elegant and clear, and their mastery of learning and arts is profound.

Within the territories of the five Indias, two kingdoms place great importance on learning: Mālava in the southwest and Magadha in the northeast. They value virtue and esteem benevolence, being both bright and keen in their pursuit of knowledge.
In this country, both heterodox and orthodox beliefs are practiced together.
There are several hundred monasteries with more than twenty thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
There are several hundred deva temples, and followers of heterodox paths are indeed numerous; most of them are those who smear themselves with ashes.
The National Gazetteer states:
Sixty years ago, there was a king named Śīlāditya (translated into Chinese as Jièrì, or "Precept-Sun").

His spiritual wisdom was lofty and brilliant, and his talent and learning were abundant and敏捷 (agile). He cherished and nurtured the four classes of living beings and revered and honored the Triple Gem.
From the moment of his birth until the end of his life, his countenance never showed a trace of anger, and his hands never harmed a living creature.
When elephants and horses drank water, they would strain it before drinking, fearing they might harm aquatic life.
Such was his benevolence.
During his fifty-odd years on the throne, wild beasts became familiar with humans, and the common people throughout the entire kingdom refrained from killing any living creature.
He established a vihāra beside his palace, exhausting every skillful artistry and providing it with complete magnificence; within it, he fashioned images of the Seven Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Every year, he regularly convened an unrestricted great assembly (paṃcavārṣika), gathering monastics from all quarters to provide them with the four types of requisites as offerings—whether these were the three robes and ritual implements, or the rare treasures of the seven precious gems.
For generations they have succeeded one another, and their noble deeds have never faltered.

Twenty-odd *li* to the northwest of the great city, one reaches a Brahmin village; beside it lies a sunken pit which, during the rains of autumn and summer, remains submerged for ten days or more, yet though it receives many streams, it holds no standing water.
Beside it, another small stūpa has been erected.
According to the records of former sages,
this was the place where a haughty Brahmin formerly fell alive into hell.
Formerly, in this city, there was a Brahmin who possessed innate wisdom and vast erudition; his learning surpassed that of the eminent scholars of his time.

He had thoroughly investigated the most profound and subtle aspects of both internal and external scriptures, and his mastery of calendrical calculations and mystical texts was as clear as looking at the palm of his hand.
His conduct was pure and lofty, and his reputation spread far and wide.
The King held him in high esteem and veneration, and the people of the country revered him.
His disciples numbered in the thousands, who tasted his doctrine and admired his character.
He would often say:
"I have appeared in the world to expound the sages' teachings and guide the common people; from ancient worthies to later philosophers, none can compare with me.

As for Mahesvara, Vasudeva, Narayana, and the World-Honored Buddha—all men are swept away by their influence, following and propagating their doctrines, all of whom depict their images and vie with one another to cultivate reverence."
"My virtue now surpasses theirs, and my fame is preeminent in this age; if I do not distinguish myself, how can I manifest my excellence?
He then had images of Maheśvara, Vasu, Nārāyaṇa, and the Buddha-Bhagavān carved from red sandalwood.
He fashioned four legs for his seat, which he carried with him wherever he went; such was his arrogance.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu from Western India named Bhadraluñci (translated into Chinese as Xiàn'ài), who was preeminent in the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*) and had profoundly mastered heterodox doctrines. His spiritual influence was pure and refined, the fragrance of his precepts was intense, and he possessed few desires and was content with little, seeking nothing from material things. Upon hearing of [Śīlabhadra’s] conduct, he sighed and said:
"What a pity!..."
"At that time, there was no one [to restrain him].
This allowed that foolish man to dare to practice such cruel deeds.
Thereupon, carrying his mendicant's staff, he traveled far away and arrived at this kingdom, where he related his long-held intention in detail to the King.
When the king saw his tattered robes, he did not yet respect him from the heart; nevertheless, he admired his lofty resolve and forced himself to pay him due courtesy.
He then prepared a seat for debate and addressed the brahmin, saying:
Upon hearing this, the Brahmin laughed and said,
"Who is this person that dares to harbor such an ambition?
He commanded his disciples to come to the site of debate, and several hundred thousand people gathered to attend and listen from before and behind him.
The worthy one wore tattered old clothes and sat upon a spread of grass.
That brahmin, however, sat haughtily upon his own seat, disparaging the True Dharma and expounding his own heterodox doctrines.
The Bhikṣu Qingbian’s eloquence flowed like a stream as he argued back and forth in circles.
After a long time, the Brahmin finally apologized and yielded.
The King then said to him:
"Having long enjoyed empty fame, you have deceived the sovereign and deluded the masses; the ancient statutes record that one who loses in debate shall be executed.
He intended to cast him into a furnace of iron, ordering him to sit upon it.
The Brahmin, driven to desperation, took refuge in him for protection.
Bhadra, moved by compassion, petitioned the king, saying:

"Great King, your benevolence and courtesy extend far and wide, and songs of praise fill the roads. You ought to spread compassionate nurture and refrain from cruelty; forgive his shortcomings and let him go wherever he pleases."
The King ordered him to ride a donkey and circulate through the cities and towns to proclaim his punishment.
The Brahmin, humiliated by this disgrace, was overcome with indignation and vomited blood.
Upon hearing of this, the bhikṣu went to comfort him, saying:

"Your learning encompasses both the inner and outer classics, and your reputation is heard far and wide. Regarding matters of honor and disgrace, you ought to be clear about when to advance or retreat.
Now, what substance is there in fame?"
The brahmin, filled with indignation, severely reviled the bhikṣu, slandered the Mahāyāna, and held the former sages in contempt.
Before his voice had even ceased, the earth split open and he fell into it alive; the traces of this event remain here.
From here, traveling southwest into the sea and then northwest for two thousand four hundred or five hundred *li*, one reaches the country of Aṭali, within the borders of South India.
The country of Aṭali is more than six thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty li in circuit.
Its inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and precious treasures are stored in abundance. Although agriculture is practiced, commerce is the primary occupation.
The soil is saline and barren, and flowers and fruits are scarce.
There grow pepper trees, whose leaves resemble those of the *shu-jiao* (Sichuan pepper).
There also grow frankincense trees, whose leaves resemble those of the *tang-li* (crabapple).
The climate is hot, with much wind and dust.
The people are frivolous and superficial by nature, valuing wealth while holding virtue in low esteem.
Their written characters, spoken language, and ceremonial regulations are largely the same as those of the country of Mālava.
Most do not believe in the merit of [meritorious deeds]; even those who have faith primarily worship celestial deities.
There are more than ten shrines where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
Traveling northwest from the kingdom of Mālava for three days, one arrives at the kingdom of Cīṭa, within the borders of South India.
The country of Kie-t'o (Kietta) is over three thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city is more than twenty *li* in circuit.
The population is dense and prosperous, and the households are wealthy and well-provided.
Having no sovereign ruler, it is a dependency of the kingdom of Mālava; its climate, products, and customs are thus identical to those of that country.
There are more than ten monasteries with over a thousand monks, who study and practice both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles concurrently.
There are several dozen deva temples, and the followers of external paths are numerous.
From here, traveling north for over a thousand *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Valabhī, also known as the kingdom of Bhillamāla.
It is within the borders of South India.
The Kingdom of Valabhī: The kingdom of Valabhī is over six thousand *li* in circuit.
Its capital city is over thirty *li* in circuit.
Regarding the products of the soil, the suitability of the climate, and the customs and character of the people, it is the same as the kingdom of Mālava.
The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and the households are wealthy; there are more than a hundred families who have accumulated wealth amounting to ten billion.
Rare commodities from distant regions are gathered in great quantities within this kingdom.
There are more than one hundred monasteries with over six thousand monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
There are several hundred deva temples, and followers of heterodox paths are truly numerous.
The Tathāgata frequently visited this country during his lifetime; therefore, King Aśoka erected commemorative monuments and constructed stūpas at all the places where the Buddha stayed.
The sites where the three past Buddhas sat, walked for meditation, and preached the Dharma are interspersed throughout as sacred traces.

The present king is of the Kṣatriya caste; he is the nephew of King Śīlāditya of the former kingdom of Mālava and the son-in-law of King Śīlāditya of the present kingdom of Kanyakubja, known as Dhruvabhaṭa (translated into Chinese as Chángyuì).
His temperament was impulsive and his wisdom shallow;
nevertheless, he was pure in faith toward the Triple Gem and established a great assembly for seven days each year, providing the Sangha with offerings of rare treasures and exquisite flavors.

Having already bestowed as gifts the price for the three robes and medicinal supplies, as well as rare and precious treasures of the seven jewels, he now ransomed them back by paying double the value.
Valuing virtue and honoring the worthy, he followed the Way and esteemed learning; thus, eminent monks from distant regions were treated with exceptional reverence.

Not far from the city, there is a great monastery established by the Arhat Ajita, where the Bodhisattvas Guṇamati and Sthiramati resided and composed their treatises, all of which are widely circulated.
From here, traveling northwest for more than seven hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Ānandapura, within the borders of Western India.
The kingdom of Ānandapura is more than two thousand li in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty li in circuit.
The population is dense and prosperous, and the households are wealthy and well-off.
There is no sovereign ruler; the country is subject to the kingdom of Mālava.
The suitability of the soil and the sequence of the seasons, as well as the rules of their written script, are likewise the same [as those of India].
There are more than ten monasteries with fewer than a thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
There are several dozen deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
Traveling westward from the country of Valabhī for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Surāṣṭra, within the borders of Western India.
The country of Surāṣṭra is more than four thousand *li* in circuit.
Its capital city is over thirty *li* in circuit and is situated on the west bank of the Mahī River.
The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and their households possess abundant wealth.
The territory is subject to the kingdom of Balāhika.
The soil is saline and alkaline, and flowers and fruits are rare.
Although the cold and heat are moderate, the winds blow without ceasing.
The local customs are frivolous and superficial, and the people are by nature fickle and impetuous.
They do not take pleasure in learning the arts, and they believe both in heterodoxy and orthodoxy.
There are more than fifty monasteries with over three thousand monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school.
There are more than one hundred deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.

The country lies on the route to the Western Sea; its people all rely on the benefits of the sea for their livelihood, making trade their profession as they exchange goods to balance supply and demand.
Not far from the city is Mount Udyāna.
At its summit lies a monastery, with chambers, halls, and corridors carved extensively into the cliffs and ridges.
The forest trees are lush and verdant, and springs and streams intersect throughout the landscape; it is a place where sages and worthies have dwelt and where numinous immortals have gathered.
Traveling north from the kingdom of Valabhī for more than one thousand eight hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Gurjara, within the borders of Western India.
The kingdom of Gurjara is more than five thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is named Viramala; it is over thirty li in circuit.
Its soil, products, and customs are the same as those of the country of Sūlastha.
The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and their households possess abundant wealth.
The followers of non-Buddhist paths are numerous, while those who believe in the Buddha-dharma are few.
There is a single monastery with over a hundred monks, who study and practice the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna teachings.
There are several dozen deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.

The king is of the Kṣatriya caste; though he is in his early twenties, his wisdom and courage are profound and far-reaching. He has deep faith in the Buddha-dharma and holds those of exceptional ability in high esteem.
From here, traveling southeast for more than two thousand eight hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Oḍḍiyāna, within the borders of South India.
The kingdom of Oḍḍiyāna is more than six thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over thirty li in circuit.
Its soil, products, and customs are the same as those of the country of Surāṣṭra.
The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and their households are wealthy and affluent.
There were several dozen monasteries, most of which were in ruins, with only three or five remaining.
There were more than three hundred monks who studied and practiced both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles concurrently.
There are several dozen deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
The king is of Brahmin descent; he has extensively studied heterodox scriptures and does not believe in the True Dharma.
Not far from the city is a stūpa, the site where King Aśoka established a hell.
From here, traveling northeast for more than a thousand *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Tiṅ-ki-ta (Tiṅgiṭa) in the region of South India.
The kingdom of Tiṅ-ki-ta is more than four thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is fifteen or sixteen *li* in circuit.
The soil is renowned for its fertility; crops grow in abundance, and it is well-suited for beans and wheat, with many flowers and fruits.
The climate is temperate and pleasant, and the people are by nature kind and compliant.
The people mostly believe in non-Buddhist paths and rarely revere the Buddha-dharma.
There are several dozen monasteries, with few monks.
There are more than ten deva temples, housing over a thousand followers of non-Buddhist paths.
The king is of the Brahmin caste; he has profound faith in the Triple Gem and honors those of virtue, such that scholars of wide renown from all quarters gather in great numbers in this kingdom.
Traveling north from here for more than nine hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Mahīśvarapura, within the borders of Central India.
The kingdom of Mahīśvarapura is more than three thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty li in circuit.
Its soil, products, and customs are the same as those of the kingdom of Oḍḍiyāna.
The people revere non-Buddhist paths and do not believe in the Buddha-dharma.
There are several dozen deva temples, most of which belong to the ash-smearing sects.
The king is of Brahmin descent and does not particularly revere or believe in the Buddha-dharma.

From here he returned to the kingdom of Kukśala; proceeding again northward through wild deserts and perilous wastes for over one thousand nine hundred li, he crossed the great river Sindhu and reached the kingdom of Sindhu, within the borders of Western India.
The country of Sindhu is more than seven thousand li in circuit.
Its capital city is called Viṣayabhūpura, and it is over thirty li in circuit.
It is suitable for grain cultivation and yields abundant winter wheat. It produces gold, silver, and brass. It is well-suited for raising cattle, sheep, camels, mules, and similar livestock.
The camels here are small and short, possessing only a single hump.
Red salt is produced in abundance, its color like that of red stone; white salt, black salt, and white stone salt are among those used as medicine in distant foreign lands.
The people are fierce by nature yet straightforward; they frequently engage in quarrels and are prone to slander.
They do not favor extensive learning, but they believe deeply in the Buddha-dharma.

There are several hundred monasteries with more than ten thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna; for the most part, they are indolent and their conduct is corrupt.
There are diligent and virtuous practitioners who dwell alone in seclusion, retreating to the mountains and forests; unremitting day and night, many have realized the fruits of sainthood.
There are more than thirty deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths reside together.
The king was of the Śūdra caste; he was simple and sincere by nature and revered the Buddha-dharma.
As the Tathāgata had frequently visited this country in the past, King Aśoka erected several tens of stūpas at the sites of sacred traces.

The Arhat Upagupta traveled repeatedly to this country, expounding the Dharma and guiding sentient beings; wherever he stayed, he left behind traces that were commemorated by the construction of monasteries (*saṃghārāma*) or the erection of stūpas (*stūpa*), which arose here and there, and may be briefly described as follows.

Along the banks of the Indus River, for more than a thousand li, there are several hundred thousand households dwelling amidst marshes and wetlands; they are fierce by nature and devote themselves solely to killing.
They sustain themselves by herding cattle, with no fixed means of livelihood.

Whether male or female, regardless of noble or lowly status, they shave their hair and beards and wear the *kāṣāya*, appearing outwardly like *bhikṣus*, yet they engage in worldly affairs, cling exclusively to limited views, and denigrate the Mahāyāna.
I have heard from the records of former sages that in the past, the common people of this land were callous and cruel, devoted solely to violent and savage acts.

At that time, there was an Arhat who took pity on their impending downfall; in order to transform them, he traveled through the air and manifested great supernatural powers and rare wonders, causing the multitude to believe and accept his teachings, and gradually guiding them with his verbal instructions.
The people were filled with reverence and joy, wishing to receive his instructions.

Knowing that the assembly’s minds were compliant, the Arhat conferred the Three Refuges upon them, quelling their ferocity and causing them all to desist from killing and slaughter. They shaved their hair, donned dyed robes, and reverently practiced the teachings of the Dharma.

As the ages have grown distant and the times have shifted, the preservation of goodness has declined while lingering customs have not yet been extinguished; though they wear the Dharma robes, they often lack precepts and virtue.
For generations, their descendants have practiced this until it became a custom.
From here, traveling eastward for more than nine hundred li and crossing to the eastern bank of the Indus River, one arrives at the kingdom of Morasuvālu, within the borders of Western India.
The country of Maulasatrūṇa is over four thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city is over thirty *li* in circuit.
The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and the households are wealthy and well-off.
It is a dependency of the kingdom of Takka.
The soil is fertile and rich, and the climate is temperate and harmonious.
The customs are honest and straightforward; the people are fond of learning and esteem virtue.
The people mostly worship heavenly deities and have little faith in the Buddha-dharma.
There are more than ten monasteries, most of which are in ruins; there are few monks, and their studies lack specialization.
There are eight deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
There is a temple of the Sun God (Sūrya), which is most magnificently adorned; its image of the Sun God is cast of gold and embellished with rare jewels.

The numinous mirror penetrates the profound darkness, and divine efficacy is secretly bestowed; female musicians perform in succession, and bright torches follow one another like the sun; offerings of incense and flowers have never ceased.

The kings and noble clans of the five regions of India have all, without exception, bestowed precious treasures here to establish houses of merit, providing food, drink, medicine, and aid to the poor and the sick.

People from various countries come here to offer prayers by the thousands; the area surrounding the celestial temple, with its ponds, pools, and flowering groves, is most worthy of excursion and appreciation.
From here, traveling northeast for more than seven hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Bhaṭṭa, within the borders of North India.
The country of Parvata is more than five thousand *li* in circuit.
Its capital city is over twenty *li* in circuit.
The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous.
It is a dependency of the kingdom of Takka.
It produces much early rice and is suitable for winter wheat.
The climate is temperate, the customs are straightforward, the people are impetuous by nature, and their speech contains vulgar expressions.
Their learning and arts are profound and extensive, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings.
There are more than ten monasteries with over a thousand monks,
who study and practice both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles concurrently.
There are four *stūpas*, erected by King Aśoka.
There are twenty deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.

Beside the city is a great monastery with over a hundred monks, all of whom study the Mahāyāna teachings; this is the very place where the former master of treatises Śrībhadra (translated into Chinese as Zuìshèngzǐ, "Most Victorious Son") composed the *Yogācārabhūmi-bhāṣya*, and it was also the original place of renunciation for the masters Bhadrapāla and Guṇaprabha.
This great monastery was consumed by a celestial fire, leaving it ruined and in a state of desolation.
Traveling one thousand five or six hundred li southwest from the country of Sindhu, one arrives at the country of Āndhra, within the borders of Western India.
The country of Āḍhavanaśīra is over five thousand *li* in circuit.
Its capital city is named Kachchheshvara, which is over thirty *li* in circuit.
Situated in a remote western border, it borders the Indus River and adjoins the seacoast.
Its dwellings are magnificent and abound with rare treasures.
Having no sovereign of its own, it is administratively subordinate to the kingdom of Sindhu.

The ground is damp and the soil is saline; foul weeds grow luxuriantly, and few fields or ridges have been cultivated. Although all varieties of grain are grown, barley and wheat are particularly abundant.
The climate is slightly cold, and the winds are fierce and violent.
It is suitable for raising cattle, sheep, camels, mules, and similar livestock.
The people are by nature violent and impetuous, and they do not favor study or learning.
Their spoken language differs slightly from that of Central India.
The local customs are simple and honest, and the people revere and honor the Triple Gem.
There are more than eighty monasteries with over five thousand monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
There are ten deva temples, most of which are inhabited by the ash-smearing heretics (pāśupatas).
Within the city is a temple of Maheśvara.
Its buildings are exquisitely adorned and its divine image possesses spiritual efficacy; the ash-smearing heretics dwell within it as their place of recreation.

In the past, the Tathāgata frequently traveled to this country, preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings and guiding the common folk to benefit the world; therefore, King Aśoka erected six stūpas at these sites of sacred traces.
Traveling west from here for less than two thousand *li*, one reaches the kingdom of Langqieluo (Lāḍha), within the borders of Western India.
The kingdom of Langqieluo extends for several thousand *li* in each of the four directions—east, west, south, and north.
The capital city of the kingdom is over thirty li in circuit and is called Sutrīśvara.
The soil is rich and fertile, and crops flourish in abundance.
The climate and customs are the same as those of the country of Āḍhyāvatī.
The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and there are many rare treasures.
Situated on the shore of the great ocean, it is the gateway to the kingdom of the Western Women (Sindh).
There is no sovereign ruler; each group establishes itself according to its river, and they do not acknowledge one another’s authority, remaining subject to the kingdom of Persia.
The script is largely the same as that of India, though the spoken language differs slightly.
Both heterodox and orthodox teachings are followed.
There are over one hundred monasteries with more than six thousand monks, who study and practice both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.
There are several hundred deva temples, and the followers of the ash-smearing heretics (pāśupatas) are extremely numerous.
Within the city is a temple of Maheśvara that is magnificent and grand, which the ash-smearing heretics venerate as their primary object of worship.
From here, proceeding northwest, one reaches the country of Bālāsī (Persia). Although it is not a country of India, it is included here as it lies along the route.
It was formerly called Bōsī, which is an abbreviation.
The country of Persia (Póluósī) is several tens of thousands of *li* in circuit.
Its capital city is called Sūlāsāṭāna, which is over forty *li* in circuit.
The land is largely riverine, and the climate is likewise distinct; it is generally warm.
Water is diverted for irrigation, and the households are wealthy and prosperous.

The region produces gold, brass, crystal, quartz, and various rare and extraordinary treasures. It is skilled in weaving large brocades, fine woolens, and variegated carpets. There are many excellent horses and camels.
The currency consists of large silver coins.
The people are by nature impetuous and violent, and their customs lack propriety and righteousness.
Their written characters and spoken language differ from those of other countries.
They possess no scholarly arts but are skilled in many crafts; whatever they produce is highly esteemed by neighboring regions.
Their marriage customs are promiscuous, and when death occurs, corpses are frequently abandoned.
They are large in stature; they wear their hair even and leave their heads bare, clothing themselves in skins, coarse woolens, or fine silk and cotton.
Households were assessed for taxes at a rate of four silver coins per person.
There were many deva temples, among which the followers of the Tīrthika Tiṇabhāva were the most prominent.
There were two or three monasteries with several hundred monks, all of whom studied the teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna.
The almsbowl of Śākyamuni Buddha is kept here in the royal palace.
To the east of the kingdom lies the city of Kalmāṣadaṃṣṭra; its inner city is not extensive, while its outer wall is over sixty *li* in circumference.
The inhabitants are numerous and their households possess great wealth.
To the northwest it borders the country of Bolor; its territory and customs are the same as those of Persia (Bālāsī).
Their physical appearance and language differ slightly [from the Persians], and they abound in rare treasures and are likewise prosperous.
To the southwest of the island of Fulin lies the Kingdom of Western Women; its inhabitants are exclusively women, with almost no men present.

Possessing many precious goods, they are tributary to the kingdom of Fulin; therefore, the King of Fulin annually dispatches men to mate with them. It is their custom that any male infants born are not raised.
Traveling north from the kingdom of Āḍhyakṣa for more than seven hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Pīṭhikā, which lies within the borders of Western India.
The kingdom of Pīṭhikā is more than three thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty li in circuit.
The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous; there is no great sovereign, and the country is subject to the kingdom of Śindhu.
The soil is sandy and saline, and the cold winds are piercingly fierce.
There is an abundance of pulse and wheat, but few flowers and fruits;
the local customs are fierce and violent,
and the language differs from that of Central India.
They do not favor the study of arts and learning, yet they are known for their sincerity and faith.
There are more than fifty monasteries with over three thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
There are more than twenty deva temples, all belonging to the ash-smearing heretics (pāśupatas).
Fifteen or sixteen li to the north of the city, within a great forest, there is a stūpa several hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka.
Within it are śarīra relics that occasionally emit a brilliant light;
this is the place where the Tathāgata, when he was formerly a rishi, was harmed by a king.
Not far to the east of here is an old monastery, which was established in the past by the great arhat Mahākātyāyana.
Beside it are the sites where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation; stūpas have been erected there as monuments.
From here, traveling northeast for more than three hundred li, one arrives at the country of Avanda, within the borders of Western India.
The country of Avanda is two thousand four or five hundred *li* in circuit.
Its capital city is over twenty *li* in circuit.
It has no great sovereign ruler and is subject to the kingdom of Sindhu.
The soil is suitable for cultivation, with rice and wheat being particularly abundant; flowers and fruits are scarce, and vegetation is sparse.
The climate is windy and cold, and the people are fierce and violent by nature.
Their speech is plain and unrefined, and they do not value academic pursuits; nevertheless, they maintain pure faith in their hearts toward the Triple Gem.
There are more than twenty monasteries with over two thousand monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
There are five deva temples, all belonging to the ash-smearing heretics (Pāśupatas).

Not far to the northeast of the city, within a great bamboo grove, are the remains of a monastery; this is where the Tathāgata in the past permitted the bhikṣus to wear *kheva* sandals (translated into Chinese as *xié*, or boots).
Beside it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; although its foundation has subsided, it still stands over a hundred feet high.
Adjacent to it is a vihāra containing a standing Buddha image carved from green stone, which occasionally emits a divine radiance on fast days.
More than eight hundred paces further south, there is a stūpa in the forest built by King Aśoka.

In the past, when the Tathāgata stayed here, the night was cold; he therefore layered his three robes over one another. When morning came, he permitted all the bhikṣus to wear double-layered cotton garments.
Within this grove is the place where the Buddha used to walk for exercise.
There are also numerous stūpas standing in close succession, all of which mark the sites where the four past Buddhas sat.
Within this stūpa are the hair and nail-clippings of the Tathāgata; whenever it reaches a fast-day (upoṣadha), they frequently emit brilliant light.
From here, traveling northeast for more than nine hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Varṇu, within the borders of Western India.
The country of Varṇu is over four thousand li in circuit.
Its capital city is more than twenty li in circuit.
The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous; the country is subject to the kingdom of Kāpiśī.
The land abounds in mountains and forests, and crops are sown according to the seasons.
The climate is slightly cold, and the customs are rugged and fierce.
The people are impetuous and violent by nature, and their aspirations are base and corrupt.
The spoken language is mostly similar to that of Central India.
They venerate both heterodox and orthodox teachings and do not favor the study of arts or sciences.
There are several dozen monasteries, many of which are dilapidated and in ruins; the monks, numbering over three hundred, all study the Mahāyāna teachings.
There are five deva temples, mostly belonging to the ash-smearing heretics (Pāśupatas).
Not far to the south of the city is an old monastery where the Tathāgata in the past preached the Dharma, providing instruction, benefit, and joy, thereby awakening all sentient beings.
Beside it are the sites where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation.

According to local tradition, one hears that to the west of this country lies the kingdom of Kāṅ-na (Kāñcī), situated among the valleys of great mountains; it has its own separate rulers and lacks a supreme sovereign.
There are many sheep and horses; among them are fine steeds that are magnificent in form and rare breeds found in few other lands, prized by neighboring regions.

Proceeding further northwest from here, crossing great mountains and traversing broad rivers, passing through small towns and cities for over two thousand li, one leaves the borders of India and arrives at the kingdom of Jāguḍa, also called the kingdom of Jāli.
*The Great Tang Dynasty Record of the Western Regions*, Scroll Eleven: The Kingdom of Siṃhala.
This was formerly the Kingdom of Siṃhala;
it is also called the Kingdom of Aśoka.
This is South India.
Its land abounds in rare treasures;
it is also called the Isle of Jewels.

In the past, there was a transformation body of Śākyamuni Buddha named Saṃghala, who was endowed with all virtues; because the people of the country honored him as their king, the nation itself was also named after him, Saṃghala.
By means of his great supernormal powers, he shattered the great iron city, extinguished the rākṣasīs, and rescued those in peril.
Thereupon, he established a capital and built towns, transforming and guiding this region and spreading the true teaching.
Upon entering parinirvāṇa, he left behind his tooth relic here in this land; as adamantine and firm, it remains undestroyed through the kalpas.
Its precious radiance shines afar, like stars sparkling in the void, like the moon gleaming at night, and like the sun gracing the day.
Whenever prayers were offered for protection against calamities, the responses came as swiftly as an echo.
When the state suffered from famine, drought, or other portents of disaster, his sincere and earnest supplications were met with the arrival of auspicious signs.
The present-day Mount Sirīṣa is the ancient kingdom of Siṃhala.

Beside the royal palace stands a Tooth Relic Shrine (Dantadhātu-vihāra), adorned with various jewels and resplendent with brilliant light; for generations, its veneration has been maintained without decline.

Now, King Arjuna of Kapiśa is a native of Su-lu; he venerates non-Buddhist heretics and shows no respect for the Buddha-dharma. Tyrannical and rebellious, he takes no pity on his people and treats the Buddha’s tooth relic with irreverent contempt.
In the third year of the Yongle era of the Great Ming, the Emperor dispatched the eunuch attendant Zheng He to that kingdom to present incense and flowers as offerings.
Zheng He exhorted King Arakunaer to revere and uphold Buddhism and to distance himself from non-Buddhist paths.
The king became enraged and was about to inflict harm upon him, but Zheng He perceived his plot and departed.

Later, he was again dispatched to bestow gifts upon various foreign kingdoms; when he went to pay his respects and receive the imperial gifts from the King of Ceylon, the king grew even more arrogant and disrespectful, seeking to plot the murder of the envoy.
Fifty thousand troops were employed to fell trees and block the road, while other forces were divided to raid the sea-going vessels.
They intended to converge at the foot of the pass, having previously prepared their stratagem.

When Zheng He and his men realized this, they hurriedly turned their ships back; however, the path was already completely blocked, so they secretly dispatched men out, who were then met by the naval forces defending it.
With three thousand troops, he entered the royal city by night via a secret path and held it.

The barbarian soldiers who had seized the sea-going ships, together with the local barbarians within the kingdom, then came from all four directions to attack, surrounding him in several layers of encirclement.

After six days of siege, He and his men captured its king; at dawn they opened the gates, cleared timber to make a path, and proceeded twenty-odd li while fighting as they went, finally reaching the boat at dusk.

When they proceeded to formally invite the Buddha’s tooth relic onto the ship, its spiritual wonders were extraordinary and its radiance was dazzling; as previously described, a thunderous roar shook the air, causing those who saw it from afar to hide themselves in awe.

Having traversed the great ocean for a total of several hundred thousand li, he encountered neither wind nor waves, proceeding as if treading upon level ground; though fierce dragons and malevolent fish emerged in profusion before him, they caused him no harm at all.
Everyone on board the ship was safe and happy.
On the ninth day of the seventh month in the ninth year of the Yongle era, they arrived at the capital.
The Emperor ordered that a magnificent sandalwood Vajra throne be prepared within the Imperial City to enshrine it.
Thus he cultivated offerings to benefit sentient beings and pray for the welfare of the common people, thereby performing immeasurable meritorious deeds.
*The Great Tang Dynasty Record of the Western Regions*, Volume XII, Twenty-two Kingdoms,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by imperial decree.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Bianji of Dazongchi Monastery: The Twenty-two Kingdoms. 1. Jāguḍa (漕矩吒) 2. Vṛji-sasthāna (弗栗恃薩儻那) 3. Andarab (安呾羅縛) 4.

Khost (闊悉多) 5. Wakhan (活) 6. Munjan (瞢揵) 7. Arni (阿利尼) 8. Garlok (曷邏胡) 9. Kirasmar (訖栗瑟摩) 10. Balūr (鉢利曷) 11. Himatala (呬摩呾羅) 12. Badakshan (鉢鐸創那) 13. Yamgān (淫薄健) 14. Kulūna (屈居勿反浪拏) 15. Dharmasthiti (達摩悉鐵帝) 16. Śākani (尸棄尼) 17. Śami (商彌) 18. Kāpiśī (朅盤陀) 19. Uṣa (烏鎩) 20. Kāśa (佉沙) 21. Cukuka (斫句迦) 22. Gostana (瞿薩旦那) Jāguḍa (漕矩吒): This kingdom is over seven thousand *li* in circuit.

The capital city of the kingdom is named Ho-si-na (Hastināpura), with a circumference of more than thirty *li*; alternatively, they reside in the city of Ho-sa-lo (Hastisāla), which is also more than thirty *li* in circumference; both are steep, formidable, and well-fortified.
The mountains and rivers are winding and majestic; the fields and mounds are broad and elevated.

Grains are sown in their proper seasons, and winter wheat grows in great abundance. The vegetation is lush and spreading, and flowers and fruits flourish. It is well-suited for saffron and produces *xingqu* grass; this grass grows by the Loma River in India.
In the city of Kāśī, there are fountains and streams that gush forth, which the people of the country benefit from using to irrigate their fields.
The climate is bitterly cold, and frost and snow are frequent.
The nature of the people is flighty and impulsive, and their dispositions are largely deceitful.
They are fond of learning the arts and possess many technical skills; they listen without achieving clear understanding, yet can recite tens of thousands of words daily.
Their written characters and spoken language differ from those of other nations.
They indulge in much empty talk and achieve little in actual fact.
Although they sacrifice to a hundred deities, they revere and honor the Triple Gem.
There are several hundred monasteries with more than ten thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna.
Now the King is pure in faith, his lineage having been inherited for generations; he is dedicated to promoting supreme merit, being both quick-witted and fond of learning.
There are more than ten stūpas erected by King Aśoka.
There are several dozen deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
It is estimated that non-Buddhists are numerous, and their followers are extremely flourishing; they revere Śiva (the "Sū-xí" character, pronounced Shì, with the second tone for the final syllable).

This deity formerly migrated from Mount Aruṇa in the kingdom of Kāpiśī to reside within the Śunahila Mountains on the southern border of this country. There he displays his majesty and exerts his power, acting with violence and malevolence; those who seek him with faith have their wishes fulfilled, while those who treat him with contempt invite calamity.
Consequently, those far and near revere and look up to him, while those high and low stand in awe and respect.

Rulers, ministers, officials, and commoners from neighboring lands of differing customs gather each year on auspicious days without prior appointment; some bring gold, silver, and rare treasures, while others offer oxen, horses, and domesticated animals, vying with one another to present offerings and collectively manifest their sincere devotion.

Therefore, gold and silver were spread upon the ground, and sheep and horses filled the valleys; no one dared to covet them, as everyone devoted themselves solely to practicing charity and making offerings.

They venerated non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthikas) and disciplined their minds through ascetic practices. A celestial deity bestowed magical spells (vidyā-mantras) upon them, which the non-Buddhists followed with great efficacy; they treated illnesses, and many benefited from being cured.
Traveling north from here for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Vṛjiṣaṭhaṇā.
The country of Vṛjiṣaṭhaṇā is more than two thousand *li* from east to west and more than one thousand *li* from south to north.
The capital city of the kingdom is named Hupinā; it is over twenty li in circuit.
The local products and customs are the same as those of the country of Jāguḍa, though the language differs.
The climate is cold and biting, and the people are fierce by nature.
The king is of Turkic descent; he has deep faith in the Triple Gem, values learning, and honors virtue.

From this country, traveling northeast across mountains and rivers, one passes through dozens of small border towns and cities of Kapisa until reaching the great mountain pass of Varṣika on the Great Snowy Mountains.
The mountain ridges are exceedingly lofty and steep; the perilous paths are precarious and prone to collapse. The trails wind and meander, and the crags and grottoes turn back upon one another.
Sometimes one enters deep valleys, and sometimes one ascends high precipices; even in the height of summer, the ground remains frozen, and travelers must pass by cutting through the ice.
After traveling for three days, they finally reached the summit of the ridge.
A piercing cold wind blew fiercely, and accumulated snow filled the valleys; travelers passing through found it impossible to set foot there even for a moment.
Even soaring falcons cannot pass beyond it; only after treading with their feet and toes do they take flight, looking down upon the various mountains as if they were mere anthills.
Within Jambudvīpa, this mountain range is preeminent in height.
Its summit is treeless, consisting only of many stone peaks that stand clustered and lean against one another, appearing as dense as a forest.
After traveling for another three days, they finally descended from the mountain range and reached the country of Andarāb.
The country of Andarāb was formerly the territory of the kingdom of Tukhāra.
It is over three thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the country is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit.
It has no great sovereign and is subject to the Turks.
The hills and mounds are continuous, while the rivers and fields are narrow and confined.
The climate is bitterly cold, with fierce winds and driving snows.
Crops grow in abundance, and it is well-suited for flowers and fruits.
The nature of the people is fierce and violent, and their customs lack social order.

They do not understand the distinction between sin and merit, nor do they value study or learning; they devote themselves solely to the worship of spirit shrines and have little faith in the Buddha-dharma.
There are three monasteries with several dozen monks, all of whom follow and practice the teachings of the Mahāsāṃghika school.
There is a stūpa there, which was built by King Aśoka.
From here, traveling northwest, entering a valley and crossing a mountain range, and passing through several small towns for over four hundred li, one arrives at the country of Kustana.
The country of Kustana was formerly the territory of the kingdom of Tukhāra.
Its circumference is reduced by one thousand *li*.
The capital city of the state is over ten *li* in circuit.
It has no great sovereign and is subject to the Turks.
The mountains are many and the rivers narrow; it is windy and cold.
Grain crops are abundant, and flowers and fruits flourish.
The people are fierce and violent by nature, and their customs lack legal codes.
There are three monasteries, and the number of monks is small.
From here, traveling northwest across mountains and valleys and passing through various cities and towns for over three hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Huo.
Huoguo (Huoguo) is the site of the ancient kingdom of Tukhāra.
It is over two thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the country is over twenty *li* in circuit.
They have no separate sovereign and are subject to the Turks.
The highlands are level and plain; crops are sown in their proper seasons, vegetation flourishes, and flowers and fruits abound.
The climate is harmonious and pleasant, and the customs are simple and honest.
By nature, the people are impetuous and fierce; they wear felt and coarse woolen garments.
Most believe in the Triple Gem, while few serve various deities.
There are more than ten monasteries with several hundred monks who study and practice both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.
Its king is of Turkic origin; he governs the various small kingdoms south of the Iron Gate, living in migratory nomadic fashion and never remaining permanently in one city.
From here, one enters the Pamir Mountains to the east.

As for the Pamir Mountains, they are situated in the center of Jambudvīpa; to the south they join the Great Snowy Mountains, to the north they reach the Hot Sea and the Thousand Springs, to the west they extend to the Kingdom of Hu (Kashgar), and to the east to the Kingdom of Wushai (Wakhan); from east to west and south to north, they span several thousand *li* in each direction.
The cliffs and ridges number in the hundreds, and the secluded valleys are steep and precipitous; ice and snow accumulate there constantly, and the cold winds are fierce and piercing.
Because it produces much leek (cong), it is called the Leek Range (Congling);
furthermore, because the mountain cliffs are a vibrant green, it was named accordingly.
Traveling eastward for more than one hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Maṅgala.
The kingdom of Maṅgala is the former territory of the kingdom of Tukhāra.
It is more than four hundred *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is fifteen or sixteen *li* in circuit.
Its soil, produce, and customs are largely the same as those of the Huo country.
It has no great sovereign and is subject to the Turks.
To the north, it reaches the country of A-li-ni (Aḷina).
The country of A-li-ni is the former territory of Tukhāra.
It borders both banks of the Oxus River (Vakṣu) and is over three hundred li in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit.
Its soil, products, and customs are largely the same as those of the Huo Kingdom.
To the east, it borders the country of Haerhu.
The country of Hushu (Halo-hu) was formerly the territory of the country of Tukhāra.
It borders the Oxus River to the north and is more than two hundred *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the country is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit.
The local products and customs are largely the same as those of Huo-guo.
Crossing steep ridges and traversing gorges and valleys from Mengjian-guo to the east, passing through several riverside towns for over three hundred li, one arrives at Kirishma-guo.
The country of Kṛṣma is the former territory of Tukhāra.
It is over ten *li* from east to west and more than three hundred *li* from south to north.
The capital city of the kingdom is fifteen or sixteen *li* in circuit.
As for its natural products and customs, they are largely the same as those of the country of Mung-kan, though its people differ in being violent, ignorant, and wicked by nature.
To the north it reaches the kingdom of Bālika.
The kingdom of Bālika was formerly the territory of the country of Tukhāra.
It is over one hundred *li* from east to west and over three hundred *li* from south to north.
The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty li in circuit.
The products of the soil and the customs of the people are largely the same as those of the kingdom of Ki-li-ssu-mo (Khaśa).
Traveling east from the kingdom of Ki-li-ssu-mo, crossing mountains and rivers for more than three hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of He-mo-ta-lo (Himatala).
The country of Himatala: Himatala is the ancient territory of Tukhāra.
It is over three thousand li in circuit.
The mountains and rivers wind and meander, and the soil is fertile.
The soil is suitable for grain cultivation, with an abundance of winter wheat; a hundred species of plants flourish and various fruits grow in great profusion.
The climate is bitterly cold, the people are violent and impulsive, they are ignorant of the retribution of sin and merit, and their physical appearance is coarse and unsightly.
Their conduct and deportment, as well as their clothing—felt, fur, and coarse wool—are quite similar to those of the Turks.
As for the women, they wear wooden horn headdresses over three feet high, with two prongs at the front:

the upper prong represents the father and the lower prong represents the mother. Depending on which parent has passed away first, one prong is removed; if both the maternal uncle and the parents-in-law have died, the horned headdress is discarded entirely.
Its former powerful kingdom was ruled by a king of the Śākya clan; to the west of the Pamir Mountains, many [tribes] were seen to have submitted to him.
