As its borders adjoined those of the Turks, it subsequently became infected by their customs and suffered their incursions; thus, in order to defend its territory, the people of this country fled to foreign lands, and within dozens of fortified cities, they each established their own rulers, living in felt tents and woolen curtains as they migrated back and forth.
To the west it borders the kingdom of Kṛṣṇa.
Traveling eastward for more than two hundred *li* through the valleys, one arrives at the kingdom of Badakshāna.
The kingdom of Badakshāna is the ancient territory of the country of Tukhāra.
It is over two thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is situated atop a mountain cliff and is six or seven *li* in circumference.
The mountains and rivers wind and flow in succession, while sand and stone spread everywhere.
The soil is suitable for beans and wheat, and it abounds in fruits such as grapes, walnuts, pears, and crabapples.
The climate is bitterly cold, and the people are by nature fierce and violent.
Their customs lack ritual propriety, and they are ignorant of learning and the arts.
Their appearance is coarse and humble, and they mostly wear felt and coarse woolen garments.
There are three or four monasteries, with few monks.
The king is simple and sincere by nature, and he has deep faith in the Triple Gem.
From here, traveling southeast through mountains and valleys for more than two hundred li, one arrives at the country of Yinvoben (Yinbujian).
The country of Yinvoben was formerly the territory of the kingdom of Duhualuo (Duhuoluo).
It is over one thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is over ten *li* in circuit.
Mountain ridges are continuous, and the rivers, fields, and plains are narrow and confined.
Regarding the products of the soil, the suitability of the climate, and the differences in human nature, they are the same as those of Bāṭṛkaṇa, with only slight variations in their language.
The king is tyrannical and violent, and lacks discernment between good and evil.
From here, proceeding southeast across ridges and over valleys along perilous narrow paths for more than three hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Kuluṇḍa.
The Kingdom of Kulūta: The Kingdom of Kulūta is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra.
It is over two thousand *li* in circuit.
Its terrain, mountains, rivers, climate, and seasons are the same as those of the kingdom of Yinvoben (Yaudheya).
Lacking social laws and regulations, the nature of the people is base and violent.
Most do not cultivate merit, and few have faith in the Buddha-dharma.
Their appearance is ugly and wretched; most wear felt and coarse woolen garments.
There is a mountain crag from which much refined gold is produced; one must cleave and split its stones before it can be obtained.
As the monasteries are few, the monks are also sparse.
The king was simple and sincere, and he venerated and honored the Triple Gem.

From here, traveling northeast, ascending mountains and entering valleys along a difficult and perilous route for over five hundred *li*, one reaches the country of Dharmasthiti, also known as Zhēnxiàn or Hùmì.
The Kingdom of Darmaṣṭīra: The kingdom of Darmaṣṭīra lies between two mountains; it is the site of the ancient kingdom of Tukhāra.
It measures more than fifteen or sixteen hundred *li* from east to west, and four or five *li* in breadth from south to north, narrowing in some places to no more than one *li*.
Bordering the Vārakṣu River, the terrain winds and turns in many curves; the hills rise and fall, while sand and gravel spread across the land. The cold wind is piercingly fierce.
Only wheat and beans are cultivated; there are few forests, and flowers and fruits are scarce.
It produces many excellent horses; although the horses are small in stature, they are resilient for long-distance travel and fording rivers.
The local customs lack propriety and righteousness, and the people are by nature fierce and violent.
Their physical appearance is coarse and unrefined, and their clothing consists of felt and coarse wool.
The eyes of the people are mostly emerald green, which differs from those of other countries.
There are more than ten monasteries, but the number of monks is small.
The city of Hūṇḍa is the capital of the kingdom.
Within it is a monastery, established by a former king of this country; he carved out the cliffs and settled the valleys to construct its halls and buildings.
In former times, this country had not yet received the Buddhist teachings, but worshipped only heterodox deities; several hundred years ago, the propagation of the Dharma first began here.
Initially, the crown prince of this kingdom fell ill; though medical arts were exhaustively applied, his condition only worsened and did not improve.
The king then went in person to a celestial shrine to offer worship and pray for deliverance.
Then the presiding priest of the shrine spoke on behalf of the deity:
"He shall surely recover; there is no need for further concern.
Hearing this, the King was filled with joy and comfort, and he turned his carriage back to return home.
On the road he encountered a śramaṇa whose deportment was dignified and worthy of admiration; struck by his appearance and attire, he asked where he had come from.
This śramaṇa had already realized the fruits of sagehood and, wishing to propagate the Buddha-dharma, had assumed this outward form.
He then replied to the king,
saying, "I am a disciple of the Tathāgata, known as a bhikṣu.
As the king was filled with anxiety, he immediately asked first:
"My son is stricken with illness; whether he lives or dies is yet uncertain.
The śramaṇa replied, "The King's ancestral spirits may be raised, but your beloved son is difficult to save."
The king said, "The celestial deity claimed he would not die, yet the śramaṇa says he must come to an end; how can the words of such a person who deceives the world be trusted?
Before long, when he arrived at the palace, his beloved son was already dead.
He concealed the matter and did not announce the death; instead, he questioned the presiding deity, who still said, "He has not died;
his ailment shall surely recover.
The King then flew into a rage, bound the presiding deity, and rebuked him, saying:
"You all dwell together in a crowd, perpetuating evil, and arrogantly exercise power and fortune.
My son is already dead, yet you still claim he will recover; such delusory deception—who could possibly endure it?"
"It is fitting to execute the presiding deity and utterly destroy the sacred temple.
Thereupon, they killed the presiding deity, removed the divine image, and cast them into the Bāhū river.
Turning their carriage back for the return journey, they again encountered a śramaṇa; seeing him, they felt reverence and joy, and bowing their heads, they apologized, saying:

"Since time immemorial we have lacked the guidance of ignorance and have stood upon the path of error; though this state of decadence has long endured, its transformation now rests with you. We pray that you will deign to look upon us and descend to our humble abode."
The śramaṇa accepted the invitation and followed him to the inner palace.
Once the burial of his son was completed, he said to the śramaṇa:

"Human affairs are entangled and one wanders through the cycle of birth and death. My son was stricken with illness, and when I asked about his fate—whether he would depart or remain—the spirit spoke falsely, saying he would surely recover."
"Previously, I received your instructions, which proved indeed not false. Thus, these teachings are worthy of veneration; I only pray that you will show compassion and guide this deluded disciple.
He then requested that the śramaṇa survey the site for the monastery and, following its prescribed dimensions, establish it accordingly.
From that time onward, Buddhism began to flourish.
Thus, the vihāra within the monastery was built for an arhat.
Inside the great vihāra of the monastery is a stone Buddha image, above which hangs a circular canopy of gold and copper, adorned with various precious gems.
When people circumambulate, the canopy likewise turns with them; when people stop, the canopy stops—its spiritual discernment is unfathomable.
I have heard from the elders that some say it is sustained by the power of the Sage’s vows, while others claim it is produced by the secret artifice of mechanical devices.
Observing its halls and buildings, the stone walls are firm and steep.
Examining various accounts, no one knows the true record.
Crossing the great mountains of this country, one reaches the kingdom of Śrīkṣetra to the north.
The country of Śrīkaṇṭha is over two thousand li in circuit.
Its capital city is five or six li in circuit.
Mountains and rivers are interconnected, and sand and stone cover the plains.
There is an abundance of pulse and wheat, but little grain cultivation; the forests and trees are sparse, and flowers and fruits are scarce.

The climate is bitterly cold, and the customs are fierce and violent; they are accustomed to slaughter and intent on theft, ignorant of propriety and righteousness, and unable to distinguish between good and evil.
They are deluded regarding future blessings and calamities and fear the disasters of the present life.
Their physical appearance is coarse and ugly, and they wear garments of coarse woolen cloth.
Their script is the same as that of the Tukhāra kingdom, though their spoken language differs.
Crossing the Great Mountains to the south of the country of Tāmralipti, one arrives at the country of Śāmbī.
The country of Śāmbī is two thousand five or six hundred li in circuit.
Mountains and rivers alternate with one another, and mounds rise and fall.
All types of grain are planted; beans and wheat are abundant, as are *pútáo* fruits. It produces realgar, which is obtained by excavating cliffs and splitting rock.
The mountain deity is violent and malevolent, frequently causing disasters; once sacrifices have been offered, one may enter and travel about in peace and safety.
If prayers are not made, wind and hail will break forth in fury.
The climate is cold and the customs are hasty.
The people are simple and honest by nature, yet their social mores lack propriety and righteousness; their intelligence and strategy are narrow and limited, and their skills and talents are shallow.
Their written script is the same as that of the Tukhāra country, but their spoken language is different.
There are many woolen garments and coarse blankets.
Its king is of the Śākya clan; he reveres and honors the Buddha-dharma, and the people of the country follow his transformation, all being pure in their faith.
There are two monasteries, but the number of monks is small.
To the northeast of the kingdom’s borders, crossing mountains and valleys and traversing perilous and treacherous terrain for more than seven hundred li, one reaches the Pamir Valley.
It is over a thousand li from east to west and more than a hundred li from south to north; its narrowest sections do not exceed ten li in width.
Situated between the two snow mountains, the cold winds are piercing and fierce; snow falls in spring and summer, and gales blow day and night.

The soil is saline and alkaline, abounding in gravel and stones, such that cultivation yields no growth and vegetation is sparse; consequently, the land has become desolate and abandoned, with no human habitation.

Within the Pamer River lies a great dragon lake, measuring over three hundred li from east to west and over fifty li from south to north. Situated within the Great Onion Range (Pamir) and at the center of Jambudvīpa, this location is the highest of all.
The water is clear and limpid like a bright mirror, its depth unfathomable; it is tinged with a dark blue-black hue and possesses an exceptionally sweet flavor.

Dwelling beneath its surface are crocodiles, chis, fish, dragons, soft-shelled turtles, alligators, tortoises, and snapping turtles; floating upon it are mandarin ducks, wild geese, swans, *shu*, and *bo* ducks. The large eggs of these various birds are cast as shells upon the wilderness, in marshy thickets, or upon sandy islets.

A great stream branches off from the west of the lake; flowing westward, it reaches the eastern border of the kingdom of Dharmaṣṭīra and joins with the Vakṣu River, flowing westward together. Therefore, to the right of this point, all waters flow westward.

A great current flows from the east of the lake; reaching the western border of the kingdom of Kāśa in the northeast, it joins with the Sindhu River and flows eastward. Therefore, to the left of this point, all waters flow to the east.
South of the Pamer River and beyond the mountains lies the kingdom of Bolor, which abounds in gold and silver; the color of the gold is like fire.
From this river, traveling southeast, one must ascend mountains and traverse perilous terrain; for many *li* there are no people on the road, and it is filled only with ice and snow.
After traveling more than five hundred *li*, he arrived at the kingdom of Kāpiśī.
The kingdom of Kāpiśī is over two thousand *li* in circuit.
The capital city of the kingdom is built upon a ridge of large rocks, with its back toward the Sītā River, and it is over twenty *li* in circuit.
The mountain ridges are continuous and the rivers and plains are narrow and confined.
Grains are scarce, while beans and wheat are abundant. Forests and trees are sparse, and flowers and fruits are few.
The plains and marshes are mostly ruins, and the cities and towns are desolate and empty.
The common people lack propriety and righteousness, and few among them pursue learning or the arts.
By nature they are fierce and violent, and they are also robust and courageous in strength.
Their appearance is coarse and unsightly, and their clothing consists of felt and coarse wool.
The script and language are largely the same as those of the country of Kucha;
however, the people are known for their sincerity and faith, and they venerate and revere the Buddha-dharma.
There are more than ten monasteries with over five hundred monks, who study the teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna.
Now the King is pure and sincere, revering and honoring the Triple Gem; his demeanor is serene and elegant, and he is devoted to learning.
Since the founding of the state, many years have passed.
He styled himself Zhìnà Típó Qúntuólá, which in the language of the Tang means "Han Rìtiān Zhǒng" (Chinese Sun-Divinity Seed).
The ancestors of this country lived in a desolate valley within the Pamir Mountains.

Formerly, the King of Pārśva married a consort from the land of Han; when he escorted her back here, he encountered military turmoil and the roads to the east and west were cut off. Consequently, he placed the princess on a solitary peak that was extremely steep and precipitous, accessible only by climbing the cliffs up and down. He established a comprehensive guard to keep watch, patrolling by day and night.
After three months had passed, the bandits were finally pacified and he wished to set out on the road home; however, the woman was already pregnant.
The envoy was filled with fear and said to his attendants:
"The King commanded me to fetch his bride, yet we have encountered this rebellion. Lodging in the wilderness by the desolate river, we cannot plan for even tomorrow."
"Moved by our King’s virtue, the demonic miasma has already been stilled; I am now about to return to my kingdom, yet my wife is pregnant.
Looking upon this, I am filled with anxiety, for I do not know where death may strike. It would be well to cast blame upon the primary culprit, so that he may later be executed."
The questioning was tumultuous, and the truth could not be ascertained.
At that time, the lady’s attendant said to the envoy, "Do not blame one another;
this is merely a spiritual communion."
"Every day at noon, a man riding a horse emerges from the solar disk and meets here.
The envoy asked, "If that is so,
how can one be cleared of this crime?"
"If we return, we will surely be executed; if we stay, they will come to attack us. Since this is the case whether we advance or retreat, what course of action is appropriate?
They all said, "This matter is no small one; who would submit to such severe punishment?"
"Exiled from our borders to await our punishment, we shall wait for the dawn and the dusk.
Thereupon, they built a palace and a guest hall atop Stone Peak, measuring over three hundred paces in circumference.
They constructed a city wall surrounding the palace, established a woman as their sovereign, and instituted officials and laws.
When the time arrived, she gave birth to a son of exquisite and beautiful countenance.
The mother governed the affairs of state while the son assumed the imperial title.

He could fly through the void and command the winds and clouds; his majestic virtue extended afar, and his influence and teachings reached distant lands, such that neighboring regions and foreign nations did not fail to submit as vassals.
When that king reached the end of his life, he was buried in a stone chamber within a great mountain more than one hundred li to the southeast of this city.

His corpse has become mummified and remains undecayed even now; it resembles the emaciated form of a person and sits upright as if asleep. One occasionally changes his clothing, and incense and flowers are constantly placed before him.
Their descendants have flourished through successive generations down to the present day.
Because their maternal ancestors were people of the land of Han and their paternal ancestors were of the race of the Sun God (Nippon-ten), they style themselves the "Race of the Han and the Sun God."
However, as for their royal lineage, their appearance is similar to that of the Central Kingdom; they wear square crowns on their heads and clothe themselves in foreign (Hu) garments.
Later generations have declined, being pressed by powerful neighboring states.
When King Aśoka ascended the throne, he constructed a stūpa within his palace.

Later, the king moved his residence to the northeastern corner of the palace and converted the former palace into a saṃghārāma for the venerable master Kumāralāta; its terraces and pavilions were lofty and spacious, and the Buddha images therein were majestic and awe-inspiring.

The Venerable was a native of the kingdom of Takṣaśilā. From his youth, he was exceptionally intelligent; having early departed from the secular world, he applied his mind to the classical scriptures and settled his spirit in the profound principles. Daily, he would recite thirty-two thousand words and, concurrently, write thirty-two thousand characters.

Thus, he was able to excel his contemporaries in learning, achieving renown throughout the age; he established the True Dharma and crushed heterodox views. His lofty discourses were pure and eminent, and there was no difficult question that he could not answer; consequently, he was universally esteemed and honored throughout the five regions of India.
The treatises he composed numbered in the dozens, all of which were widely propagated and studied by everyone; he was, in fact, the founding master of the Sautrāntika school.
At that time, there were Āryadeva in the south, Nāgārjuna in the west, and Kumāralāta in the north, alongside Aśvaghoṣa in the east—these four were known as the "Four Suns Illuminating the World."

Therefore, when the king heard of the Venerable One’s eminent virtue, he raised an army and mobilized his people to invade the kingdom of Takṣaśilā; having subdued it, he established this monastery to manifest his reverence and provide a place for veneration.

Traveling more than three hundred li southeast from the city, one arrives at a great stone cliff where there are two stone chambers; in each, an arhat has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).

He sits upright and is difficult to move; his form appears that of a frail person, yet his skin and bones remain incorruptible. Having already lived for over seven hundred years, his beard and hair grow continuously, so the assembly of monks shaves his hair and changes his robes every year.
To the northeast of the great cliff, one crosses ridges and traverses dangerous terrain for over two hundred li to reach Bontongrangshara (in the language of Tang, "Blessed Abode").
It is situated on an eastern spur of the Pamir Mountains amidst four surrounding peaks; the area covers more than a hundred *qǐng*, with the center sinking slightly lower.
Snow accumulates there throughout both winter and summer, and the winds blow with piercing cold.
The fields are saline and barren, so crops do not flourish; lacking forests and trees, there is only sparse, low-lying grass.
Although it was hot during the day, there was much wind and snow; as soon as people entered, clouds and mist would arise, causing great hardship for the traveling merchants due to these perils.

I have heard from the elders that in the past there was a merchant with more than ten thousand followers and several thousand camels. Carrying their goods in pursuit of profit, they encountered wind and snow, and both men and animals perished.

At that time, there was a great arhat in the kingdom of Kāpiśī who, observing from afar, took pity on their perilous distress. Desiring to employ his supernatural powers to rescue those submerged in calamity, he had just arrived at this place when the merchants had already perished.

Thereupon, he gathered all manner of rare treasures and assembled everything he possessed; he constructed dwellings, accumulated wealth and provisions, purchased land from neighboring states, and sold households in border cities to provide relief for those traveling to and fro.
Consequently, the traveling merchants and caravans now all receive comprehensive provisions.

From here, proceeding eastward down the eastern ridge of the Pamir Mountains, one ascends perilous peaks and crosses deep ravines; the mountain paths are treacherous and winds and snow follow one after another. After traveling more than eight hundred li, one emerges from the Pamirs and arrives at the kingdom of Wusha (Uṣa).
The Kingdom of Uḍeṇa: The kingdom of Uḍeṇa is over one thousand *li* in circuit.
Its capital city is over ten *li* in circuit and borders the Sindhu River to the south.
The soil is fertile, crops are abundant, forests are lush, and flowers and fruits grow in great profusion.
Various types of jade abound, including white jade, black jade, and green jade.
The seasonal cycles are harmonious, and wind and rain follow their proper courses.
The customs lack ritual propriety and righteousness; the people are by nature fierce and unruly, prone to guile and deception, and possess little sense of shame.
Their written characters and spoken language are largely the same as those of the country of Kucha.
Their appearance is ugly and wretched, and they wear skins and coarse woolens for clothing;
nevertheless, they are able to revere, believe in, and honor the Buddha-dharma.
There are more than ten monasteries with fewer than a thousand monks, who study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hinayana teachings.
For several hundred years, the royal lineage has been extinct; there is no separate sovereign, and the country is subject to the rule of Kapiśa.
More than two hundred li west of the city, one reaches a great mountain.

Its atmosphere is dense and imposing; clouds arise from its rocks as they are struck by the wind. The cliffs and precipices are towering and jagged, appearing on the verge of collapsing yet not yet fallen.
At its summit stands a stūpa of magnificent and extraordinary construction.

According to local tradition, several hundred years ago, a mountain cliff collapsed, revealing within it a bhikṣu sitting with eyes closed. His stature was immense, his appearance withered and emaciated, and his hair and beard hung down, covering his shoulders and veiling his face.
A hunter who had seen him reported it to the king, and the king personally went to observe and pay his respects.
The people of the capital, both men and women, arrived unbidden; they burned incense and scattered flowers, vying with one another to offer worship.
The king said:
"Who is this person?
How magnificent he is!"
A bhikṣu replied:
"This one with long, hanging hair and beard, yet wearing the kāṣāya robe, is an Arhat who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).

Now, those who enter the meditative absorption of cessation have previously set a limit; some say it is upon hearing the sound of the *ghanṭī*, while others say it is when waiting for the light of the sun to shine—once such a stimulus occurs, they arise from that concentration."
If there were no physical sustenance, they would remain silent and unmoving; sustained by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), their bodies would not undergo decay.
However, the substance of solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) perishes as soon as one emerges from concentration.
"It would be appropriate to pour ghee and oil over it to make it moist, and only then strike it to awaken the settled mind.
The King said, "Is this so?"
He then struck the *gandi*.
As its sound barely resonated, this arhat suddenly looked up with wide-open eyes;
after a long while, he said, "Who are you people?"
"You have a most humble appearance and are clad in monastic robes?
He replied, "I am a bhikṣu."
He asked, "Indeed,
where is my teacher, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, now?
He replied:
"His entry into Great Nirvāṇa has already been long ago.
Upon hearing this, he closed his eyes and, filled with regretful longing, immediately asked again:
"Has the Tathāgata Śākyamuni appeared in the world?"
He replied, "The one who manifested his numinous spirit to guide the world has already entered parinirvāṇa.

Upon hearing this, he bowed his head again; after a long time, he rose, ascended into the void, and displayed supernatural transformations, transforming himself into fire to cremate his own body, leaving his remains to fall to the earth.
The king collected his bones and erected a stūpa.

From there, traveling north for over five hundred li through mountainous wastes and desolate wilderness, he reached the kingdom of Khosta (formerly called Shule), which was named after its capital city.
The correct pronunciation should be Śrīkṛtati;
the Sūle (Khotan) term is still somewhat corrupted.
The kingdom of Kāśa is over five thousand *li* in circuit.
The land consists mostly of sandy deserts with little arable soil.
Crops flourish in abundance, and flowers and fruits grow profusely.
It produces fine felt and coarse woolens, and its inhabitants are skilled in weaving fine cotton cloth, carpets, and rugs.
The climate is mild and pleasant, with wind and rain following their proper seasons.
The nature of the people is fierce and violent; their customs are full of guile and deceit. They hold little regard for ritual and righteousness, and their learning and arts are superficial.
Regarding their customs, when a child is born, its head is pressed flat; their appearance is coarse and vulgar, and they practice tattooing while having green eyes.
As for their script, it takes its model from India; although there have been deletions and corruptions, much of its original structure remains.
The language and intonation differ from those of other countries.
The people are sincere in their faith in the Buddha-dharma and diligently cultivate merit and virtue.
There are several hundred monasteries with more than ten thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna.
Because they did not investigate the underlying principles but mostly chanted the texts, there were many who could recite and master the Tripiṭaka as well as the *Vibhāṣā*.
From here, traveling southeast for more than five hundred li, crossing the Sītā River and over a great sandy ridge, one arrives at the country of Cīnabhukti (formerly called Juqu).
The Kingdom of Cīnakuṭa: The kingdom of Cīnakuṭa is over one thousand *li* in circuit.
Its capital city is over ten *li* in circuit; it is steep, lofty, and impregnable, and its registered households are numerous and prosperous.
The hills and mounds are continuous, and the ground is strewn with gravel and stones; it borders two rivers and is quite suitable for cultivation.
Grapes, pears, and crabapples grow there in great abundance.
The climate was windy and cold, and the people were volatile and violent.
Their customs were characterized solely by deceit and fraud, and they openly practiced robbery and theft.
Their script was the same as that of the kingdom of Kustana, though their spoken language differed.
Their adherence to ritual and righteousness is slight, and their learning and arts are shallow and superficial.
They place sincere faith in the Triple Gem and take pleasure in seeking merit and blessings.
There are several dozen monasteries, most of which have fallen into ruin; the remaining monks number over a hundred, and they study the Mahāyāna teachings.
On the southern frontier of the kingdom lies a great mountain, its cliffs and ridges towering and steep, its peaks and crags layered one upon another;
the vegetation withstands the cold, remaining lush through both spring and autumn;
the mountain streams are deep and rapid, with cascading waters pouring forth in all directions.
Cliffside niches and stone chambers are scattered like chess pieces across the crags and forests.
Many Indian practitioners of spiritual fruition, frequently exercising supernatural powers, travel great distances with ease to dwell and rest here.

Because there were many Arhats who attained parinirvāṇa here, there are numerous stūpas; even now, three Arhats still reside within a rocky cave, having entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). Their bodies appear emaciated, and their hair and beards grow constantly long, so the śramaṇas go there from time to time to shave them.
In this country, the number of Mahāyāna sūtra sections is particularly numerous; among all places where the Buddha-dharma has reached, none is more flourishing than this one.
There are some ten collections consisting of one hundred thousand stanzas each, and from these downward, the various streams are truly vast.

From here, proceeding eastward across ridges and over valleys for more than eight hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Kustana—translated into the language of Tang as "Earth-Milk," which is its elegant local appellation.
In the vernacular it is called the Kingdom of Huannuo; the Xiongnu call it Yudu; the various Hu peoples call it Xidan; and in India it is called Qu dan.
The old name, Yutian, is a corruption.
The Kingdom of Kustana: The kingdom of Kustana is over four thousand *li* in circuit.
Deserts and sand dunes occupy more than half its extent, while the arable land is narrow and confined.
It is suitable for grain cultivation and produces many varieties of fruit.
It produces woolen carpets and fine felt, and its inhabitants are skilled at spinning and weaving silk and gauze.
It also yields white jade and black jade.
The climate is mild and pleasant, though it is subject to whirling winds and flying dust.
The common people understand propriety and righteousness, and their natures are gentle and respectful.
They are fond of studying the classics and arts, and are broad-minded and proficient in various skills.
The populace is wealthy and happy, and all households live in peace and security with their established occupations.
The state prizes musical sounds, and its people delight in song and dance.
Few wear garments of fur, coarse wool, or felt; most dress in *si*, *zhou*, and white cotton cloth.
Their physical deportment conforms to ritual propriety, and their social customs are well-ordered.
Their written script and legal codes follow those of India; they have slightly modified their forms and styles, with some general evolution.
Their language differs from that of other nations, and they hold the Buddha-dharma in high esteem.
There are more than one hundred monasteries with over five thousand monks, most of whom study and practice the Mahāyāna teachings.
The king is highly skilled in martial arts and holds the Buddha-dharma in deep reverence; he claims to be a descendant of Vaiśravaṇa.
In ancient times, this country was desolate and uninhabited, and the god Vaiśravaṇa resided there.

After Prince Aśoka had his eyes gouged out in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā, King Aśoka, in a fit of rage, punished his ministers and exiled the noble clans to the north of the Snow Mountains, where they dwelt among the wilderness valleys.
The exiles, pursuing their livelihoods, reached this western frontier; they selected a chieftain of noble stature and enshrined him as their king.
At that time, the son of an emperor from the eastern lands, having been banished for his offenses, resided on this eastern frontier; urged by his subordinates, he likewise proclaimed himself king.
As the years accumulated, the teachings and customs became obstructed.
Each, while engaged in hunting, encountered others in the wilderness; there they inquired about their ancestral lineages and consequently vied for seniority.
His words were full of anger, and he immediately desired to engage in battle.
Someone advised him, saying:
"Why are you so hasty now?"
"Since we have engaged in this decisive battle while hunting, we have not yet exhausted our military prowess.
It would be appropriate to return and train our troops, then assemble again at an appointed time.
Thereupon, they turned their carriages back and returned to their respective kingdoms, where they inspected and trained their warhorses and supervised and encouraged their soldiers.
When the appointed day arrived, the armies met, their banners and drums facing one another.
On the morning of the battle, the Western Lord was at a disadvantage; [the victor] pursued the fleeing enemy and subsequently decapitated him.

The Eastern Lord, riding on his momentum for victory, gathered the remnants of the fallen state and moved the capital to a central location, where he was just beginning to construct city walls and moats.
Fearing that he lacked sufficient land and apprehensive that his undertaking might fail, he issued a proclamation far and wide, seeking anyone who understood the principles of geography.
At that time, there was a smearing-ash ascetic carrying a large gourd filled with water,
who approached and said, "I know the topography of the earth.
He then poured the water out in a winding stream, tracing its course until it returned to its starting point, after which he hurried away and suddenly vanished from sight.

Relying on that water-mark as a foundation for its walls and foundations, they were thus able to commence construction; this is where the kingdom was governed, and it is here that the current king has his capital.
The city is neither lofty nor steep, yet it is difficult to overcome in attack; from ancient times until now, no one has been able to conquer it.

That king had moved the capital and established his city; having accomplished great deeds in founding the state and pacifying the people, he was now advanced in years and approaching old age, yet he still lacked an heir and feared the extinction of his lineage.

Thereupon, he went to the abode of the deva Vaiśravaṇa to pray for an heir; from the forehead of the divine image, an infant emerged, and he carried him back in his carriage, whereupon the people of the country celebrated with joy.
Fearing that he would not live long because he did not drink milk, they immediately went to a shrine and earnestly requested him to be nourished there.
Suddenly, the ground before the deity rose up, forming the shape of a breast; the divine child suckled from it and thus grew to maturity.
With wisdom and valor illuminating the past and his moral influence spreading afar, he subsequently established a divine shrine to honor his ancestors.
From that time until the present, successive generations have maintained this tradition; as the rulers of the state, they have presided over the realm without losing their ancestral lineage.
Consequently, the divine temple now contains many rare treasures, and offerings and sacrifices are performed there without fail at their appointed times.
Because it was nourished by the milk of the earth, it became the name of the kingdom.

To the south of the royal city, at a distance of more than ten li, there is a great monastery (mahāvihāra) built by a former king of this country for the arhat Vairocana (translated into Chinese as Biàozhào, "Universal Illumination").
In the past, before the Buddha-dharma had yet reached this country, an Arhat came from the kingdom of Kaśmīra to this grove to sit in quietude and practice meditative concentration.
At that time, someone who saw him was struck by his appearance and attire, and reported the matter in full to the king.
The king then went there in person to observe his demeanor and said,
"Who are you, staying alone in this secluded forest?"
The Arhat said,
“I am a disciple of the Tathāgata, dwelling in seclusion and practicing meditative concentration.
Your Majesty should plant the seeds of merit by extensively praising the Buddha’s teachings, constructing a monastery, and summoning the assembly of monks.”
The king asked,
"What virtues does the Tathāgata possess, and what divine powers does he have, that you, though dwelling as a bird, diligently and with hardship follow his teachings?
He replied:
"The Tathāgata, out of compassion for the four modes of birth, guides those within the three realms; sometimes manifesting and sometimes concealing himself, he displays both birth and extinction.
Those who follow his Dharma transcend birth and death, while those who are deluded by his teaching remain entangled in the net of craving."
The King said, "It is truly as you have said;
the matter transcends mere discussion. Since you are called a Great Sage, please manifest your form for me.
Once I have been granted the opportunity to behold you, I shall establish [a monastery] for you, dedicating my heart with faith to propagate the teachings."
The Arhat said, "When a king builds a monastery, a spiritual response occurs once the work is completed.

If the King would indeed grant his request and construct a saṃghārāma, people from far and near would all gather; the Dharma assembly would be celebrated with joy, yet there would still be no *gaṇḍī* to strike for summoning the assembly.
The King said to the Arhat, "The monastery is now complete; where is the Buddha?
The Arhat replied:
"When one is sincere, the sagely discernment is not far off.

The King then made a formal request, whereupon he suddenly beheld a Buddha image descend from the sky and bestow a *ghanṭī* upon him; thereupon, he became filled with sincere faith and propagated the Buddhist teachings.
More than twenty li to the southwest of the royal city is Mount Gośṛṅga (translated into Chinese as "Ox Horn").
Two peaks rise up, and its cliffs and precipices are cut off on all four sides. Within these cliffs and valleys stands a monastery, where the Buddha image occasionally radiates brilliant light.

In the past, the Tathāgata once came to this place and briefly expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the sake of devas and humans; he prophesied that this land would establish a kingdom where the bequeathed teachings would be revered and upheld, and the Mahāyāna would be practiced and followed.

On a rocky crag of Ox-Horn Mountain there is a great stone chamber, within which resides an Arhat who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) to await Maitreya Buddha; for several hundred years, offerings have been made to him without interruption.

Recently, a cliff collapsed, blocking the entrance and path. The king raised an army wishing to clear away the fallen rocks, but immediately swarms of black bees flew out and stung the multitude with their venom; for this reason, the stone gate remains unclosed to this day.
More than ten li to the southwest of the royal city, there is the Dīrghabhāvana Monastery.
Within it stands a lacquered clay image of the Buddha, which originally came from the kingdom of Kuci and was established here.
Formerly, there was a minister in this country who was censured and lived in exile in Kuci, where he constantly paid homage to this image.

Later, when he was granted permission to return to his own country, he continued to offer his sincere devotion from afar. After midnight one night, the image suddenly arrived of its own accord. The man then donated his residence to establish this monastery.
Traveling more than three hundred li west from the royal city, one arrives at the city of Bālgāī.

Within it is a seated image of the Buddha, over seven feet in height; its marks and signs are perfectly complete, and it stands with a majestic and imposing presence. On its head it wears a jeweled crown, which occasionally radiates brilliant light.
According to local tradition,
it was originally in the kingdom of Kaśmīra and was subsequently requested to be moved here. Formerly,
there was an arhat whose śrāmaṇera disciple, when approaching the end of his life, requested a sour rice cake.
An Arhat, observing with his divine eye, saw that this flavor existed in the kingdom of Gostana; he exercised his supernatural powers to travel there and seek it out.
After the śrāmaṇera had eaten it, he made a vow to be reborn in that country, and as a result, his long-held wish was fulfilled, for he became a prince.
Having succeeded to the throne, his majesty commanded both near and far; he subsequently crossed the Snow Mountains to invade the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
The King of Kaśmīra assembled his cavalry, intending to resist the invading enemy.
At that time, an Arhat admonished the king:
"Do not engage in battle; I am able to repel them.
He then expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the King of Kustana.
The king had not yet believed this and still intended to raise an army.
The Arhat then took the robe the king had worn as a novice monk in a previous life and showed it to him.

Upon seeing the robe, the king attained the knowledge of his past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*). He apologized to the King of Kaśmīra, and they became friends; he withdrew his troops and returned, escorting the Buddha image that had been venerated during his time as a novice, following the army to pay homage and invite it [to his realm].

When the image reached this location, it could not be moved; consequently, a monastery was constructed around it, and monks were invited to reside there. The king removed his precious crown and placed it upon the head of the image; the one currently worn by the statue is precisely that which was bestowed by the former monarch.
One hundred and fifty or sixty *li* to the west of the royal city, in the middle of a great sandy desert along the main road, there is a mound;
it is a burial mound of rats according to local tradition.

I was told by the local people that in this sandy desert, the rats are as large as porcupines, their fur being of various colors such as gold and silver. They serve as the chieftains of their respective tribes, and whenever they emerge from their burrows to roam or rest, the rest of the rat colony follows them as attendants.

In the past, the Xiongnu led several hundred thousand troops to raid and plunder the frontier cities, stationing their army near the Mausoleum of the Mice. At that time, the King of Gostana led several tens of thousands of soldiers; fearing he might not be a match for them, he recalled his long-standing knowledge of the extraordinary nature of the mice in the desert, though he had not yet regarded them as divine.
When the invaders arrived, there was no one to whom they could turn for help; the ruler and his ministers were struck with terror and knew not how to devise a plan.
They would have been content to perform sacrifices once more, burning incense and imploring the rats, hoping that their spirits might manifest and provide some measure of military assistance.
That night, King Gostana saw a large rat in a dream,
which said:
"I wish respectfully to assist you."
"I pray that you will mobilize the troops early so that we may join battle at dawn; we shall surely achieve victory.

King Gostana, knowing that there was divine protection, accordingly readied his cavalry, issued orders to his generals and soldiers, and set out before daybreak, charging forward in a surprise attack.
When the Xiongnu heard of this, there was none among them who did not feel fear.

Just as they were about to mount their horses and don their armor, the mice gnawed through all the horse saddles, human garments, bowstrings, leather bindings of the armor, and indeed every strap and fastener, severing them all.
When the invading troops arrived, [the enemy] was bound with their faces to the ground and executed.
Thereupon, their generals were killed and their soldiers taken captive; the Xiongnu were struck with awe and terror, believing they had been protected by divine spirits.

King Gostana, moved by the profound kindness of the mice, established a shrine and instituted sacrifices; for generations his descendants have maintained this reverence, regarding it with exceptional esteem and wonder.
Thus, from the sovereign above down to the common people below, all perform these sacrificial rites in order to seek blessings and protection.
Passing by the cave, he dismounted from his carriage and hurried forward; he prostrated himself to pay his respects and offered sacrifices to pray for blessings.
Whether it was clothing, bows, and arrows, or incense, flowers, and delicacies—having thus presented his sincerity, he received much merit and benefit.
If offerings and sacrifices are not performed, calamities and portents will follow.
Five or six *li* to the west of the royal city is the Samāja Monastery.
Within it stands a stūpa over one hundred feet high, which manifests many auspicious omens and frequently emits a divine radiance.
In the past, there was an Arhat who came from afar and stayed within this forest, emitting a great radiance through his supernormal powers.
At that time, the king was on an upper terrace at night when he saw from afar the forest illuminated by this light. He then inquired of those nearby, and they all replied:
"There is a śramaṇa who has arrived from afar; he sits in meditative seclusion within the forest, manifesting supernormal powers."
The king then ordered his carriage and went in person to observe him.
Having beheld this wise and enlightened man, his heart was filled with reverence; admiring his virtue without ceasing, he invited him to the inner palace.
The śramaṇa said:
"All things have their proper place; one should direct one's will toward where they belong.
Deep forests and marshy wetlands are what the heart delights in."
"High halls and deep chambers are not what I have heard of.
The King’s reverence increased further; he held him in profound esteem and built a monastery for him, erecting a stūpa.
The śramaṇa accepted the invitation and stayed there.
After a short while, the king was moved to find several hundred grains of śarīra; filled with great joy, he thought to himself:
"How late it is for the śarīra to manifest its response!"
"Would it not be a most excellent site to place it beneath a stūpa at an early date?
He then went to the monastery and explained his intention in detail to the śramaṇa.
The arhat said:
"O King, do not grieve; we shall now enshrine it.
It is appropriate to enclose it successively within caskets made of gold, silver, copper, iron, and large stone."
The king commanded his artisans, and in less than a day their work was completed; the relics were placed upon precious carriages and conveyed to the monastery.
At that time, the royal retinue and hundreds of officials who came to witness the procession of the śarīras numbered in the tens of thousands.
The Arhat then raised the stūpa with his right hand and placed it within the palms of his hands, saying to the king, "You may now deposit it below.
He then dug a pit in the ground to install the casket; when this task was completed, he lowered the stūpa, and it was set down without any tilting or damage.
The onlookers marveled at what they had never before experienced; their faith in the Buddha grew ever more profound, and their resolve to revere the Dharma became firm.
The King said to his officials:
"I have often heard that the power of the Buddha is inconceivable and his spiritual penetrations are unfathomable."
Sometimes he manifests a hundred billion emanated bodies, or adapts his traces to appear among humans and devas;

he may lift the entire world within the palm of his hand, yet sentient beings have no perception of motion or stillness, as he expounds the nature of phenomena with an eternal voice, and sentient beings attain awakening according to their respective kinds.
This represents spiritual power that is not shared with others and wisdom that transcends words.
Though its divine manifestation has already vanished, its teaching still endures.
Those who partake of its harmony and drink of its bounty, savoring its essence and admiring its influence, can still attain this spiritual resonance and deeply rely upon its blessings.
"Exert yourselves, all of you!
You should hold [the Dharma] in profound reverence; that the Buddha-dharma is profound and subtle is thereby made clear.
Five or six *li* to the southeast of the royal city is the Maśa Monastery, which was established by the former queen of this country.
In ancient times, this country was unaware of silkworms and mulberry trees. Hearing that they existed in the eastern lands, it dispatched an envoy to seek them.
At that time, the ruler of the eastern state kept them secret and refused to grant them, strictly ordering the frontier guards not to allow the seeds of mulberry trees or silkworms to pass out.
The King of Kustana then humbled his words and lowered his demeanor, seeking a marriage alliance with the Eastern Kingdom;
the ruler of that land, possessing a mind inclined toward the distant realms, granted his request.
The King of Kustana dispatched an envoy to welcome the bride, instructing him thus:

"You deliver this message to the daughter of the Lord of the Eastern Land: 'In our country, we have never before possessed the seeds of silk, cotton, mulberry trees, or silkworms; you may bring these with you so that we may make garments for ourselves.'"

Upon hearing these words, the woman secretly sought his seed; she placed the cocoons of the mulberry silkworms within the lining of her cap. When they reached the checkpoint, the officials searched everywhere, yet they did not dare to inspect the princess’s cap.

He then entered the kingdom of Kustana and halted at the former site of the Mashe Monastery; there, having prepared the full ceremonial rites, he was welcomed into the palace, and mulberry seeds for silkworms were left behind in this place.
As the spring begins, they plant the mulberry trees; once the month for silkworms arrives, they again attend to gathering and rearing them.
At first, they still feed the larvae with various leaves, but from that time onward, the mulberry trees cast a continuous shade.
The Queen Mother then engraved this upon stone as a decree, forbidding injury or slaughter;
only when the silkworm moths had all flown away could the cocoons be processed.
Should anyone dare to violate this, the manifest deities shall offer no protection.
Consequently, he established this monastery for the First Sericulture Rite.
Several withered mulberry trees are said to be the original trees from which the species was first propagated.
Therefore, in this country, silkworms are not killed; should anyone secretly take silk, the silkworms will invariably fail to thrive in the following year.
More than one hundred *li* to the southeast of the city is a great river flowing toward the northwest; the people of the country benefit from it, using it to irrigate their fields.
Later, the flow was cut off, which the king found deeply strange and anomalous.
Thereupon, he ordered his carriage and questioned the arhat monks, saying:
"The waters of the great river have been the source of sustenance for the people of this land; now that the flow has suddenly ceased, where does the fault lie?"
"Is there injustice in your governance, or is your virtue not all-pervasive?
If not so, why are the retributions so severe?
The Arhat replied:
“Great King, your governance of the kingdom has brought about a pure and harmonious transformation.
That the river’s flow was severed was the doing of a dragon;
you should quickly offer sacrifices to seek its favor, and it shall restore the former benefits.”
The King, thereupon turned his carriage back to perform a sacrifice to the river dragon.
Suddenly, a woman appeared, treading upon the waves, and said:
"My husband died long ago; I have no one to turn to for my livelihood."
"This is why the river's flow has been cut off and the farmers have lost their livelihood.
If Your Majesty selects a noble minister from within your kingdom to be my husband, the water will flow as it did before."
The king said, "I have heard you with respect; do as you wish.
Thereupon, the dragon set his heart upon the king's chief minister.
Once the King had turned his carriage back, he said to his subordinates:
"Ministers are the vital pillars of the state;
agricultural pursuits are the sustenance for the people's lives."
"If the state loses its stabilizing pillar, it will fall into peril; if the people are deprived of food, they will die.
Between the matters of peril and death, which course of action is appropriate?
The great minister rose from his seat, knelt, and replied:
"For a long time I have been humble and unworthy, yet I have erroneously been entrusted with a heavy responsibility.
I have constantly thought of repaying the state, but have not yet encountered the right opportunity; now that I am selected for this office, I dare to fulfill my profound duty."
If it benefits the myriad subjects, why begrudge a single minister?
A minister is but an assistant to the state;
the people are the very foundation of the state. I pray that Your Majesty will not hesitate further.
"It would be fortunate for you to cultivate merit by establishing a saṃghārāma.
The King granted his request, and the work was completed in no time.
His ministers further requested that he enter the Dragon Palace early; thereupon, the officials and commoners of the entire nation held a farewell banquet with drums and music.
The minister then donned white robes, mounted a white horse, and took his leave of the king, respectfully bidding farewell to the people of the land.

He drove the horse into the river; though he stepped upon the water, he did not sink. Having reached midstream, he brandished his whip and traced a line across the water, which parted in two. Thereupon, he vanished.
Shortly thereafter, a white horse emerged from the water, carrying a large sandalwood drum and a sealed letter.
The letter read in general terms:

"Your Majesty has not overlooked one so humble as I, mistakenly including me among those chosen by the divine. I pray that you cultivate much merit, thereby enriching the state and benefiting your ministers."
He hung this great drum in the southeast of the city, saying, "If an enemy force approaches, the drum shall resound first.
Thereupon the river began to flow, and it remains useful to this day.
As the years have passed and time has drifted far away, the dragon drum has long been absent.
At the place where it was formerly suspended, there is still a drum today.
The monastery by the side of the pond is now dilapidated and ruined, with no monks remaining.

More than three hundred li to the east of the royal city, within a vast wilderness, there is a tract of land spanning several tens of *qǐng* that is utterly devoid of grass; its soil is reddish-black.
According to the elders, they say:
"This was the site where an army was defeated."

In the past, the military forces of the eastern kingdom, numbering one million, launched a western expedition. At that time, the King of Gostana also marshaled several hundred thousand cavalrymen to resist the powerful enemy from the east; having reached this place, the two armies encountered one another and immediately engaged in battle.
The Western army suffered a defeat; seizing the advantage, they slaughtered the survivors, captured their king, killed their generals, and executed the soldiers until not a single one remained.
Blood flowed so profusely that it stained the ground—the traces of which still remain here.
Traveling eastward from the battlefield for more than thirty *li*, one arrives at the city of Pāmā.
There is a standing image of the Buddha carved from sandalwood, over twenty feet in height.
It manifests many miraculous responses and frequently emits a brilliant light.
Whenever anyone suffers from illness, if they apply a gold-leaf image to the site of the pain, they will recover immediately; if they pray with a sincere heart, their requests are mostly fulfilled.
According to local tradition,
it is said that this image was formerly made by King Udayana of the kingdom of Kauśāmbī while the Buddha was still in the world.
After the Buddha passed away, it flew through the air from there and arrived here in the city of Ho-lo-lo-kia to the north of this country.

When he first arrived there, the people of the city were peaceful, happy, and wealthy; however, they were deeply attached to false views and did not hold him in high esteem or respect. They merely passed along the account of his origins, regarding him as a deity rather than a noble being.
Later, an arhat paid homage to this image; the people of the country were struck with alarm, marvelling at his appearance and attire, and they rushed to inform the king.
The king then issued an order, decreeing that this strange man should be covered in sand and dust.
At that time, the arhat’s body was covered in dust and sand, and he had no food to sustain himself.
There was a man who felt great compassion; having previously always revered and paid homage to this image, upon seeing the arhat, he secretly provided him with a meal.
As the Arhat was about to depart, he said to the man:
"Seven days from now, sand and soil shall rain down, filling this city until not a single soul remains."
"You should know this and quickly devise a plan for escape;
otherwise, you will suffer the same calamity as I have.
Having finished speaking, he departed and suddenly vanished.
The man entered the city and related everything to his relatives and friends; yet among those who heard him, there was none who did not mock him.

On the second day, a great wind suddenly arose, blowing away the foul soil, and rain fell, filling the streets with various jewels; the people then cursed the one who had told them [of the coming rain].
This man, knowing for certain that this was inevitable, secretly opened a tunnel and exited beyond the city walls to dig it out.
On the seventh night, after midnight, rain of sand and earth filled the city.
The man departed through the passageway and traveled east toward this country, stopping at the city of Pāmā.
As soon as he arrived, the image also came there; it was immediately enshrined here for worship, and no one dared to move it.
I have heard from ancient records that when the Dharma of Śākyamuni comes to an end, the Image will enter the Dragon Palace.
Now, the city of Alakāvatī has become a great mound of earth, and many kings of various nations and powerful elites from distant lands desire to excavate it in order to take its precious treasures.
Just as he reached its side, a violent wind suddenly erupted, smoke and clouds gathered from all directions, and the way was lost.

Crossing the Śatadru River to the east, he entered the sandy desert and traveled over two hundred li until he reached the city of Ni-rang, which was three or four li in circuit and situated in the midst of a great marsh.
The marshy ground was hot and damp, making it difficult to tread upon;
the reeds grew so rank and luxuriant that no path remained, except for the road leading toward the city, which alone permitted passage.
Therefore, all those who travel back and forth must pass through this city, which Kustana regards as the frontier defense of its eastern border.

From here, traveling eastward, one enters the Great Flowing Sands; these sands drift and spread, gathering and dispersing according to the wind, leaving no tracks for people to follow, so that many eventually lose their way.
The four directions stretch out vast and boundless, with no way to discern one's destination; for this reason, people collect and pile up remains of the deceased as markers.
Water and grass are scarce, and hot winds are frequent;
when these winds arise, humans and livestock become dazed and confused, thereby falling ill.
At times he heard songs and whistling, or heard wailing and crying.
Amidst these sights and sounds, he became dazed and lost all sense of where he was; consequently, there were frequent deaths and losses, which were clearly caused by malevolent spirits.
After traveling more than four hundred *li*, he reached the ancient kingdom of Dūlā.
The country had long been desolate, and its cities were all overgrown with weeds.
From here, traveling eastward for more than six hundred *li*, he arrived at the ancient kingdom of Jermadhāna, which is the land of Niemo (Nemaza).
The city walls stand towering, but human habitation has been cut off.
Traveling northeast from here for over a thousand li, one arrives at the ancient kingdom of Navapa, which is the land of Loulan.

I have charted the mountains and rivers and examined the territories and lands; I have detailed the rigidity or flexibility of national customs and recorded the climatic influences of the soil and water. Since movement and stillness are not constant and preferences differ, these matters are difficult to verify exhaustively and cannot be explained through mere hearsay.
Wherever I have traveled, I have briefly recorded the general outline, citing what I have heard and seen, and noting those who aspire to transformation.
Thus, from the time the sun sets until its rise, all are bathed in the grace of your benevolence; wherever the wind of your influence reaches, all look up to your supreme virtue.
"To unify the world and bring it under a single rule within the four seas—how could this have been achieved merely by a single-wheeled carriage dispatched on a mission across ten thousand *li*?
The postscript and eulogy state:
"How magnificent! Is it not so? That the Dharma King manifested in this world!"
The spiritual transformations operate in hidden movement, and the divine way is empty and penetrating.
It exhausts form and consciousness throughout the sands of worlds, and severs arising and passing away within the kalpas of dust.
When form and consciousness are exhausted, though one responds to birth, there is no birth.
He manifested departure and extinction, yet demonstrated that there is no extinction.
How could it be that he truly descended his spirit into Kapilavastu and merely vanished in transformation at the Śāla trees?

We know for certain that he responded to beings by manifesting spiritual efficacy and displayed traces in accordance with conditions; he succeeded to the lineage of the Kṣatriyas and inherited the legacy of Śākya, continuing the honor of the world within while excelling in the Way beyond the mundane.
Thereupon, he set aside the golden wheel to preside over the Dharma-realm and unfurled the jade-white hair-tuft to radiantly comfort all living beings.
His Way permeates the ten directions, and his wisdom encompasses all things.
Though he transcends the realm of the ineffable and the formless, he extends his protection within the sphere of sight and hearing.
He turns the Wheel of Dharma thrice throughout the great trichiliocosm, and with a single voice, he stirs eloquence among all beings.
The eighty thousand gates are distinguished in their variety, and the twelve divisions of scripture provide their essential synthesis.
Thus, wherever the teachings of the voice reach, beings hasten toward the Forest of Blessings;
wherever the influence of these exemplary ways stirs, they are driven forward into the Domain of Longevity.
The achievements of the sages and worthies are magnificent, and the principles governing heaven and humanity are complete!

Yet, they forgot both movement and stillness within the forest of the firm and solid, and left behind both coming and going within the realm of illusion and transformation; they could not continue what depends upon conditions, nor did they achieve the state of non-existence.
The Venerable Kāśyapa carefully selected the Arhats to repay the Buddha’s kindness and compile this treasure of the Dharma.
The four Āgamas encompass its source and flow, while the Tripiṭaka summarizes its essential pivot.
Although various sectarian schools have arisen, the Great Treasure remains intact.
From his miraculous descent until his secret passing, his sacred traces have manifested in a thousand transformations and his divine portents in ten thousand varieties.
The inexhaustible spirit becomes ever more manifest, and the teaching of non-action grows ever more renewed.
These are fully preserved in the scriptures and recorded in detail in the biographies and annals.
Nevertheless, various discourses remain entangled and conflicting opinions run amok; from beginning to end, few have been able to provide an orthodox exposition.

If even for these recorded accounts of specific events, various theories remain as diverse as this, how much more so for the profound mystery of the True Dharma and the remote transcendence of its ultimate principles? When scrutinizing their deep significance, the texts are largely deficient.
Therefore, those of former generations who cultivated meritorious virtue followed the tracks of the lost scriptures,
while the eminent scholars of later times treaded upon the traces of the fragmented texts. Thus,
the great principles remained stifled and unmanifest, and the subtle words were incomplete and left without inquiry.
The transmission and gradual spread of the Dharma have spanned many years, beginning from the Han dynasty and continuing through to the present sagely era.
This magnificent enterprise of translation has perpetuated its beauty and radiated its brilliance in continuous succession.

The profound Way has not yet been fully unfolded, and the True Doctrine remains obscure; this is not merely a matter of the concealment or manifestation of the Sage’s teachings, but is surely due to the causes and conditions of the King’s transformation of the world.

Our Great Tang, presiding over and instructing all under heaven, spreads its influence of trust beyond the seas, examining the bequeathed rules of the Sages and rectifying the ancient statutes of the former Kings.
The revelation of this Image-Teaching has flourished as a grand instruction; the Way does not function in vain, for its propagation depends upon those of illustrious virtue.

Consequently, the profound meanings of the Three Vehicles have been obscured beneath a thousand years, and the lingering spiritual power of the One of Ten Strengths has remained hidden beyond ten thousand li.
"The Way of the Gods has no fixed direction, while the teachings of the Sages have a locus for manifestation; that they become evident only when conditions meet is indeed a truth worthy of belief.
Now, as for the Dharma Master Xuanzang: he drew his clear currents from Lake Leize and branched his vast source from the Gui River;
he embodied the auspiciousness of supreme virtue and harbored the pure essence of central harmony."
Treading the Way in harmony with virtue, he dwelt in integrity and cultivated his conduct;
planting the seeds of fortune through past causes, his destiny coincided with a flourishing era.
He withdrew from the dust of the mundane world to dwell in leisure at a place of learning, honoring the elegant instructions of former masters and looking up to the noble virtues of past sages.
Carrying his book-box, he followed teachers to study; traveling abroad to seek instruction, he roamed through the lands of Yan and Zhao and toured the regions of Lu and Wei;
he crossed the Three Rivers to enter the central region of Qin and journeyed through the three Shu provinces to reach the Wu-Hui area.
Scholars of profound learning and eminent talent have all diligently sought instruction from him;
the world’s most illustrious sages have repeatedly declared their resolve to seek the Dharma under him.

Having heard his remaining discourses and examined the collective deliberations of the assembly, I observe that they vie with one another to champion the doctrines of their own specialized schools, while all harbor envy toward the studies of other paths.
His sentiments were stirred as he sought the source of truth, and his resolve was set upon detailed investigation.

Coinciding with the universal order of the four seas and the peace throughout the eight directions, on the first day of the middle month of autumn in the third year of the Zhenguan era, he bared his robes and set out upon the road, traveling far toward the west with his monk’s staff in hand.

Relying on the imperial transformation to seek the Way and riding upon profound blessings to travel alone, he emerged from the narrow passes of the Iron Gate and the Stone Gate, and traversed the perils of Mount Ling and the Snowy Mountains; in a mere shift of the hourglass sands, he reached India.
He proclaimed the national ethos to foreign lands and disseminated the Great Transformation to distant regions.
Having personally received the study of the *Brahma* language, he consulted with sages;

when long-standing doubts arose, they were resolved through the examination of clear texts, and when profound principles were encountered, they were explored by extensively questioning those of superior talent.
He opened the treasury of his spirit to investigate principle and expanded his divine mind to embody the Way.
Hearing what had never been heard before and attaining what had never been attained before, he is a beneficial friend to the site of practice and a true craftsman of the Dharma-gate.
Thus it is known that his fame was far-reaching and his virtuous conduct lofty; he had accumulated learning throughout three winters, and his reputation spread ten thousand *li*.
The scholars of India all looked up to his magnificent virtue; they called him a "repository of the scriptures" and also hailed him as a "General of the Dharma."
The disciples of the Hīnayāna were called Mokṣadeva, which in the language of Tang means "Deva of Liberation";
the assembly of the Mahāyāna were called Mahāyānadeva, which in the language of Tang means "Deva of the Mahāyāna."
This was done to exalt his virtue by transmitting his illustrious title and to honor him by deliberating upon a magnificent name.

As for the profound meanings of the Three Wheels and the subtle words of the three requests, he investigated their origins and currents in depth and exhaustively mastered their branches and leaves. His wisdom shone forth in brilliant awakening, and his principles flowed with serene harmony; the meanings of the questions he posed are detailed in a separate record.

Soon thereafter, his mastery of profound principles reached the mysterious depths, and a pure influence spread far and wide; his learning was already vast and his virtue already flourishing, whereupon he traveled across mountains and rivers and wandered through the outskirts and towns.

Leaving the city of Māyā, he entered the Deer Park; he roamed the Staff Grove and rested in the Cock Garden. Turning his gaze back toward the land of Kapilavastu, he cast his eyes upon the city of Kuśinagara.
The site of his descent into birth shares its lush splendor with the rivers and plains;
the traces of his hidden spiritual presence face the suburban mounds in vast solitude.

Surveying these divine vestiges, my sentiments deepen; gazing up at this profound legacy, I sigh eternally—not merely out of sorrow for the "Grain of Wheat" that mourned the Yin dynasty, nor only out of lament for the "Millet Separation" that pained the Zhou.

Thus, I have meticulously expounded upon the historical accounts of Śākyamuni and set forth the flourishing achievements of India; I have extensively gathered information on the local customs and topography, preserving various divergent traditions.
As the years have swiftly passed and the cycles of cold and heat have repeatedly shifted, my heart remains yearning for that Land of Bliss, never forgetting the traces of its origins.
I have obtained one hundred and fifty grains of the Tathāgata’s bodily relics;
one golden Buddha image, including its halo and pedestal, measuring sixteen inches in height;

and one golden Buddha image modeled after the likeness of the Buddha at the Dragon Cave on Mount Prāgbodhi in the kingdom of Magadha, including its halo and pedestal, measuring thirty-three inches in height.

One sandalwood image of the Buddha depicting the first turning of the Wheel of Dharma at the Deer Park in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, with a total height including the halo and pedestal of one chi and five cun;

one sandalwood image of the Buddha depicting the portrait of the King of Kauśāmbī, who, out of longing for the Tathāgata, had a likeness carved in sandalwood, with a total height including the halo and pedestal of two chi and nine cun;

and one silver image of the Buddha depicting his descent from the celestial palace to tread upon the precious steps in the kingdom of Kapitha, with a total height including the halo and pedestal of four chi.

One gilt bronze Buddha image, three chi and five cun in height including the halo and pedestal, modeled after the image [of Śākyamuni] preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other scriptures at Vulture Peak in the kingdom of Magadha;

one sandalwood carved Buddha image, one chi and three cun in height including the halo and pedestal, modeled after the image left behind by the subduing of the venomous dragon in the kingdom of Nagarahāra;
and one image modeled after the one that toured the city to perform transformative teachings in the kingdom of Vaiśālī.

The writings are called "Heavenly Writings," and the speech is termed "Heavenly Speech";
the phrasing is elegant and subtle, while the phonology flows in cycles;
sometimes a single word encompasses multiple meanings, and sometimes a single meaning is synthesized from many words.
The sounds have their modulations, and the tones are regulated as clear or deep.

The Sanskrit texts possess profound significance; their translation must rely on enlightened individuals. The purport of the sutras is subtle and mysterious; their meaning depends upon those of eminent virtue.
If one were to edit it with the brush and refine it with the musical scales of *gong* and *shang*, this would truly be unsatisfactory and certainly not a sound argument.
In transmitting the profound purport of the scriptures, one must strive for ease of understanding; provided that it does not deviate from the original essence, this is what constitutes excellence.
Excessive refinement leads to affectation; excessive plainness leads to rusticity.
If one is candid yet not overly refined, and eloquent yet not overly plain, then one may avoid great error; only then can one be said to be capable of discussing translation.

Fortuitously relying on the arrival of this auspicious era,
I have joined the ranks of the *yuán* and *hóng* amidst my meager talents as a swallow or sparrow. Thus,
I have charged this mediocre talent with the compilation of this local gazetteer.

My learning is not extensive in antiquities, nor do my writings possess elegant refinement; yet, I have polished my dullness and encouraged my failing strength, exerting myself though weary as one who drags a lame horse.

Having reverently received the records of his intent, I have arranged the texts in their proper order, and with the provision of official stationery and writing implements, I have compiled this record.
My wisdom is shallow and my abilities limited, with many omissions and deficiencies;
at times my expressions are redundant, yet I have not yet managed to prune them away.

In the past, Sima Zichang possessed the talent of a true historian; when he compiled the *Shiji*, following the legacy of his father, he sometimes recorded names without surnames, or counties without prefectures.
Therefore it is said that even the refined mind of a single person, when its thoughts are manifold and its writings redundant, finds itself lacking leisure;
how much less, then, could the intelligence of the most ignorant succeed in being detailed and complete?

As for the differences in climate and customs, the records of boundaries and local products, the classifications of character and intellect, and the seasonal variations of heat and cold, these have all been recorded in full detail regarding their excellence or deficiency, with careful preservation of their fundamental facts.
As for the surnames of the Hu and Rong peoples, their respective nations are well known;
as for the customs and transformations of India, the pure and the turbid are clearly distinguished. A brief outline has been recorded here, as detailed in the preceding preface.
The protocols for guests, the rites of celebration, census figures, the number of effective soldiers, and those who have donned the dyed robes are not matters for detailed record.

Nevertheless, because the Buddha employs supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to reach sentient beings and manifests spiritual transformations to bestow instruction, it is said that when the divine way penetrates the profound mysteries, its principles transcend the realm of humans; and when spiritual transformations manifest in both the hidden and the visible, these events arise beyond the scope of the mundane world.

Therefore, regarding the regions where the Buddhas descended to bestow their auspiciousness and the sites where former sages left behind their enduring fame, I have briefly cited these vestiges of spiritual power and roughly set them down in this record.
As the terrain and roads wind and turn, and the borders and frontiers intersect and overlap, I have recorded them according to my travels rather than arranging them in a systematic sequence.
Therefore, throughout India, there are no distinct boundaries between territories; I have recorded these scattered accounts at the end of this work to provide a brief indication of their domains.
Those described as "visited" are places where I personally traveled and stepped upon;
those cited as "reached" are records based on hearsay.
Sometimes he records events directly, and sometimes he elaborates upon them with refined prose.
